# The History of the WALDENSIANS
## Divided into three parts

->Of which<-

**The first deals with their origin, pure faith, and the persecutions** which they suffered throughout all of Europe during a period of more than 450 years.
**The second contains the History of the Waldensians, otherwise named** the Albigensians <note>The Albigensians were a medieval religious group in Southern France, often associated with the Waldensians by later Protestant historians seeking a lineage of "pure" Christianity.</note>.
**The third comprises the Doctrine and Discipline which they shared** among themselves, together with the refutation of the doctrine of their adversaries.

### Copy of the Privilege <note>In the 17th century, a 'Privilege' was an exclusive license granted by the government. It acted as an early form of copyright, protecting a printer's investment by preventing others from publishing the same work for a set number of years.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring floral motifs and a central vase-like element.</image-desc>

THE STATES GENERAL <note>The sovereign governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note> of the United Netherlands have consented and granted, and do hereby consent and grant, to Nicolaes Vincensz. van Spieringx-hoeck, Book-printer, living in Dordrecht: That for the period of the next six years, he alone shall be permitted in the United Provinces to print and publish a certain translation which he has had made of a book entitled the *History of the Waldensians, divided into three parts: the first, dealing with their origin, beginning, and the persecution which they suffered throughout all of Europe for more than four hundred and fifty years. The second part, the histories of the Waldensians, otherwise named the Albigensians, and the third part, containing the doctrine and discipline which they held in common, as well as the refutation of their enemies, compiled together from various authors by Jean Paul Perrin of Lyon.* Forbidding all and any inhabitants of the United Netherlands from reprinting the aforementioned translation, which the said Spieringx-hoeck has had made, in whole or in part within the aforementioned period of six years, or bringing it into the United Netherlands if printed elsewhere, to be sold therein, without the consent of the aforementioned Nicolaes Vincensz. van Spieringx-hoeck, under penalty of forfeiture of the reprinted copies, and additionally the sum of two hundred Carolus guilders <note>The Carolus guilder was a standard currency in the Habsburg Netherlands, named after Emperor Charles V.</note>, one-third of which is to be applied to the benefit of the Officer who shall make the legal claim, the second third for the benefit of the Poor, and the remaining third for the benefit of the aforementioned Spieringx-hoeck. Done at the Assembly of the highly mentioned Lords States General, in The Hague, on the 22nd of May, in the year 1624.

->*N. vander Meer. vt.* <note>The abbreviation "vt." stands for "vidit," indicating the official has reviewed and verified the document.</note><-

->By order of the same.<-

->*I. Goch.*<-

# Preface.
### 2

...shines like the dawn, **Beautiful as the Moon, Pure as the Sun, Terrifying as battle arrays with flying banners?** <note>original: "Verschrickelijck als de Slachordens met vliegende banieren." This is a quote from the Song of Solomon 6:10, used here to describe the Church as both beautiful and a formidable spiritual force.</note> This question seemed appropriate for me to use as an introduction to address Your Honors with reverence regarding this same History. In this saying, there are two principal things to note: 1. That which is asked and spoken of here, namely the **bride**. 2. That which is said of her, namely the radiance she possesses and gives off.

The one being asked about here is the same who, among other titles in the *Song of Solomon*, is called the **beloved Bride**. 

<margin>Song of Solomon 5:1, 6:9.</margin>
Under this title, one understands and addresses the **Church of Christ on earth**, which Christ has chosen for eternal life from the entire human race; which He gathers, protects, and maintains through His Spirit and Word in the unity of Faith, from the beginning of the world to the end. She is called the **Bride** not without reason. Seeing that just as a bride is loved and cherished by her bridegroom, so too is she loved by Christ her husband, to whom He has betrothed himself with an unbreakable and everlasting marriage-vow. For it is to her that it is spoken in **Hosea 2:18-19** <note>In modern Bibles, this is usually numbered as Hosea 2:19-20.</note>:

> I will betroth you to me forever; I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in grace and in mercy. Yes, I will betroth you to me in faithfulness, and you shall know the Lord.

With this address, the close connection and unbreakable unity between Christ and His Church is specifically expressed through the words *betroth* and *entrust*; for it is certain that marriage promises and vows are held as the most binding of all. Indeed, it is assured with the promise of *righteousness* and *justice*, indicating that He intends for these to be upheld by both sides—namely, that He would keep and protect His church in righteousness and justice, and on the other hand, that the Church would cling to Christ her Bridegroom with Faith and Trust. And because these parties are very unequal—the Church being entirely unworthy of such a union—the cause is shown to be God’s mercy and grace. And therefore, because this is a very wonderful and great marriage, the Apostle Paul says of it in **Ephesians 5:32**: *This mystery is great, but I speak of Christ and the Church.* Indicating that the physical marriage between Man and Wife is a [reflection of] this great mystery...

A true representation by ascent and steps <note>This "ascent" refers to the idea that the Church grows more visible and powerful over time, like the sun rising in the sky.</note>:

Her rising is shown by the **Dawn**, for just as the Dawn shows itself with a small light and glimmers in the midst of the darkness, so has the Church likewise shown herself in the **Old Testament**, being enclosed in a very small number, especially in the time of the first Elders of the first age. 
2. After the flood. 
3. Of the **Patriarchs** under **Abraham**, **Isaac**, and **Jacob**, in **Chaldea**, **Mesopotamia**, **Egypt**, and **Canaan**. Likewise in the **New Testament**, beginning in the Disciples and followers of Christ, still consisting in a very small number.

2. Her progress, increase, and spreading is shown by the **Moon**, **Sun**, etc. As those things that, gradually spreading themselves more, growing up and becoming greater, also show themselves with greater radiance; like a Moon shining in the darkness of the night, as happened in the Old Testament under the descendants of the Patriarchs, when the church spread herself more and more and increased, as in Egypt and thereafter: and in the New Testament was spread by the **Apostles** through many Cities and Lands. 

3. Until she, increasing with time and growing more and more, finally has come to such great glory and prestige that she, like the Sun above the Stars, so also above all gatherings

-># Preface.<-

gatherings of heathens and unbelievers have been cleared out, as happened in the **Old Testament** under the **Judges** and **Kings**. And in the **New Testament**, having been spread throughout the whole world, and having obtained powerful Emperors, Kings, and Princes as Sovereign Lords: in which state she <note>The Church, often personified as a woman or bride.</note> was also no less disciplined before her persecutors and enemies, like **battle arrays**, when these, being well-equipped, march toward their enemies with flying banners to destroy and annihilate them.

Yet just as the **Dawn**, **Sun**, **Moon**, etc., are often so covered and darkened by clouds, mists, eclipses, etc., that they cannot be seen or provide light to people at all, so it likewise happens to the **Church**. And these metaphors depict the Church not only insofar as they shine and give light, but also insofar as they do *not* shine and do *not* give light. Therefore, **Ambrose**, in the fourth book of his work on the six days of Creation, applies this same comparison of the Sun and Moon to the state of the Church, saying: *That the Church has her rising and increase of light, but also a waning of the same.* <note>original: "Dat de Kercke hare opganck ende aenwassen des lichts als ooc een afneminge van het selve heeft."</note> To this, **Augustine** adds in Epistle 48: *That she is sometimes entirely covered by the multitude of scandals.* <note>In this context, "scandals" refers to spiritual stumbling blocks or moral failings within the community that obscure the Church's true nature.</note> For in the same way, the Church in the Old Testament was darkened and hidden from the eyes of men in the time of **Elijah** under the reign of **Ahab** and **Jezebel**; likewise during the time of the **Babylonian captivity**. And in the New Testament, during the time of the first persecutions, when the Church had to hide herself in caves and dens, and was pushed so far back that her enemies triumphed and boasted over the extermination of the Christian name. For on a certain commemorative coin struck by **Diocletian**, <note>A Roman Emperor (reigned 284–305 AD) known for the "Great Persecution" of Christians.</note> this inscription appears: **The name of the Christians, who were overturning the Republic, having been deleted.** <note>original Latin: "Nomine Christianorum deleto qui Rempub. Euertebant."</note> And in such a state she is shown in **Song of Solomon 2:14**, by the **Dove** that lives in the clefts of the rock, and in **Revelation 12:6**, by the pregnant woman in labor who, being pursued by the **Dragon**, had to flee into the wilderness.

But just as one sees the **Dawn**, **Sun**, and **Moon** break through the mists and clouds to spread their light, so the Church has every time raised her head again and obtained a good outcome, spreading and expanding herself in the midst of the darkness and the unbelievers of the earth. Just as the examples of the Old and New Testament continually prove. And let this be enough regarding the rising and setting of the Church herself.

<meta>This page continues the metaphorical comparison of the Church to celestial bodies and military formations. The previous page ended with the idea that the Church in the Old Testament was sometimes hidden from the eyes of men, just as the sun is hidden by clouds.</meta>

-># Preface.<-

2. What further and especially must be noted in this presentation are some of its particular qualities, which are depicted and painted here with these four things as if with their living colors. For 1. One sees among other qualities in the **Dawn**, in the **Moon**, **Sun**, and **Battle Arrays** altogether, a beauty elegant beyond measure.

1. In the **Dawn**, because of the light and radiance, as it first appears with a dark, then a gilded redness, then with a clear light and brightness, driving away the darkness.

2. In the **Moon**, because of its radiance with which it illuminates the night more than other stars.

3. In the **Sun**, because of its brilliance and clear light that illuminates everything and drives away the darkness entirely, even hiding and covering the stars through its radiance.

4. In the **Battle Arrays**, because of their order and arrangement. Also because of the delightful display of the flying and swaying banners, etc.

Yet it should be noted that these things do not have their light and beauty from themselves, but through communication <note>In this context, "communication" refers to the theological concept of *communicatio*, where properties are shared or bestowed from a higher source to a lower one.</note>: for the **Dawn** and **Moon** receive it from the **Sun**, the **Sun** from its **Creator**, and the **Battle Arrays** from the **Commanders** <term>velt-oversten: military generals or field-marshals</term> who arrange and equip them; for otherwise, it is but a confused and disorderly multitude.

2. One sees in these things a noticeable instability, change, and various forms. In the **Dawn**, seeing that it shows itself more clearly, joyfully, and pleasantly at one time than at another; for it is also covered and darkened by clouds and thick mists. Besides that, one sees in the same the instability and change of the place of its appearance according to the variety of time and season of the year. Likewise, the **Sun** and **Moon** do not always appear equally bright but are sometimes darkened by clouds and **eclipses**.

Furthermore, they also do not always appear in one and the same place and time, but change their rising and setting, climbing and descending, according to the season of the year. And that the **Battle Arrays** are likewise subject to their changes is well-known.

3. One sees that these also have their adversaries, against whom they must struggle, while the darkness is contrary to and fights against the **Dawn**, the **Sun**, and the **Moon**. The **Battle Arrays** have their enemies, against whom they are set and to whom they are terrifying.

4. Yet even though in this contrast, the **Dawn, Sun, Moon, etc.** are outwardly obscured by clouds or other things, they cannot in themselves be deprived of their light; for with that light, they finally overcome and drive away the darkness, breaking through it.

Here then, through these qualities, is shown the character and appearance of the Church of Christ here on earth, concerning among other things: 1. Her Beauty. 2. The changes to which she is subject. 3. Her Struggle. 4. Her invincibility and endurance.

I. One sees that the **Beauty of the Church** is depicted with this presentation, generally through these four things together, but especially through the **Moon**, as it is said, **Fair as the Moon.** And just as beauty is a property of these things—and especially of the **Moon**—so also is Beauty a property of the Church, in the same way that it belongs to these things and especially the **Moon**, so it also belongs to the Church. And therefore, she is properly adorned with this title of honor and greeted by Christ, her Bridegroom <note>The "Bridegroom" is a traditional Christian metaphor for Jesus Christ, based on various biblical passages.</note>, in Song of Solomon 1:15 and 6:4: *See, my love, you are beautiful, beautiful you are,* etc. Likewise, in Song of Solomon 1:8 and 6:1, she is called the *Fairest among women* <note>original: "Schoonste onder de wijven"</note>, which is to say, surpassing in beauty all the gatherings of the Godless, the worldly, and the unbelieving. This is also testified to by the Prophet David in Psalm 45:14: *The King's Daughter is all glorious within.* And Psalm 84:1 <note>The original text cites Psalm 83:1, but the verse "How lovely are your dwellings" is found in Psalm 84 in most English Bibles.</note>: *How lovely and how beautiful are your dwellings, Lord of Hosts.* In these places, the Church is understood under the names "King's Daughter" and "Dwelling of the Lord."

Yet just as neither the Dawn, nor the Sun, nor the Moon possess their radiance, light, and shining—in which their beauty especially consists—of themselves, nor even the Battle Arrays, as has been said; so likewise the Church does not have her beauty of herself. Indeed, just as the place where the Dawn appears is dark before the lighting of the Sun, and just as the Moon is a dark or at least a faintly glowing creature—indeed, even the Sun itself, if it were not enriched with the light of God—so would the Church have absolutely no beauty or elegance of herself. On the contrary, she was highly disfigured, stained, filthy, and abominable, just as the state and appearance of the Church is shown to have been of herself in Ezekiel 16:3, 4, and 5. There, she is addressed thus: *Your origin and your birth is of the land of the Canaanites; your Father was an Amorite, and your Mother a...*

-># Preface.<-

4. Yet, although in this comparison, the **Dawn**, **Sun**, **Moon**, etc., may be outwardly darkened by clouds and so forth, they can nevertheless not be robbed of their light within themselves; for with it they eventually overcome and drive away the darkness, breaking through it.

Through these qualities, the nature and appearance of the **Church of Christ** here on earth are shown, specifically regarding: 1. Her **Beauty**. 2. The **changes** to which she is subject. 3. Her **Struggle**. 4. Her **invincibility** and **endurance**.

1. We see that the **Beauty of the Church** is depicted through this presentation—generally through these four things together, but especially through the **Moon**, as it is said, *Fair as the Moon.* <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 6:10.</note> And just as beauty is a quality of these things, and especially of the Moon, so too is Beauty a quality of the Church; since it belongs to her in the same way it belongs to these celestial bodies, it also belongs to the Church. Therefore, she is properly adorned with this title of honor and greeted by Christ, her Bridegroom, in Song of Solomon 1:15 and 6:4: *See, my love, you are beautiful; you are beautiful,* etc. Likewise, in Song of Solomon 6:1, she is called the *fairest among women*—that is, surpassing in beauty all the gatherings of the godless, the worldly, and the unbelieving. This is also testified by the Prophet David in Psalm 45:14: *The King’s daughter is all glorious within.* And in Psalm 84:1 <note>The original text cites Psalm 83:1, following older Dutch numbering.</note>: *How lovely and how beautiful are your dwellings, O Lord of Hosts.* In these places, the Church is understood by the names "King’s Daughter" and "Dwelling of the Lord."

Yet, just as neither the **Dawn**, nor the **Sun**, nor the **Moon** possess their brilliance, light, and radiance—in which their beauty especially consists—from themselves, nor do the **armies** <note>referring to "Slachtordens" or "armies with banners" mentioned in the previous section</note> as has been said; so likewise the Church does not have her beauty from herself. Indeed, just as the place where the Dawn appears is dark before the rising of the Sun, and as the Moon is a dark (or at least weakly glowing) creature—yes, even the Sun itself, if it were not enriched with the light of God—so the Church would have no beauty or elegance whatsoever from herself. On the contrary, she was highly misshapen, stained, filthy, and abominable. The state and appearance of the Church as she is in herself is shown vividly in Ezekiel 16:3, 4, and 5, where she is addressed thus: *Your origin and your birth are from the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite, and your mother was...*

This has especially moved me to undertake the labor and effort of translating this History from the French into our Dutch language, and thus to make this great miracle of God known to the Dutch Reformed Church of Christ. In our church, little or almost no knowledge is found regarding the state of this ancient Church of Christ among the Waldensians <note>A medieval movement that predated the Reformation by centuries; they were often called "The Poor Men of Lyon" and were later claimed by Protestants as their spiritual ancestors.</note>; I am certain that what is found within these pages will be edifying. This Church of Christ, as it existed among the ancient Waldensians before and until our current century, we now present and dedicate—now equipped in Dutch, confessing her faith in the Dutch language, and presenting her admonitions, teachings, and rebukes in the Dutch language with proper submission and offering of service—To Your Honors:

1. As to fellow supporters of the same ancient religion of the Waldensians, now flourishing by God's grace in the Reformed churches of these United Netherlands, and especially embraced, maintained, and protected in this famous city of Dordrecht <note>Dordrecht was a vital center for Dutch Protestantism, most notably as the site of the Synod of Dort (1618–1619) which solidified the doctrines of the Reformed Church just five years before this translation was published.</note>. This has been achieved through much labor, cost, and effort, with the highest joy and fatherly care, both by Your Honors and by your parents and ancestors, who have been so graciously blessed by God for the prosperity of the church and the benefit of the pious citizens.

2. As to my commanding Lords and patrons, who have bound me to them with great affection through many benefits and kindnesses. Since I am in turn bound to acknowledge these with dutiful service and proper gratitude, I have desired to humbly dedicate and assign this modest labor of mine to Your Honors, as a small token of my goodwill, for the advancement of God’s honor and the service of His Church. I very humbly pray that, although it is a small gift, you will nonetheless accept it with the same affection with which it is presented by Your Honors' most humble servant, according to Your Honors' natural kindness. I further pray to God that He may enrich me through His gifts of grace, so that I may be fit to repay my debt of gratitude with proper service for the advancement of God’s honor and the edification of the members of His Church. Furthermore, may He graciously keep Your Honors under His protection for the advancement of the honor of His Holy name, the service of His Holy Church, and the welfare of the common good. Amen. In Your Honors' City of Dordrecht, this 16th of July in the year 1624.

# The Author to the Reader.

THE Church of God, which is scattered throughout the world, must be esteemed more worthy than the world itself. This is the purchased and acquired property of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified for her. There is no good in the world to be valued except that which is found within her: but just as our Savior, for the advancement of our salvation, invites us to enter into her and remain within her; so Satan labors against this, to keep men away from her unto their damnation. He blinds them so that they might accept as the church one that is not the church; he maintains them in errors and misleads them through worldly splendor, and causes them to despise the true church—primarily because she, while being here in the world, is subject to persecutions, in which those who do not honor the master will likewise not love his servants.

Consequently, since they recognize no other as Christ's church except that very one which, for many centuries, has triumphed over the blood of the Martyrs she killed: they ask with shameless audacity where and in what region the Catholic <note>Here used in the sense of "universal," though the author is critiquing the Roman Catholic claim to the title.</note> church then was, if that one, which for so long a time has peacefully enjoyed this title, was not the true one? Where was she then (they say) hidden during the last five past centuries? They insist that one should at least point out a single person who, within the span of so many years, believed the very things that have been put forward in our time under the name of the **Reformation**.

This present history of the Christians called the **Waldensians** and the **Albigensians** <note>The Waldensians (from Peter Waldo) and Albigensians (Cathars) were medieval groups in France and Italy. While historically distinct, Protestant writers often grouped them together as early witnesses of "pure" Christianity against Rome.</note> shall sufficiently answer all those who are able to read it without passion. For in it, it appears that more than 450 years ago, there was a great multitude of people, especially in various Kingdoms and Territories of Europe, who held a faith *that in all points corresponds and accords with the word of God, and with that doctrine which is accepted in the Reformed churches:* which people, under the darkness of the **Antichrist**, sighed, and were among them like precious pearls in mud or filth, and like roses among the thorns. The world gaped at them as miserable, even wicked people; but God looked upon them as his children, gave them eyes to see, ears to hear, and a heart or understanding to comprehend his truth. And just as God paved a way for his judgments, surrendering those who had rejected his word to a spirit of confusion <note>original: "tuymelgeest," a term used in the 17th century to describe a staggering spirit of error or spiritual dizziness, often referencing Isaiah 19:14.</note>, so he paved a way for his mercy when he drew this remnant out of those temples that were flaunted and decorated with idolatry. He worked powerfully within them through the holy internal ministry of his Holy Spirit, making them temples of the same, and thus preserving them from the outward service which was then stained with the countless fabrications of men.

The writings of these same Waldensians and Albigensians, which until now have been miraculously preserved, testify and prove in this History the purity and sincerity of their faith, and justify them against the slanders of their enemies. It shall appear that they have retained the **Apostles' Creed**, as well as the **Athanasian Creed** <note>Two of the most ancient statements of Christian belief; the author uses them to prove the Waldensians were orthodox Christians, not heretics.</note>, as the foundations of their faith; the law of the Most High as the rule of their obedience; the **Lord’s Prayer** as a prescription for their prayers; and finally, that they maintained the **Sacraments** in the same purity as they were instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise, they lived under a good and holy **Discipline** <note>The system of church governance and moral oversight.</note>, ordering and fitting their manner of life to that very word which was the rule of their faith. Notwithstanding all of this, we shall yet show that for these very things—without which no one can be a sincere Christian man—they were nevertheless fearfully condemned to death...

[banish]ed, exiled, murdered, burned, cursed, and persecuted by the force of arms.

One therefore asks in vain where the Church of Christ was in previous times and centuries: since it is certain that this almost countless multitude, whom the Popes have had put to death through their courts, was the Church—even if they opposed the Roman Church and the Popes in those matters where they were contrary to the Church of God itself.

But since the first article of the truth—which these faithful and godly martyrs sustained and maintained—comes from the eternal God, who is without beginning or end, and since nothing true or lasting can be found outside of His word, it necessarily follows that when this God speaks, then human reason must stand still; indeed, then all human inventions and fancies must vanish, even if they were as old as the lie itself. Furthermore, one must likewise admit that those people who, in past centuries, believed in the one God alone through Jesus Christ, were true members of the Church; indeed, that they were the <term>Catholic Church<note>The author uses "Catholic" in its original sense of "universal," arguing that the persecuted believers were the true universal body of Christ, rather than the Roman Catholic institution.</note></term>, in whatever region of the earth they may have been. It is now certain and evident, from the teaching and the confession of faith of those believers discussed in this present **History**, that they placed their hope only in the living God, and that they expected salvation and life through no other than the Son of God. 

Since these same people were therefore slaughtered, strangled, and killed, what injustice is done by those who—sharing in and defiling themselves with these same sins and cruelties through their bloodthirsty desires—pretend to look for the Church of past centuries among those believers whom people like them have killed? Indeed, should they not also thank God along with us, because all the efforts and violence of Satan have been in vain and powerless? For despite these efforts, the church has nevertheless survived in the persons of these servants of God; indeed, it has even maintained the victory and conquest through faith, triumphing in the midst of and through **Martyrdoms** and oppressions. We have not measured these in this **History** by the cruelty of the torments, but rather by the justice and goodness of the cause itself.

Seeking out and tracing this blood trail, through the certain proofs of faith and the steadfastness of millions of witnesses who sealed the truth with the loss of their lives, shall serve to promote God’s honor. Therefore, those whose hearts God shall awaken through His touch to enlarge this **History**—by the true account of things of similar substance and matter that occurred near their birthplaces—will greatly promote the edification of the Church. It is certain that there is hardly a Kingdom, State, Principality, City, Village, or Hamlet in Europe to be found where this innocent blood has not been shed. By contributing what God has done in past centuries to our knowledge of the Church, we may understand in what place and how God has preserved her.

And in such a holy occupation, one must not fear the venom of evil tongues, the slanders of **Atheists** or the godless, or the mockery of worldly mockers. An unhealthy stomach desires nothing but what is contrary to it; the wicked likewise can praise nothing except that which agrees with their corrupt nature. If the slanders of the wicked had been able to withhold from us the service we owe to God and His Church, we would not have written even three full lines of this **History**, or we would have abandoned the pursuit. For many bit at it and slandered it at the first news that we were researching it: what then will they not do now, seeing in it that which they never thought we could defend with such shining truth?

# Of the First Part,
### Of the History of the Waldensians.

The First Chapter.
That God has at all times raised up laborers for the gathering of His Saints: At what time Waldo began to teach, and with what fruit; who he was, as well as those who were named Waldensians after him.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'G' featuring a bird (possibly a swan or pelican) amidst floral flourishes.</image-desc>

God has never left himself without witness; from time to time he continually raises up instruments to proclaim his grace. He enriches these same individuals with the necessary gifts for the building up of his Church; he gives them his Spirit as a leader and his truth as a guiding line, so that they might distinguish the Church which began in Abel from the one which began in Cain <note>The author uses the biblical figures of Abel and Cain to represent the "true" persecuted church versus the "false" persecuting church, a common theme in Reformation-era historiography.</note>. He teaches them to describe the Church through faith, and faith through the Holy Scriptures. He strengthens them in the midst of the most difficult persecutions, making them acknowledge that the Cross is profitable, since the believers, by means of the same, exchange the earth for heaven; and that the children of God are in no way lost, even if they are murdered or cast into the fire for the sake of righteousness. One also finds in their very blood and ashes the seed of the Church.

<column-break/>

This same thing, which one has been able to observe in all ages, has been observed in a special manner among the Christians named the Waldensians <note>The Waldensians (or Vaudois) are a pre-Reformation Christian movement that began in the 12th century, emphasizing poverty and lay preaching.</note>. These were raised up at that time in which Satan held men in ignorance, having entangled the greater part of those who called themselves Christians in the great sin of the earth—namely, Idolatry—the Kings and Princes themselves employing all their power to confirm the same, delivering all those to death who wished to keep themselves free from the wounds that are inherent to idolatry.

It happened around the year of our Lord one thousand one hundred and sixty that the penalty of death was set for all those who would not believe that (the sacramental words having been spoken by the Priest) the body of our Lord would be in the Host <term>Host: the wafer used in the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term> under the appearance of the bread and the wine, its roundness and whiteness; yes, that very body as thick and also as large as it was on the tree of the Cross, the bread disappearing and being transubstantiated or changed into the flesh of Christ. There was also a command to worship the same Host, for which the streets were decorated with carpets, before which one knelt, which one called God, before which one beat their breast, and which was enclosed in monstrances <term>Monstrance: an open or transparent vessel of precious metal used in the Catholic Church to display the consecrated Host</term> to be worshiped, just as people still do today—

<summary>This page introduces the Waldensians as a divinely preserved group of believers who emerged during a period of perceived spiritual darkness to oppose the doctrine of Transubstantiation and the worship of the Host.</summary>

follows today.

This teaching, previously unknown to the Apostles—who had never spoken of such a mystery—and unheard of in the early Church, which never had any Teacher who instructed them in this **personal sacrifice** <note>This refers to the "sacrifice of the Mass," which the author argues was a later invention unknown to the early Christians.</note> for the living and for the dead, caused many Christians to be struck with terror. They preferred to suffer temporal death rather than oppose such idolatry, fearing that by adhering to it, they would face hell.

<margin>Guido de Perpignan in his *Flower of the Chronicles*.</margin> **Peter Valdo**, being a citizen of **Lyons**, was the most courageous in setting himself against such fabrications. He also rebuked many other failings in doctrine that had crept into the Roman Church over time, saying that the Church had abandoned the faith of Jesus, and that she was the **Babylonian Whore** <note>A common Reformation-era pejorative for the Roman Catholic Church, referencing the Book of Revelation.</note> and that **unfruitful Fig Tree** which the Lord had cursed in ancient times.

That one must not obey the Pope, seeing as he was not the head of the Church.

That the monastic life was a foul conduit <note>The Dutch *stinckende pype* suggests a "stinking pipe" or "foul channel," implying monasticism was a corrupting influence.</note>, and the monastic vows were the brands and marks of that great Beast.

That **Purgatory**, the Masses, the dedication of churches, the veneration of saints, and the remembrances for the dead were nothing other than the snares of the devil and the nets of greed.

<margin>See the *Sea of Histories*, folio 203. Claude Rubis in his *History of the City of Lyons*, page 269.</margin> Valdo was therefore listened to with greater attention because he was held in high esteem for his learning and godliness. Furthermore, he gave great alms from his possessions to the needy; and besides feeding them with physical bread, he exhorted them above all to seek **Jesus Christ**, the true bread of souls.

<column-break/>

<margin>The *History* of Monsieur du Thou, page 455. Louis Camerarius in the *History of the Orthodox Brethren of Bohemia*, page 7. Guido de Perpignan in his *Flower of the Chronicles*. The *Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth* <note>original: "Catalogus testium veritatis"</note>, page 535. Simon Deuoi-on in his book *The Account of the Alterers of the Church*.</margin> Various historians have written that he made a firm resolution to lead an irreproachable life, approaching as closely as he could the life of the Apostles. This came about through a fatal incident that occurred unexpectedly and without warning. Namely, that being in the company of certain friends one evening after supper, while they were being merry together, one of the company fell dead to the earth. This greatly terrified all who were present. Indeed, Valdo was touched to the core by this, and through that arrow of Divine justice, he was moved to an unusual repentance. He devoted himself to the reading of the **Holy Scriptures**, seeking his salvation therein. He published some treatises of the Ancient Fathers and continually instructed the poor who flocked to him to share in and enjoy his alms.

The Archbishop of Lyons, named **Jean de Belles-mains** <note>OCR: Ioan. de Belles Mayons. Jean de Belles-mains was the Archbishop of Lyons from 1182 to 1193.</note>, having been warned that Valdo made a profession of teaching the people and that they freely rebuked the failings, the excess, and the pride of the Popes and their clergy, forbade him to put forward such arguments anymore or to instruct anyone further, seeing as he, being a **layperson**, was exceeding his calling. He ordered him to cease under penalty of **Excommunication** <term>Banne: a formal ecclesiastical censure or excommunication</term>, and further threatened to proceed against him as a **Heretic**.

Valdo replied to this that he was not able to remain silent...

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Peter Valdo’s defiance against the religious authorities in Lyons. The previous page established Valdo’s rejection of various Roman Catholic doctrines, such as the Mass and the Pope's authority.</meta>

->of the History of the Waldensians.<-
A 2

In a matter so weighty as the salvation of mankind, Valdo felt he would rather obey God—who commanded him to speak—than men who commanded him to remain silent.

Following this answer, the Archbishop exerted his best efforts to have him captured, but he could not succeed. As Valdo was of a noble family and much beloved by many, he remained openly within Lyons under the favor and protection of his friends for a period of three years.

Pope Alexander the Third, the third of that name <note>Pope Alexander III (reigned 1159–1181) was known for his conflict with Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and for presiding over the Third Lateran Council.</note>, having understood that many people within Lyons were already casting doubt upon his pretended sovereign power over the Church, and fearing that this beginning of rebellion would further assault his high dignity, banished Valdo and his adherents. He commanded the Archbishop of Lyons to proceed further against them through ecclesiastical censures, even to their complete eradication.

<margin>Claude de Rubis in his *History*, page 269. Albertus de Capitaneis, in the book *Of the Origin of the Waldensians*, page 1.</margin> Claude Rubis relates that Valdo and his followers were entirely driven out of Lyons; and Albertus de Capitaneis says that they could not be completely rooted out. Furthermore, we have been unable to learn more of this first persecution, other than that those who escaped from Lyons—who after Valdo were called Waldensians—followed him, and thereafter scattered from one another into various groups and places.

### The Second Chapter.

That the scattering of Valdo and his followers was the means that God used to spread the teaching of Valdo throughout nearly all of Europe.

<column-break/>

<margin>Albertus de Capitaneis in the book *Of the Origin of the Waldensians*, page 1. Claude de Rubis in the aforementioned place, page 269.</margin> Albertus de Capitaneis relates that Valdo, departing from Lyons, betook himself to **Dauphiné** <note>A province in southeastern France.</note>. And Claudius de Rubis believes that he frequented the mountains of the said province, and that he met there a rough people, yet well-suited to receive the instructions of his faith. And it is true that the churches of the Waldensians which have survived the longest, and which are still the greatest in number above other places in Europe, are those located in Dauphiné and the surrounding areas, which originate from the same—namely those of **Piedmont** and **Provence**.

<margin>1. Vignier in the same part of his *Historical Library*, page 130. 2. Dubravius in the *History of Bohemia*, in the 14th book.</margin> 1. Vignier says that he departed for **Picardy**, and that in a short time he achieved such success there that many people followed his teaching, and that they suffered great persecutions for the same shortly thereafter. For, as 2. Dubravius relates, a short time later King Philip Augustus <note>Philip II of France (1165–1223), who significantly expanded the French royal domains.</note>, being incited by the clergy, took up arms against the Picardy Waldensians. He destroyed and razed three hundred manor houses of the gentry who followed their side, destroyed several fortified cities, and pursued them as far as **Flanders**, where they had fled, and caused a great multitude of them to be burned.

<margin>See the *Sea of Histories*.</margin> This persecution drove many away and caused them to flee to **Upper Germany**, where they were likewise severely persecuted shortly thereafter, most notably in the land of **Alsace** and along the Rhine River by the Bishops of **Mainz** and **Strasbourg**. These bishops caused thirty-five citizens of Mainz to be burned in the city of **Bingen**.

Bingen, and within Mainz, eighteen others, who all endured death with great steadfastness, just as eighty others were burned at Strasbourg following the persecution by the Bishop of that place. ### The Third Chapter.
#### By what names the *Waldensians* were called by their enemies, as well as with what slanders they burdened them.

The Monks of the Inquisition, being mortal enemies of the Waldensians, were not satisfied with daily handing them over to the hands of secular justice; they additionally burdened them with stains of infamy, accusing them of being the authors of all the heresies in the world. They claimed these people were the dregs of society, and frequently charged the Waldensians alone with all the "monsters" <note>In this context, "monsters" refers to unnatural or blasphemous religious errors.</note> they themselves had concocted, as if the Waldensians were nothing but a hostel and refuge for all kinds of errors. They first called them Waldensians after Valdo, who was a citizen of Lyons, as well as Albigensians after the region of Albi. <margin>Vaudois.</margin>

And because those who followed the teaching of Valdo departed from Lyons stripped of all human means, having had to leave the greater part of their goods behind, their enemies mockingly named them <term>Pauperes de Lugduno</term> <note>original: "Pauperes de Lugduno", meaning "The Poor of Lyons".</note>.

In Dauphiné <note>A province in southeastern France.</note>, they were mockingly named <term>Chaignards</term> <note>original: "Chaignards", meaning "Dogs".</note>. <margin>Chaignards.</margin>

And as a portion of them crossed the Alpine mountains, they were named <term>Transmontani</term> <note>original: "Transmontani", meaning "Those from across the mountains".</note>. <margin>Transmontains.</margin>

And after one of the disciples of Valdo named Joseph, who preached in the Diocese of Die in Dauphiné, they were called Josephites. <margin>Iosephistes.</margin>

In England, they were called Lollards after the name of Lollardus <note>Likely referring to Walter Lollard, a 14th-century preacher, though the term "Lollard" has debated origins.</note> who preached there. <margin>Lollards.</margin>

After two priests who taught the doctrine of Valdo in Languedoc, one named Henricus and the other Esperon, they were called Henricians and Esperonists. <margin>Henriciens. Esperon:</margin>

After one of their <term>Barbes</term> <note>original: "Barbes", a term used by the Waldensians for their pastors, meaning "uncles" or "elders" in their dialect.</note>, meaning Pastors or Teachers, who preached in the Albi region named Arnoldus Hot, they were called Arnoldists. <margin>Arnoldistes.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the third chapter of the history of the Waldensians, detailing the various derogatory names and labels applied to the group by their opponents across different regions of Europe.</meta>

# of the History of the Waldensians.
<sig>A 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: commanded</meta>

<margin>Siccars, Fratricelli.</margin> In Provence, they were named in an unknown way of speaking or tongue as *Siccars*, that is, "cutters" or "carvers" <note>original: "voorsnijders"; this term may refer to the way they were perceived as "cutting away" from the church or perhaps to a specific trade.</note>. In Italy, they were named *Fratricelli*, as if one said "Little Brothers," because they lived together like brothers in true unity.

<margin>Insabathas.</margin> And since they observed no other day of rest except Sunday, they were therefore named *Insabatati* or *Insabathas*, as if to say "without Sabbath" or "keeping no Sabbath."

And because they were constantly subject to and endured suffering, they were given a name from the Latin word *Pati*, which signifies "to suffer," being called *Patarins* or *Patarieus*, that is, the "suffering" or "patient" ones.
<margin>Patariens. Patarius.</margin>

And as they, like poor travelers, were fleeing and traveling from one land to another, they were called *Passagenes*, that is, "passers-by" or "wanderers."
<margin>Passagenes.</margin>

In High Germany, they were called *Gazares*, which is as much as to say "cursed" or "abominable and exceptional villains."
<margin>Gazares.</margin>

In Flanders, they were called *Turlupins*, as if one said "dwelling with wolves," because due to the persecutions they were often forced to hide and remain in the wilderness and the forests.
<margin>Turlupins.</margin>

Sometimes they were named after the names of the regions or districts where they lived, such as from Albi, the *Albigensians*; from Toulouse, the *Toulouzans*; from Lombardy, the *Lombards*; from Picardy, the *Picards*; from Lyon, the *Lyonists*; from Bohemia, the *Bohemians*.
<margin>Toulouzains. Lombards. Piccards. Lionistes. Bohemiens.</margin>

Sometimes, in order to make them more hateful, they were

<column-break/>

accused and held to be accomplices of the ancient heretics, which occurred under ridiculous pretenses. For because they made a profession of purity, both in their lives and faith, they were therefore called *Catharri* <note>The Cathars, or "Pure Ones," were another medieval group often confused with the Waldensians by their persecutors.</note>. And because they denied that the Host, which the mass-priest displays in the Mass, could be God, they were therefore named *Arrians*, as if they were forsaking the divinity of the Son of the eternal God. And as they maintained and defended that the power of the Emperors and the Kings of the Earth does not depend on the power of the Popes, they were therefore called *Manicheans*, as if they established "two principles" <note>The Manicheans believed in a dualism of good and evil; the accusers here imply that separating church and state power was a form of dualism.</note>. And for other idle reasons that they imagined for themselves, they were called *Gnostics*, *Cataphrygians*, *Adamites*, and *Apostolics*.
<margin>Catharres.</margin>
<margin>Arriani.</margin>
<margin>Gnostiques. Adamites. Apostoliques.</margin>

Sometimes they were subjected to even greater grievance and violence: for Matthew Paris calls them "knaves" or "rascals." The compiler of the *Treasury of Histories* calls them *Bougres* <note>original: "Bouggers"; a derogatory term derived from "Bulgarian," often used as a slur for heretics.</note>. Rubis relates that whenever anyone spoke of a Sorcerer, they were named with the name *Valdois* <note>Waldensian</note>. And what is more, he works hard to prove that they were indeed such. Which presumption must be answered in a more suitable place, where they shall be acquitted of these and similar accusations that their enemies have laid upon them. From whose books we have collected the following.
<margin>Bougres. Sorciers.</margin>

The third slander with which they were burdened was that they held goods in common among themselves, and even held women in common.

The fourth slanderous stain was that they rejected <term>infant baptism</term> <note>The Waldensians often emphasized believer's baptism or questioned the efficacy of the rite as performed by the Roman Church.</note>.

### Chapter 4.

#### How the Waldensians are acquitted of the slanders contained in the previous chapter, based on the writings they have left behind.

Whether the Waldensians of Bohemia were a remnant of the people who followed Peter Waldo <note>original: "Valdo"</note>—as there are those who hold that he ended his life in Bohemia after departing from Germany, having escaped the hands of the Bishops of Mainz and Strasbourg—or whether they were other people who had likewise embraced the same faith as the Waldensians, it is at least certain that they were severely persecuted under King Ladislaus, King of Hungary and Bohemia. <margin>Ladislaus.</margin> And we have in our hands a certain defense of these same Waldensians, written in the <term>Gascon tongue</term> <note>The author refers to the Occitan language used by the Waldensians in the Alpine regions and spread to their colonies.</note>, which they sent to the King (whom they call Lancelau) to clear themselves of the many slanders laid upon them by their enemies. We also have that book which they titled **A ico es la causa del nostre Despartement de la Gleisa Romane**, that is, **See, this is the cause of our separation from the Roman Church.** And as they respond there to the first slander—namely, that they held their gatherings in dark places where, once the candles were blown out, their enemies said they committed horrific incest—we shall transcribe their answer from the said defense in their own words and language, for greater certainty and edification.

<margin>In the letter to King Ladislaus, page 2.</margin>
Among other things (they say) they bark and snarl like evil, growling dogs, [claiming] that it is a law among us to say: "Yield yourself to everyone who desires you," and that we fulfill our lusts in hidden and dark caves, without distinction with all those who come before us, yes, even if they were our own natural mothers, daughters, wives, or sisters. But how could that actually be the case, seeing that indeed, in the case—

<column-break/>

Among other things, they preach—like annoying, growling dogs—that we have as a law: "Give yourself to everyone who asks," and that we give ourselves to our delights in hidden, dark caves with whoever we encounter, whether mother, or daughter, or wife, or sister. <note>original Occitan: "Entre las autras cosas illi predican... o sia de maire, o de filla, o de moller, o de soror."</note> Yet for forty years and more, there has been no fornication among us that was not punished. Nor even such debauchery, as our good life and deeds are the destruction of their [the accusers'] way of life.

->The 1st Book, of the 1st Part<-

...in forty full years past—during which it has pleased God to preserve and protect us—no one has ever heard it said that any <term>fornication</term> <note>original: "hoererije"</note> among us has gone unpunished, nor has any indecency been committed; so much so that our lives and works themselves rebuke and prove, or put to shame, the lives of those who accuse us.

And since they speak of themselves to their own praise, and such a defense might seem weak and faint, look then here at what they have written elsewhere against fornication, which alone shall be enough to prove that they have been entirely estranged from devilish desires, and from wishing to defile themselves through <term>incest</term> <note>original: "bloet-schanden," literally "blood-shame."</note>.

<margin>
From the Book of the remedies for the sin of Unchastity, in the 21st chapter.
</margin>
The sin of unchastity pleases the devil wonderfully well, but displeases God; it also greatly wrongs our neighbors, seeing as through it a person obeys that most despised part or member of his body more than God, who has forbidden it. The foolish woman robs not only her husband of his goods, but also herself. He who gives himself to this sin keeps faith with no one; from this it came that David had his faithful servant Uriah put to death in order to obtain his wife. Amnon destroyed his sister Tamar. This sin ruins the inheritance of many, as is told of the Prodigal Son, who wasted his goods with an unchaste and excessive life. Balaam chose this very sin to provoke the children of Israel to sin, by occasion of which twenty-four thousand of them were put to death. This sin was the cause of Samson's blindness, it led Solomon astray, and many others perished because of the beauty of women. Fasting, prayer, and absence or avoidance serve as remedies against this sin. For one may overcome all other sins by fighting against them; but in this one, a person becomes the victor by fleeing and by not approaching it. Of which we have an example in Joseph. We must then pray to the Lord daily, that He...

<column-break/>

<margin>
From the Book of the remedies for the sin of Lust, chapter 21. <note>original: "Libro del rea medi del pecca de Luxurca." This column provides the original text in the Occitan language used by the Waldensians.</note>
</margin>
The sin of lust pleases the devil much, and is very shameful to God, and injurious to the neighbor, because man obeys the vilest part of his body more than God who has forbidden it. The foolish woman takes not only from the fool his things, but also herself. He who works in this vice keeps faith with no one, wherefore David caused his faithful servant to be killed for his wife. Amnon corrupted his sister Tamar. This vice takes the inheritance from many, even as is said of the Prodigal Son who dissipated his substance living luxuriously. Balaam chose this sin before all others to cast down the children of Israel and make them sin, for which sin twenty-four thousand men were killed. This sin blinded Samson, perverted Solomon, and many perished through the beauty of woman. Fasting and prayer are the remedy for this sin, and drawing oneself back. For other vices we can overcome by fighting, but this one by fleeing and not approaching it. Example in Joseph. We must therefore pray to the Lord every day, that He take from us the sin of lust and give to us the gift of understanding and of chastity.

# The History of the Waldensians,
**B**
<meta>catchword: of the</meta>

...may [God] keep this sin of unchastity far from us, and may He grant us understanding and purity.

<margin>In the book of virtues, in the chapter on marriage.</margin>
Against the second deceptive accusation—namely, that they were supposed to maintain that one is permitted to put away his wife—they answered: That **Marriage** is a bond that may not be untied except by the coming of death, unless it be for <term>fornication</term> <note>original: "hoererije"</note>, just as our Lord Jesus Christ says. And St. Paul in 1 Cor. 7 says: that the wife shall not be separated from the husband, nor the husband from the wife.

<margin>In the book of the Waldensians titled "On Virtue," in the chapter on marriage.</margin>
To the third slander regarding the "community of goods" and of "wives": they answered concerning marriage, that the same was instituted by God in the earthly Paradise: and that it is a fitting remedy to avoid fornication. And that St. Paul, speaking of the same, said that every man shall have his own wife, and every woman her own husband. Likewise, that the man must love his wife as Christ loved His Church, and that those who are married must live holily together with their children in the fear of the Lord.

Marriage is a bond not to be loosed, which cannot be untied until death, except as Jesus Christ says, for the reason of fornication. And Saint Paul in 1 Cor. 7 says: Do not depart the wife from the husband nor the husband from the wife.

Marriage was ordained by God in Paradise. It is a remedy to avoid fornication. And of this Saint Paul says, let each one have his own wife, and each one have her own husband. <margin>This is evident by the legal proceedings they have in hand, in which Commissioners [ordered] the 12 <term>bands</term> <note>Likely referring to groups of officials or legal districts.</note> against the usurpers of the Waldensians' property for the restitution of the same.</margin>
As far as property is concerned, it is certain that everyone has possessed his own goods at all times and places. In <term>Dauphiné</term> <note>A historical province in southeastern France.</note>, when the Archbishops of <term>Embrun</term> <note>original: "Ambrun."</note>, Jean and Rostan, stripped them of their property; and when the Lord of Argentière and Montaimar, as well as Arroas de Bonne, drove the Waldensians living in the Valleys of Fraissinière and Argentière from their lands, the restitution of each individual inheritance was pursued by the particular owners from whom they had been taken. The Waldensians of <term>Provence</term> are still presently demanding from the Pope those goods that were added to his domains through <term>confiscation</term>; each individual owner provides proof of the parcels and goods they inherited from their grandfathers from <term>immemorial times</term> <note>A legal term meaning a time so long ago that no living person remembers its beginning.</note>, without there ever having been any "community" among them that would diminish the lawful ownership which every person has over his grounds and estates according to the law.

<margin>This is evident by the treaties regarding the "Manner" and other petitions made by the Waldensians of Provence.</margin>

### Concerning the fourth Slander, regarding baptism: namely, that they withheld the same from small children: they are exonerated by the following words/

<margin>
In the book of the Waldensians entitled Spiritual Almanac. folio 45.
</margin>
Neither the time nor the places for those who must be baptized is ordained: but love and the edification of the Community and the congregation must serve as a rule in this, etc.

Also, for this reason one comes to offer the speechless children for baptism: which those who are most closely related to these little children are bound to do; such as their Parents or friends, or those to whom God has given such love.

<column-break/>

"Neither the time nor the place is ordained in which those who ought to be baptized must be, but charity and the edification of the Church, and of the congregation, ought to be the rule in this, etc." <note>original: "Lo temps non es ordena ni encara lo luoc en aquilli ique devon esser baptiza, ma la carita & L'edification de la Gleisa, & de la cōgregation, deo esser regla en aizo. & ch." (Occitan)</note>

Also. "Therefore one comes to present the children for Baptism, and this they must do who are most closely related to the children, such as their parents, and those to whom God has given charity." <note>original: "Item. Emperzo la se ven a presentar li enfant al Baptisme, & aizo devon far aquilli a qui li enfant lor tocan plus pres de ser parents, & aquilli a qui dio na donna la charita." (Occitan)</note>

---

<column-break/>

<note>The following text returns to a single column layout across the width of the page.</note>

It is indeed true that for several hundred years, being forced to have their children baptized by the Priests of the <term>Roman Church</term> <note>original: "Roomscher Kercke"</note>, they postponed and delayed doing so as long as they were able; and this because they had a horror of the human inventions added to the institution of this <term>Sacrament</term> <note>original: "Sacramēts"</note>, all of which they held to be true pollutions of the same. And since their Teachers, whom they called by a common word <term>Barbes</term> <note>Meaning "uncles" in the Occitan dialect, a title of respect for Waldensian pastors</note>, were often traveling for the service of their Communities, and thus they could not have their children baptized through their service, they sometimes kept them unbaptized for a considerable time. Observing this, the Priests stained them with the aforementioned slander, which has been held as true not only by their enemies, but even by many of those who have recognized their life and faith as good in all other points.

The fifth slander was that they worshiped their Barbes (that is, Teachers), prostrating themselves before them. To clear the <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval proto-Protestant movement</note> of this, it is only necessary for the reader to take the trouble to see what they taught concerning the worship of the one God alone, in the explanation they give in the book of their teaching on the first commandment of the Law of God.

<margin>
Checked by the legal proceedings made by the same Albert against the Waldensians of the Alpine mountains.
</margin>
They have (it is true) shown great reverence to their Teachers, as to those who served them with the word of reconciliation and maintained them in love, finding themselves bound to this by the promptings of their consciences. But that they would have intended to show to a creature the honor which is owed to God the Creator alone: this cannot be said except with false slander, no matter how violently and cruelly their mortal enemy <term>Albertus de Capitaneis</term> <note>An inquisitor and legal official active in the late 15th century, known for his campaigns against the Waldensians in the Alps</note> in the Bishopric of Turin had them tortured.

The sixth slander: that they maintained that one might never swear an oath.

<margin>In the book named the *Spiritual Almanac*, in the explanation of the 3rd commandment. Heb. 6. Is. 6.</margin>
They have said that there are lawful oaths tending to God’s honor and to the edification of one's neighbor, citing what the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: that men swear by the one who is much greater than themselves, and the oath serves for confirmation to put an end to all strife. The seventh slander intended to make them hateful to the people, as if they had placed the Pope on the same level as the Turk regarding the expansion of the Church and the Kingdom of Christ, saying that the Pope sinned mortally when he sent out **Crusades** <note>The original Dutch uses 'Croiſaden' and 'Cruys-baerden' (Cross-bearers), referring to the military expeditions authorized by the Pope.</note>—that is, Cross-bearers—against the **Saracens** <note>A common historical term for Muslims during the medieval period.</note>.

<margin>In the book of the *Causes of the Separation from the Romish Church*, page 235.</margin>
In their defense, it should be noted that they did not complain about the beginning of the wars against the Turk, but because the Popes, under the pretext of the same, stripped the Church both of its temporal goods and of Divine blessing: deceiving the unlearned through their **Bulls** <note>Official edicts or charters issued by the Pope.</note> and **Blessings**, who all too willingly accepted the Popes' lies, indeed, buying and paying for them dearly. Furthermore, they considered it evil that the Pope caused them to be attacked by the Crusades of the Pilgrims and persecuted as heretics without having heard them or having proved them to be such.

"The Pope, by such Indulgences, ordained in various ways the despoiling of the whole Church of its goods of Fortune and of its divine goods. For by such blessings he deceives the hearts of the innocent; but they [the Popes] wish to seize [wealth] affectionately and with much price for the lie." <note>original: "Lo Papa per Tali Indulgenzas ordena en diverſas manieras deſpoilla tota la Gleiſa de li bien de Fortuna, & de li bien diuin. But they were not the only ones who rebuked the greed or the vengeful spirit of the Popes in the matter of the Crusades.

...[Man was] driven out of Paradise because he had sinned there: and even the Angels fell from Heaven, so that they might serve as an example for those who should come after, to teach them and prove to them that it is neither the place, nor its own greatness and dignity, that makes a person holy, but the innocence of life.

<margin>Response of the Waldensians, which they titled: *The Light and the Treasure of Faith*, fol. 214.</margin>
Against the ninth slander, namely that they were said to have taught that the government may sentence no one to death, they said:

That it is written, that one shall not let the evildoer live. And that without the hatred of sin, the teaching is not useful, nor are judgments recognized, nor would crimes be punished. And that therefore righteous anger is a mother of good order, but that unwise patience or tolerance is the seed of crimes, giving the evildoers the reins to do evil.

<column-break/>

<note>original: "Lo es eſcrit, non laiſſares Viore lo mal faitor, ſi la ira non ſare la doctrina non profitare ni li judici non ſaren diſcerni ni li pecca non ſaren caſtiga. Donc la juſta ira es maire de la diſciplina, & la patienza ſen raſon ſemena li vici, & laiſſá prevaricar li mal."</note>
It is written, you shall not let the evildoer live; if there is no anger <note>referring to "righteous anger" or zeal against sin</note>, the doctrine shall not profit, nor shall judgments be discerned, nor shall sins be punished. Therefore, just anger is the mother of discipline, and patience without reason sows vices and lets the wicked stray.

---

It is true that they found it evil that the authorities delivered them to death without taking any knowledge of their case, but only upon the accusation of the Priests <note>original: "Papen," a derogatory term for Catholic clergy</note> and Monks who were their opposing parties and judges, because they had discovered and called out the abuses that the same had forced into the Church, and therefore condemned them as Heretics and handed them over to the secular arm—that is what they called the government.

Therefore, they considered it a cruel naivety in the authorities to believe such embittered people as the aforementioned Priests were, and to cause so many poor, innocent people to die upon their accusation, without having heard or questioned them.

The tenth slander was intended to make them hateful to Kings and Princes, namely that they supposedly taught that a layman being in a state of grace has more power than a Prince who is in mortal sin.

<margin>Response, regarding the causes of their separation from the Roman Church, p. 41.</margin>
Against this deceit they answered: that every person must be subject to those placed over him, to obey them, love them, keep peace with them, and honor them with double respect, in subjection, in obedience, in willingness...

<column-break/>

<note>original: "Vn chaſcun deo eſſer ſotmes a li devant pauſa, creyre a lor meſeimes amar lor, aver paz cum lor, coler lor de doble honor, en ſubjection, en obedienza, en prompteza, & en pagament."</note>
Every person must be subject to the powers placed over them, to believe them, to love them, to have peace with them, to honor them with double honor, in subjection, in obedience, in promptness, and in payment <note>referring to taxes or tribute</note>.

The eleventh slander was based on the claim of the Waldensians, namely that the Pope has no power over the Kings and Princes of the earth, but that they depend directly on God alone. For from this, their accusers took the opportunity to call them <term>Manichaeans</term><note>Followers of a dualistic religion that believed in two equal opposing forces of good and evil; here the Pope implies that denying his supreme authority suggests a belief in two separate divine principles.</note>, as if they were establishing two primary principles.

<margin>In the book named *The Treasure of Faith*, article 2.</margin>
Against this slander they answered: We believe that this Holy Trinity has created all things, visible and invisible, and that He is the one Lord over all that is heavenly, earthly, or hellish, as is said by St. John. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

<column-break/>

<note>original: "Nos crefen que aquesta sancta Trinita ha crea totas cosas, vesiblas, & es Seignorador de las cosas celestials, terrenals, & enfernals, coma es dict en sanct Iohan. Totas cosas sons faitas per luy & sensa luy non es faita alcuna cosa."</note>
We believe that this holy Trinity has created all things, visible, and is Lord of the things celestial, terrestrial, and infernal, as is said in Saint John. All things were made by Him, and without Him nothing was made.

<column-break/>

The origin of this slander was found in the <term>Extravagantes</term><note>A collection of papal decrees not included in the earlier official codifications of Canon Law.</note> of Pope Boniface VIII, who, subjecting the authority of Emperors to his own, says of his own power: <note>original: "Quicunque huic potestati resistit dei ordinationi resistit, nisi duo (sicut Manicheus) fingat esse principia"</note> "Whoever resists this power resists the ordinance of God, unless (like a Manichaean) he imagines there to be two principles." That is: All who resist this power, resist God’s ordinance, unless they, like the Manichaean, wish to invent two principles. *On Superiority and Obedience. Canon Unam Sanctam. Law 1, title 8.*

The twelfth slander alleged that they believed that everything done with a good intention was good, and that everyone shall be saved through that which he does with a good intention.

<margin>Rainerius, *Book on the Form of Heretics*, article 38.</margin>
No other answer is needed for this deception than what the monk Rainerius—who stained them with this accusation—says elsewhere: namely, that they maintained that no one is saved except through their faith, which he calls a "sect." A liar ought to have a better memory of his own sayings so that he does not speak against himself, as he does here.

<margin>In the book *On the Cause of Their Separation from the Roman Church*, page 273.</margin>
And to show that they did not hold such a belief, what they said about the <term>Antichrist</term><note>The Waldensians often identified the institutional corruption of the Papacy with the biblical Antichrist.</note> is sufficient: namely, that he forced his errors in with strength, under the appearance of good intention and under the cover of faith.

<column-break/>

<note>original: "A quel serf se nes intra par lo passa, fot la forza de le fe, & fot bona intention."</note>
That serpent <note>possibly 'servant' or 'serpent' in the original dialect</note> has entered therein through the past, under the force of the faith, and under good intention.

The thirteenth Calumny was that they held that one could kill priests or damage them in their <term>tithes</term><note>A tenth of one's income or produce paid as a tax to the church.</note>, and withhold these from them without a burden of conscience.

### Of the History of the Waldensians.

<margin>As appears from the trials conducted by <term>Albertus de Capitaneis</term><note>A 15th-century inquisitor known for his harsh persecution of the Waldensians in the Alpine valleys.</note> and other monks and inquisitors against the Waldensians of <term>Dauphiné</term><note>A former province in southeastern France.</note>. In the book of the Waldensians, concerning the persecutions, page 274.</margin>
It is certain that if the Waldensians had been able to spend their tithes for another use than the maintenance of those whom they had called out and labeled as mute dogs, sleeping watchmen, and lazy bellies—those who were deceiving and were also being deceived—they would have done so without fail. However, in the meantime, it is not found that they caused any disturbance because of it. It clearly appears that of those things which they were permitted to use according to their own will, they gave very little or nothing at all to such men. They did not concern themselves with their masses or their prayers for the dead, about which the priests also complained, taking from this the material to accuse them as heretics. And as for their supposed desire for revenge, see how they themselves have spoken of it:

<columns>2</columns>

The Lord, knowing well that we would be delivered up, says thus: *Matthew 10:17.* Guard yourselves from men; but he neither teaches nor counsels his elect that they should kill anyone, but rather *Luke 6:35.* that they should love their enemies. When his disciples said to him: *Luke 9:54.* "Do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?" Christ answered them: "You do not know by what spirit you are driven." Furthermore, the Lord speaks to St. Peter: *John 18:11. Matthew 26:52.* "Put your sword back in its place," etc. Likewise, temporal enemies must be despised and endured with patience, for nothing new is happening in this. We are here as the threshing floor of the Lord to be threshed and beaten, just as the corn is separated and purified from the chaff.

<column-break/>

<note>original (Occitan/Vaudois): "Lo Segnor sabent aquisti livrament dis garda vos de li home: ma el non enseigna ne conseilla li seo eslit occire alcun ma de amar li enemic..."</note>
The Lord, knowing of this deliverance, says: "Guard yourselves from men." But he does not teach nor counsel his elect to kill anyone, but rather to love the enemy. When the disciples said: "Do you wish that we say that fire should descend from heaven and consume them?" Christ, responding, said to them: "You know not of what spirit you are." Also, the Lord said to Saint Peter: "Return your sword to its place," etc. Likewise, temporal adversities make us practice contempt [for the world] and carry ourselves with patience, for no new thing has happened to us. We are here the hard threshing of God, to be fanned like the grain of wheat from the husk.

<columns>1</columns>

The last slander which we have gathered from the writings of the enemies of the Waldensians is that with which Mr. <term>Claudius de Rubis</term><note>Claude de Rubis (1533–1613) was a Catholic jurist and historian from Lyon who wrote polemics against the Waldensians and Protestants.</note> defames them in his History of the City of Lyon, namely that, having departed from Lyon and moved to the Alpine mountains, they became, along with the country folk there, *broom-riders*, which is to say, sorcerers. # Of the History of the Waldensians.

[God] has an abomination of these things. And for the sake of these sins, he shall destroy you at your entrance.

And in the book of Leviticus it is said <margin>Leviticus 20.</margin>: Whoever turns to the sorcerers and soothsayers, to go whoring after them, I will set my hand against him [and cut him off] from his people.

## The First Book, of the First Part

...doubt the City of Geneva and the Estates of the Cantons that have accepted the Gospel. They have no other substance for this <note>The "substance" refers to the grounds for accusing the Reformers of sorcery.</note> than that in such places, sorcerers are often condemned to death, following the command <margin>Exodus 22:18</margin> of God, who does not want the sorcerer or the sorceress to be allowed to live. He would have made a better conclusion if he had said that in those places where the Reformation has been introduced in our time, no fellowship or conversation is held with sorcerers at all. For this reason, they put to death as many as can be found; unless he wished to say that to condemn sorcerers is nothing other than to follow them and be favorable or helpful to them, and that sentencing them to death is nothing other than a kind of heresy.

But on the contrary, it truly happens in those places that heresy and sorcery either accompany or follow one another, where those very people who present themselves as teachers of the people are frequently found to be sorcerers themselves. Various personages have complained about this, having written with heavy hearts of that which they knew was all too common <note>original: "in swane ginc"; an idiom meaning something was widespread or in vogue</note> among their priests and monks—nay, what is more, even among some Popes.

<margin>Bodin in his book on demon-possessed people. Book 4, chapter 5, page 211. <note>Referring to Jean Bodin's *De la démonomanie des sorciers* (1580), a foundational text on the prosecution of witches.</note></margin> Bodin has noted that the same has been found in countless legal verdicts, where he recounts that quite often the priests are not only sorcerers themselves, or that the sorcerers have an understanding with the priests, but that they have even allowed themselves to be brought to perform the Mass for the
