### Of the History of the Waldensians.

...nor any trace of wrongdoing, nor any ceremonies or worship of the Roman Church; instead, they found that there was nothing of those villainous acts with which they were charged. Rather, they found that they observed Sundays, had their children baptized according to the manner of the early Church, and taught them the Articles of the Christian faith and the commandments of God. The King, having heard the report of these commissioners, said with an oath: "That they were far more honorable people than he and all his folk."

<margin>This is recounted in the memorial notes of the Archbishop of Embrun named Rostain, handled by the Counselor Vulçon.</margin> This same King, having heard that in Dauphiné, and namely in the valley of Fraissinière, in the Diocese of Embrun, there were certain people who lived like beasts <note>In the Middle Ages, "living like beasts" was a common accusation used to dehumanize remote rural populations or "heretics" to justify their persecution.</note>, without religion or worship, also having an ill opinion of the Roman religion, sent thither one of his confessors with the Official of Orléans to find out what was going on. This confessor and his companion traveled to the place, where they questioned the Waldensians who lived in that same valley regarding the matters of their faith and conduct. The Archbishop of Embrun—who was eagerly waiting for the properties of these Waldensians to be added to the domains of his Archbishopric, as they would be forfeited by reason of heresy—urged the aforementioned commissioners very hard to condemn them as heretics in haste. But the same commissioners would not fulfill his desire, but excused them as much as they could; indeed, to the point that before their departure, the King’s confessor, while staying at the Angel Inn <note>original: "Herberghe vande Enghel"</note> in Embrun, declared in the presence of many bystanders: "That he wished he were as good a Christian as the very lowliest of the inhabitants of the valley of Fraissinière."

<column-break/>

<margin>Note.</margin> King Francis I, the first of that name and successor to King Louis XII, having heard that the parliament of Provence was causing much suffering to the Waldensians living in Mérindol, Cabrières, and other surrounding places, wished to be informed of the faith, life, and manner of these same Waldensians. Therefore, he commanded Guillaume du Bellay, Lord of Langey <note>Guillaume du Bellay (1491–1543) was a French diplomat and general known for his fairness and historical writings.</note>, then lieutenant in Piedmont, to diligently investigate this matter. Whereupon the same Lord sent two persons to Provence, both honorable men, whom he commanded to inquire into the life and religion of these Waldensians as well as the proceedings of the Court of Parliament against them. These two deputies reported to the Lord of Langey that the greater part of the province of Provence declared that the said Waldensians were a very industrious people. They reported that about two hundred years ago, they had moved from the land of Piedmont to settle in Provence, where they had taken over several hamlets that had been ruined by war, as well as other abandoned and uncultivated land, under the title of <term>quit-rent land</term> <note>original: "Chijnsgoet" – land held by paying a fixed annual rent to a lord rather than providing military or labor service.</note>, making it fertile through their labor. And through the investigations they conducted in the land of Provence, they found that these Waldensians of Mérindol were peaceful people,

# The First Book, of the First Part

...beloved by all their neighbors, people of good morals, keeping their promises or holding to their word, and paying their debts faithfully without letting themselves be brought to court for them; a friendly and compassionate people, who did not allow anyone among them to suffer want, giving alms to strangers and poor travelers according to their means. Furthermore, the inhabitants of Provence declared that those of Merindol <note>Merindol was a prominent Waldensian village in Provence, later famous for the brutal massacre of its inhabitants in 1545.</note> were known among other countrymen by the fact that they could never be provoked to slanderous words or to naming the Devil, nor to swear any oath, unless it were in the making of some condition or contract, or before a court of law. Likewise, they were recognized by this: that if they were in any company where wanton talk or blasphemies were heard, they would quickly withdraw themselves from such company.

Thus we see how many of the Waldensians' enemies have spoken honorably of them, being driven to do so by the power of the truth. We must now further examine in what esteem they were held by those who, after them, held the same faith with them.

### The Sixth Chapter.
#### Testimonies given to the Waldensians by many great personages who made profession of the Reformed Religion.

<margin>Theodore Beza in his *Portraits of Pious Men*.</margin>
Theodore Beza <note>A major French Protestant Reformer and successor to John Calvin in Geneva.</note> has called the Waldensians the seed of the purest ancient Church, and this because they were so miraculously preserved in the midst of the darkness and errors with which Satan had possessed these recent centuries or times.

<margin>Constans on the Revelation.</margin>
Constans, in his commentary on the Revelation of John, proves that the Reformation of the Church in the West began in France by means of Waldo, and that from this source, it spread across the rest of Europe.

<margin>Bullinger in his preface to the Revelation, Folio.</margin>
Bullinger <note>Heinrich Bullinger was a Swiss Reformer and successor to Zwingli in Zurich.</note> speaks of the Waldensians in this manner: "What shall we say then? It has been more than four hundred years," says he, "that through France, Italy, Germany, Poland, Bohemia, and other regions of the world, the Waldensians have made profession of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, and through various writings and constant preaching have pointed out and denounced the Pope as the true <term>Antichrist</term> <note>At the time, "Antichrist" was a common theological term used by Reformers to describe the Papacy, which they believed had usurped Christ’s authority.</note>, of whom the Apostle St. John had foretold, and that he must therefore be avoided. These same people, being surrendered to various cruel torments, have with great constancy given public testimony of their faith through glorious martyrdoms, and they still do the same today; it has never been possible to root them out, notwithstanding that the same has often been attempted even by the most powerful Kings and Princes, being incited by the Pope; and it is God," says he, "who has hindered all their labor and efforts."

->of the History of the Waldensians.<-
D
<meta>catchword: Martinus</meta>

<margin>Wesenbecius <note>Petrus Wesenbecius was a 16th-century scholar and jurist who wrote a famous oration defending the Waldensians.</note> in his Oration on the Waldensians.</margin> **Luther** confessed that he had hated the Waldensians as a lost people, until, having become acquainted with the godliness of their faith through their confessions and writings, he noticed that a great wrong had been done to these honorable people, whom the Pope had condemned as Heretics. He stated they were, nonetheless, worthy to receive the honor and praise of the Holy Martyrs. Furthermore, he found in these same Waldensians a thing that was very much to be wondered at—and never before heard of in the Papal Church—namely, that the aforementioned Waldensians, having abandoned all human teachings, meditated on the Law of the Lord day and night, occupying themselves therewith. He noted they were also experienced in the Holy Scripture and very well practiced in it. On the contrary, those who are called "our Masters" <note>This refers to the "Magistri Nostri," a title for the Scholastic theologians of the Roman Catholic universities whom the Reformers often mocked for knowing logic but not the Bible.</note> in the Papacy so greatly despised the Holy Scriptures that among them were found those who, in all their lives, had never once looked well at the Bible, even though they boasted of its glorious title.

Moreover, having read the confession of the Waldensians, he said that he thanked God for the great light that God had shared with them, rejoicing with them because now, all suspicion having been removed on both sides (by which one might have held the other suspect of Heresy), they had come so close to one another and were brought together in the same sheepfold under the only Shepherd and Bishop of our souls, who be praised into eternity.

<column-break/>

**Oecolampadius** <note>Johannes Oecolampadius was the primary Reformer of Basel and a close associate of Zwingli.</note> wrote in the year 1530 this following letter to the Waldensians in Provence.

<margin>This Letter is found in the book of **Georgius Morel** <note>A Waldensian pastor who traveled to Switzerland and Germany to align Waldensian theology with the Reformation.</note> on the Waldensians, regarding the conference he held with Oecolampadius and Bucer.</margin> We have understood with great pleasure through your faithful Shepherd **Georgius Morel**, what your faith and religion is, and in what manner you people speak of it. We therefore thank our most kind Father, who has called you in this age to such a great light, through the midst of the darkness which is spread through the whole world and the disorderly power of the Antichrist. And therefore we acknowledge that Christ is among you. Consequently, we also love you as brothers; and would to God that we might in deed make you feel that which we would be ready to do for you all, even if it were very difficult to do. For the rest, we would not want that which we write to be interpreted as if we, out of pride, attributed any authority to ourselves: but rather as reasons spoken to our Brothers out of love and Brotherly friendship. The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has shared with you an exceptional knowledge of his truth, more than with many other nations, and has blessed you with a Spiritual blessing. Insofar as you remain steadfast under his grace, he has yet much greater treasures with which he can enrich you and make you perfect, so that you may grow up to the measure of the inheritance of Christ.

The signing of this letter was thus:

**Oecolampadius** wishes to the well-beloved brothers in Christ, who are called the Waldensians, the grace of God the Father, through his son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit.

<margin>In the same place.</margin>
Praise be to the Lord God and Father, who has preserved Your Lordships <note>original: "V. L." (Uwe Liefden), a respectful 16th-century form of address</note> until now in such great knowledge of His truth, and has inspired you to investigate the same, having made you capable of it. Note here, then, the nature of true faith: namely, that as soon as it is known somewhere—even as a small spark of Divine clarity—it carefully preserves what has been given to it by God. St. Paul serves us as an example in this, who in all his epistles shows the care he had to advance the glory of God. And truly, if we pray with a good heart that the name of God be hallowed, and His Kingdom come, then we shall never pursue any matter with such great diligence as this: namely, that the truth be known and confirmed even where it is not, and that it may be advanced in places where it is already planted. Only one thing grieves us primarily: namely, that we are now occupied with other affairs, and therefore do not have the leisure to answer you at such length as we would have wished.

# The First Book, of the First Part

...the Papists <note>A term used historically by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics, often in a derogatory sense.</note> have acted against the Waldensians just as the Pagans once did against the early Christians, accusing them of killing their own little children in their secret meetings.

<margin>Notable History of the Reformed Churches of France. Vol. 1. book 1. p. 35.</margin>
The author of the *History of the Reformed Church in France* speaks of the Waldensians as follows: The Waldensians, he says, have from time out of mind, beyond human memory, set themselves against the abuses of the Roman Church. They have therefore been so persecuted—not only by the "sword of God’s word" <note>This refers to theological debate and scripture-based arguments.</note> but also with all kinds of violence and cruelty, along with a million slanders and false accusations—that they were forced to scatter to whatever places they could reach. They wandered through the wilderness like poor wild beasts. Nevertheless, the Lord preserved the survivors in such a way that, despite the madness of the whole world against them, they have maintained themselves until now in three regions located very far from one another: namely in Calabria <note>A region in Southern Italy.</note>, Bohemia, and Piedmont <note>A region in Northern Italy at the foot of the Alps.</note>, and the surrounding lands. From there, they scattered into the districts of Provence about two hundred and seventy years ago. As for their religion, they did not adhere to the Papal superstitions. For this reason, they were continually burdened and tormented by the Bishops and Inquisitors <note>original: "Kettermeeſters," literally "masters of heretics."</note>, who for that purpose abused the power of the secular judges. Thus, it is a visible miracle of God that they have been able to survive at all.

<margin>Jean Chassagnon</margin>
Jean Chassagnon <note>A 16th-century French historian and author of a history of the Waldensians.</note> describes what follows regarding them: it has been

<column-break/>

<margin>In his History of the Waldensians.</margin>
written of the Waldensians, he says, that they rejected all the institutions and traditions of the Roman Church as useless and superstitious; they did not hold the Clergy and Prelates in high regard. Because of this, being banished and driven from the land, they spread into many different places such as Dauphiné, Provence, Languedoc, Piedmont, and into Apulia, Calabria, Bohemia, England, and elsewhere. Some have written that a portion of the Waldensians departed for Lombardy, and there they multiplied so greatly that their teaching spread through all of Italy and even reached Sicily. Despite such a vast scattering, they steadily maintained unity and brotherhood with one another for a period of 400 years, living in great simplicity and in the fear of the Lord.

# Of the History of the Waldensians
<sig>D 3</sig>

...[Papi]sts <note>original: "Papisten." A term used by reformers to refer to those loyal to the Pope.</note> in France, they then began to oppress them for very unjust reasons, and labored to bring upon them the hatred of the peoples; and especially of the Kings, so that by this means they might be completely rooted out.

<margin>Vignier in his *Historical Library*, page 130.</margin>
Vignier <note>Nicolas Vignier (1530–1596) was a royal physician and historian to the French King, known for his vast chronological works.</note> mentions the Waldensians in his *Historical Library* and testifies that they suffered long and heavy persecutions, and yet nothing was able to prevent them from maintaining the doctrine they had received from the earlier Waldensians, handing it down from hand to hand to their children.

<margin>Holagaray in his *History of Foix*, pages 120 & 121.</margin>
Holagaray <note>Jacques Olhagaray was a 16th-century historian who documented the history of the southern French regions where the Waldensians and Albigensians were active.</note> sets the Waldensians and Albigensians <note>The Albigensians were a religious group in southern France also targeted by the medieval Inquisition; they are often grouped with Waldensians in Protestant histories.</note> against the Bishop of Rome <note>The Pope.</note>, specifically in all the points of doctrine that were publicly preached and commanded by his power. This refers to those doctrines found and invented by the same, which conflict with the Word of God. And he further testifies that among them were intelligent and very learned men to strengthen and support their faith against the monks.

<margin>Matthias Illyricus in the *Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth*, page 534.</margin>
Matthias Illyricus <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575) was a Lutheran reformer who compiled the "Catalogus testium veritatis" to prove that there were always people who disagreed with the Roman Catholic Church before Luther.</note> in the Register that he collected of the witnesses of the truth, writes that he noticed from the writings of Waldo <note>Peter Waldo, the 12th-century founder of the Waldensians.</note> which he has in his possession, written on a certain old parchment, that Waldo was a learned man, and that he did not have the Biblical Books translated into the common tongue by others, but that he worked on it himself.

It is certain that the enemies of Waldo and of the Waldensians will not

value these aforementioned testimonies, because they will place both these witnesses and those they testify about on the same level, considering them both to be heretics. It was about forty years ago that the Lord of Vignaux, a Pastor in the churches of the Waldensians in Piedmont <note>A region in northwest Italy where the Waldensians lived for centuries in mountain valleys.</note>, described what follows here in his notes or memoirs. He set these down concerning the origin, antiquity, teaching, religion, manners, ordinances, persecutions, confession, and progress of the people called the Waldensians.

"I who write this," he says, "can testify that I was sent among these people to preach the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, which I have now done for forty years. I did not have to labor to turn them away from the ceremonies and customs of the Roman Church, nor to put out of their hearts and minds the Pope, the Mass, Purgatory, and similar things. In these matters, they had long before me become Doctors or masters—despite the fact that the greatest multitude [among them] knew neither A nor B <note>A Dutch idiom meaning they were completely illiterate.</note>."

### Chapter Nine

#### Names of the pastors of the Waldensians who have taught them over the past four hundred and fifty years, and who have come to our knowledge.

<margin>1160.</margin>
Valdo <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140 – c. 1205), the merchant from Lyon who founded the "Poor Men of Lyon" or Waldensians.</note> began to teach the people—who after him were named Waldensians—in the year of our Lord eleven hundred and sixty.

<margin>In the 1st table of the Differences of Religion, page 150 <note>Refers to a work by Philips of Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde (1540–1598), a prominent Dutch statesman and theologian.</note>.</margin>
The Lord of Saint-Aldegonde observes that at the same time Waldo had established himself in Lyons, God also raised up others in Provence and Languedoc, among whom the most prominent were a certain Arnaud, an Espernon, and a Joseph; after whom they were named Arnaudists, Josephists, and Esperonists. Although, because their teaching was first accepted within Albi in the district of Albigeois, they were commonly called Albigensians. Thus, the Waldensians on one side and the Albigensians on the other were like the two Olive Trees or the two lights of which St. John speaks <note>A reference to Revelation 11:4, often interpreted by reformers as representing the true witnesses of the Gospel throughout history.</note>, from which the oil and the light were spread to all the ends of the Earth.

In the same vein, he says, followed Peter Bruys <note>Pierre de Bruys (fl. 1117–1131), a French popular reformer and contemporary of Henry of Lausanne.</note>, for whom some called them Petro-Bruysians.

He was followed in the teaching, he says, by one named Henry; one of whom had been a Priest and the other a Monk. They taught in the Dioceses of Arles, Embrun <note>original: "Arbrun"</note>, Die, and Gap, from which they were driven and then accepted into Toulouse.

<margin>Ibid. p. 151.</margin>
A certain Bartholomew, who was a native of Carcassonne,

<column-break/>

established (he says) the churches in Bulgaria, Carinthia <note>original: "Kernte"</note>, Dalmatia, and Hungary, and appointed the ministers, just as Matthew Paris <note>Matthew Paris (c. 1200–1259), an English Benedictine monk and chronicler.</note> recounts, calling him "Pope and Bishop." To this he brings the letter which the Bishop of Porto <note>original: "Portvenſchen Biſſchop"</note>, being the Pope's Legate in those quarters, wrote to the Archbishop of Rouen and to his Suffragans, seeking help and assistance against them, until they were finally forced to retreat into the deserts, following the prophecy of the Revelation, saying: That the woman with child who bore the man-child <note>Revelation 12:1-6.</note>, and is the true Church of God, would be so persecuted that a flood of water would be cast out of the throat like a river after her to swallow her up, and that she would be forced to flee to the Wilderness, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, or the time of forty-two months, or of twelve hundred and sixty days.

Reinerius <note>Reinerius Saccho (c. 1200–1259), an inquisitor and former member of the Waldensians who wrote a famous treatise against them.</note> recounts two of the most prominent Bishops of the Waldensians: namely, a certain Balazinanza of Verona, and a Johannes de Lugio, who taught among them after those named above, around the year 1250.

# The First Book, of the First Part
<meta>catchword: Stepha-</meta>

Lollardus <note>likely Walter Lollard (d. 1322), a teacher often associated with the spread of proto-Protestant ideas</note> was likewise held in great esteem among them, both because of a certain exposition he made of the Revelation of John, and also because he had brought and preached the knowledge of their teaching in England. After whom the Waldensians there were named Lollards.

The Waldensians of the Valleys of Angrogna, of Dauphiné, Provence, and Calabria, have had the following as <term>Barbes</term> <note>The term "Barbe" (meaning "uncle" in the local dialect) was used by the Waldensians for their pastors to distinguish them from Catholic priests (referred to as "fathers").</note>, of whom they have preserved the memory from over three hundred years ago: namely:

### From Provence.

Angelus of La Coste.
Daniel of Valence and John of Molines. These two were sent to Bohemia to serve the Churches of the Waldensians gathered in that Kingdom; but they betrayed the Churches and did them much harm, for they revealed to the enemies of the Waldensians everything they had learned of their small flocks or meetings, from which a great persecution arose. This caused the Churches of Bohemia to write to the Waldensian Church in the Alpine mountains that for such callings henceforth, they should only promote such persons whose faith, loyalty, honesty, and—through the passage of time—good knowledge and proof had been given.

The last Barbes they had were George Maurel and Peter Mascon, who in the year 1530 were sent to Germany to discuss religion with Oecolampadius <note>Johannes Oecolampadius (1482–1531), a prominent reformer in Basel</note>, Bucer <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a leader of the Reformation in Strasbourg</note>, and others. Peter Mascon was taken prisoner at Dijon.

## of the History of the Waldensians.

<sig>E 3</sig>

<margin>1560.</margin>Stephen Negrin and Louis Paschalis were sent to Calabria in the year 1560 to the churches of the Waldensians of Montalto, San Sisto, and others located nearby. Stephen Negrin was taken prisoner and led to Cosenza, where he died of hunger in prison.

Louis Paschalis was brought to Rome, where he was condemned to be burned alive. This took place in the presence of Pope Pius IV and his Cardinals, whom he summoned to appear before the throne of the Lamb <note>A reference to the Judgment Seat of Christ, common in martyr literature</note> to give an account of their cruelties.

<margin>This is known from the collection of legal proceedings found in the cabinet of the late Lord of Avençon, Archbishop of Embrun, obtained when Embrun was captured. These cases were against the Waldensians of Freissinières and L'Argentière.</margin>There were many others as well, as can be seen from the trials conducted against the Waldensians of Dauphiné, which have fallen into our hands. In these records, many other <term>Barbes</term> <note>The Waldensian term for their pastors, literally meaning "uncles."</note> or ministers are mentioned, who were often thrown into prison and delivered to death by the monks of the Inquisition, who had them spied upon even on the peaks of the Alpine mountains as they traveled from one to another. Yet this small number is sufficient to show that, despite their enemies' utmost diligence to completely root them out, the eternal God has nevertheless not failed to provide laborers for His harvest when it was necessary, to preserve even until now thousands of people. Especially in Dauphiné and Provence, there are those who have every reason to boast of being descended from the ancient Waldensians, and of having inherited more of their zeal and godliness than of their earthly goods, which the persecutors have wrested from them.

This is as the Pope still does today, who has newly attached the ancestral estates of the Waldensians—who held property in the <term>Comtat Venaissin</term> <note>An area in southeastern France that was then an independent territory ruled directly by the Pope.</note>—to the so-called Apostolic Chamber <note>The administrative treasury of the Papacy.</note>. He would also gladly take their lives under the pretext of heresy, if he could; so far is he from considering at any time restoring those same goods to them, as he has been requested in vain. His officers reward them more with empty words and false countenances than with actual deeds, truth, or sincere intent.

But since the reader, not knowing who these <term>Barbes</term> or pastors were, might hold them in less regard, we shall include in the following chapter what we find in their writings. These shall serve as proof of their faith, calling, and the exercise of their office, and as a demonstration of their zeal and godliness.

### The Tenth Chapter,

->Concerning who the <term>Barbes</term> <note>Literally "uncles," the respectful Waldensian term for their pastors.</note> or pastors of the *Waldensians* were, what their calling was, and with what zeal and faithfulness they performed their offices.<-

<margin>Raynerius, *On the Form of Heretics*, fol. 8.</margin>
The Monk Raynerius <note>Raynerius Sachoni (c. 1200–1259), an inquisitor and former member of the Cathars who wrote extensively—and often inaccurately—about dissenting groups.</note> has said many things regarding the calling of the Waldensian Pastors that never occurred: such as that which he attributed to them, namely that they had a supreme Bishop and two others following him, whom he named the Eldest Son and the Youngest Son. Additionally, a Deacon: [claiming] that he laid hands on the others with the highest authority and sent them wherever he saw fit, like a second Pope. Against such deceptive allegations, here follows what is found in their own writings concerning the calling of their Pastors.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Taken from the book of George Maurel and Peter Masson, page 8. <note>These were Waldensian leaders who sought contact with the Protestant Reformers in the 1530s.</note></margin>
All those (they said) who are to be accepted as Pastors among us, while they are still with their parents, ask us to be received into the service [of the ministry], and that we would pray to God for them, that they might be made fit for such a heavy office; which the same petitioners do solely to show their humility.

<column-break/>

All those who are to be received from among us, while they are still with their people, pray—if it pleases our people—that they be received into the Ministry, and that it would please them to pray to God afterward, so that they may be made worthy of so great an office. But the aforementioned petitioners do not do these things for any other end, except to demonstrate humility. <note>original Occitan: "Tuit aquilli li qual devon esser receopu, d'entre de nos, quand illi font encara cum lor gent..."</note>

<column-break/>

They are given lessons, and are made to learn by heart all the chapters of St. Matthew and of St. John, and all the Epistles called Canonical, as well as a good portion of the writings of Solomon, of David, and of the Prophets.

<column-break/>

And they are taught lessons, and are made to learn by heart all the chapters of Saint Matthew and of Saint John, and all the epistles which are called Canonical, a good part of Solomon, of David, and of the Prophets. <note>original Occitan: "Et lor enseñan leçons, & lor facen empenre de cor tuit li capitol de Sanct Matheo..."</note>

<column-break/>

Thereafter, if they have good testimonies, they are accepted with the laying on of hands into the office of preaching.

<column-break/>

And then, if they have good testimony, they are received with the imposition of hands into the office of preaching. <note>original Occitan: "Et pois si illi auren bon testimoni son receopu cum l'imposition de las mans en l'offici di lapredication."</note>

# Of the History of the Waldensians.
<meta>catchword: Christ,</meta>

<columns>2</columns>

Those who were most recently accepted <note>The junior pastors or apprentices.</note> may not do anything without the permission or consent of those who were accepted before them; and likewise, the first <note>The senior pastors.</note> must not undertake anything without the consent of their companions, so that all things proceed with order.

We Pastors gather all together once a year to handle our common affairs together in a general assembly.

The food and that which is necessary for our clothing is shared and provided in full sufficiency out of goodwill and as if in alms, by the people whom we serve and teach.

The money given to us by the people is brought to the aforementioned general assembly and delivered there in the presence of everyone; it is received by the Elders <note>original: "Outsten."</note>, and a portion of it is handed over to those who must travel, according to what is found necessary for their expenses, and a portion of the same money is given to the poor.

If any of our Pastors falls into the sin of unchastity <note>original: "oncupsheyt."</note>, he is cast out from our company, and the office of preaching is forbidden to him.

Among other powers that God has given to His servants is the right to choose the Leaders of the people and the Elders <note>original: "Ouderlinghen."</note> for their offices, according to the variety of their work—

<column-break/>

The junior <note>original Occitan: "Lo sequent."</note> must not do anything without the permission of the senior <note>original: "devant pausa."</note>. And similarly, the seniors must not do anything without the permission of their companions, to the end that all things be done among us with order.

We Pastors assemble ourselves all together once a year to treat our affairs together in a general Council.

Food and the things with which we are covered are administered to us and given freely, and in the place of alms, very abundantly by the good people whom we teach.

The money which is given to us by the people is brought by us to the predicted general Council, and delivered in common before us all; it is collected by our elders <note>original: "maior."</note>, and part of it is distributed to those who have to travel, as it is seen to be necessary for them, and part of the said money is given to the poor.

When any of our predicted pastors falls into the sin of dishonesty <note>original: "deshonesta," here meaning unchastity or sexual immorality.</note>, he is cast out of our company and prohibited from the office of Preaching.

Among the other powers God gives to His competent servants is that they choose the governors of the people, and priests <note>original: "preires," used here in the sense of elders or ministers.</note> for their offices, according to the diversity of the work in the unity of Christ,

# The First Book, of the First Part

...things, nor disputes, nor deceit, nor cunning, nor usury, nor ill will, nor discord: And do not tolerate or keep among you any people of a bad life, nor those who give offense or a bad example among you, but let love and faithfulness rule among you and every good progress: the one dealing with the other just as each would want to happen to himself: For otherwise it is not possible that anyone can be saved, or obtain the grace of the Lord or of men in this world, or the glory in the other; and it is necessary that the leaders, above all, keep a hand to this, likewise those who rule and are superiors: for if the head is sick, then all the limbs are ill. Therefore, if you desire and hope to possess eternal life, to be in good esteem, to have a good name, faith, and prosperity in this world both in temporal and spiritual goods, then cleanse yourselves of all disorder, so that God may always be with you, who never forsakes those who hope in Him. But know this for certain, that God does not hear, nor dwell with sinners, nor also in the soul that gives itself to ill will, nor also with people who are subject to sin.

Therefore, let everyone make the ways of his heart straight, and shun the peril, if he does not wish to perish in the same.

Nothing else at this time, except that you wish to put these things into practice: and may the God of peace be with you all, and accompany us in our true, devout, and humble prayers, saving...

<column-break/>

...people <note>original: "ple", likely the end of "pueple"</note> among you; but charity and fidelity <note>original: "carita & fidelita"</note> reign among you and every good example, treating one another even as each would want to be done to himself: For otherwise it is not possible for anyone to be saved, nor to have the grace of God, nor of men in this way, nor the glory in the other. And all this belongs principally to the maintainers and favorers, the rulers and governors. For when the heads are infirm, all the members together suffer. Therefore, if you hope and desire to possess eternal life <note>original: "vita æterna"</note>, and a good voice, and good fame, and good credit, and to prosper in this world in spiritual and temporal goods: purge yourselves of all disordered life among you, so that God may be always with you, who never abandons those hoping in Him. But know this for certain, that God does not hear, nor inhabit with the sinners, nor in the malevolent soul, nor with the man subject to sins. Therefore, let each one place his heart upon his way, and flee the peril if he does not want to perish in them.

Nothing else for the present, except that you put these things into effect, and may the God of peace <note>original: "Dio de paz"</note> be with all of you, and accompany us in true, devout, and humble orations, saluting all the faithful and lovers of Christ. Amen.

Therefore, let each one place his heart upon his path, and flee the perils if he does not wish to perish in them.

Nothing else for the present, except that you put these things into effect, and the God of peace be with you all, and accompany us in true, devout, and humble prayers, greeting all the faithful and beloved of Christ. Amen.

### The 4th Article.

These aforementioned books teach this: that there is namely one God, who is Almighty, All-wise, and alone is good; Who has made everything according to His goodness. For He made Adam in His image and likeness; but that through the envy <note>original: "nijt"; referring to the biblical concept that death entered the world through the devil's envy (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24).</note> of the devil, and through the disobedience of Adam, sin came into the world; and that we are sinners in Adam and through Adam.

### The 5th Article.

That Christ was promised to the Fathers, who received the Law; so that they, by recognizing their sins, their injustice, and their unfitness <note>original: "onbequaemheyt"</note> through the Law, would long for the coming of Christ, to the end that He might satisfy for sin, and fulfill the Law Himself.

### The 6th Article.

That Christ was born at the time ordained by His Father, namely when all wickedness overflowed; and that not because of good works, for they were all sinners. But so that He might show us grace and mercy, being truthful.

### 4.

The above-said books teach this: That there is one God, all-powerful, all-wise, and all-good, who by His goodness has made all things. For He formed Adam in His image and likeness. But that by the envy of the Devil, and by the disobedience of the said Adam, sin entered into the world, and that we are sinners in Adam, and by Adam.

### 5.

### 6.

That Christ was born at the time given by God His Father, that is to say, at the hour when all iniquity abounded, and not for good works alone. For all were sinners, but so that He might show us grace and mercy as one who is truthful.

### The 11th Art.

We have a horror of all human inventions / as coming from the Antichrist / <note>As noted on the previous page, the Waldensians used the term "Antichrist" to describe the ecclesiastical systems they believed had corrupted the Gospel.</note> which bring about disturbance / and hinder the freedom of the Spirit.

### The 12th Art.

We believe that the Sacraments are signs of certain holy things / or visible representations of invisible grace: holding it as good that the believers shall sometimes use these visible signs or representations as opportunity allows: and yet we believe and hold / that these same believers can be saved / even if they do not receive these signs / when they / namely / have no place or opportunity / where they might receive or use them. <note>This highlights a "spiritual" understanding of the sacraments; while they are valued, the physical act is not considered strictly necessary for salvation if a believer is prevented from participating by circumstance.</note>

other manners, & similar things, & principally the masses.

### The thirteenth Chapter.

#### Another confession of the Faith of the Waldensians.

->The first Article.<-

<margin>Taken from the book of Carolus du Moulin, <note>original: "Carolus du Moulin" refers to Charles Du Moulin (1500–1566), a famous French jurist who wrote about the history and rights of the Waldensians.</note> on the Monarchy of the French. page 65.</margin>We believe that there is but one God alone / who is a Spirit / Creator of all things / and Father of all / who is above all / through all and in all / whom one must worship in Spirit and truth / upon whom alone we rely / and from whom alone we boast to have our life / nourishment / clothing / health / sickness / prosperity and adversity / whom we love / as being the author and origin of all good / and whom we fear as the one who knows the hearts.

->The second Article.<-

<margin>John 4.</margin>We believe that Jesus Christ is the son of God / the image of the Father / that in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead / through whom we know the Father / who is our intercessor and mediator / and that there is no other name under Heaven given to Men / in which we must be saved / in whose name alone we call upon the Father / and use no other prayers / than those / which are contained in the Holy Scripture or which in substance agree with them.

->The third Article.<-

We believe that the Holy Spirit is our comforter / proceeding from the Father and the Son / by whose inspiration we perform our prayers / being renewed by him / who works all good works in us / and through him we have the knowledge of all truth.

->The fourth Article.<-

We Believe that there is one Holy Church / which is the assembly of all the elect and faithful who have been from the beginning of the world / and shall be until the end: of which our Lord Jesus Christ is the Head: which is governed by his word / and led by the Holy Spirit / in which all good Christians must walk: For she prays without ceasing for all / and her word is acceptable to God / outside of which no one can be saved.

->The fifth Article.<-

We hold that the Ministers of the Church / such as the Bishops and Pastors / must be blameless / as much in life as in teaching: otherwise / that they must then be deposed from their office / and others installed in their places: and that no one may presume to take this honor upon themselves / other than he who is called by God like <term>Aaron</term> <note>Aaron, the brother of Moses, was the biblical model for a divinely appointed priest. This emphasizes their rejection of self-appointed or purely political church appointments.</note>, feeding the flock of God not for dishonest gain: also not as having power or lordship over the <term>clergie</term> <note>original: "clergie," referring here to the congregation or the lower-ranking church members.</note>: but as being from the heart the example of the Flock / in speech / in conduct / in love / in faith and in purity.

# The 1st Book, of the 1st part
<page-num>50</page-num>
<header>The 1st Book, of the 1st part</header>

->The sixth Article.<-

We acknowledge that the Kings, Princes, and Regents <note>The term "Regents" refers to any ruling official or governor in authority.</note> are ordained and confirmed as Ministers of God, whom one must obey / for they bear the sword for the protection of the innocent / and for the punishment of evildoers: for which cause we are bound to show them honor / and to pay taxes. From which no one may exempt themselves / as that is forbidden by the Example of our Lord Jesus Christ / who even willed to pay tax / without wishing to take on earthly authority.

->The seventh Article.<-

We believe that in the Sacrament of Baptism, the water is the outward and visible sign / which represents to us that which / through the invisible power of God working in us / happens within us: namely the renewal of the Spirit / and the mortification <note>original: "doodinghe"; the spiritual practice of putting to death the sinful nature.</note> of our members in Christ Jesus / through which we likewise are received into the Holy assembly of the people of God / testifying and declaring before the same / our faith and change of life.

->The eighth Article.<-

We believe that the Holy Sacrament of the Table or the Lord’s Supper of the Lord Jesus Christ, is a Holy remembrance and thanksgiving / for the benefits that we have received through his suffering and death / which one must do or keep together in faith and love / and examine oneself / and thus Eat of this bread / and partake of his blood / just as is written in the Holy Scripture.

->The ninth Article.<-

We believe that Marriage is good and honorable / Holy and instituted by God / which must not be forbidden to anyone / so long as there is no hindrance / by the word of God.

->The tenth Article.<-

We acknowledge that those who fear God / seek those things that please God / and labor to bring forth good works / which God has prepared for them to walk in / such as his love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, temperance, <note>These "good works" align with the biblical "Fruits of the Spirit" found in Galatians 5.</note> and other good works / contained in the Holy Scripture.

->The eleventh Article.<-

On the contrary, we confess that one must guard oneself against false teachers / whose aim is to draw the people away / from the true worship that belongs to God the Lord alone / and to cause them to rely on the creatures <note>This refers to created things, including icons, saints, or worldly objects, rather than the Creator.</note> and to trust therein / as well as to abandon the good works that are set forth in the Holy Scripture / and to perform others which are devised by men.

->The twelfth Article.<-

We hold for the measure of our faith / the Old and New Testament / and we agree with the common confession of the Faith / with the Articles which are contained in the Apostles' Creed <note>original: "Symbolum der Apostelen"</note> / namely these:

### The Sixth Article.

We acknowledge that Kings, Princes, and Regents are ordained and established as Servants of God, whom one must obey; for they bear the sword for the protection of the innocent <note>original: "onnooselen"; in this context, it refers to the law-abiding or harmless citizens</note> and for the punishment of evildoers. For this reason, we are bound to show them honor and to pay taxes <note>original: "schattingen"</note>. From which no one may exempt himself, as this is forbidden by the Example of our Lord Jesus Christ, who himself chose to pay taxes without wishing to take up earthly authority.

### The Seventh Article.

We believe that in the <term>Sacrament of Baptism</term> <note>A sacred rite signifying spiritual cleansing and initiation into the church</note>, the water is the outward and visible sign which demonstrates to us that which—through the invisible power of God working in us—happens within us: namely, the renewal of the Spirit and the mortification of our members in Christ Jesus, through which we likewise are accepted into the Holy assembly of the people of God, testifying and declaring before the same our faith and change of life.

### The Eighth Article.

We believe that the Holy Sacrament of the Table, or the Supper of the Lord Jesus Christ, is a Holy remembrance and thanksgiving for the benefits we have received through his suffering and death; which one must do or hold together in faith and love, and examine oneself, and thus Eat of this bread and share in his blood, just as is written in the Holy Scripture.

### The Ninth Article.

We believe that Marriage is good and honorable, Holy and instituted by God, which must not be forbidden to anyone, provided there is no hindrance according to the word of God.

### The Tenth Article.

We acknowledge that those who fear God seek those things that please God, and labor to bring forth good works which God has prepared for us to walk in—such as his love, joy, peace, patience <note>original: "lijdt saemheyt"</note>, benevolence, goodness, temperance, and other good works contained in the Holy Scripture.

### The Eleventh Article.

On the other hand, we confess that one must guard oneself against false teachers, whose aim is to draw the people away from the true worship that belongs to God the Lord alone, and to cause them to rely on and trust in creatures <note>This likely refers to the intercession of saints or the use of icons</note>, as well as to abandon the good works presented in the Holy Scripture in order to perform others devised by men.

### The Twelfth Article.

We hold as the measure of our faith the Old and New Testament, and we agree with the common confession of Faith, with the Articles contained in the <term>Apostles' Creed</term> <note>Latin: "Symbolum Apostolorum"; the foundational statement of Christian belief</note>, namely these:

<note>The following section returns to a single-column layout across the full width of the page.</note>

The faith of the <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval Christian movement that preceded the Reformation, emphasizing poverty and the authority of the Bible.</note> is sufficiently known from the contents of the previously related holy and pure teachings. Notwithstanding this, they have nevertheless been persecuted for that same faith for more than four hundred and fifty years, and would also still be persecuted for it today, if they could be caught in those places where human institutions are prized above God's Word. For even if it is the case that Satan is put to shame and his kingdom destroyed by the clarity of the Gospel, he still does not cease to keep those people—whose minds he has blinded—under the yoke of <term>idolatry</term> <note>In this context, the author refers to religious practices not strictly mandated by the Bible, which the Waldensians and later Protestants viewed as false worship.</note>. Furthermore, he continues to restrain and compel them by force under the tyranny of his laws, rewarding the ignorance and error—which people love by nature—with the darkness in which they take their pleasure and delight. But just as the eternal God has not wanted to permit the faith of His pious servants and Martyrs to be buried in the earth, so He wants their steadfastness to be revealed for our edification and example. Therefore, having now shown in this first book that the Waldensians believed for salvation that which they were required to believe, we will in the following book show and reveal what has come to our knowledge regarding their suffering for righteousness.

The Waldensians have had no worse nor crueler enemies than the Popes: Because (says the Monk Reinerius, among all those who have risen against the Roman Church) the Waldensians have been the most harmful and destructive, because they have opposed it for a very long time. Secondly, because this sect (he says) is universal, for there is hardly any land where it has not set foot. Thirdly, because, while all others provoke horror through their blasphemies: the Waldensians, on the contrary, display a great appearance of godliness, because they live righteously before men, and believe and feel rightly concerning God in all things, and maintain all the articles of the Christian faith; yet they slander the Roman Church and hate it, and in this, he says, they are easily believed and followed by the people.

<column-break/>

And elsewhere, the same author says that the first lesson which the Waldensians give to those whom they draw to their following is the study [of Scripture]; they teach them from the words of the Gospel and the Apostles how the followers of Christ must be, saying that those alone are the successors of the Apostles who follow their manner of life. From this, he says, they conclude that the Pope, the Bishops, and the Clergy, who seek and possess the riches of this world, do not follow the life of the Apostles, and therefore, since they are not the rightful leaders of the Church, it was by no means the intention of our Savior Jesus Christ to entrust his pure and well-beloved Bride to such men, who defile her more by evil examples and wicked works than they seek to preserve her in her purity, just as she was received in the beginning, namely pure and spotless.

# The Second Book, of the First Part

...against the excess and pomp, against greed, against pride, and against the errors that had been introduced by the Popes, such that they were persecuted by them even unto death.

The means the Popes used to root them out were first their thunderbolts and excommunications, their Rules or Canons, Constitutions, and Decrees; and moreover, they directed toward them everything that might make them hated by the Kings, Princes, and peoples of the earth, delivering them to Satan as much as they were able, forbidding their subjects from holding any kind of fellowship or company with them, judging them useless and unworthy of any offices, honors, provostships, inheritance, and the making of Wills, even to be buried in the common Churchyards, judging their goods confiscated or forfeited, and their children disinherited; and they did not stop there, but whenever they could capture them, they then further condemned them to be delivered over to the secular arm <note>The "secular arm" refers to civil authorities who carried out physical punishments, such as execution, which the Church itself officially avoided performing.</note>, ordering their houses to be razed and torn down, and assigning their fixed and movable property as forfeited to the Treasury <note>original: "Fiscael"</note> or to others who should first seize them. And of all such sentences of theirs, we still presently have the originals in hand, just as the Popes themselves gave them to their Instruments or Officers whom they used for the execution of the same, just as we likewise have the original minutes of the mandates given concerning the

<margin>

Giving to the informers a full third part or some other portion of that which was confiscated, and further sentencing all who concealed them or showed them favor to the same punishments.

But even this means was considered too slight against a matter pressing so hard upon them, as was the conduct and proposal of the Waldensians, who, regardless of all such thunderbolts <note>The Dutch *Blixems* refers to "papal thunderbolts," or the formal decrees of excommunication intended to strike fear into the public.</note>, nevertheless continued in their way; and therefore they did not stop preaching that the Pope was the Antichrist, the Mass an abomination, the Host <note>The consecrated bread used in the Mass.</note> of the same an idol, and Purgatory a fable or idle fiction. Which points, once accepted, were sufficient to cause the Pope’s power to topple over completely, as well as to dry up all the rivers and streams of profit and the riches of his so-called Clergy.

Therefore then, Pope Innocent the Third, who succeeded in the place of Pope Celestine the Third of that name around the Year 1198, took another means in hand than that which the Bishops had previously used and followed; for he authorized certain Monks for this purpose, into whose hands he placed the full power of the Inquisition, who drew up their legal processes, and also handed them over to the Secular <note>original: "Politijcken"</note> Judges, which was done only with full and absolute power, and followed a shortened path, yet with much greater cruelty; while

<column-break/>

the people were thus dragged by thousands before the Magistrates, who handed the same over to the Executioners. And through this it happened that within a few years the whole of Christendom was unsettled and moved by such a piteous and lamentable spectacle, seeing the throwing into fires and the hanging on gallows of all those who placed their trust for salvation in Jesus Christ alone, and rejected all idle hope and comfort which men had devised for their own benefit and profit’s sake. Which was the sole and total fruit of the aforementioned Inquisition, of which more shall be spoken in the following chapter.

#### Of the Inquisition: by whom this was first put into operation, and with what cunning the Waldensians were tormented thereby.

# The Second Book, of the First Part

...certain Bishops and Monks sent out so that they might go and preach in the places suspected of holding the Waldensian faith. But these preachers, as the compiler of the <margin>The Treasury of Histories in the Year 1206.</margin> *Treasury of Histories* relates, converted only a few people. For among the multitude, he says, there were few who returned to the "right faith" <note>By "right faith," the author refers to the Roman Catholic Church, likely written from a perspective critical of the Church's efforts.</note>.

In the Land of Narbonne <note>A region in Southern France, then a stronghold of the Waldensian and Albigensian movements.</note>, two Monks were employed for this purpose: namely, one Pierre de Chasteauneuf with one Dominic <note>Saint Dominic (1170–1221), the founder of the Dominican Order.</note>, who was born in Caleruega <note>original: "Cahorre"</note> in Spain, to whom an Abbot of Cîteaux was also joined; and besides these, there were many other priests and Monks, and among others a Bishop of Castres <note>original: "Cestre"</note>, who all likewise traveled there.

The aforementioned Monk Pierre de Chasteauneuf was struck dead <note>His assassination in 1208 was the immediate catalyst for the Albigensian Crusade.</note> in this business, and for that reason was later canonized—that is, recorded by the Pope among the number of the saints.

But Dominic did not stop from harassing and persecuting the Waldensians, both in deed and with words. This Monk, seeing himself grow in regard and authority thereby, founded a certain Order of mendicant <note>term: "mendicant" (Monks who took a vow of poverty and lived by begging or charity rather than from land ownership)</note> Monks, who were later named the Dominicans after him; and this Monk was also later canonized, and his Monastic Order confirmed by Pope Honorius. The Pope declared that he had been exhorted to do this in a dream, for it seemed to him that he saw the Roman Church falling down, and that Dominic supported and held it up with his shoulders. Therefore, the Pope commanded that in recompense for this, this Order should have the first place among the mendicant Monastic Orders.

It is said of this Monk that while his mother was still carrying him in her body, she dreamed that she bore a dog which threw out flames of fire from its throat. His followers interpreted this to his advantage, saying that it indicated and signified that he would be that hound who would spew out the fire that would consume the heretics. But on the contrary, those whom he daily delivered to death might well say with truth that he was that dog who had set the whole of Christendom on fire, and that the flames coming from his throat served to indicate, depict, and signify those hellish and blazing Sentences which he pronounced against the Christians.

Meanwhile, this Monk knew how to arrange and promote his affairs and those of his Monks so well that even during his lifetime, before his death, he had caused a great multitude of fine houses to be built, as much in the lands of Languedoc, Provence, Dauphiné, and Spain as elsewhere. For these, he likewise obtained great income and Rents, both from the generosity of those who were well-affected toward this Order of his, and especially from the confiscated goods of the Waldensians. For these, Count Simon de Montfort <note>The military leader of the crusade against the heretics in Southern France.</note> similarly gave him great liberties and alms, thus "cutting wide straps from another’s leather" <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to be generous at someone else’s expense—in this case, using property seized from the Waldensians.</note>.

This Monk conducted himself in the Inquisition as the head of the same...

### Of the History of the Waldensians.

H 2

...ans <note>The text continues from the previous page: "Dominicanen" (Dominicans).</note>, working so much according to the sense and will of the Popes, that from that time until now the Monks of his Order are employed in the Inquisition.

The power granted and given to these Monks, the Inquisitors, was unlimited and absolute; for they could assemble the people, by the ringing of bells, whenever it pleased them or seemed good to them; they could proceed against the Bishops themselves, and if they were found at fault in the matter, they could initiate proceedings against them and place them in prison; they could also open the prisons or release prisoners without anyone's objection. All kinds of accusations were valid; a sorcerer or a whore were, in matters of alleged heresy, considered undeniable witnesses. One only had to accuse, and this could be done either by the living voice or by throwing slips of paper at the feet of the Inquisitor; for the trials were conducted without re-examination <note>original: "recolement" — a legal term for the formal re-reading of a witness's testimony to them to confirm its accuracy</note>, without confrontations <note>original: "voorhooftbrenginghen" — literally "bringing before the forehead," meaning a face-to-face confrontation between accuser and accused</note>, even without an opposing party, without witnesses, and without any other Law except the pleasure and the will of the Inquisitor or "Heresy-master." To be wealthy was akin to a crime of heresy and stood close to it, for he who had something to lose was on the path to being ruined and lost, either as a heretic or at least as a <term>favourer</term> <note>term: "favourer" (from the original "Fauteur") — a legal category for someone who supported, hid, or failed to report a heretic</note> of heretics; a single bad

<column-break/>

suspicion or second thought was enough to silence the mouths of Fathers, Mothers, and blood relatives, and to prevent all prayers and mediation for the accused. Indeed, if anyone merely requested to provide him with only a glass of water, or to arrange for a little straw for him to lie upon within some stinking hole, that person was immediately treated as a favourer of heretics—no more and no less than if he had been a criminal offender who deserved death—and brought to the same or worse extreme distress. Consequently, no Advocate dared to undertake the defense of his closest blood relative or the most special friend he might have had. No Notary would have dared to receive any instrument or written document serving to the benefit of the accused. Nay, what is more, once someone was entangled and caught in the nets of the Inquisitors, he was never again secure or free from them; it was always to be begun and done again anew; for if he were once let out and released, that occurred only provisionally and until further or other notice. Indeed, even death did not end the punishment, as they have also left us their sentences against the buried dead bod- <note>The text breaks off here; the full word is "lichamen" (bodies), referring to the practice of exhuming and burning the remains of posthumously convicted heretics.</note>

The people in general, even the most powerful and wealthy, were essentially forced to worship these Monks, the Inquisitors, and to give great gifts and presents for the building of their houses and the founding of their Monasteries, fearing that they would otherwise be accused or suspected of heresy, or at least that they would not be considered or held zealous enough in the Faith by these Holy Fathers. Indeed, they were not even allowed to lift their eyes to the Host <note>the consecrated bread used in the Mass</note> when it was shown by the Priest <note>original: "Pape" — a term often used pejoratively by Protestants for a Catholic priest</note>, until it was otherwise found good, permitted, and ordered by the Fathers, the Inquisitors or Heresy-masters.

were? It was answered by the same Prelates: That such people could not be excused, for (they added) who is so much a stranger that they could be unaware that the Waldensians have been punished and condemned for a very long time? And who does not know that they have been persecuted for many years, with such great cost, labor, and much sweat by the Catholics? And yet, comparing this statement of the Prelates with what Georgius Morel wrote in the year 1540, it must be no small miracle of God that, notwithstanding all the bloody persecutions from the time of Waldo <note>Peter Waldo, the 12th-century merchant credited with starting the Waldensian movement</note> in the year 1160 until the aforementioned year 1530, even then—according to the declaration of Georgius Morel—more than eight hundred thousand people remained who made confession of the Waldensian faith.

<margin>Georgius Morel in his memoirs <note>original: "memoria le aſteet"</note> page 54. 800,000.</margin> As for the deceptive dealings practiced by the aforementioned Heresy-masters <note>Inquisitors</note> in the execution of their offices, we would have no knowledge of them, except for what some believers who escaped from the Spanish Inquisition might have been able to inform us: but it did not please God that these arch-deceits remained hidden, and that we would not obtain copies of them that were written by their own hands. See here then the Inquisitors' crafty deceits, which served them as rules and instructions in conducting the trials of the Waldensians.

<column-break/>

1. It is not expedient or advisable to dispute concerning the faith in the presence of laypeople <note>Ordinary people who were not members of the clergy</note>.

2. No one must be held as converted if he will not accuse all those whom he knows to be such as he himself is.

3. He who does not accuse others who are as he is must be cut off from the church as a rotten limb, so that the healthy members are not corrupted by him.

4. When anyone is handed over to the Secular Judge <note>The civil authority responsible for carrying out the death penalty, as the Church technically did not execute people themselves</note>, one must see to it carefully that he is not permitted to offer his defense or to show his innocence before the people: for if he is put to death [having spoken], the people would be scandalized; and if he goes free, danger to the faith would arise therefrom.

5. One must carefully avoid promising life before the people to the one who is condemned to death (namely, if he wishes to convert), considering that no heretic would let himself be burned if he could escape through such a promise; and if he promised conversion before the people, and life was not granted to him upon it, then the people would be offended and believe that he was being put to death unjustly.

Note, they said, that the Inquisitor or Heresy-master <note>original: *Kettermeeſter*</note> must always hold the act as a certainty without any conditions, and only inquire about the circumstances of the matter, saying: "How often have you made your confession to the heretics? 7. The Heresy-master may look into a book as if he had recorded therein the life and dealings of the accused, along with everything he is being questioned about. <note>This was a psychological tactic to make the prisoner believe the Inquisitor already had evidence against them.</note>

If he then answers: "Since I must die, then I would rather die in this my faith than in the faith of the Roman church," <note>original: *Roomſcher kercke*</note> then hold it for certain that he was previously only feigning a desire to be converted, and for that reason he must be brought to Justice. <note>In this context, "Justice" typically refers to being handed over to the secular authorities for execution.</note>

<column-break/>

then, that the Heretics are even more strengthened and stiffened, seeing that they also out-argue <note>original: *wtſtrijcken*</note> the learned men in this way.

10. Likewise, one must well observe that the Heretics never answer directly, and when they are pressured by many questions, they then commonly object that they are simple and unlearned people, and therefore do not know how to answer. And seeing that the bystanders are moved to pity for them—as if they were being wronged—holding them for simple and innocent people, they then take heart from this and feign to cry like poor miserable people; and pleading with their judges, they work hard to be freed from the Inquisition, saying: "My Lord, if I have erred in any matter, I shall gladly accept the penance <note>original: *boete*</note> for it: But help me to be freed from this shame, into which I have come through hate and envy, without having committed a crime." But the courageous Heresy-master must by no means be moved by such flattery and pleading, nor give any belief to such feigning.

### The Third Chapter.
### Of the Churches of the Waldensians in Dauphiné, and of the persecutions they have suffered, which have come to our knowledge.

THE Churches of the Waldensians in Dauphiné have been scattered for many hundreds of years in various regions and districts of this Province; they have had churches in Valentinois, where even now there are places in which, from time immemorial, the faith of the Waldensians has been received and passed down from the Father to the

<column-break/>

Son; such as the places of Faulques and Beauregard in Valentinois, and Baulme near Crest. From these places, the trial records have fallen into our hands concerning certain private persons of these locations who were accused by the Heresy-masters as followers of the Waldensian faith, now already over three hundred years ago.

But the most famous churches of the same Province are those of the Valleys of Freissinières near Embrun, and of Argentière, and of the Louise Valley. This last was, because of the Waldensians, named *Val Pute*, <note>original: *Val Pute*, likely from the Latin *Vallis Puta* or *Vallis Putida*.</note> which is to say the "Stinking Valley," as if in this valley there had been nothing else but a brothel and a flood of all kinds of unrestrained behavior and villainy. This same valley has been completely rooted out. On the other side of the Alpine mountains, there is a valley named the Valley of Pragela, which they likewise inhabited from time immemorial; this valley is situated under the Archbishopric of Turin, being even now populated and inhabited by the descendants of the very first Waldensians, of whom one has heard mention in former times. From the inhabitants of this valley were populated the valleys in the region of Piedmont, namely La Perouse, Saint Martin, Angrogne, and others. Likewise, the Waldensians in the regions of Provence and Calabria also descended and sprouted from the aforementioned places in Dauphiné and Piedmont. In this Valley of Pragela, there are currently six beautiful churches, each having its own Pastor, and each...

Just as all the aforementioned books were collected among the inhabitants of these valleys, which in former times was one of the most secure retreats or places of refuge of all that the Waldensians had in Europe, being surrounded and enclosed on all sides by almost insurmountable mountains, in whose caves and caverns they withdrew and maintained themselves in times of persecution.

<margin>Derived from his memorial notes on the Waldensians.</margin> The Lord of Vignaux <note>Jean de Vignaux was a pastor who documented Waldensian history and collected their ancient manuscripts.</note>, who was one of the first pastors to teach among them long before the free exercise of the Reformed Religion <term>Reformed Religion: Protestantism, specifically the tradition following the teachings of Calvin.</term> in France, cannot satisfy himself enough in recounting the straightforwardness, sincerity, and godliness of this people, whom he found fit to receive the preaching of God’s word—which their ancestors had so dearly loved, and in which they had instructed their descendants.

<column-break/>

And this is truly a matter of great wonder: that despite this people being enclosed and surrounded on all sides by the enemies of their faith, and in such constant danger of being captured as soon as they stepped outside their houses, they could never be turned away by any worldly consideration from their holy purpose to serve God—taking His word as the rule of their faith, and His law as the rule of their obedience. And in this purpose, they have been blessed and strengthened by God above all Christians in the whole of Europe, so that even while their speechless little children had scarcely left the nursing of the breasts, the fathers and mothers already took a special delight and a great pleasure in instructing them in the faith and Christian doctrine. Through this, it happened that these children became so capable and powerful that they put to shame many elderly but unlearned people living elsewhere for their ignorance.

...driven, who, not being satisfied with instructing their people with good admonitions on Sundays, went furthermore during the week along the villages and hamlets to instruct and admonish, not sparing themselves despite the steepness and unevenness of the craggy rocks, the harshness of the air, and the roughness of the land. There, they had to climb high mountains to visit their sheep <note>A metaphor for the congregation, reflecting the Waldensians' identity as a rural, pastoral community.</note> and bring them the nourishment and food of their souls. This they did not neglect even when these same people were in the summer following the cattle upon the summits of the rocks; and there, they performed Christian services and admonitions in the open fields. It was, then, in these valleys that one saw the people listen to God’s word with attention and reverence; there, Christian discipline was practiced with fruit. There the people prayed with fervor when they returned from work; in the evening when night arrived, and in the morning at the crack of dawn, before they began any work, they called upon the Lord—first within their houses, and thereafter in the church—for His help in their deeds, thoughts, words, and labor. Thus, they committed themselves to their work under the protection of the living God, whom they loved, honored, and worshipped. In that place alone, one traced more simplicity and zeal than in many other places where pleasures hold the upper hand. Yet, they were not such unrefined boors that they did not have many persons among them who could read and could express their affairs with a fitness of words and reason—especially those who occasionally traveled down to the lower districts. They also had schools for their convenience, in which their little children were instructed, and they lacked nothing that they deemed useful for the advancement and spreading of God’s glory.

<column-break/>

The first persecution that has come to our knowledge is that which was stirred up by a certain monk who was an Inquisitor <term>Inquisitor: An official of the Catholic Church tasked with identifying and suppressing heresy.</term> or "Master of Heretics," belonging to the order of the Friars Minor <note>Also known as the Franciscans.</note> named François Borelli. He was commissioned in the year 1380 to investigate and gather information regarding the sect of the Waldensians in the Dioceses of Aix, Arles, Embrun, Vienne, Geneva, Aubonne, Savoy, the County of Venaissin, Dyois, Forez, and Selon, according to the contents of his Bull <note>A formal decree or public letter issued by a Pope.</note> obtained for that purpose from Pope Clement the Seventh, who then held his seat at Avignon <note>During the Western Schism, competing popes resided in Avignon, France, rather than Rome.</note>.

<margin>This Bull was retrieved from the Chamber of Accounts in Grenoble.</margin>
The Pope was moved and stirred up to issue this decree by the too-close proximity of these same Waldensians, for which reason he wished to purge the Dauphiné <note>A historical province in southeastern France.</note> of them, because they held him to be the Antichrist.

However, it did not go well for the Mayors of Freissinières <note>A high-altitude valley in the French Alps that served as a refuge for Waldensian communities.</note> named Michel Ruffi and Jean Girard. For these men, having been summoned to appear before the same Archbishop to answer both for themselves and for the inhabitants of their valley, replied that they had nothing to answer or say to the aforementioned Archbishop, as their case was pending before the King and his council. They therefore protested, requesting a copy of the charges. Nevertheless, being forced to answer despite all their protests to the contrary, **Michel Ruffi**, shaking his head, answered in his own language: **"Look, what madness!"** <note>original: "Veici Rages"</note>. And being further pressed, he said again: **"Look, is this not a fine argument?"** <note>original: "Veici una bella raison" – likely intended sarcastically to highlight the absurdity of the proceedings.</note> The Archbishop, embittered and enraged by such contempt from these Mayors, sent them to the fire and had them burned without any further pretense of justice.

But it did not go well for this Archbishop for long afterward; for he died (not without a clear sign of God’s justice and wrath) very shortly after the aforementioned execution. And so the persecution by this Archbishop and his Commissioner, Jean Veyleti, ended in the year 1487.

However, in the dealings and trials conducted by this monk Jean Veyleti, we have noticed and observed an extraordinary cunning and villainy. For having obtained these trial records, we found among them small slips of paper on which this Commissioner had recorded the answers of the accused simply, as they came from their mouths. But we later found these same simple answers expanded in the formal trial records, and often stated contrary to or entirely different from the *summary* <note>original: "sumptum" – the initial raw notes of a statement used as the basis for a formal legal document.</note>, which the aforementioned answers noted in the trials actually contained. In this, he twisted the meaning of the accused, making them say what they themselves had never thought.

For example, when asked if he did not believe that as soon as the sacramental words were spoken by the priest in the Mass, the body of Christ was in the host <note>The bread used in the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, as large and great as it was on the wood of the Cross? When the **Waldensian** <note>original: "Waldench"</note> answered "No," then this Veyleti or his clerk recorded the answer from his mouth thus: "That he had confessed that he did not believe in God."

Likewise, when asked: "Should one not call upon the Saints?" and having answered "No," they then wrote that he had blasphemed the Saints and spoken ill of them.

Behold, such was the bad faith of the Monk-Inquisitors, even in such a weighty matter. And it is also not without certain proof of God’s providence that such villainies have been preserved and remain to this day, so that we may now demonstrate by what kind of spirit those men were driven. These were the men who, having oppressed and finally killed and burned the believers and members of the Church of Christ through manifold deceptions, nevertheless dare to ask where the Church and the believers—whom they themselves destroyed—were before our coming.

Now, if the reader is eager to know how such trial records fell into our hands: this likewise occurred through the providence of God. Those very people who committed and carried out these cruelties and villainies against the Waldensians—namely these same Archbishops of Embrun, Jean and Rostain, and others—had locked up and preserved these papers and trial records in their coffers and chanceries. They remained there until this same city was snatched from the hands of the conspiring Leaguers <note>The Catholic League was a major faction during the French Wars of Religion that opposed the Huguenots and sought to eradicate Protestantism.</note> in the year 1585, and restored to the obedience of the King by the Lord Marshal of Lesdiguières. At that time, all the trials and proceedings that had been instituted against the Waldensians over many hundreds of years were thrown out into the streets because of the fire that the enemies themselves had set in the Archbishop’s house, in order to protect a certain

<column-break/>

While "brune" literally means brown, the text translates it here for the reader as "black."
