Being present there at that time, the Lord of Calignon (who during his life was the Chancellor of Navarre) and the Lord of Vulson (currently a Councilor of the King in the Court of the Parliament of Grenoble) saw to it that these same cases and trials, formerly conducted against the Waldensians, were picked up and gathered. From these records, we have drawn what pertains to the cruelties and faithless dealings of these Monk-Inquisitors and their followers, as well as all that shall follow hereafter concerning the Waldensians in Dauphiné <note>A province in southeastern France.</note>, and the persecutions by the Archbishops of Turin carried out by their commissioners against the Waldensians of Pragela.

Until now, we have not heard of the Waldensians being attacked by open warfare; but this began with Albert de Capitaneis, the Deacon of Cremona. Having been sent out against them by Pope Innocent VIII in the year 1488, he began to request help from the King's Governor in the land of Dauphiné, named Hugues de la Palu. To this end, the Governor took up soldiers and proceeded to the place that the aforementioned Albert had designated, saying that the Waldensians were staying there: namely, in the Valley of Loyse <note>Now known as Vallouise.</note>. And it is true that they were then entirely rooted out, so that this valley was later settled and populated with new people and inhabitants. Not a single household of these **Waldensians** ever appeared to settle there again, which is a certain sign that all the inhabitants of every nature and lineage perished and died there together.

These Lieutenants of the King, having thus annihilated and destroyed the inhabitants of the **Val Louise**, and fearing that the Waldensians living nearby would take it over again, and that they would then at some time have similar trouble to drive them out once more, gave the property and holdings of the same valley to whomever he pleased and as he saw fit. The sentence was pronounced in the Great Church of **Embrun**, and afterwards posted on a large tablet upon the church doors. Below it were placed thirty-two Articles of the Faith of the Waldensians. ->Against the Mass.<-

->The Invocation of the Saints.<-

And other things that were put forward by the **Waldensians**. Also, that every man burning with lust may carnally know any woman, whoever she may be, without falling into sin thereby, because the Apostle says that it is better to marry than to burn, and because it is said in the Gospel, *whoever can receive it, let him receive it* <note>original: "qui potest capere capiat"</note>, translating it as: he who can seize it, let him seize it.

Now, it so happens that the very same <term>Information</term><note>The official investigative records or depositions.</note> upon which they founded their sentences has fallen into our hands. From these records, this deception has been uncovered to their own conviction and shame. For there was not one of the witnesses—notwithstanding that the majority of those heard were priests or monks who were interrogated by this Monk—who did not answer that he had never known such things to exist among the **Waldensians**.

...were taught and practiced or committed.

In these sacks of trials against the **Waldensians**, there is, among others, a trial conducted against two **Barbes**<note>The term "Barbe" (meaning uncle) was the title used for Waldensian pastors or ministers to distinguish them from the Roman Catholic "Father."</note>, who were both captured in the year 1492 on the heights of **Costeplane**. One was named **Francois Gerondin** and the other **Pierre de Iacob**. When these men were asked how it happened that the cause of the Waldensians had increased so much and had spread across so many places for such a long time, the Monk <note>The inquisitor recording the testimony.</note> recorded the following as the answer of **Barbe Gerondin**: that the unrestrained lives of the Priests was the cause of it, as well as the fact that the Cardinals were greedy, proud, and unchaste. He stated that it was well known to everyone that there was neither Pope, nor Cardinal, nor Bishop who did not have their concubines; likewise, there were few or none who did not have their <term>Bardachen</term><note>From the Italian "bardassa," referring to young male companions or favorites, often implying a sexual relationship.</note> with whom they committed their <term>buggeries</term><note>A historical term for sodomy or sexual deviance.</note>. Therefore, the **Barbes** of the **Waldensians** could easily persuade the people that the religion of such scandalous men could not be good, because their works were so wicked and evil.

And immediately thereafter: When the same **Barbe** was asked what their teaching was regarding unchastity, they <note>The inquisitors.</note> made him answer: That unchastity is no sin, unless it be committed between a mother and her child. But how could the **Barbes** have drawn people away from the **Roman Church** by condemning the unchastity of the Priests, if they themselves had taught that unchastity is no sin?

Furthermore, being

<column-break/>

asked why **Incest** committed between a mother and a child is a sin, they made him answer: that it is a sin because it is forbidden by God.

Further asked where God has forbidden the same, they made him answer that Jesus Christ said to St. John before his Ascension: *Garda te dove fer ay failly una volta non tornar piu.*<note>Original in Occitan dialect: "Garda te dove fer ay failly una volta non tornar piu." Translated: "Watch yourself, where you once came out, do not return again."</note> That is: "Watch yourself, and do not re-enter that place from which you once came out." All these things were set down and recorded, not only according to the dictation of the aforementioned Monk, but also with the consent or approval and signature of the Counselor **Ponce** and of a certain **Oronce**, Judge of **Briançon**. From this, the monopoly and conspiracy of these <term>Kettermeesters</term><note>Literally "Heresy-masters," the Dutch term for Inquisitors.</note> is evident; as they were not satisfied with persecuting the **Waldensians** through open violence, but also attempted to suppress them with the stains of slander, attributing to these **Barbes** such dull and absurd answers. Yet, as will appear in its proper place (namely in the explanation they give of the Seventh Commandment), these men were exceptionally well-practiced in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, it is pure deceit and falsehood to say that they would have forged such an absurd and improper tradition, especially in a matter where they never failed to bring forth everything taught to us in God’s Word against excess, unchastity, and whoredom.

This persecution was most miserable, for as soon as the **Waldensians** were condemned for Heresy, they were by this...

In the year 1494, commissioners were appointed by order of the Pope to deal with the **Waldensians** of **Dauphiné**—otherwise named **Chagnards** <note>A derogatory nickname likely derived from the word for "dogs."</note>, that is, the **Dogs**. We do not mention her here for the sake of her steadfastness <note>The author implies she may have lacked the courage of other martyrs, but her testimony is historically valuable.</note>, but because she spoke many things in her defense that are relevant to this history. When she was asked whether she had seen or heard any **Barbes** <note>Waldensian pastors or ministers.</note> of the **Waldensians**, she answered no. <column-break/>

confessed that twenty-five years ago, two men in gray clothes had come to the house of her husband, and that after the evening meal, one of these asked her: *“Have you never heard tell of a handful of people in the world, without whom the world would otherwise perish?”* <note>original: "Naves vous iamais auvi parlar, dun plen pung de mond, que si non era tot lo monde seria a fin"</note>. Upon this, the man answered her that he had come there to speak to her of that small flock, and to show and teach her who they were, saying that they were those who had learned from the commandments of God how one must serve God. And for that reason, they wandered through the world to teach the world how they must worship and honor God, and to reform the abuses of the **Roman Church**. He also told her, among many other things: that we must not do to another that which we do not want to happen to us <note>The Golden Rule.</note>; that one must worship God alone, as He is the only one who can help us, and not the deceased saints; that one must not swear <note>The Waldensians followed a strict interpretation of the Bible regarding the prohibition of taking oaths.</note>; that one must maintain marital fidelity; that one must keep the Sunday holy, and that it is not necessary to keep the other holy days; that the clergy had too many possessions; and that this was also the reason why they kept harlots and...

### of the History of the Waldensians.
L
<meta>catchword: one</meta>

He [the Archbishop] said he would write to the Pope and Cardinals and send them the account of everything that had happened against them, and would ask for advice on how he should conduct himself in this matter. But afterward, this Archbishop informed them that he had been unable to obtain any answer.

In the meantime, King Charles VIII <note>King of France, reigned 1483–1498</note> having died, this Archbishop departed for the anointing or Coronation of King Louis XII in the year 1498. Having learned of this, and clearly perceiving that they had no good to expect from Rome in their favor or benefit—and that the Archbishop meanwhile remained satisfied, keeping the use of their property which had previously been confiscated and seized by his predecessors and attached to his Archbishopric, and that it would now grieve him to restore the same—the inhabitants of Freissinières <note>A valley in the High Alps known for its Waldensian population</note> decided to send word to King Louis XII. They petitioned him through a formal request that he would have their property restored to them, which the aforementioned Archbishop, the monks who served as Inquisitors, and many others were withholding from them. The King referred this matter to his Chancellor and Council. When the Chancellor spoke of it with the Archbishop, he replied that the restitution of the requested property did not concern him in the least, seeing as the same property had been confiscated by the Inquisitors long before he came to the Archbishopric of Embrun. However, he claimed that at that same time in Paris were a president of Grenoble and the Councilor Rabot, who would be able to answer regarding this article, as they themselves had condemned the Waldensians. Yet the Waldensians strongly maintained that the Archbishop should be the primary one charged with restoring their goods, as many fine portions of their property were attached to the domains of that same Archbishopric; and whenever they demanded them back, this Archbishop referred them to the Pope, which acted to the prejudice of what the late King had ordained.

<column-break/>

The High Council <note>The Grand Conseil, a high judicial body in France</note>, having taken knowledge of the case of the Waldensians of Freissinières, ordained that no new actions should be taken in the matter until the King had written to the Pope to obtain Papal Commissioners. These commissioners, joined with the same Archbishop acting as ordinary <note>An "ordinary" is a church official, like a bishop, with regular jurisdiction over a territory</note>, were to finally bring an end to this case.

Following this, a certain Confessor <note>The King's personal priest and spiritual advisor</note> of the King and the Official of Orleans <note>The "Official" was the presiding judge of the ecclesiastical court in Orleans</note> were nominated as Papal Commissioners. They arrived at Embrun in the year 1501, on the 4th day of July.

...they sent a herald to me to deliver the King’s letters; having received these, I offered my obedience and requested that they stay at my house, just as my Lord the Confessor <note>Jean de Rely, the Bishop of Angers and confessor to King Charles VIII and Louis XII</note> had promised me while we were in Lyons <note>The city of Lyon</note>. In the year 1560, the Waldensians of Fraissinière and Pragela had established their Churches, provided with their Teachers or Pastors, who maintained them in the practice of their Religion during the time when all those who made profession of the Reformation were being persecuted unto death. In the same year, President Truchon delivered a certain premeditated and extraordinary speech or Oration before the assembly of the Estates of Provence, aimed at the complete eradication of the Waldensians of Fraissinière and Pragela: saying that this <term>old leaven</term><note>A biblical metaphor (from 1 Corinthians 5) used here to describe the Waldensian faith as a lingering corruption that would infect the whole region of Dauphiné if not destroyed.</note>, which was sufficient to ruin all of Dauphiné if no precautions were taken against it, had to be removed and destroyed. In the assembly of these Estates, it was resolved and decided to root them out with open violence and arms. And to that end, commissions were issued to recruit soldiers and to march toward those Valleys: but while the <term>drums</term><note>Original: "Trammels," referring to military drums used to summon recruits.</note> were being beaten and they were busy recruiting soldiers in the land of Provence, the unexpected death of King Francis II broke and nullified this plan and decision, and the Waldensian Churches have since remained in existence, as they still remain today through the singular grace of God.

### Chapter Four.

### Concerning the Churches of the *Waldensians* of Piedmont, along with the persecutions they have endured, as far as we have obtained knowledge of them.

The Waldensians have had famous churches since time immemorial in the valleys of Piedmont: Angrogna, Perosa, the valley of San Martino, Luserna, and in other places situated thereabouts. It is held for certain that they came from the Waldensians of Dauphiné <note>A province in southeastern France.</note>, from Pragelato, Freissinières, and other places located above them. For, having multiplied so greatly in those same places that the land could not sustain them all, they were consequently forced to spread their dwellings far and wide as they arrived. They always welcomed one another with hospitality, showed brotherly friendship, and whenever they were distressed by turmoil, they likewise came to one another's aid with a heartfelt love, sparing neither their lives nor their property for their mutual preservation.

The first turmoil that the Waldensians of Piedmont experienced arose from the report of the Priests who had been sent to them by the Archbishops of Turin, saying: that the people over whom they had been given charge did not live according to the faith and customs of the Roman Church. Specifically, that they made no offerings for the dead:

<column-break/>

that they heeded neither Masses nor confessions; and that they also did not seek to obtain for themselves, through the customary means, deliverance from the punishments and pains of <term>Purgatory</term><note>In Catholic theology, an intermediate state after death for purification; the Waldensians rejected this doctrine.</note>. Therefore, the Archbishops of Turin persecuted them to their utmost power, making them hateful to their Princes. The Princes, however, understood the contrary from the good testimony that the neighboring peoples gave of them, regarding their friendly conduct and way of life; namely, that they were simple people, God-fearing, well-mannered, without falsehood or malice, loving uprightness and honesty, always ready and willing to serve their Prince, and that they very gladly showed all obedience and bounden duty with diligence to the same. Furthermore, they were so agreeable to the neighboring peoples living around them that those neighbors continually labored to entice and draw their young people to Piedmont for their service; indeed, they even sought out nurses and <term>wet-nurses</term><note>Original: "Minne," women hired to breastfeed and care for infants.</note> among them to raise their little children. Consequently, the same Princes remained for a long time in the resolve that they would in no way vex or molest them. But the Priests and Monks who frequented those areas, drawing no profit from their faith, burdened them with countless calumnies and slanders; and whenever they came to Piedmont to maintain their trade and business, the same always ambushed some of them, whom they then—having captured them—immediately delivered into the hands of the <term>Inquisitors</term><note>Original: "Kettermeesters," literally "masters of heretics."</note>. Which Inquisitors

Then, holding these two cobblestones in his hands, he spoke thus to them: "When I have eaten these stones which you see here, then you shall bring to an end the Religion for which you now make me die." And after that, he threw the stones away onto the earth.

They also dispatched chosen troops of "Christ-people" to Vaucluse in Dauphiné, to overrun the valley of Pragelato and, by occupying them with their own defense through alarms, thus prevent the other Waldensians of Piedmont, their neighbors, from sending them any help. Yet this happened through a special providence of God: that they divided their troops into bands, more out of arrogance and defiance than out of good leadership. ### The Fourth Chapter.

#### Of the Churches of the Waldensians of Piedmont, together with the persecutions they have endured, as far as we have obtained knowledge of them.

The Waldensians have, from time immemorial, had renowned churches in the valleys of Piedmont, Angrogna, Perosa, the St. Martin Valley, Lucerna, and other nearby places. It is held for certain that they came from the Waldensians of Dauphiné, from Pragela, Freissinières, and other neighboring places. For having multiplied so greatly in those same places that the land could not sustain them all, they were consequently forced to spread their dwellings far and wide as best they could. They also always welcomed one another with brotherly friendship and showed such kindness; and whenever they were distressed by turmoil, they likewise came to each other's aid with heartfelt love, sparing neither life nor goods for their mutual preservation.

The first turmoil experienced by the Waldensians of Piedmont arose from the reports of the Priests who had been sent to them by the Archbishops of Turin, saying: that the people over whom they had been given charge did not live according to the faith and customs of the Roman Church. And specifically, that they made no offerings for the dead:

<column-break/>

that they cared for neither Masses nor <term>auricular confession</term><note>The practice of confessing sins privately to a priest.</note>: and also that they did not seek to obtain for themselves, through the usual means, deliverance from the punishments and pains of <term>Purgatory</term><note>In Catholic theology, a place of purification for souls before entering Heaven.</note>. Therefore, the Archbishops of Turin persecuted them to the utmost of their power, making them hateful to their Princes. These Princes, however, understood the contrary from the good testimony that the neighboring peoples gave of them, regarding their friendly conduct and way of life; namely, that they were simple people, God-fearing, well-mannered, without falsehood or malice, loving sincerity and honesty, always ready and willing to serve their Prince, and that they very gladly performed all obedience and dutiful service with diligence toward him. Moreover, they were so agreeable to the neighboring peoples living around them that these neighbors continually worked to entice and draw their young people to Piedmont for their service; indeed, they even sought out wet nurses and nannies <note>Original: "voesters ende Minne"</note> among them to raise their small children. Consequently, these same Princes remained for a long time in the resolution that they would in no way vex or molest them. But the Priests and Monks who associated with them, drawing no profit from their faith, burdened them with countless calumnies and slanders; and whenever they came to Piedmont to maintain their trade and business, the same always ambushed some of them, whom they then, having captured them, immediately delivered into the hands of the <term>Inquisitors</term><note>Original: "Kettermeeſters," literally "heretic-masters."</note>. Which Inquisitors—

<margin>Vignaux in his memoirs, page 7.</margin>

...[confessors] handed them over to the executioner, so that there is hardly a city in all of Piedmont where someone of them has not been killed. For Jordan Tertian was burned at Susa; Hippolyte Rossier was burned at Turin; Villermin Ambroise was hanged on the heights of Meane; as was also Antoine Hiun; Vgon Chiamp of Fenestrelles, being imprisoned at Susa, was taken from there to Turin, where his intestines or entrails were first torn out and poured into a basin, and after that he was cruelly tortured and put to death: and among these servants of the Lord, there are some who had already defended and confirmed the known truth more than two hundred and fifty years ago, some over one hundred and fifty years. But among others, the steadfastness and bravery of one named Catelan Girard is very remarkable and to be wondered at; standing on the woodpile at the stake, at the place where he was burned at Revel in the <term>Marquisate of Saluzzo</term><note>A historical state at the foot of the Alps, now part of the Italian province of Cuneo.</note>, he requested two street stones or cobblestones. The bystanders refused to hand them to him, as they feared he wanted to harm someone with them; but having declared that he did not wish to do so, they finally handed them to him. He then, holding these two cobblestones in his hands, spoke thus to them: "When I have eaten these cobblestones which you see here, only then shall you bring to an end the religion for which you now make me die"; and after that, he threw the cobblestones away onto the ground.

<margin>Vignanx in his memoirs, folio 74</margin>

That burning and scorching of the fires lasted until the year 1488. Then they decided to attack the Waldensians with open force, because they noticed that, besides many being drawn to the knowledge of God because of the persistence and courage of those whom they thus publicly killed, they would, moreover, by that means, never be able to reach their goal. For this purpose, they then recruited <term>Crusaders</term><note>The original Dutch 'Christen-volck' (Christian-folk) refers here to a volunteer militia or army granted indulgences by the Pope to fight against perceived heretics.</note> to join with Albert de Capitaneis, Commissioner of the Popes <term>Sixtus the Fourth</term><note>Pope from 1471–1484, known for the Sistine Chapel and the Spanish Inquisition.</note> and <term>Innocent the Eighth</term><note>Pope from 1484–1492, who issued the bull 'Summis desiderantes affectibus' which intensified the persecution of heretics.</note>. There were 1,800 soldiers listed on the rolls, besides a great multitude of the inhabitants of Piedmont who also ran from all quarters for the sake of plunder; all these took their way together toward Angrogna, Lucerna, La Perouse, St. Martin, Praviglerm, and Biolet, which lies in the Marquisate of Saluzzo.

<column-break/>

They also dispatched selected troops of Crusaders to Vaucluson in Dauphiné, to overrun the valley of Pragela, and by occupying them with alarm for their own defense, thus to prevent them from sending any help to the other Waldensians of Piedmont, their neighbors. Yet this occurred through a special provision of God, that they divided their troops into bands, more out of arrogance and defiance than out of good planning. For even though it gave every man business and occupied them in their defense, such that they could not help one another, they nevertheless so diminished their power with this that they were defeated everywhere: but especially...

...safety in the valley of **Angrogna**<note>A key valley in the Cottian Alps, historically a stronghold for the Waldensian movement.</note>, where they used the greatest force. Because this new attack by the enemy forces could not occur without them receiving warning in the meantime—that the same was being done against them—they had also prepared themselves to meet and welcome them, holding their positions at the entrances and narrow passages where a few men were able to hold back a great multitude. They had armed themselves with long wooden **targes** or shields<note>A targe is a concave shield used for defense during the late Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> which covered their bodies entirely, and in which the arrows of their enemies remained stuck without hurting or damaging them. The front ranks being thus equipped and covered, the others behind them could very advantageously use their hand-bows and crossbows under the protection of these aforementioned shields. And as the enemy nevertheless stubbornly advanced and approached the passages to win them, the women and children fell on their knees, crying out in their language: **"O God, help us!"**<note>original: "O dio Aiutaej"</note>. But while the enemies were mocking this, and specifically among others a certain captain nicknamed **Saquet**, who was mockingly imitating these women, he was killed in the meantime and plummeted down from the mountain, falling into a deep pit which to this day is still called the **Pit of Saquet** after his name. At the same time, it also happened that a certain captain named **The Black of Mondovì**<note>original: "Le Noir de Montdenj"</note>, against those women who were firmly calling upon God, crying **"Mine, mine, they are making the passage!"**<note>original: "I miej, I miej, Faranno la passada." This likely refers to the captain's boastful claim that the women were his "prey" as they broke through.</note>

<column-break/>

was likewise struck in the throat by an arrow shot and killed. When the soldiers noticed this, and saw that pieces of the rocks and the throwing of stones and arrows covered them, they all took to flight, so that the majority of them plummeted down from the stone cliffs.

This people noted in this alarm yet another working of the **providence** and arrangement of God: namely, that when the enemies approached a certain place which by nature and situation is the strongest in the entire valley of Angrogna, called **The Meadow of the Tower**<note>original: "Le pre de la tour" (Pra del Tor). This was the famous natural fortress and spiritual center of the Waldensians.</note>, where they might have fortified themselves and thus made themselves masters of the same valley, God then sent them such a thick cloud and such a dark mist that the enemies could hardly see one another. They had neither the trouble nor the time to inspect the suitability of the place, nor to remain there; for the Waldensians, regaining their courage, drove the enemies further into flight, so that they were entirely dismayed. Not seeing where they were going, the majority threw themselves down from above and fled away in a heap, leaving behind their weapons and the booty they had obtained upon entering the valley, where they had spilled the wine and flour and loaded their baggage-carriers and servants with the most precious moveable goods—leaving it all behind.

God, moreover, has [touched] the heart of their **Prince of Piedmont**...

Therefore, it was again shown / to her highness / that all those / who at other times had wished to bring down these people by the force of arms / had met with ill success and perished / because the locations of their dwellings were advantageous to them / and that the narrows and passages of the land were better known to them / than to those who came to attack them. <meta>This page continues the account of the Great Synod of Angrogna in 1535. Having decided to formally align their ancient traditions with the Reformation, the Waldensian leaders and families are now confirming a specific set of doctrinal articles that define their faith in contrast to Roman Catholic practice.</meta>

# of the History of the Waldensians.

...[accepted] by all those present, who promised to uphold, maintain, believe, and preserve the same without any contradiction, as being in accordance with the teaching which had been taught to them from father to child for many hundreds of years past, and drawn from the word of God.

### Article 1.

**That divine service <note>original: "Godtsdienst"; referring here to the act of worship and religious practice.</note> cannot be practiced otherwise than through the Spirit and truth: for God is a Spirit, and all those who wish to speak with God must speak with Him in the Spirit.**

### Article 2.

**All those who have been saved, and those who shall yet be saved, were chosen by God before the foundation of the world was laid.**

### Article 3.

**Those who are ordained to salvation shall not be damned.**

### Article 4.

**All those who advocate for and defend free will <note>The Waldensians here side with the Reformers' view that human will is bound by sin and requires God's sovereign grace for salvation.</note> completely deny predestination and the grace of God.**

### Article 5.

**No work can be called good except that alone which is commanded by God; and likewise, there is no work that is evil except that which God has forbidden.**

### Article 6.

**A Christian person may swear by the name of God without sinning against what is written in the Gospel of Matthew in the 5th Chapter, provided that he who swears does not use the name of God in vain. For one does not swear in vain when the taking of an oath serves God's honor and salvation.**
**Likewise, one may swear before the law <note>original: "voor het rechte"; meaning in a court or before a magistrate.</note>, because he who serves the authorities—whether he be a believer or an unbeliever—has received his power from God.**

<column-break/>

### Article 7.

**Auricular confession <note>The practice of confessing sins privately to a priest.</note> is not commanded by God; and it is determined according to Holy Scripture that the true confession of a Christian person consists in confessing to God alone, to whom honor and respect are due. There is another kind of confession which takes place when one is reconciled with one's neighbor, of which we are exhorted in Matthew 5. The third kind of confession is when one has sinned publicly and before the eyes of all men; therefore, one also makes an acknowledgment of guilt and confession publicly and before the eyes of all men.**

### Article 8.

**We must rest from our labor on Sunday as zealots for the honor and respect of God: out of love for our servants, and to apply ourselves to hearing the word of God.**

### Article 9.

**It is not permitted for a Christian person to avenge himself on his enemy in any way.**

# The Second Book, of the First Part

### Article 10.

**A Christian person may serve in the office of the magistracy <note>original: "ampt der overheyt"; referring to serving as a government official or civil leader.</note> among Christians.**

### Article 11.

**There is no certain time appointed for a Christian to fast, and one does not find in God's word that the Lord has commanded such a thing, nor designated any specific days for it.**

### Article 12.

**Marriage is not forbidden to any persons, of whatever quality or condition they might be.**

### Article 13.

**Whoever forbids marriage teaches a doctrine of the Devils.**

### Article 14.

**He who does not have the gift of abstinence <note>original: "onthoudinge"; the ability to remain celibate without sinning.</note> is bound to marry.**

### Article 15.

**The Ministers of the Word of God must not move from place to place, unless it happens for the great benefit of the Church.**

### Article 16.

**It is not contrary to Apostolic fellowship that ministers should possess something of their own in private, in order to support their households.**

<column-break/>

### Article 17.

Concerning the matter of the Sacraments, it is concluded from the Holy Scripture: that we have only two Sacramental signs which Jesus Christ has left us; the first of which is Baptism, and the other the Lord's Supper. These we receive to show how our perseverance in the faith is, just as we promised when we were little children and were baptized. Likewise, it is in memory of the great benefit that Jesus Christ did for us when He died for our redemption and washed us through His precious blood.

These Articles having been concluded among them, the priests <note>original: "Papen"; a derogatory term for Roman Catholic clergy at the time.</note>—who were among them at that time and frequented the area to receive the income from the parishes—were terrified and amazed. They lost all hope that these people could ever be brought back to the obedience of the Roman Church through any force, much less by their own will. And noticing that the door to their profit was now closed, they departed without speaking a single word.

Thus, the Mass was banished from the Valleys <note>The Alpine valleys of Piedmont, the traditional home of the Waldensians.</note> of these Waldensians by their own departure and withdrawal. And because they only had New Testament books and some books of the Old Testament which were translated into their Waldensian language, they also resolved to have the entire Bible printed as quickly as possible, especially since their books were only written by hand...

Shortly after this, war arose between King Francis, the first of that name, and the Prince of Piedmont, which was very advantageous for these poor people; for during the disturbances and confusion of the war, they remained unmolested. This continued until finally Pope Paul, the third of that name, petitioned the Parliament of Turin to suppress this people and to punish them through the law as soon as they were handed over by the Inquisitors as very harmful Heretics. Therefore, this Parliament caused a very great multitude of them to be burned within Turin, following the example of the other Parliaments of France, which also at this time burned all those who were being called Lutherans <note>At this time, "Lutheran" was often used as a general slur for any Protestant, regardless of their specific denomination.</note>.

But they greatly worsened their situation thereby, for the King charged them that they must live according to the laws of the Roman Church, or that, if they did otherwise, they would be punished as Heretics. He commanded the Court of the Parliament of Turin to ensure that all his subjects living under their jurisdiction lived in his Religion. He added to this that he did not have the Lutherans burned throughout his entire Kingdom of France only to keep a remnant or a "nest-egg" <note>original: "hauwer"; referring to a small surviving group kept in reserve.</note> of them alive within the Alpine mountains.

This Parliament then diligently applied itself to fulfill this Mandate of the King...

# The Second Book, of the First Part

<meta>catchword: him</meta>

...of the King to be put into work and carried out; and has therefore commanded them upon pain of death, that they should immediately dismiss their Ministers, and take on Priests to sing Masses for them, and that they should henceforth live like all other subjects of the King. But they answered that they could in no way obey such commands, because the same were contrary to the commands of God, whom they wished to obey in matters of religion rather than men.

Yet it is beyond doubt that the Parliament would have forced them by violence to this very thing—which they refused upon a simple command—if the King had not had business elsewhere.

Therefore the Parliament had to content themselves with persecuting those through the <term>Inquisition|A powerful office within the Catholic Church tasked with rooting out and punishing heresy.</term>, and receiving from the Monks those whom they sent to the fire. But thereafter, in the year 1555, this Parliament greatly increased the persecution; for after they had burned a certain bookseller named Bartholomeus Hector within Turin (because he, in his death, showed great steadfastness and piety, and greatly edified the bystanders, even moving them to pity and weeping, so that they, through a general clapping of hands and gestures, which they performed at his speeches and prayers that he made to God, justified and acquitted him;) this Parliament took cause from this to do their utmost and to use the King’s power

During these heavy persecutions, the Protestant Princes of Germany prayed for them, requesting King Henry II <note>original: "Henricus de tweeden"</note> that he would be willing to let them live peacefully and remain in their religion, in which they had lived from father to child for many centuries. <margin>1559.</margin>

<margin>This war is printed in a separate treatise and is also found in the history of the martyrs of our time in the 8th book, page 532.</margin>

But since the histories and the accounts of these wars have been brought to light elsewhere, we shall make no longer account of them, it being noteworthy what we shall only note here: namely, after the Lord of Trinity with his military army had been defeated, and finding that the "lion's skin" <note>original: "Leeuwen hupt" – likely "huyt" (skin), a metaphor for brute force</note> or force had not suited or succeeded for him, he put on the "fox's skin" and turned to <term>guile|deceptive tactics; original: "archistisheypt," likely a typo for "arglistigheyt"</term>, showing those people that what had already passed had only happened due to a lack of mutual discussion and through misunderstanding, rather than through ill will or hatred from His Highness toward them; [he claimed] that his soldiers had also overstepped because of the great resistance they had encountered, but that he henceforth wished to be an instrument of their preservation.

Also, our enemies, having gained this advantage over us, and there being no one left among us who might comfort, advise, rebuke, or exhort us, will without doubt do their utmost to keep the entry and the gate always closed, and thus prevent the return of our Shepherds. By their service we have been so worthily instructed and taught, and also sufficiently strengthened against all kinds of temptations. And since they will not cease to accuse us as rebels when we invite them back, it is better that we do not deprive and rob ourselves of the fruits of their ministry."

Lord la Trinité, at the least, would not allow them to send anyone after them. Having then for a long time struggled with one another and being in disagreement over the decision of what they ought to do, and finally seeing a fortress being built, through which they would always be kept under constraint and in check if they allowed its progress to continue; and moreover being afraid that if they undertook anything against those who were building and working on it, their deputies—whom they had in **Turin**—would be put to death in retaliation; they were for these reasons most dazed and astonished. Yet, considering how they had been falsely deceived by that "fine smooth-talker" <note>Dutch: 'schoonen klappaert', a derogatory term for a deceptive chatterer or silver-tongued deceiver</note> Lord la Trinité, they overcame and set aside all the imaginings they had, deciding that they must entrust the outcome to the providence of God, as well as reconciling themselves with God through fasting and prayer. Having done this, they summoned their **Shepherds** <note>Pastors</note> back and sought help from their neighbors in **Pragela** <note>Pragelato, a nearby valley</note>. These neighbors also rushed to them with their weapons; and seeing in their churches the altars and images that Lord la Trinité had already caused to be placed there, they broke down those same altars to the ground, even tearing out their foundations, and smashed the images into pieces. They also besieged the aforementioned fortress, captured it, and slew all those who resisted them; they also repelled the reinforcements sent to relieve this fortress, putting them to flight and slaying a great multitude of them.

<column-break/>

For which reason Prince **Emanuel Philibert** <note>The Duke of Savoy (1528–1580), who initially sought to suppress the Waldensians by force</note>, being very enraged, wished to avenge this upon the deputies whom he was holding in prison. But Lady **Marguerite** <note>Margaret of Valois, Duchess of Savoy, who was known for her sympathy toward the Protestants and often acted as a mediator</note>, speaking for them, softened the Prince as much as she could, pointing out to him that those of **Angrongne** <note>Angrogna, a central Waldensian valley</note> must have received some warning of the treatment his Highness had inflicted upon their deputies, and that seeing themselves on the path to being completely lost, they had out of necessity taken up this improper means in order to be preserved. It so happened that his Highness, through the urging and instigation of the **Nuncio** <note>The Papal Ambassador</note> or Legate of the Pope, had meanwhile forced these deputies to attend Mass, and there made them ask forgiveness from God, the Pope, and the Holy Mother the Roman Church, as well as making them promise that they would live according to her commands; and that being done, had them led back to prison, waiting until his aforementioned fortress would be completed. Seeing himself now far excluded from his purpose and expectation, he accepted and agreed to the treaty <note>The Treaty of Cavour (1561), a landmark agreement granting limited religious freedom to the Waldensians</note> that had been proposed by Lady Marguerite, under which they have lived until now; which treaty we omit to set down here, because it is contained elsewhere in their histories.

# The History of the Waldensians.
<meta>catchword: vera-</meta>

<margin>1570.</margin>
The extremity that came upon them occurred in the year 1570. For their **Prince** <note>Duke Emmanuel Philibert of Savoy</note>, having then committed and entered himself into an **offensive league** <note>A military alliance between Catholic powers intended to suppress the Protestant Reformation across Europe</note> or treaty against the Protestants—joined by many other Princes of Europe—also began to harass his aforementioned subjects in the Waldensian Valleys. ...ven Copin, sitting at the table in his lodgings during supper time with many other merchants, there was one among them who began to speak of the diversity of religions. He said many things that tended toward the shame and dishonor of the Waldensians <note>The Waldensians were a pre-Reformation Christian movement that faced intense persecution for their beliefs, which centered on simplicity and the authority of the Bible.</note> of Angrogna <note>Angrogna is a valley and municipality in the Piedmont region, historically a stronghold for the Waldensian faith.</note> and the surrounding areas. Therefore, he answered this chatterer who proposed such discourse, in favor and defense of his religion. This man, seeing himself rebuked, said to Copin: "Are you then also a Waldensian?" To which Copin answered, "Yes." "Do you then not believe," he continued, "that God is in the Host?" <term>Host: The bread or wafer used in the Christian ceremony of the Eucharist, which Catholic doctrine teaches becomes the actual body of Christ.</term> "Not I," said Copin. Whereupon the other replied, "Then what a false religion is yours." "My religion," spoke Copin, "is as true as it is true that God is God, and as true as I hold it for true that I shall die." The next day after this, Copin was summoned before the Bishop of Asti <note>A city in the Piedmont region of modern-day Italy.</note>, who

<column-break/>

announced to him that he had been informed of the scandalous remarks he had made yesterday evening within his inn; that he must therefore confess his error or fault if he wished to obtain a pardon for it, or otherwise that he would have him punished for it. Copin answered boldly that he had been provoked and called to such a response, and that he had spoken nothing that he would not be willing to **defend, even at the peril of his life: that he had some possessions in the world, also a wife and children, but that he would gladly lose or turn away from the affection and love he bore them, so that he would not love them against his soul and conscience.** And as far as his conduct was concerned, he said further, if the Bishop wished to inquire among the merchants of Asti, they all knew him well and knew that he was a man of honor, and they would give testimony that he had never wronged anyone as long as he had associated and traded among them; and since he was a merchant, he should therefore be permitted to carry out that for which he had come there, namely his trade, without being troubled or harassed.

...be mindful of what I have often set before you, namely that God added fifteen years to the life of King **Hezekiah**: <note>original: "Hiskia"; a reference to the biblical story in Isaiah 38:5 where God miraculously grants King Hezekiah a longer life.</note> but that he has lengthened it much more for me, for it is a long time ago that you saw me as one dead, and yet I am still alive, and I hope, and also hold for certain, that he will preserve me yet longer, so long as it shall serve the honor of his name and the advancement of my salvation, through the grace that he shall grant me. Written from the prison at **Ast**, this 16th of September, 1601.

The **Bishop of Ast** <note>Asti, a city in the Piedmont region of modern-day Italy.</note> was meanwhile very troubled, not knowing what he should do with this man: for if he released him, he then feared the scandal, and that many would embolden themselves to speak openly against the **Roman religion**: <note>referring to Roman Catholicism</note> on the other side, there was a clause in the treaty made between Her Highness on one side, and the **Waldensians** on the other, which exempted and freed them from such faults with these words: *And in the event that they were questioned regarding their faith, being in Piedmont among the other subjects of Her Highness, then they shall be permitted to answer thereupon, without thereby falling into any real or personal punishment.* Since this **Copin** had been brought in first, he had to be declared innocent and free; but the Bishop did not want it said that he had been imprisoned unjustly. So that the blame for this man's death would not be laid upon him,

<column-break/>

and so that he would also not have to set him free and release him, he sent his trial records to **Pope Clement VIII**, to know what he should do therein. Now, what the answer was that the Bishop received from the Pope regarding this has not been discovered; but nonetheless, this man was found dead in prison very shortly thereafter, not without sign and appearance of having been strangled, out of fear that if they had put him to death publicly, he might have edified others <note>meaning to strengthen the faith of others</note> through his confession and steadfastness. Being dead, they sentenced him to be further burned; and for that reason, the body was dragged out of the prison, his sentence was read in the public square, and the body thrown into the fire. Behold, that is then the last of the **Waldensians**, and those who have come to our knowledge, who was persecuted unto death for his faith.

<summary>Barthélemy Copin concludes his final letter to his wife before being found strangled in his prison cell, likely to prevent a public execution from inspiring other Waldensians. Despite his death, his body was publicly burned by the authorities in Asti.</summary>

# The History of the Waldensians.
O 4
<meta>catchword: sen (the end of the word 'onderwesen', meaning 'instructed')</meta>

### The Fifth Chapter.
### Of the Waldensians living in the Valleys of Maties and Meane and in the Marquisate of Saluces, together with the last persecutions they suffered.

In the time when the Waldensians of **Dauphiné** <note>A province in southeastern France.</note> spread themselves through **Piedmont**, there were some who remained in the Marquisate of **Saluces** <note>Saluzzo, a town and former principality in the Piedmont region of Italy.</note> in the Valleys of **Maties** <note>Mattie</note> and **Meane** <note>Meana di Susa</note>, and the places situated around there. These were not spared during the persecutions which their co-religionists from the Valleys of **Angrogne**, **St. Martin**, and others were suffering. Their only refuge then was to flee through the aforementioned Valleys, especially when the Governors of the said Marquisate persecuted them by order of the Kings of France, who condemned to death all those within their Kingdom who in any way agreed with their faith. It is now true that King **Henry the Great** <note>Henry IV of France, who ended the French Wars of Religion.</note> of blessed memory, having granted his subjects an **Edict of Pacification** <note>The Edict of Nantes (1598), which granted religious rights to French Protestants.</note> or of peace, the Waldensians who were then in the said Marquisate enjoyed the same privileges alongside other inhabitants of the realm: but when, by a certain treaty entered into with the **Duke of Savoy**, the land of Bresse was ex-

<column-break/>

changed for the Marquisate of Saluces, the poor Waldensians were deprived of the free exercise of their religion throughout the extent of the Marquisate. For at the insistence of the **Nuncio** <note>A diplomatic representative of the Pope.</note> of Pope **Clement the Eighth**, he not only forbade them the free exercise of their religion, but furthermore, by a new **Proclamation** <note>original: "Placcaet"; an official public decree or edict.</note>, banished all those within the said Marquisate who practiced any religion other than the **Roman** <note>Roman Catholicism</note>. And to ensure that they would immediately have to clear out, a great multitude of Monks were sent to the same Marquisate and the Valleys, who went from house to house, questioning and examining the consciences of every person. After which followed an exile of more than five hundred households, who betook themselves to France, but especially to Dauphiné. And so that in the places where they had departed and settled, they would not be accused of being banished from their land for some villainous acts they might have committed, but rather that it would be recognized that only zeal for their religion had made them wanderers, they published this following declaration in the Year 1603.

Amen.

### The Sixth Chapter.
### Of the Waldensians living in the New Lands, together with the persecution they have suffered.

<margin>1570.</margin>
The "New Lands" mentioned here are situated in the Alpine mountains, on the borders of Piedmont, Dauphiné, and Provence, of which Barcelonnette is the capital city. In these lands there are several villages located in the richest and best parts of this country, and among others one named Jausiers <note>A village in the Ubaye Valley, known for its long-standing Waldensian presence.</note>, which has been inhabited by the Waldensians from time immemorial. These people remained there for a long time without the Princes of Piedmont becoming aware of the presence of this folk within their lands; but the priests brought them into hatred and accused them because they brought the clergy no profit, not living like other peoples who gave them great offerings for the living and the dead. Thus, when His Highness <note>Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy (1528–1580).</note> persecuted those who had abandoned the laws of the Romish Church, these people were likewise not forgotten, especially when the governors of this valley were opposed to them.

These were also among those who, in the year 1576, were ordered and forced to attend Mass or to leave the land of His Highness. In this situation, they judged they could do nothing more profitable than to join with others who, being threatened with similar exile, took refuge with the Protestant Princes. They requested these Princes to speak and intercede for them with their Prince, so that he would not so trouble them for the sake of their faith, in which they had lived from father to child for many hundreds of years. During those centuries, their Princes have had no other subjects who have shown them more faithful obedience than they; declaring that they still did not wish to fall short in their dutiful obligation of submission and the payment of taxes, which they had very gladly paid at all times and given to their Princes. They were still ready to persevere in showing obedience to his commands, if only they might be left unmolested and untroubled in their mind or conscience.

## The Second Book, of the First Part

...showed that only the love of his Master—which he felt for those Christians who shared the same faith as him—had moved him to pray for them; that His Highness might allow them to live peacefully in the practice of their Divine Worship and religion, without coercing their consciences <note>original: "Confcientien"; the internal moral sense of right and wrong.</note>. He argued that his Master and Lord would accept this kindness as if shown to him personally, and by this, the Princes of Germany <note>original: "hoogh duytslant"</note>, who were likewise requesting the same through him, would be greatly indebted to him. Furthermore, God would be merciful to him, and his subjects would be more faithful to him, if he did not show himself relentless in this matter. He noted that the turmoils occurring everywhere in all the states of Kings and Princes—who had sought to subject the very souls of their subjects through weapons, as well as use force to make them return <note>To the Catholic Church.</note>—should have made all other Princes wiser, particularly those who had not yet reached such extremes. More so, since those who had not used such severity had won the hearts of their subjects, causing them to remain all the more loyal. And since he had this same means in his hand, they humbly prayed that he would also choose to follow the examples of those merciful Princes.

It appeared from the answers of His Highness that this intercession was not pleasing to him; this became even more apparent from the consequences or the actions that followed afterward. For he answered: That although he did not inquire nor ask how

<column-break/>

the Prince and Count Palatine of the Rhine <term>Count Palatine: the Elector Palatine, one of the most powerful Protestant rulers in the Holy Roman Empire</term>, nor the other Princes of Germany, were governing their subjects, and that he, being a Sovereign Prince, had to give no account to anyone for his will, pleasure, and motives: nevertheless, he greatly thanked the aforementioned Princes and all others who showed such love toward him, his state, and his subjects, wishing them rest and peace. But he stated that the calamities which had arisen among them from the diversity of Faiths had moved him to desire only one religion in his state—namely, the very one he had found there previously and in which he had been raised. He feared that under the cloak of religion and freedom of conscience, he would still have to dispute with his subjects as if they were his fellows or companions regarding what he possessed by right title as master, just as had happened to various Princes of Europe who, in such dealings, had been unable to keep their subjects under any rule as Sovereigns. <meta>This page continues the Duke of Savoy's response to the intercession of the German Princes. On the previous page, the Duke began explaining his sovereign right to govern his subjects' religion. ### of the History of the Waldensians.

...maintained by a certain Decree <note>original: "Placaet"; an official proclamation or edict.</note>, which he caused to be observed unbreakably. If any wanton spirits seeking novelties were found outside those valleys under his State, he had them punished as rebels. He considered that, just as the aforementioned Princes felt compassion for his subjects to let them enjoy the practice of their religion, he himself was likewise certain that they could not find it wrong (in their excellent fairness and prudent judgment) that he provided for his own security and the preservation of his state by punishing the rebellious. Regarding their intercession, he would further investigate and inquire into the condition of his subjects who made profession of their religion and give them relief.

And because they specifically spoke to him about a certain Minister named Giles <note>Jean Gilles, a Waldensian pastor who had been imprisoned.</note>, whom he kept locked in a certain cave, he had him pulled out from there and placed in a chamber; and after he had taken information regarding the charges—namely, that he had allegedly written to those in Geneva to the detriment of Her Highness <note>Likely referring to the Duchess of Savoy, Margaret of France, who was often more sympathetic to the Protestants than her husband.</note>—he released him.

He also dismissed a certain Castellan <note>A governor or warden of a castle and its surrounding territory.</note> of the Meane valley, not approving of what the same had done against the Waldensians of the aforementioned valley.

<column-break/>

But for the rest, this aforementioned Councilor <note>The envoy returning to the German Princes.</note> was hardly halfway back on his journey when the persecution doubled in intensity, becoming much stronger than before. Among other actions, the Governor of the New Lands <note>Likely referring to the territories of Nice (Nizza), then part of Savoy.</note>, at the end of the following month of November, caused it to be proclaimed by trumpet blast: that all those who within a month did not wish to go to Mass must leave the lands of His Highness within that same time, on pain of losing life and property. In this situation, these poor people could find no way out except at the risk and peril of losing their lives. For in Provence, they burned all those whom the Parliament of Aix had captured, who were then called Lutherans <note>At this time, "Lutheran" was often used as a catch-all term for any Protestant heretic, regardless of their specific denomination.</note>. In the lands of Honoratus, the Count of Tendes, such people were also handed over to the executioners. Gonzaga, the Duke of Nevers, the King's Governor in the Marquisate of Saluces <note>Saluzzo.</note>, likewise put them to death. In Dauphiné, the Archbishop of Ambrun <note>Embrun.</note> let them all rot in foul holes and pits, or let them die of hunger and cold in the Brown or Black Tower—all those he could surprise and get into his hands. They were banished from the land of Piedmont. There was then no other escape left for these people but along and over certain very high mountains, almost impossible to climb; and as—

**The Second Book, of the First Part**

...then, being in the heart of winter, covered with snow and ice, in order to reach the Valley of Freissinière <note>A high alpine valley in the Dauphiné region, known as a refuge for the Waldensians.</note> by night, if it were possible.

They then set out together toward this mountain, around the high feast of Christmas, during the harshest time and weather of the entire year: but before they could reach halfway up the mountain, the greater part of the women and small children were already overcome and half-dead from the cold; and as night took them by surprise on the summit of this mountain, they were forced to remain lying there on the ice, where a great many of them had already died by the following day. The others, who escaped this danger and distress, took their leave for the Valleys of Freissinière. After the houses of these poor people had remained uninhabited and empty for a long time, no one nevertheless wanted to take over their houses and estates, much less build upon them. Therefore, the Governors permitted the same Waldensians to return and live there, and they were thus endured and tolerated in the confession of their faith; but if they wished to enjoy the practice of their religion, they had to travel for that reason outside the State or jurisdiction of their Prince. And כך the valley was resettled with people once more. This is all that we have found and learned of them, although they were also persecuted from father to son, and from time to time, alongside other Waldensians of Dauphiné and Piedmont: but the trial records <term>Processen</term> <note>original: "Processen"; refers to the official legal documents and transcripts of the inquisitorial trials.</note> regarding this have not come into our hands.

### The Seventh Chapter.
### Concerning the Waldensians in Calabria, as well as the persecutions they suffered.

<margin>1370.</margin>
**A**round the year of our Lord 1370, the Waldensians of Pragela and Dauphiné found themselves bound in such great numbers within a narrow and cramped land: that out of necessity, they had to give permission to a certain number of their young people to go search for some other regions that might be suitable to live in, and to cultivate and work the land. These people found uncultivated and poorly inhabited land in Calabria, which was nevertheless fertile, as they judged from the surrounding lands. Seeing then that the land was fit to bring forth wheat, wine, olives, oil <note>original: "Olpe"; likely a transcription error for "Olie" (oil) or referring to legumes.</note>, and chestnuts, and that there were mountains suitable for grazing cattle and obtaining wood for easy construction: they approached the Lords <note>The local feudal landowners.</note> of those places to negotiate with them regarding the conditions or terms of their residence within their lands. These same Lords received them kindly and reached an agreement with them, mostly to the advantage of the aforementioned new vassals or subjects, regarding their rights and justice, accord-

### of the History of the Waldensians.

...agreeing, namely, regarding the rents, tithes, tolls, fines, or penalties, in case they might fall into any dispute and wrangling or other failings; after a certain region had been pointed out and designated for them, the greater part of them returned to announce to their elders what they had encountered in a rich land, one well-suited to enjoy an abundance of all kinds of earthly blessings. For this reason, they then obtained from their elders and kinsmen such things as they were given to begin their households. Many of them entered into the state of marriage and took their wives with them, returning together to Calabria, where they built certain small towns, namely: **St. Xist**, **La Guardia**, **Vaccarizzo**, **Rose**, **Argentina**, **St. Vincenzo**, and **Montalto**. <note>These settlements in Calabria became prosperous Waldensian enclaves. Today, Guardia Piemontese still retains traces of the Occitan language brought by these medieval migrants.</note>

The Lords of these lands considered themselves quite fortunate to have met such good subjects, who had made their lands populous and overflowing with all sorts of fruits; but especially because they found them to be honest people, upright of mind, showing them all due duties and proper respect, which one might expect from the very best subjects in the world.

Only the pastors and priests <term>miſpapen</term> <note>Literally "Mass-priests"; a term used here to distinguish Catholic clergy from the Waldensian's own spiritual leaders.</note> complained about them, because they did not live, regarding religion, like other peoples, as none of their children stepped for-

<column-break/>

ward to become priests or Beguines <term>Bagijnen</term> <note>A lay religious order of women who lived in semi-monastic communities; the Waldensians notably avoided sending their children into Catholic religious orders.</note>, nor did they concern themselves with the chanting, wax candles and taper-lights, the ringing of bells, or even the soul-masses <note>Masses performed for the deceased to assist their passage through Purgatory, a practice the Waldensians rejected.</note> that were performed for the deceased. And even though they had built some churches, they nonetheless refused to decorate them with any images, nor did they go on pilgrimages; they had their children taught and instructed by certain schoolmasters who were strangers and unknown men, to whom they showed more honor than to the priests themselves, paying the priests no more than their tithes, according to the agreement they had made with the Lords. Consequently, the priests said it was to be feared that this people must have a peculiar faith which prevented them from binding and mingling further with the native inhabitants, and that they must hold a bad opinion of the **Roman Church**. But the Lords of those places, fearing that if the **Pope** came to notice that a people living so close to his seat was rejecting and despising the laws and institutions of the Roman Church, he might have them rooted out, restrained the pastors so that they would not make complaints against these people, as they were otherwise honest folk who had made the whole land rich,

The same Inquisitor <term>Inquisitor: Dutch "Kettermeester," literally "heretic-master," an official tasked with identifying and punishing those who deviated from Catholic doctrine</term> Panza then departed for St. Agatha <note>Sant'Agata di Esaro in Calabria</note>, where he handed over a large multitude of these people to the secular judge. Furthermore, Pope Pius IV <note>Pope from 1559–1565</note>, seeking their total extermination, also sent the Marquis of Butiane, promising him that if he performed this good service for the Holy See and cleansed the land of Calabria of the Waldensians who had taken firm root there, he would then reward his son with a Cardinal’s Hat. But this Marquis carried out his assignment with little effort. This was because the Inquisitor monks, together with the Viceroy of Naples <note>The representative of the Spanish crown who governed the Kingdom of Naples</note>, had already killed nearly everyone they could catch. Additionally, they had sent the bravest and strongest men away to the Spanish galleys <term>galleys: ships where prisoners were forced to row as a form of grueling and often fatal hard labor</term>, banished the fugitives forever, and either sold or killed the women and children.

<column-break/>

Regarding their ministers <note>Waldensian pastors or "barbes"</note>, the situation was the same. Stephen Negrin was taken to the prisons of Cosenza <note>original: "Cossence"</note>, where he died of hunger. Louis Paschalis <note>original: "Ludovicus Paschalis," a prominent Waldensian preacher</note> followed him there, where he was condemned to be burned alive. Pope Pius IV desired to witness the final punishments and torments of this man—who had maintained and defended the claim that the Pope was the Antichrist <note>A common Protestant and Waldensian identification of the Papacy with the biblical figure of the Antichrist during the Reformation era</note>—and wished to satisfy his eyes with the sight. He therefore attended the execution in person, accompanied by many Cardinals. But this Pope would have surely preferred to be elsewhere, or that Paschalis had been completely mute and speechless, or that the gathered crowd had all been deaf, because Paschalis spoke many things from the Word of God concerning the Pope which greatly displeased him. Thus this man died, calling upon God with such great fervor that the bystanders were deeply moved, while the Pope and the Cardinals ground and gnashed their teeth in spite.

Behold, that is the end of the Waldensians of Calabria, who were thus completely exterminated. For if any of those who fled have returned, they have completely subjected themselves to the laws of the Roman Church, to live according to them.

### The Eighth Chapter.
### Concerning the Waldensians living in Provence, as well as the persecution they have suffered.

The Waldensians living in Provence in the places called Cabrières, Mérindol, La Coste, and other surrounding places, are believed to have originated and descended from the Waldensians living in Dauphiné and Piedmont, as can be shown by the families who bear similar names; among whom some are found who could point out their lineage and migration. These people, for the same reasons previously related regarding those from Calabria, also settled in Provence, namely to somewhat relieve their former Valleys <note>The "Waldensian Valleys" in the Cottian Alps, the ancestral home of this group</note> of the great multitude of people who lived there. And although the region where they settled was entirely desolate at the time of their arrival, they nevertheless made it fertile within a few years through the blessing of the Lord, making it suitable for harvesting wheat, wine, olive oil, chestnuts, and other fruits in great abundance.

The very first persecutions they endured have not come to our knowledge, notwithstanding that today we still find the commissions issued against the Waldensians living in Provence by the Popes or Antipopes <term>Antipopes: rival claimants to the papacy; at this time, several resided in Avignon rather than Rome during the Great Schism</term> who resided at Avignon and lived very close to them; namely, those of the Archdeacon of Cremona, Albert de Capitaneis <note>A legal official and inquisitor notorious for organizing crusades against the Waldensians in the late 15th century</note>, and of the Franciscan monk, François Borelli, who held commissions against them in the year 1380 to gather information against the Waldensians in the Dioceses of Aix-en-Provence, Arles, and Salon. And as they had already departed and were living in that same province in the year 1228, when the Archbishops of Aix, Arles, and Narbonne met in Avignon to assist the Inquisitors <term>Inquisitors: Dutch "Kettermeesters," literally "heretic-masters," officials tasked with identifying and punishing religious dissenters</term> with counsel in the case of the Waldensians—according to what they said then (as was previously related), that the Inquisitors had captured such a great multitude of Waldensians that, far from being able to provide them with food, they could not even provide enough stone and lime to build prisons for them—thus it is certain that the Waldensians of Provence, who lived, so to speak, right at the gates of the Papal Palace and throughout the County of Avignon, were not forgotten. But as we have no specific documents in hand through which we might prove those persecutions in detail, we shall include nothing else here except that for which we have sufficient proof.

<margin>1506.</margin>

Around the year 1506, when this good King <note>Louis XII of France, known as the "Father of the People"</note> was informed that there was a certain kind of people in Provence who did not live according to the ordinances of the Roman Church, and that they were in every way abominable and horrific—allegedly committing many crimes and villainies, the mere memory of which was terrifying—being such that they were accused of the very same things that had formerly been held against the Christians of the early Church. Therefore, he placed the matter in the hands of the Court of the Parliament of Provence to take notice of it and to punish them according to the circumstances and findings of the case. But after that court had been occupied with the matter, and as the King understood that many innocent people were being put to death, he stayed the hands of the court, not wishing them to proceed with their executions until he could know for certain what kind of people these were who had been portrayed to him as such great godless men. To this end, he sent out Mr. Adam Fumée, his Master of Requests, who reported back to him that what he had been told concerning the Waldensians was very far from the truth, since they could not be convicted of any sorcery or adultery; instead, they lived in all things as pious and honest people, doing wrong to no one. They had their young children baptized, and those among them were instructed in the articles of faith and in the commandments of God; they were diligent in hallowing and keeping Sundays; and the word of God was purely taught and explained among them. Likewise, a certain preaching monk named Parvi, who was the King's Confessor and who had also been commissioned by the King in this matter alongside the aforementioned Master of Requests, testified to the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>Vesembecius in his oration on the Waldensians. Having heard these things, the King added an oath, saying: "Indeed, these men are better than me and the rest of my Catholic people." <note>original: "His auditis Rex iureiurando addito, Me, inquit, & cetero populo meo catholico, meliores illi viri sunt."</note></margin>
When the King heard this, he declared with an oath that these people were more pious than he himself and his other subjects who were Catholic. This persecution having been thus halted by King Louis XII, they continued until the time of King Francis, the first of that name. And as there was talk in France at that time of the Reformation in matters and points of religion, they sent two of their Barbes <note>A term for Waldensian pastors, literally meaning "uncles," used to distinguish them from the "Fathers" of the Catholic Church</note>, namely George Morel of Fraissiniere in Dauphiné, and Peter Masson of Burgundy, to Johannes Oecolampadius, a Minister at Basel; to Capito and Martin Bucer at Strasbourg; and to Berthold Haller at Bern, in order to confer and treat with them concerning their faith, as well as to seek advice from them on many points for which they requested further clarification. The letters that Oecolampadius and Bucer wrote to them have been inserted at length earlier in the first book of this History, in the sixth chapter, where it was shown how many great personages among those who made profession of the Reformation...

### The Eighth Chapter.
### Concerning the Waldensians living in Provence, as well as the persecution they have suffered.

The <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval religious movement that preceded the Reformation, following the teachings of Peter Waldo and emphasizing the authority of the Bible.</note> living in Provence—in the places near Cabrières, Mérindol, Coste, and other surrounding areas—are believed to have sprung and descended from the Waldensians living in Dauphiné and Piedmont. This can be demonstrated by the families who bear the same names, among whom some are found who could point out their ancestry and their journey of departure. For the same reasons as previously related concerning those of Calabria, these people also settled in Provence: namely, to somewhat relieve their original Valleys of the great multitude of people who lived there. And although the region where they settled was entirely a wilderness at the time of their arrival, they nevertheless made it fruitful in a few years, through the blessing of the Lord, making it fit for harvesting wheat, wine, olive oil, chestnuts, and other fruits in great abundance.

The very first persecutions which they endured have not come to our knowledge; nevertheless, we still find today the commissions that were issued against the Waldensians living in Provence by the Popes or the <term>Antipopes</term> <note>Rival claimants to the Papacy who resided in Avignon rather than Rome during the Western Schism.</note> who resided at Avignon and lived very near to them. Specifically, there were those of the Archdeacon of Cremona, Albert de Capitaneis, and the Franciscan monk, François Borelli, who held these commissions in the year 1380 to gather information against the Waldensians in the Dioceses of Aix-en-Provence, Arles, and Salon. And since they had already departed and were living in that same Province in the year 1228—when the Archbishops of Aix, Arles, and Narbonne were gathered in Avignon to assist the <term>Inquisitors</term> <note>original: "Kettermeesters," literally "masters of heretics," officials appointed to root out dissent from Church doctrine.</note> with counsel in the case of the Waldensians—it was said then (as has been related before) that the Inquisitors had captured such a great multitude of Waldensians that it was impossible to provide them with food, and they could not even procure enough stones and lime to build prisons for them. Thus, it is certain that at that time the Waldensians of Provence—who were living, so to speak, right before the gate of the Papal Palace and all around the County of Avignon—were not forgotten. However, because we have no specific documents in hand by which we might prove those particular persecutions, we shall include nothing here other than that for which we have sufficient evidence.
