## of the History of the Waldensians.

<margin>1506.</margin>Around the year 1506, when this good King <note>King Louis XII of France.</note> was informed that there was a certain kind of people in Provence who did not live according to the ordinances of the Roman Church, and that they were in every way hideous and abominable, committing many villainies and foul deeds—the mere memory of which was horrific—being the very same things that were once attributed to the Christians of the early Church; he therefore placed the matter in the hands of the Court of the Parliament of Provence, to take notice of it and to punish them according to the circumstances and findings of the case. After the said Court had been occupied with this, and as the King understood that many innocent people had been put to death, he stayed the hands of the same court, not wishing them to proceed with their executions until he had certainly learned what kind of people these were who had been depicted to him as such great godless ones.

<margin>Vesembecius in his oration on the Waldensians.</margin>To this end, he sent out Mr. Adam Fumée, his <term>Master of Requests</term> <note>A high-ranking judicial official who handled petitions and legal reviews for the King.</note>, who reported back to him that what had been told to him regarding the Waldensians was very far from the truth; while they could not be convicted of any sorcery or adultery, they lived in all things as pious and honest people, wronging no one. He reported that they had their children baptized, and that those among them were instructed in the articles of faith and in the commandments of God; that they carefully observed and kept the Sundays; and that the word of God was purely taught and explained among them. Likewise, a certain preacher monk named Parvi, who was the King's confessor and who had also been commissioned by the King in this matter alongside the aforementioned Master of Requests, gave the same testimony.

<column-break/>

Having understood this, the King declared with an oath that these people were more pious men than himself and his other subjects who were Catholic.

<margin>Vesembecius in the oration on the Waldensians: <note>original Latin: "His auditis Rex iureiurando addito, inquit, & cetero populo meo catholico, meliores illi viri sunt."</note> "Having heard these things, the King, adding an oath, said: 'They are better men than the rest of my Catholic people.'"</margin>This persecution having been thus halted by King Louis XII, they persisted until the time of King Francis, the first of that name. And since the Reformation in matters and points of religion was then being discussed in France, they sent two of their <term>Barbes</term> <note>The Waldensian term for their pastors or elders, derived from the word for "uncles" to distinguish them from Catholic "fathers."</note>, namely Georgius Morel of Fraissiniere in Dauphiné, and Petrus Masson of Burgundy, to Johannes Oecolampadius, minister at Basel; to Capito and Martin Bucer at Strasbourg; and to Berthold Haller at Bern, in order to confer and treat with them concerning their faith, as well as to seek advice from them on many points for which they requested further explanation. The letters which Oecolampadius and Bucer wrote to them have been inserted at length earlier in the first book of this History, in the sixth chapter, where it was shown how many great personages among those who made profession of the Reformation...

### The Epistle of the Waldensians of Provence.
### To Master Oecolampadius. <note>Johannes Oecolampadius (1482–1531) was a prominent German-born Reformer based in Basel, Switzerland.</note>

<column-break/>

->Greetings to My Lord Oecolampadius.<-

<note>original: "Salut a Monseigneur Oecolampadio." This left column is translated from the original Occitan/Waldensian dialect.</note>

Because many, in their accounts, have brought it to our ears that in almost all things you are filled with the blessing of His Spirit, as is known by the fruits. Therefore, we have come from a distant region to you with a firmly joyful heart, hoping and trusting much that the said Spirit will enlighten us through you, and will clarify many things for us which are in doubt to us, and firmly covered by the fault of our ignorance and sloth; and this, as I show you, is to our heavy loss and that of the people whom we do not sufficiently teach. So that you may understand at once: we, such as we are, teachers of a poor and small people who have remained for more than four hundred years <note>This "400 years" refers to the Waldensian claim of a continuous tradition of faith dating back centuries before the Reformation.</note> among the most cruel thorns, but yet not without the great favor of Christ, as all the faithful would easily judge; for they have been delivered often by the said favor, when pricked and tormented by the said thorns, so that you may give counsel to us and confirm our weak ones.

<column-break/>

->Salvation be unto you, Master Oecolampadius.<-

<note>This right column is translated from the Dutch version of the letter.</note>

As we have understood from various persons, and the rumor has come to our ears; that God, who is almighty, has filled you with the blessing of His Holy Spirit, as the fruits prove. Therefore we also, from a far-situated province, with a glad and joyful spirit, take our refuge in you, hoping and trusting that the Holy Spirit will enlighten us through your means, and will clarify many matters about which we are doubting, which are as yet hidden from us due to our ignorance and sloth, and—as it is to be feared—to our great disadvantage, as well as that of the people whom we do not sufficiently instruct. For so that you may know once and for all what the truth is: we, such as we are, poor teachers of this small handful of people, have for over 400 years lived in the midst of cruel thorns, and yet not without the great grace of Christ, as all the faithful here may easily testify; for this people has often been delivered through the same grace when they were pricked and tormented by these thorns. Therefore we now come to your lordship to obtain counsel from you and to be strengthened in our weakness.

# The Second Book, of the First Part
### Page 132

...being all similar to the Decree <term>Arrest: A formal legal ruling or judicial decree, in this context from the Parliament of Provence.</term> of King Ahasuerus <note>A biblical king from the Book of Esther.</note>, given at the request and persistence of Haman against the people of God, as is told in the History of Esther. For besides the fact that the summoned men and women, for contumacy <note>Legal defiance or failure to appear in court when summoned.</note> or disobedience, are condemned by that same Decree to be burned alive, and their children and households banished, it was furthermore decided that the village of Mérindol should be made entirely uninhabitable, and that the woods for two hundred paces all around it should be cut down and leveled. All of this was done and decided by Decree without these people ever having been heard.

The King, having been informed of this Decree, sent the Lord of Langeai <note>Guillaume du Bellay, Seigneur de Langey (1491–1543), a French diplomat and soldier tasked by the King to investigate the Waldensians.</note> to Provence to investigate the customs and faith of the Waldensians <note>A medieval Christian movement that sought to follow Apostolic poverty and simplicity; they were later embraced by the Protestant Reformation.</note>. Having understood that these people had been accused of many things of which they were not guilty, King Francis, the first of that name, sent letters of grace. These were not only for their alleged "default"—that is, failing to appear before the court on the appointed day—but also for all others in the land of Provence. By these letters, he expressly commanded the Parliament that they should not henceforth presume to proceed as harshly as they had done in times past. But when these letters were introduced, they submitted a request, seeking to be allowed to answer through an attorney. Francois Chai and Guillaume Armand ap-

<column-break/>

-peared on behalf of all the people and requested in their name that they might be shown from God’s word where they were in error, declaring themselves ready to abjure <note>To formally renounce a belief or heresy under oath.</note> and abandon all heresy if it were shown to them that they had fallen into any. To this end, they submitted their confession of faith in writing, so that if anything were found therein that could be rebuked by Holy Scripture, the specific points they must recant might be pointed out to them. If nothing blameworthy were found, they asked that they no longer be troubled with so many and great persecutions, as it was to be feared that the judges, thinking they were only striking at men, might also be found to be waging war against God in His truth and against those who uphold it. 

But all their requests served no other purpose than to embitter the judges even more; for their judges, being seized by prejudice and firmly believing that these people were heretics, never wished to take the trouble to even inquire if such a thing were true. Instead, they made all their conclusions and sentences in favor of the Papists <note>Original: "Papen," a common contemporary term for Roman Catholics, often used by those in the Reformed tradition.</note> who accused and complained against them. But all their petitions served for nothing else than to embitter their judges even more. For their judges, being preoccupied with prejudice and firmly believing that these people were heretics, never wished to take the trouble to find out if the same were actually true; instead, they made all their conclusions and sentences in favor of the Priests who accused and complained against them. King Francis, being informed of these inhuman cruelties carried out in consequence of the aforementioned Edict <note>original: "Arrest" — referring to the 1540 Edict of Mérindol which ordered the destruction of the Waldensian villages.</note>, was greatly displeased by it. Thus, at the end of his life, being distressed and oppressed by the gnawing of his conscience—principally because everything had been done in his name and under his authority—and being grieved that he himself could not punish those who had shed so much innocent blood before his death, he charged his son Henry to take vengeance for the same.

In consequence of this, after the death of his father, he issued Edicts in the year 1549, by which he took the cause of the Waldensians of Provence upon himself. Yet, nevertheless, no one was strangled and hanged for it except for the Advocate Guerin alone, because he had poorly and falsely informed the King when he dismissed and revoked the first stay of the case against those of Mérindol, from which the execution of the aforementioned Edict of the Parliament of Mérindol followed in the manner previously described. And all the others who were also guilty of these cruelties escaped, solely out of consideration and the notion that it was not fitting or timely to do anything more for the sake of the <note>The term "Lutherans" was often used by 16th-century authorities as a general label for all Protestants and dissenters, regardless of their specific sect.</note> Lutherans.

Regarding the rest who had escaped the terrible murder, some of them moved to Geneva, others to Switzerland and High Germany <note>Southern Germany and German-speaking Swiss regions.</note>; some others remained near their properties, occasionally going there in a stealthy manner to cultivate the land. And so, they gradually returned with their households to their homes, which they repaired and tidied up again during the time when it was permitted to them through the benefit of the edicts. These later became the seed of the very beautiful Churches which are gathered there again today, flourishing in godliness and purity as much as any other Churches in the entire Kingdom of France.

Book II, of Part I
<meta>catchword: Waldensians</meta>

### Chapter Ten.
### Concerning the Waldensians living in Austria, and concerning the persecutions they suffered.

A great number of the Waldensians made their home in Austria, where they were severely persecuted, as is sufficiently evident, even if we had no other evidence than the *Chronicle of Hirsauge*. It is recorded there that around the year 1400, a large number of them were burned in the city of Crema <note>Likely Krems an der Donau in Lower Austria</note>, which is located in that same Duchy of Austria. Furthermore, what caused the persecutors the most suspicion was a certain discourse or story from one of them; while he was being executed in Vienna, the capital city of Austria, he said during his torture that there were more than eighty thousand in that province who held the same faith that he did.

<margin>See the *Chronicle of Hirsauge*.</margin>

Around the year of our Lord 1467, when the Hussites <note>Followers of the reformer Jan Hus in Bohemia</note> established their churches and separated themselves from the Roman Church, they understood that in Austria, near the borders of Bohemia, there were still churches of the ancient Waldensians. They learned that there were excellent and learned men appointed as their pastors and that the teaching of the Gospel was powerful among them. To discover the truth of this matter, they dispatched two of their brothers, or pastors, along with two elders, with the commission

<column-break/>

to learn about the condition of these small groups, as well as the reasons why they said they had separated from the Roman Church, along with their origin and progress. Additionally, they were to report on the conditions and events of their own beginnings in Bohemia, and explain the reasons for which they had likewise separated themselves from the Papal Roman Church. While on their way, having diligently searched for and found these Waldensians, they declared to them how they followed and practiced nothing other than what was ordained by our Savior Jesus Christ and taught by his Apostles, holding themselves entirely to the Institution of the Son of God regarding the Sacraments.

<margin>Joachim Camerarius in the *History of the Churches of the Brethren in Bohemia and Moravia*. P. 104. <note>original: "Ioachimus Camerarius in Hist. de Ecclesiis Fratrum in Bohemia & Moravia. P. 104."</note></margin>

The Waldensians received them with great pleasure, hearing that in Bohemia there were likewise many people who had given glory to God and had abandoned the abuses and idolatries of the Roman Church. They exhorted them in the name of God to proceed in what they had so laudably begun for the knowledge and maintenance of Heavenly truth and the confirmation of good discipline. As a sign of the great joy they received from this, and of the holy company and fellowship they declared they wished to keep with them, they blessed them, praying to God for them and laying hands upon them.

The Waldensians told them how God had miraculously preserved them for many hundreds of years, notwithstanding the very great and many persecutions they had continually suffered. And thereafter, they—the same Bohemian Brethren—let them depart in a friendly and polite manner. These brethren told their own brothers everything they had seen and done on their journey, which gave them an incredible pleasure. From that time on, a holy affection arose between them, to deal with one another for their common edification as often as possible. In consequence of this, the Bohemian Brethren visited the Waldensians in Austria through their letters, making it known to them that they had received a special comfort through the recent dealings held via correspondence. However, just as they did not desire to be accomplices in any of their faults, so they could not remain silent—without showing a lack of love—about those things they found worthy of reproach in them. This was, namely, that they allowed their own weaknesses far too much, while they, after having known the truth, still kept themselves hidden in the Popish churches <note>A term used by reformers to refer to the Roman Catholic Church</note>, attending the idolatries <note>The reformers often used this term to describe the Catholic Mass and the use of religious images</note> which they nonetheless condemned, and thus shamefully desecrating and defiling themselves; for one must believe with the heart, but also confess with the mouth unto salvation. Furthermore, they felt obliged to admonish them regarding the gathering of gold

<column-break/>

and silver; for even if their objective was good—namely, to be able to help one another in times of persecution—nevertheless, because each day has enough of its own burden or oppression, and such anxiety does not befit those who must always look before them and gather for themselves treasures in Heaven, they condemned or rejected that which was found to be excessive in them, and which they might ultimately make the most of or hold as the principal thing.

<margin>
Joachim Camerarius, *History of the Churches of the Brethren in Bohemia and Moravia*, p. 105. <note>original: "Ioach. Camerarius hist. de Eccleſiis Fratrum in Bohemia & Moravia"</note>

The Waldensians in Austria thanked them from the bottom of their hearts for this, praying that they would wish to maintain the same holy affection toward them, and that they would wish to share, on their behalf, that which could serve their fellowship, and that they would wish to choose a time and place to deal more broadly. For, as they had long known their own faults which had been pointed out to them, they had not been able to use proper means against them. But they hoped that together they might take good resolutions, both concerning these and other various matters. When the time was approaching to send to the appointed place where they should meet, they doubted whether the matter might be discovered, and that such danger was to be expected on both sides. Moreover, it was shown to the Waldensians that they had been tolerated, even though there was sufficient knowledge of their faith...

### The eleventh Chapter.
### Of the Waldensians living in Upper Germany, together with the persecutions they suffered, of which we have proof.

<column-break/>

**A**lthough it is the case that immediately after Peter Waldo, with those who followed him to Upper Germany, had appeared, the persecution against them—driven by the Bishops of Mainz and Strasbourg along the Rhine—was so fierce that on one day, and in one fire, eighteen were burned together; yet we find that in the time of Emperor Frederick the Second, around the year 1213, all of Upper Germany, but especially the land of Alsace, was full of Waldensians. The investigation begun against them was so strict and sharp that they had to depart from there secretly and flee to various places to escape the persecution. This flight served to great profit and advantage: for these were so many Teachers, spread out to make the purity of the Faith known to many people.

<margin>
Dubravius in *History of Bohemia*.

He carried out and practiced this charge with extreme cruelty, and that against all sorts of people, without any regard or excuse, indeed even not sparing the Priests, whom he robbed of life and property.

In the year 1391, the monks in Saxony and Pomerania captured the number of four hundred and forty-three Waldensians, who confessed that they had been raised and instructed in their faith by their ancestors from long ago, and that their teachers came from Bohemia.

In the year 1457, the monks, the Inquisitors of the Bishopric of Eichstätt <note>original: "Eisten"</note> in Upper Germany, discovered many Waldensians, whom they put to death. These had among them twelve *Barbes* <term>Barbes: A title for Waldensian pastors, derived from the regional word for "uncle," used to distinguish them from Catholic "Fathers"</term>, who taught and instructed them.

One must not forget nor omit the thirty citizens of Mainz <note>original: "Mentz"</note> who were burned in the city of Bingen because they were known to have the faith of the Waldensians; nor also the twenty-four whom the Bishop of Strasbourg had cast into a fire; nor also that which Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a German Benedictine abbot and historian</note> relates: that the Waldensians confessed at the same time that their number and multitude were so great that they could travel from Cologne all the way to Milan, always finding lodging throughout this long journey with people of their religion, and that their houses had a certain mark on the roofs, as well as around the doors and gates, by which they could recognize them.

For Johannes Maiyerus <note>original: "Iohannes Maiyerus"</note> places him in the order or number of holy men who, through a divine revelation, had predicted many future things that occurred in his time. This same man, preaching and teaching the same doctrine that the Waldensians taught, was captured in Upper Germany by the monks, the Inquisitors, and having been delivered to the secular judge, he was burned at Cologne. This same man made a commentary on the Revelation of John <note>original: "Openbaringe Ioannis"</note>, in which he noted and pointed out many things that were said regarding the Roman Antichrist. ### The Twelfth Chapter.
### Of the Waldensians who have been persecuted in England.

**E**ngland is one of the very first places that was converted through the acceptance of the Gospel; for not long after Waldo had departed from Lyons, there were believers there who were sentenced to death because they were Waldensians, namely eleven years after the scattering and expulsion of the Waldensians from the city of Lyons.

<margin>Matthew Paris in the *History of England* in the aforementioned year 1163. Jean Bass in the *Chronicle of London* 1210. Thomas Walden, Englishman, in the 6th book of the *Sacraments*, book 12, chapter 10, page 204, column 3.</margin>

For Waldo departed from Lyons in the year 1163. And Matthew Paris notes that the monks, the Inquisitors, already had the Waldensians in England banished in the year 1174. And Jean Bass mentions one who was banished within London in England in the year 1210, solely because he was satiated and soaked through <note>meaning: deeply imbued or saturated</note> with the teaching of the Waldensians. Thomas Walden, an Englishman, describes that in the time of Henry the Second of that name, King of England, the Waldensians were severely persecuted there, and that they were then called Publicans <note>original: "Publicanen"; a common medieval term for various "heretical" groups, often those seen as dualists or anti-establishment</note>: And that those in whom no sufficient causes were found to condemn them to death were marked or branded with a glowing key upon their foreheads, so that they might thereby be known to everyone.

<column-break/>

The faith of the Waldensians then became more widely known among the English through the wars that were waged for that reason against the Albigensians; and the more so because—as the Lord of Popelinière has well noted—of the proximity of the lands of Count Raymond of Toulouse and the land of Guienne <note>Aquitaine, which was under English rule during this period</note>, which the English were then possessing, together with the kinship or alliance of the King of England, being the brother-in-law of the said Count Raymond. Through this, the English had good opportunity and occasion not only to give one another mutual help and assistance in their wars, but also to obtain full knowledge of the faith of these same Albigensians—which was the same and one with the faith of the Waldensians—so that from this knowledge they might judge and defend more surely that extreme violence, with great injustice, was being used against them for the cause of religion. From this it happened that the Englishman was often compelled to protect himself against those who, under the cover of religion, attacked and made war upon his lands.

<margin>Popiliniere, in his *History of France* in the 1st book.</margin>

Brother Reinard Lollard was at this time the powerful instrument through whom God wished to be served, so that through exhortations and living examples, the knowledge of this doctrine—for which the Waldensians were delivered unto death—might be shared with the English. This doctrine was accepted by John Wycliffe, as it stands noted in a book dealing with the origin and...

### The Fourteenth Chapter.
### Of the Waldensians who were persecuted in Poland.

Around the year 1330, many people were found in the Kingdom of Poland who confessed to having accepted the faith of the Waldensians. The Bishops there had recourse to the means ordained and established by the Pope for that purpose, namely the Inquisition, through which they delivered many of these people into the hands of the executioners. The author of the *Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth* <note>referring to the work of Matthias Flacius Illyricus</note> writes that he has among his records the formula or the instruction for the Inquisitors <term>Kettermeesters: literally "masters of heretics," the official title for the inquisitorial judges</term> which they used and followed in this persecution.

<margin>Flacius Illyricus in the Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth, page 539.</margin>Vignier relates that upon departing from Picardy, many of those who had been persecuted there moved to Poland.

# The First Book of the History of the Albigensians.

### The First Chapter.

Who the *Albigensians* were, what their faith was, and what people are included under this name of *Albigensians*. When and by whom they were instructed in the same faith; in what high regard their Pastors or Teachers were held; by whom and in what *Councils* they were condemned; how they increased in number; and which Cities and great Lords strengthened and followed their side: For what doctrines the Popes hated them and persecuted them unto death.

<margin>
Rainerius on the Method of Hereticating <note>original: "Rain. de Forma hereticandi"; Rainier Sacchoni was a 13th-century inquisitor who wrote extensively on heretical groups.</note>
</margin>
The Albigensians, who are discussed in these histories, are not different in faith from the **Waldensians** <note>A proto-Protestant movement that began in the 12th century, emphasizing poverty and the Bible as the sole rule of faith.</note>; they are distinct only because of the location and the region of **Albi**, after which they were named due to their residence and origin. The Popes condemned them as Waldensians; their Legates or deputies made war upon them as though they held the faith of the Waldensians; the monk Inquisitors prepared and initiated legal proceedings against them as Waldensians. The common people also persecuted them as such, and they themselves considered it an honor—beyond their knowledge of the purity of the doctrine they held in common with the Waldensians—that this title and surname was extended to them. Consequently, many historians have also called them Waldensians. We shall therefore distinguish them from the Waldensians not because of their faith, but because of the place of

Jacques de Ribera in the Collections of the City <note>original: "Jac. de Riberia in collectaners vrbis"</note>

their residence, and because of the particular wars which they suffered and endured for more than fifty years.
<margin>
Of Toulouse <note>original: "Thoulouzane"</note>
</margin>

Under this name, we also include the subjects of the Counts Raymond of **Toulouse**, both the father and the son, as well as the subjects of the Count of **Foix** and **Comminges**, and all those who followed their side, fought for their religion, and suffered the same persecutions.

They received the faith of the Waldensians shortly after the departure of **Peter Waldo** from Lyon. The instruments used for this work were **Peter de Bruys**, a certain **Henry**, a **Joseph**, an **Espernon**, and **Arnold Hot**, after whom they were later named: **Petrobrusians**, **Henricians**, **Josephists**, **Esperonnists**, and **Arnoldists**. Afterward, the *Abbot* returned to the general chapter. But the Bishop and the two monks remained traveling through the land, preaching for a long time. They converted some of the common or lowly people; but of the great [nobles], there were few who returned to the true faith.

Auxerre on the side of the Bishops; and on the other side, on behalf of the Albigensians, were R. de Bot and Antoine Rivière. Arnold Hot was the Pastor for the Albigensians, who was deemed fit for such a business. Arnold was the first to arrive at the appointed day and place. And after him came the Bishop Eulus <note>Likely Fulk (Foulques), the Bishop of Toulouse.</note>, and the Monk Dominic, a Spaniard <note>Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican Order.</note>, with two legates or representatives of the Pope, namely Pierre de Castelnau <note>original: "Pierre Chastel." A papal legate whose later assassination triggered the Albigensian Crusade.</note> and Raoul de Lust; the Abbot of Candeil, P. Bertrad, Prior of Auterive: also the Prior of Palats, and many other priests and monks.

The Theses or the Propositions put forward by Arnold were these:

### I.
That the Mass, with Transub-

<column-break/>

stantiation <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the literal body and blood of Christ.</note>, is an invention and fabrication of men, and was instituted neither by Christ nor by his Apostles.

### II.
That the Roman Church is not the Bride of Christ, but a Church full of unrest, and one that is drunk on the Blood of the Martyrs <note>A reference to the "Whore of Babylon" in the Book of Revelation, frequently used by Reformers to describe the Papacy.</note>.

### III.
That the Polity <note>The organizational structure or governance.</note> of the Roman Church is neither good nor holy, nor was it instituted or confirmed by Christ.

Arnold sent these propositions to the Bishop, who requested fifteen days' time to answer them, which was granted to him. On the appointed day, the Bishop did not fail to appear, bringing a long and large document. Arnold Hot requested that he be heard in response to it in an open field <note>Meaning a public, accessible space.</note>, saying that he wished to answer everything contained therein with a living voice, asking the listeners not to let it weary them if he were long in doing so, as he was answering a document that was also long. They promised to listen to him with attention without him being disturbed. He then spoke and argued against it at various hours, for four days long, and with such great wonder from the bystanders and such confirmation of his cause, that all these Bishops, Abbots, Monks, and Priests wished they had never...

For he shaped his answers exactly as the articles were set down in the writing itself, all with such order and clarity that the listeners could well understand that even if the Bishop had written much, he had nonetheless proven or concluded nothing that could be drawn to the advantage of the Roman Church against Arnold's propositions.

And this being done, Arnold thereafter requested that, since the Bishops and he himself were bound and held, from the beginning of these negotiations, to confirm and prove their declarations and sayings through the word of God alone, that therefore the Bishops and <term>Priests</term><note>original: "Papen." A term used by Dutch Protestants for Roman Catholic clergy, often with a polemical or derogatory edge.</note> should be charged to prove that the <term>Mass</term><note>The central act of worship in the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, just as they sang it, piece by piece, was instituted by the Son of God, and likewise also sung by his Apostles, from the start or the <term>Introit</term><note>original: "Introitus." The opening chant or prayer of the Mass.</note> of the mass, until the end of the same, or the <note>original: "Ite missa est." The Latin dismissal at the end of the Mass, meaning "Go, it is the dismissal."</note>: But the Bishops could not show that any of the pieces of the same were instituted for that action or such practice by Jesus Christ or his Apostles. Because of this, the Bishops suffered shame and embarrassment. For Arnold had now brought them to the <term>Canon of the Mass</term><note>The most solemn part of the Mass, containing the prayer of consecration.</note>, which they hold to be the principal part of their Mass, and proved that the Mass was then not the Holy <term>Lord’s Supper</term><note>The Protestant term for Communion or the Eucharist, emphasizing its origins in the Last Supper.</note>. For, said he: If the mass were that Supper which the Lord instituted, then after the consecration, all of that would

<column-break/>

remain: which was there in the Lord’s Supper, namely the bread: But in your mass the bread does not remain: for through <term>Transubstantiation</term><note>The Catholic doctrine that the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the actual Body and Blood of Christ during the Mass.</note>, the bread disappears; therefore the mass without the bread is not the Lord’s Supper, where that bread remained.

For Jesus Christ broke the bread.

St. Paul also broke the bread *as* bread.

On the contrary, the Priests break, as they say, not the bread, but the body of Christ.

Therefore the Priests do not do the same thing that Jesus Christ, nor St. Paul, did.

Upon this contradiction which Arnold wished to make between the Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Mass, in order to show that the same was from neither Christ nor his Apostles; the Monks, Bishops, Legates, and Priests departed, without wishing to listen further, fearing that they might cause the bystanders to have such imaginings and reflections as might greatly weaken and disturb their faith in the Mass.

Moreover, how has the Monk been able to know that the Albigensians were defeated, if no judgment or verdict was ever pronounced?

Around the same time, many other disputations were held, such as at **Serignan** and at **Pamiers**: but these served only to deceive the Albigensians; for while and in the meantime as the Bishops of **Toulouse** and the Bishop of **Osma** <note>original: "Onezimonde," likely referring to Diego de Acebo, Bishop of Osma.</note> disputed at Pamiers, and the two Legates with **Arnold** at Montreal, B. de Villeneuve, who was the magistrate and arbiter in the dispute on behalf of the Bishops, announced that nothing

### The Third Chapter.

### The end of the disputations over Religion was the beginning of the wars, stirred up by the Pope and his legates; the pretext of the Pope to proclaim the Crusade against the Albigensians. Count Raymond humbles himself before the legate of the Pope, is scourged by the legate, and deprived by the Pope of the County of Venaissin; he becomes the head of the Army of the Crusade against those of Béziers.

When **Pope Innocent** had his army of the **Crusade** ready and spread it around the lands of the Albigensians, then one disputed no further, except with <term>faggots</term><note>original: "mutsaerden." Bundles of wood used for burning heretics at the stake; the author implies that the time for words had passed and the time for executions had begun.</note>, and the masters and disputants were the **Executioners**, and the Monks, the **Inquisitors**, were the Harpies. With these the Pope was helping himself toward the rooting out of the Albigensians. And this intended Crusade was advanced under the pretext of making war against **Count Raymond of Toulouse**, because of the death of a certain preacher Monk, who was [killed] by the Albigensians.

The **Pope** likewise wrote to all **Christian Princes**, asking that they should prepare themselves to earn the same **pardon** or **indulgences** against the **Albigensians** as they were accustomed to earn when they traveled across the **Sea** against the **Turks** <note>Referring to the Crusades to the Holy Land.</note>. But the **King** answered that he was far too occupied with the war against **Emperor Otto** and **John, the King of England**. "Among the **Barons**," he said, "there are enough who will undertake the journey for the sake of the **Pardon**."

**Count Raymond**, having been warned of what was being built against him in **Europe** at the urging of the **Pope**, sent **Ambassadors** to him and prayed that he would not condemn him unheard, assuring him that he was not guilty of the death of **Brother Peter of Chasteauneuf**, and moreover, that he was certain the **Murderer** had fled to **Beaucaire**. He further complained of the malice of his **Enemies**, who had so falsely informed [the Pope] regarding this **Murder**. But it was all in vain; for before his excuses reached **Rome**, the army of **Pilgrims** <note>In this context, "Pilgrims" refers to the Crusaders who took a vow to fight for the Church.</note> was in

The **Clergy**, who had gathered great multitudes of **Pilgrims** in their **Dioceses**, were the **Bishop of Sens**, the **Archbishop of Rouen**, the **Bishop of Clermont**, the **Bishop of Nevers**, the **Bishop of Lisieux**, the **Bishop of Bayeux** with the **Bishop of Chartres**, and many others; each **Bishop** accompanied by the **Pilgrims** of his jurisdiction, to whom the **Pope** promised **eternal life** in **Heaven**—though he would not have given them a single **farthing** <note>Original: "oortken," a very small Dutch coin.</note> on earth—and that without letting them know that in such wars, more **blows** often fall than **misses** <note>A play on words in the original Dutch between "slagen" (blows) and "misslagen" (misses or mistakes).</note>. This gathering of **Pilgrims** occurred in the **Year 1209**.

In such a state of affairs and circumstances, it was now necessary to set force against force, or at least to come to submission. The latter was considered the easiest, yet also the most perilous. For to go and surrender oneself into the hands of one's **enemy**, and at his discretion, therein lay great danger to be feared. Nevertheless, **Count Raymond** appeared at **Valence** before the **Legate** of the **Pope** named **Milo**.

# The First Book

**Count Raymond** was ordered to strip himself completely naked outside the Church of **St. Gilles**, wearing only linen breeches on his feet, otherwise barefoot, bareheaded, and with his shoulders bare. After this, a stole <note>A liturgical vestment worn by clergy, here used as a symbolic leash.</note> was placed around his neck, and pulling him along by this stole, he was led nine times around the grave of the late **Brother Peter of Castelnau**, <note>original: "Br. Peter van Chasteauneuf." A Papal Legate whose assassination in 1208 triggered the Albigensian Crusade.</note> who was buried there in the same church. Meanwhile, as he walked around the grave, he was scourged with rods held in the hand of the **Legate**. **Count Raymond** protested against this unusual or extraordinary penance imposed upon him for a sin he had not committed himself, for he had not struck the monk dead. But the **Legate** answered that even if he had not killed him himself, nor ordered him killed, nevertheless, because the killing had occurred in his land and because he had not pursued the killers, the murder was deservedly and properly attributed to him. He was told he must satisfy the **Pope** and the **Church** through this humility or penance if he wished to be reconciled with both. He had to be whipped in the presence of **Counts**, **Bannerets** <note>Lords entitled to lead men under their own banner.</note>, **Marquises**, **Prelates**, and a great multitude of people. He was also made to swear over the *Body of the Lord* <note>original: "Corpus domini." The consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note> (as they call it) and certain

</margin>

relics which had been brought there for that purpose, that he would henceforth be obedient to the **Pope** and the **Church** for the rest of his life. Furthermore, he was sworn to wage an eternal, deadly, and irreconcilable war against the **Albigensians** <note>A Christian sect in Southern France deemed heretical by the Catholic Church.</note> until they were completely rooted out or brought to the obedience of the **Roman Church**. Having sworn this solemnly and publicly, though under duress, the **Legate**—to honor him more and to bind him further to keep his oath—appointed him as the head and general commander of the army of **Pilgrims**, <note>term: "Pilgrims" (Pellegrims). The **Legate** did this to drive the **Albigensians** to despair, taking away all hope that they might be helped by the Count, who had not only renounced and abjured their faith but now also held the commission to persecute them.

<margin>Béziers.</margin>For he <note>Count Raymond VI of Toulouse.</note> considered that if he allowed himself to be used against the Albigensians, he would be sinning against his own conscience and showing himself to be an opponent and enemy to those of whom, until that time, he had been a leader and principal protector. By doing so, he would bind himself into an eternal slavery to the **Pope** and his **Legates**. On the other hand, if he attempted to escape from the army of the **Crusaders**, he would give them new cause to persecute him; for in such a case, they would have rightfully pursued him as a perjurer, a relapsed heretic <note>original: "weder vervallen." A technical legal term for someone who fell back into heresy after recanting, often carrying a death sentence.</note>, and a traitor. If he were then captured, he would run the risk of losing his life, his property, and his friends all at once. Yet, if he followed the command laid upon him by the **Legate**, he would then be the instrument of the loss and ruin of **Béziers**, the total destruction of the subjects of his nephew, the **Count of Béziers**, and indeed of his nephew himself.

In this distress of spirit, he chose and resolved to remain in the army of the **Pilgrims** <note>original: "Pellegrims." Crusaders often referred to themselves as pilgrims because they took a religious vow.</note> for a few more days, and then to request leave from the **Legate** to travel to **Rome** to humble himself before the **Pope**, which they could not well refuse him. Meanwhile, the army began to approach the city of **Béziers**. Battering rams, slings, "cats" <note>A 'cat' or 'chatt' was a mobile covered gallery used to protect besiegers as they approached a wall to undermine it.</note>, and breastworks were prepared. The stone-throwers, siege engines, and other tools of war were positioned and made ready to attack and scale the city with a general assault, for which

<column-break/>

such a great multitude of ladders were erected that it was impossible to ward off or withstand the furious attack and violence for which the **Pilgrims** were preparing.

The **Count of Béziers** <note>Raymond Roger Trencavel, the 24-year-old nephew of Raymond of Toulouse.</note> came out of the city and threw himself at the feet of the **Legate Milo**, seeking mercy for the city of **Béziers**. He humbly pleaded that the **Legate** should not punish the innocent and the guilty with the same and equal penalties, which would undoubtedly happen if the city were taken by force (which was easy to do for such a large and powerful army as the one brought there to scale the city from all sides). He argued that much blood would be shed on both sides which could otherwise be avoided; that within **Béziers** there was still a great number of **Roman Catholics** who would all be caught and brought to the same ruin, which was contrary to the intention of the **Pope**, who only wished the Albigensians to be punished. And even if the Legate did not wish to spare his subjects for their own sake, he hoped he would consider the Count's own person, his age, and his profession, seeing as the loss would fall upon him—who was still a minor <note>original: "minderjarich." Though Trencavel was an adult, he is portrayed here as young and deserving of mentorship/mercy.</note> and a very obedient servant of the **Pope**, having been raised in the Roman [faith].

Understanding this, the Catholics sent their Bishop to the Legate <note>The Papal Legate, Arnaud Amalric, who led the crusade.</note> to humbly pray that he would not include them under the punishment of the Albigensians, since they had always adhered to the Roman Church, of which he, as their Bishop, had good knowledge. But the Legate, becoming enraged, declared and protested with terrible threats and high words and oaths that unless everyone in the city confessed their fault and together submitted to the Roman Church, they would all perish by the edge of the sword, without any regard for their Catholic status, age, or sex: For everything would be surrendered to fire and sword. And immediately he ordered that the city be summoned to surrender at his discretion. This being refused, he set all the heavy artillery and war engines in motion, had great stones thrown, and began the assault and general scaling of the walls.

# The First Book

...that the **Count of Béziers** <note>Raymond Roger Trencavel, the 24-year-old Viscount of Béziers and Carcassonne.</note> was still young and a **Roman Catholic** himself, who could also greatly advance the conversion of those who had placed their trust in him.

The **Legate** <note>Arnaud Amalric, the Cistercian abbot leading the Crusade against the Albigensians.</note> requested that the **King of Aragon** <note>Peter II of Aragon, who attempted to mediate the conflict.</note> withdraw for a moment, so that they might deliberate among themselves and consider what course of action would be found best.

Once the King was called back, the Legate informed him that, in view of his intervention and intercession, he would take the Count of Béziers into grace. Therefore, the Count and twelve others of his choosing might leave with their equipment and baggage, as they saw fit. But as for the people who were within the City of **Carcassonne**, they would not leave except at his <margin>Note.</margin> discretion—that is, at his mercy or lack thereof—from which they should nevertheless expect the best, since he was the Pope’s Legate. However, they were required to leave entirely naked—whether they were men, women, maidens, or children—without even a shirt or any covering upon their bodies. Furthermore, the Count of Béziers was to be placed in secure custody, and his goods were to remain the property of the future Lord of the Land, who would be chosen to hold it.

The King of Aragon deemed this treaty unworthy to be presented to the Count of Béziers, yet he nonetheless fulfilled his duty. Having presented and announced these terms, the Count of Béziers told him that he would never surrender under such useless, foul, and unjust conditions, but would instead seek to protect himself and his subjects with the means that God might grant him for that purpose.

The King of Aragon then departed, but not without showing great displeasure at such unjust procedures and actions.

<column-break/>

The **Governor** <note>original: "Stadthouder." Here referring to the military commander of the crusading army.</note> ordered that all the heavy equipment or artillery be brought into play and that the city be taken by force. However, he was forced to witness with great displeasure and distress that a large portion of his **Pilgrims** <note>original: "pelgrims." Crusaders were legally considered pilgrims on a holy journey to earn spiritual rewards.</note> were killed there. For those within the city cast down a great multitude of stones upon them, as well as fire with pitch and sulfur, and boiling hot water. A great multitude of arrows was also seen raining down upon the attackers, so that the earth was covered by them, and the city moats lay filled with the dead bodies of pilgrims. These dead caused an unbearable stench for both the army and the city.

This hard shock or setback caused the remaining Pilgrims to scatter across the fields, as they had now completed their term of **forty days** <note>To earn a full indulgence—the forgiveness of sins—a crusader was required to serve for forty days.</note>, during which they had "earned Heaven." They had no further desire to gain more after such a fine and great victory and conquest, especially as they feared they might exchange their current good fortune for death in battle.

The **Governor** <note>In the Dutch text 'Stadthouder'; here referring to the Papal Legate, Arnaud Amalric, who held supreme authority over the crusading army.</note> being very troubled because his people were reduced to such a small number, and now being entirely without hope of capturing this so weighty and well-situated place—which was needed to quarter those who would hereafter take up the leadership of the Church’s army—he devised the following military ruse, which also succeeded for him. The **King**, having been called back in, was told by the **Legate** that out of respect for his mediation and intercession, he would take the **Count of Béziers** into his grace. Therefore, the Count and twelve others alone might come out with their equipment and baggage, as they saw fit; but as for the people who were inside the **City of Carcassonne**, they would not come out except at his <margin>Note.</margin> discretion—or at "mercy or lack of mercy" <note>This historical phrase refers to unconditional surrender, where the victor has total power over the lives of the defeated</note>—from which they should nevertheless expect the best, since he was the Pope’s **Legate**. The **King of Aragon** considered this treaty unworthy to be presented to the **Count of Béziers**, but nevertheless he fulfilled his duty and discharged himself of the task. Having then presented and stated the terms, the **Count of Béziers** said to him

<column-break/>

that he would never come out on such useless and unjust conditions, but would seek to defend himself and his subjects with whatever means God would grant him.

The **King of Aragon** then departed, but not without showing great dissatisfaction over such unjust procedures and actions.

The **Governor** <note>The Papal Legate, acting as the military commander of the Crusade</note> commanded that all the heavy equipment or artillery should be brought into play, and that the city should be taken by force. But with great displeasure and annoyance, he had to see that a large number of his **pilgrims** <note>original: "pelgrims" — crusaders were legally considered pilgrims and received spiritual indulgences for their service</note> died there. For those from the city threw a great multitude of large stones down upon them, as well as fire with pitch and sulfur, and boiling hot water. A great multitude of arrows was also seen raining down on the attackers, so that the ground was covered with them, and the city moats lay filled with the dead bodies of **pilgrims**. These dead caused an unbearable stench, both for the army and for the city.

This harsh shock or setback caused the **pilgrims** who remained to disperse through the fields, as they had now completed their period of forty days, during which they had earned Heaven <note>A reference to the plenary indulgence granted to crusaders who served for forty days</note>. They were no longer eager to gain anything more after such a fine and great victory and conquest—the more so because they feared that they might trade their good fortune for blows.

The inhabitants of Carcassonne, having learned of the imprisonment of their Lord, burst into lamentation. They were seized with such great dismay and terror that they no longer thought of anything, nor were they concerned with anything except how they might escape. However, all means of flight had been taken from them, and it seemed impossible, for they were surrounded on all sides by trenches and bulwarks, and the fortifications were full of soldiers. While in such distress and consternation, one of them said that he remembered hearing an old man among their ancestors say that within Carcassonne, under the earth, there was a certain canal or conduit <note>The Dutch uses "canal ofte gotier," referring to a secret subterranean passage.</note> so large and wide that many people walking upright could pass through it at once. He said this canal led to the **Castle of Cameret** or **Caberet** <note>The Castles of Lastours-Caberet, a major stronghold of the Albigensian resistance.</note>, located three miles from Carcassonne; if they could find the mouth or entrance to it, then God had prepared and sent them a miraculous deliverance. mouth of the same being found, they all set out together towards nightfall with their wives and children, taking with them only some food, and that for only a very few days. With bitter lamentations, they thus abandoned their houses and furniture, filled with all kinds of goods, and went on an uncertain venture to find the means by which they might escape by fleeing, dragging along their little children and very old people. Furthermore, they were mutually distressed by the miserable crying and untimely wailing of the wives and women. However, the next day they arrived at the aforementioned castle, and from there they were scattered and wandered away from one another—some here, others there—some to **Aragon**, others to **Catalonia**, others to **Toulouse**, and to other cities on their side, wherever it pleased God to lead each one of them.

The next morning, the **Pilgrims** <note>The "Pilgrims" refers to the Crusaders, who took a vow and wore the cross as if on a pilgrimage, though their purpose was military.</note> were greatly astonished because they had heard no noise at all throughout the entire night, and even more so because they saw no one appearing now that it was day. Being therefore in doubt, they moved a little closer to the city walls, fearing that this might be a bait to lure them into a trap <note>original: "int nette te lacken," literally "to lure into the net."</note>. Nevertheless, perceiving nothing that might cause them further concern, they climbed up the breaches or breaks in the walls and entered the city.

### Chapter Six.

The Legate Milo appoints and confirms **Simon de Montfort** as a certain head over the army of the Church; De Montfort accepts this charge; **Count Raymond** is absolved by the Pope; The Count of Béziers dies; The **King of Aragon** is displeased with Count Simon; Many desert Count Simon, withdrawing themselves from his obedience; He requests a new **Crusade** from the Prelates.

THE city of Carcassonne having come under the power of the Legate, he decided to make it a seat of the war and an arsenal or armory against the Albigensians. Therefore, he gathered all the Prelates and Great Lords who were still in

<column-break/>

his army to deliberate on how this war, which they saw would still last a long time, should be managed in the future. Furthermore, he proposed to them that although he deemed it necessary that a Legate or Governor of His Holiness should be constantly present in the army of the Church to confirm everything that occurred there, there must also be a secular head or commander of the war—specifically one who was powerful, wise, brave, and of great authority. This leader would command absolutely in all matters that arose and resolve all military affairs through his wise and prudent management. Since the ecclesiastical or spiritual persons were not capable or fit to lead the armies and conduct the war, they should therefore consult among themselves to cast their eyes upon one of the military lords to whom the conquered lands might be entrusted. Likewise, the management and care of this holy war would be placed upon him until the Pope should provide otherwise.

These nominated and chose the **Count Simon de Montfort** <note>A French nobleman who became the primary leader of the Albigensian Crusade.</note> from near Paris. **Count Simon de Montfort**, being General of the holy army of the Church, lodged himself within Carcassonne with four thousand **Pilgrims** <note>The Dutch *Pelgrims* refers to the crusaders who had taken up the cross; they were technically considered pilgrims on a holy journey.</note> who remained with him from the original great recruitment of three hundred thousand men. Therefore, one had to have willing, paid soldiers for the guarding of this place.

From the court of the King of France, he traveled further to Rome, where he received absolution from **Pope Innocent III** himself, as the Pope alone was able to grant such absolution, having reserved that right for himself. The Pope also received him kindly and politely, and honored him with a very rich and precious mantle and with a ring of great value. Furthermore, he gave him full forgiveness and remission concerning the murder, declaring him sufficiently justified in that regard.

The **Count of Béziers** <note>Raymond Roger Trencavel, who had surrendered Carcassonne to protect his people.</note>, being imprisoned at Carcassonne, died shortly after **Count Simon de Montfort** was placed into possession of his lands. This death was not without great suspicion that he had been poisoned. Count Simon showed himself to be very grieved by this death and had him buried with great pomp in the Great Church of Carcassonne. He ordered the body to be carried with the face uncovered so that none of his subjects should doubt that he was truly dead.

Among other reasons that Count Simon <note>Simon de Montfort, the leader of the Albigensian Crusade.</note> had used to encourage the Pilgrims <note>The Crusaders were often called "Pilgrims" because they took a religious vow and wore the cross on their clothing.</note>, the most prominent was that this place was cursed above all others, because since the year 1180—which was then thirty years ago—no Mass had been celebrated there.

This place was situated on the river Agout, five miles from Carcassonne on the side leading toward Toulouse. The Count of Foix, having received certain news of their arrival, lay in ambush on their path, where he defeated and slew them all, so that no one escaped except a certain Count, who fled at the first encounter to Count Simon to bring him the news. Whereupon Count Simon had the Count of Foix pursued with fourteen thousand men, but in vain: for he had already withdrawn into Moissac <note>Original: Moissacard.</note>.

When this siege had lasted for six months, the city of Lavaur was finally taken by storm and scaling; and everything there was put to the edge of the sword. Except for eighty noblemen whom Count Simon had hanged and strangled, just as Aimery was also hanged on a gallows that was much higher than the others; the Lady of Lavaur was thrown into a pit and then stoned to death within it.

In all this, one reads of no more than a single act of courtesy that the soldiers of Count Simon are said to have shown, namely this: that a certain nobleman, having learned that many women and girls were shut up in a house, requested them from the General, who granted them to him. This nobleman then had them led to safety, healthy and sound, so that they suffered no indignity nor received any villainy <note>A euphemism often used in period accounts to indicate that the women were protected from sexual assault.</note>.

# The History of the Albigenses

We must now return to Count Raymond of Toulouse, who, having returned from Rome with letters from the Pope, sent word to the Legate Milo that he was reconciled with the Pope and that he had received full absolution <note>Formal release from guilt or punishment for sin.</note> or a stay of proceedings from him, and that he had also received gifts from him. However, this is recounted differently in the *Treasury of Histories* <note>Original: "Threſoir der Hiſtorien," a reference to a historical source or chronicle.</note>. For it is stated there that the Pope wrote to the Bishop of Rodez, to Master Milo, and to Master Fredize, that insofar as the Count could sufficiently clear and discharge himself before them regarding the death of Brother Peter <note>Peter of Castelnau, a papal legate whose murder in 1208 was the primary catalyst for the Albigensian Crusade.</note>, as well as regarding the heresy <note>Original: "Ketterijë."</note> of which he was accused, they should then grant him his absolution. This clause gave power back to the Legate to re-examine the Count on these matters, which was nothing other than dragging him back to the beginning of his miseries.

Count Simon <note>Simon de Montfort, the military leader of the Crusade.</note> urged the Legate to proceed in the case of Count Raymond, either condemning and sentencing him or absolving and acquitting him. He did this so that he might know whether to recognize him as a friend or an enemy of the Pope and the Church, and consequently whether to leave him in peace or wage war against him.

The Legate ordered Count Raymond to appear in person, so that he might know once and for all how the Count and his subjects intended to live with him—specifically with Count Simon and the Church.

<column-break/>

Count Raymond replied that neither he nor his subjects had anything to do with those people; since he had made his peace with the Pope, which could not be unknown to the Legate, seeing as he had shown him the Bull <note>A Papal Bull, a formal decree or public letter issued by the Pope.</note>. He insisted that they should therefore leave him unmolested.

Count Simon and the Legate wrote back to him, stating it was necessary for him to come to them to fulfill the requirements of the Bull. To this he replied that he would much rather take the trouble to go to King Philip of France, and to the Emperor, or even back to Rome to the Pope himself, to complain about the injustice they were doing to him, rather than place himself further into their hands.

Since the Legate then noticed that he could not trap him through letters, he decided that he would catch him with the "fox's tail" <note>An idiom meaning to use flattery, cunning, or deceptive persuasion.</note>. They therefore sent Folquet, the Bishop of Toulouse, to him, and instructed him on how he should behave to deceive the Count. Folquet was a very suitable instrument to carry out this premeditated treachery. He went to Count Raymond and insinuated himself into his friendship with feigned protestations of service; furthermore, he showed displeasure and regret over the misunderstanding that had arisen between the Count and the Legate. He declared a wish that he might improve the situation, even at the risk of his own blood, offering him all help and friendship: since he more...

<meta>This page follows the excommunication of Count Raymond VI of Toulouse and details the impossibly harsh conditions—often called the "Articles of Arles"—imposed upon him by the Crusaders, leading to a breakdown in negotiations.</meta>

# The First Book

1. That the Count of Toulouse shall grant leave to all his men-at-arms, without retaining even a single one.

2. That he shall be submissive and obedient to the Church, and moreover repair all damages suffered and pay all costs and burdens incurred.

3. That in all his lands, only two kinds of meat shall be eaten. <note>This restriction was likely a monastic-style dietary penance intended to humble the entire population of the region.</note>

4. That he shall cause to depart from his lands all Heretics <term>Ketters: specifically the Cathars, whom the Church viewed as a major threat</term> and their allies.

5. That he shall deliver into the hands of the Legate and the Count of Montfort all those whom they shall name to him, to do with them according to their will and pleasure; and this within one year.

6. That no one in all his lands, whether noble or common, shall be permitted to wear any clothing of value, other than black and coarse hooded cloaks.

7. That all fortified or strong places and castles suitable for defense belonging to him shall be leveled and torn down.

8. That none of his Noblemen shall be permitted to live in any City or Castle, but shall keep their dwellings in the open country in a farmhouse, like other countryfolk or peasants.

9. That he shall not be permitted to levy any tolls in his lands, except those from ancient times.

10. That every householder shall pay annually to the Governor four Toulouse <term>deniers: a common medieval silver coin</term> or pennies.

11. That whenever the Count of Montfort or any of his people travel through his lands, they shall not have to pay for anything they consume.

12. That having followed and fulfilled all that is written above, he shall be required to travel across the Sea to wage war against the Turks, without returning back here except by command of the Legate.

13. That after the fulfillment of all these things, the Legate and the Count of Montfort would return all his lands and lordships to him, when it should please them.

<column-break/>

Having communicated these Articles to the King of Aragon <note>Peter II of Aragon, who was Raymond’s brother-in-law and initially tried to mediate the conflict.</note>, he deemed them so unjust that he refused to remain in that place any longer. Instead, he advised the Count of Toulouse to mount his horse and leave immediately, fearing they might seize his person and secure him until the Articles were fully carried out, or that they might have him put to death—as they seemed to intend—in order to obtain his property. And since the same King of Aragon had previously advised the same Count Raymond against trusting the Legate or Count Simon any further, he now reproached him for his past carelessness, addressing him in the Gascon language: *They have paid you well.* <note>original: "Pla-bous an pagat"</note>

The Legate and Count Simon, being greatly dissatisfied because this prey had escaped them, realized well that he would no longer allow himself to be ensnared by them. Therefore, they saw that they would have to obtain by force what they had not been able to acquire through their legal sentences.

Count Simon had brought the King of Aragon over to their side, who was his <note>The King of Aragon was the feudal overlord and brother-in-law to Raymond of Toulouse, making him Raymond's most powerful protector.</note> only support on earth, next to God. The manner in which they accomplished this was as follows. The Legate wrote to him, stating that he would obtain very great praise and perform a notable service to the Pope and the Church if he would once more allow himself to be used as a mediator of peace; they humbly begged him for this reason that he would come to *Narbonne*, where they would see to laying or preparing a good foundation for this.

He then traveled there. The first arguments they presented to him were to reconcile the *Count of Foix* with the Church and *Count Simon*. This was a calculated maneuver, undertaken to strip *Count Raymond* of this man's help. Thereafter they stated and made known to him that *Count Simon* desired to live with him as with the best kinsman and friend he had in the world: that to this end he desired to bind himself more closely to him, if he would accept the daughter of *Count Simon* for his eldest son. And they proposed such conditions to him that he granted his son to the same daughter of *Count Simon*.

<column-break/>

For the fulfillment and following this alliance, the King of Aragon gave to Count Simon the possession of the County of Béziers, which he had never before been willing to grant him; nor the land of Carcassonne, which he now likewise received of his own accord. But the very worst thing for Count Raymond of Toulouse and the Count of Foix was this: that they made him swear that he would no longer favor the Albigensians <term>Albigensians: a dualist religious sect in Southern France targeted by the Church during the Albigensian Crusade</term> from then on, but would keep himself neutral in this war of the Church against them.

Count Simon, having obtained that which he desired—namely the alienation of the King of Aragon from the Count of Toulouse and the Count of Foix—seized his opportunity and assailed and attacked both the one and the other with violence.

And because the Albigensians had far too many people in this siege, it was deemed best that Count Raymond should take a portion of the army and go to conquer certain robber-nests <note>original: "roofnesten" – a derogatory term for the small fortified outposts held by the Crusaders that harassed the local countryside.</note> by which the army was being harassed. Count Simon admitted the mistake he had made by allowing himself to be enclosed within Castelnau-d’Arry, as he, being the leader, ought to have been in the field to generally provide and care for what was necessary for the preservation of all those places that stood under his command.

<column-break/>

He then left within this place, with supreme command, a man named Guy de Levis, called the Marshal of the Faith <note>Guy de Levis was one of Simon de Montfort's most loyal lieutenants; the title "Marshal of the Faith" reflects the religious nature of the Crusade.</note>. To break through, Simon made a sortie against the besiegers, letting some troops hold up the fight until he had made his escape.

Count Raymond, having learned that Count Simon had escaped, was therefore very displeased—more for the shame than for the actual harm he imagined. For the rumor had already spread that the General was "in the cage," and that he would not get out of there except bare-headed, with a rope around his neck, crying for mercy. Each leader complained to the other about this: the Count of Foix because they had left him in a cruel fight without sending reinforcements, and Count Raymond because Simon had escaped extreme danger without anyone having realized it.

Finally, they decided to break up the siege because of the approaching winter and a great number of newly-enlisted Pilgrims <term>Pilgrims: This refers to the Crusaders, who were granted the same spiritual indulgences as pilgrims to the Holy Land.</term> who were steadily approaching. They well guessed that Count Simon would not spare them, as he possessed the Pope’s Bull, which stated that they went straight to Heaven if they perished in this war—being as pure of sins as, perhaps, the stick of a poulterer after he has cleaned out the dirty chicken coops with it <note>This is a satirical jab by the author at the concept of Papal indulgences, suggesting the "purity" granted to the Crusaders was as superficial as a stick used to scrape filth.</note>.

Count Simon became entirely defiant and puffed up, mocking all this great and useless preparation of the Albigensians, and especially because they had thus let him...

Count **Raymond** <note>Raymond VI, the Count of Toulouse.</note> pleaded on the other side that the King of **Aragon** should not abandon their cause; he offered him his life and property to fight under his command or to follow him in the war.

The King of **Aragon**, driven by these requests and prayers, and also moved with mercy and compassion for the oppressed, finally took up arms and sent this letter of defiance to Count **Simon** <note>Simon de Montfort, the leader of the Albigensian Crusade.</note> through two trumpeters: "Labor without delay to carry out the Pope's will, or else struggle against your Lord; and if you fall into my hands, you shall pay for it. It is your bounden duty to do as I wish, and I desire that this shall be done before I commit myself to arms for your destruction."

Count **Simon** knew well how to make use of this little letter of defiance: for he sent it to various quarters of Europe, demonstrating through the Bishops and Monks who preached the **Crusade** that from now on, one was not dealing with the Counts of **Toulouse**, **Foix**, and **Cominges**, or the Prince of **Béarn**, but with a mighty King who had set himself up as a head of the **Albigensians**. Therefore, if he were not given extraordinary help, the cause of the Church would be finished; and thus he pleaded with all good Christians, and especially the King of **France**, to come to his aid in this holy war and hour of extreme need.

### of the History of the Albigenses.

On the other hand, the King of **Aragon** has written to the King of **France**, stating that Count **Simon de Montfort** <note>Simon de Montfort was the primary leader of the Albigensian Crusade, known for his military prowess and perceived cruelty.</note> had his soul puffed up and inflamed with many conceits that far exceeded the grasp of his senses and his power: that all his intentions were only adorned and covered with the appearance and cloak of religion, while in truth his objective was solely to be King in deed, and Simon in name alone. He therefore very humbly prayed the King—both through his letters and through his agents—that he himself should not involve himself in this war on one side or the other. This request he also obtained from the King, as it vexed him to see his subjects continually drawn into the bloody war of the **Waldensians** <note>Though the text mentions Waldensians, it refers generally to the various groups targeted by the Albigensian Crusade, including the Cathars.</note>, and that under the pretense and deceit of Papal pardons or placards; as he also saw that such great lords, who were his good friends, were thus troubled by Count Simon.

When Count Simon learned that the King of **France** had made himself neutral, it greatly vexed him, and he knew not where to take refuge except in the threats of the **Legate** <note>The Papal Legate, the official representative of the Pope, who wielded immense power to excommunicate rulers.</note> to excommunicate the King of **Aragon** if he continued to proceed. The Legate sent ambassadors and letters to him, to which the King of Aragon replied in this manner: "Go, quickly now, and tell your master that I shall come to visit him and bring him the answer with ten thousand men-at-arms, and that he should make himself ready to defend; I shall teach him to mock his equals."

<column-break/>

Each one then made himself ready. Count Simon sent to **France** the Archdeacon of **Paris** and Master **James of Vitry** <note>Jacques de Vitry was a prominent theologian and historian who actively preached the crusade against the Albigensian 'heretics'.</note> to preach a Crusade. However, King **Philip Augustus** did not wish to permit that people should be recruited within his kingdom; nonetheless, a great multitude of people set out from **Auvergne**, from **Normandy**, and from around **Lyon**. These pilgrims <note>The term 'pilgrim' was often used at this time to describe those taking up the cross for a Crusade.</note> arrived before the King of **Aragon** had his army ready, which gave Count Simon a great advantage. In the meantime, he captured **Grane**; he also made raids into the **County of Foix**; he captured **Tudelle** in the Albigensian region and murdered all those he found there, without distinction of sex or age. He likewise besieged and won **Saint-Antonin**, and there had thirty persons, being the most prominent of that place, hanged and strangled in cold blood after he had once granted them their lives. Furthermore, he allowed a certain monastery of monks there to be plundered. In addition, he besieged **Penne** and took it by agreement <term>apoinctement (terms of surrender)</term>, as well as **Marmande**; he secured for himself the **Castle of Biron**, situated by the sea.

Those who were at **Muret**, where they saw this game <note>original: "spel"; here used metaphorically to describe the "action" or "play" of the battle.</note> play out from a distance and from beyond the reach of weapons, had among them a monk who attributed all the honor of this remarkable victory to the Crusaders. He claimed that it was obtained through the power of the benediction or blessing which the **Bishop of Comminges** had given over the army of the **Pilgrims** <term>Pilgrims: A term often used in contemporary accounts to refer to the Crusaders, who took vows similar to those of religious pilgrims.</term>, promising the **Pilgrims** Heaven without having to suffer any of the pains of Purgatory; and should they perish, they would be welcomed into heaven as true Martyrs. Furthermore, he claimed that while the battle lasted, all the clergy betook themselves into a church, where they prayed so fervently that their shouting sounded more like howling than praying.

The historian of **Languedoc** also relates that they held a great advantage because they had received the blessing of the Bishops, and also because they had worshipped the wood of the True Cross held in the hands of the **Bishop of Toulouse**.

On the other hand, the **Albigenses** recognized in this an extraordinary proof of God's judgment; namely, that the **King of Aragon**, on this day, looked more to his own power and foresight than to the help of God. But nevertheless, they did not lose heart or cast their courage away, even though they lost fifteen thousand able-bodied men that day. Nor did they despair or lose faith in the justice and goodness of their cause, as theirs was not the first army to be defeated in a righteous dispute, nor was it the first time an unjust and evil cause was supported by victory.

# of the History of the Albigenses.

The city having been given into his hands, and having gathered the **Legate** and the **Bishops** of his retinue in his tent, it was decided there that this city should be handed over to the **Pilgrims** <term>Pilgrims: In this context, the term refers to the Crusaders, who were granted the same spiritual benefits as pilgrims to the Holy Land.</term> for plundering, and that it should be entirely dismantled <note>To "dismantle" a city in the Middle Ages meant to tear down its defensive walls and towers, leaving it vulnerable to future attack.</note>, with the exception of the **Castle of Narbonnes** <note>This refers to the Château Narbonnais, the ancestral castle of the Counts of Toulouse, located on the city walls.</note>. At this time, the new **Legate** of the **Pope** arrived, named **Bonaventura**, along with other **Pilgrims**, namely: the **Bishop of Beauvais**, the **Count of Saint Paul**, the **Count of Savoy**, the **Count of Alençon**, the **Viscount of Melun**, **Mathieu de Montmorency**, and other great lords who accompanied them. The **Legate**, seeing such a great multitude of **Pilgrims**, feared that **Prince Louis** would want to establish order over many places that the **Albigenses** still held, which would then have worked to the disadvantage of the **Pope's** power, under whose name these conquests or takeovers were being made and carried out. For in truth, hardly any of the great Lords were rightfully warred against solely for the sake of religion, seeing as they so often sought refuge with the **Pope** as the source of all their misfortune; this was indeed a poor seeking of help for them, as they never brought anything back from **Rome** but fair words and very harmful consequences.
