The Legate Bonaventura employed similar cunning and deceit against Count Raymond of Toulouse. He advised him to go to Rome, where he might settle his affairs more peacefully with the Pope himself than with Count Simon <note>Simon de Montfort, the military leader of the Crusade</note>; this was said to be all the more necessary because he was charged and accused of causing the death of his own brother, Count Baldwin. Baldwin had been imprisoned at the Castle of Olme in the land of Cahors for bearing arms against Raymond. This deed was of such a nature that it made him hateful before God and men, and his enemies greatly magnified it to incite the Pilgrims <note>term: Pilgrims; here referring to the Crusaders who took a formal vow to fight</note> to come and take revenge. They claimed that Baldwin had been denied a confessor at the end of his life and that he had prayed to God to raise up good Christians to take heed of the wrong done to him by his brother, as if by a second Cain <note>A biblical reference to the first fratricide</note>.

This young Lord had been raised in England until that time, where he could no longer restrain himself; seeing his father at war and in constant infamy, he resolved to involve himself to deliver his father, either through negotiation and agreement or by force of arms.

The case of Count Raymond was debated, pleaded, and weighed before the Pope. The Abbot of Saint-Thibéry likewise defended their cause very courageously. Having returned from Rome, they requested the execution of their Bull from the Legate, demanding the restitution of their lands. But the Legate told them that there were certain restrictions within the same, and that time was needed to settle and bring those matters to an end. He stated that in the meantime, they should allow the good fruits of their improvement or conversion to be seen, and that by so doing, they would obtain what the Pope had ordained, but not otherwise.

When the Counts saw clearly that they had been deceived, they resolved to put their hands back to the work <note>This marks the resumption of armed resistance by the House of Toulouse against the occupying Northern French forces.</note>.

### The Second Chapter.

Simon de Montfort hastens there, and after much fighting, he is finally killed there by a stone thrown by a woman; his army is put to flight.*

The first military campaign and feat of Raymond, son of Count Raymond of Toulouse, was the conquest and capture of **Beaucaire**, which city he mastered. After that, having starved out the castle, Count Simon—being unable to relieve it—made an agreement or accord <note><term>accord</term>: a formal treaty of surrender or capitulation</note> for those who were inside; namely, that they should depart from there carrying only what they could manage of their baggage, equipment, or gear. Count Simon lost a hundred noblemen there, whom he had stationed in a secret ambush near the city; those within the city, having become aware of them, fell upon them and hacked them to pieces.

The young Count Raymond distinguished himself so greatly through his bravery in this siege that he gave Count Simon enough to understand and consider: that his son Amaury would have this young Lord as a thorn in his foot <note>An idiomatic expression meaning a persistent and painful obstacle or source of irritation.</note>, who would cause him as much trouble as his father had caused Simon in his own time.

Following the decision of the Council, the Pope henceforth wrote to him as nothing less than a Monarch, qualifying him or naming him the **Skilled Soldier of Jesus Christ and Invincible Defender of the Catholic Faith.** <note>original: "Ad-extre Gendarme de Iesus Christ: Inuincible propugnateur de la foy catholique." The Pope’s generosity, "cutting wide strips from another man’s leather" <note>An old Dutch idiom meaning to be generous with property that does not belong to you.</note> and giving away that which he had no right to give, caused him <note>Simon de Montfort</note> to travel to the King of France to be placed in possession or ownership of the Duchy of Narbonne, of the County of Toulouse, along with all the lands that the Crusaders or Pilgrims—belonging to the King's fiefs—had won from those whom he called heretics or their supporters. This he indeed obtained from the King. He says that the religious devotion or Christian affection of the people toward him was so constant and so great that there was no one who did not consider himself blessed if he could but touch the hem of his garments.

Through these aforementioned marriages, Count Raymond gained the time and opportunity to assemble his troops and to strengthen himself against a great force. When the Legate <note>A high-ranking papal representative</note>, seeing that Count Simon was very dismayed, spoke to him thus: "Do not be frightened by anything, for we shall very shortly regain the city and murder all the inhabitants and bring them to nothing; and if any Pilgrims should perish in the fight, they shall go to Heaven as Martyrs." He insisted that they should henceforth be certain of this and remain without fear. Upon this, one of the foremost Captains said to him: "You speak very boldly, my Lord Cardinal. And if my Lord the Count believes you, he shall gain little advantage. For you and all the other Prelates of the Church are the cause of all this evil and destruction, and you shall be so even further, if one chooses to believe your sort."

And while the fight was still enduring, the Count of Foix also arrived there with fresh <term>soldiers</term> <note>original: "Chrijchs-volck." Literally "war-folk" or troops.</note>, both from among his own subjects and certain troops of Navarrese and Catalans, who drove the Count of Montfort’s forces in a fury to the banks of the Garonne. There, in astonishment and dismay, they threw themselves in great heaps and sought refuge within the ships, whereby many drowned and smothered in the river. And Count Simon himself, even as he was fully armed, also fell into the water with his horse, so that he had to be pulled out with great effort and labor.

Count Raymond therefore ordained a general assembly at Saint-Sernin <note>original: "S. Saornin." The Basilica of Saint-Sernin was a central religious and gathering point in Toulouse.</note>, where he exhorted the people to thank God for the fortunate beginning of the victory they had obtained

<column-break/>

over their enemies, and told them that they should henceforth be of good courage and hope for improvement. He furthermore exhorted everyone to help build, position, and operate the heavy equipment or artillery against the Narbonnais Castle <note>The Château Narbonnais was the main stronghold and residence of the counts, then held by the Crusaders.</note>, showing that the enemy, by losing this place, would thereby be brought to his complete downfall; and that by capturing it, they would be secured and liberated. Such that in a short time, and in almost no time at all, the rams, <term>culverins</term> <note>original: "Slanger-stucken." Early long-range cannons, named for their serpentine shape.</note>, <term>cats</term> <note>original: "Catten." Mobile wooden galleries or sheds used to protect soldiers while they approached or undermined walls.</note>, stone-throwers, hurling engines, <term>trebuchets</term> <note>original: "Blydden." Massive counterweight siege engines.</note>, and other instruments and heavy equipment which were in use at that time, were made ready. Being provided with all their necessary tackle, they were set against the Narbonnais Castle. **Which caused those inside to tremble greatly.**

Count de Montfort, being on the plain or open field of Montolieu, held counsel and asked how he should behave in such a troublesome siege against such courageous enemies. The Bishop of Toulouse, in order to comfort him, said to him that he must have good courage, for the Lord Cardinal had sent messengers with his letters throughout the whole world to promote help and assistance for him, and that he would therefore very soon have enough folk.

All the open country was hostile to **Count Simon**, resulting in a great famine in his camp. In contrast, everything was in abundance within the city of **Toulouse**. This was, he says, a miraculous event or a wonder: and from it his successors could clearly perceive that they were maintaining and committing an unjust cause. This was not regarding the punishment of those who strayed from the faith, for that was considered a very profitable and praiseworthy thing; but rather because they were oppressing their subjects too much, piling misery upon misery upon them, shaming and dishonoring their wives and daughters <note>The Dutch "schoffierende" implies sexual violence or public humiliation.</note>, in order to oppress and overburden them in every way—even those who fulfilled their guilty duty and showed every devotion of good subjects, sparing no one. Furthermore, they unjustly withheld other people's property from them. Even assuming they had been heretics, as **Montfort** claimed, could they not, in less than the blink of an eye, come to better reflection and improve their lives? But as I believe (he says further), it was ambition or the greed for power which blinded him, as may easily be recognized by the evil treatment and maltreatment, violence and oppression committed by him against the innocent <note>The word "onnosel" here carries the double meaning of "harmless" and "undeserving of harm."</note> people of **Toulouse**, who honored him, cherished him, and wished him well as their Lord. This skirmish and scattering occurred in June, the day after **St. John the Baptist’s Feast Day**, in the year 1218.

But it is also well worth noting in this matter that he was not cast down and brought low until after he had been proclaimed by three different Councils and declared to be the Monarch or Potentate of his conquered lands, as well as the head of the army of the Church, the restorer, the son, servant, and the favorite of the Church, and the protector of the Faith—after he had become worshipped or most highly honored by the people, feared by the great, and the terror of Kings. And see now how, like that ambitious or power-hungry brother-murderer and violator **Abimelech**, who was killed by a piece of a millstone that a woman threw down from a tower, which broke his skull; so this destroyer of many nations, destroyer of cities, swallower of other men's states and goods...

### Chapter Three.

**Count Raymond regains all that Count Simon had taken from him in Agenois; the Count of Foix likewise obtains Mirepoix from Rogier de Leni; the Count of Cominges reconquers the lands that were withheld from him by a certain Joris; prosperous success for the Albigenses in Lauragues; a Crusade of little value after the death of Count Simon; Prince Louis captures Marmande; returns to France after he had summoned the city of Toulouse to surrender.**

### Chapter IV.

**The war of the Albigensians takes on a different appearance, owing to the death of Pope Innocent III, through the change of the Legate, through the passing of Count Raymond of Toulouse, through the death of Raymond the Count of Foix, and of Lady Philippe de Moncade, the mother of the Count of Foix, and the death of the monk Dominic.**

<column-break/>

The Legate Bertrand Bonaventura, having grown weary because of the long duration of the war, and noticing that the danger of it far exceeded the profit and the pleasure, used and put forward as his excuse his extreme old age, wishing to withdraw from the war and return to Rome. Adding to this that **Pope Innocent III** having died, **Pope Honorius** his successor—who had not directed this war through his authority from the beginning, and thus did not know how much was at stake in this war, nor how it ought to be conducted—necessarily had to be instructed by his Legate or Governor regarding its continuation and the great profit that was coming to the Church from it. Bonaventura then prayed the Pope that he would be pleased to deputize another Governor, and furthermore, he pointed out to him that the necessity of this war was such that not only did the loss of all those lands already conquered from the Albigensians hang in the balance—since they would recover them very easily if one did not strengthen themselves against them—but also that it would soon be over for the Roman Church, seeing as the teaching of the **Waldensians** <note>A proto-Protestant movement following the teachings of Peter Waldo, emphasizing poverty and the Bible.</note> and Albigensians was diametrically opposed to the power of the Popes, and was overturning and destroying the institutions of the Church.

Regarding this Crusade, the Legate Bertrand had written to King Philip <note>Philip II Augustus of France.</note> in this manner: "Do not fail to find yourself with all your power and might in the quarters of Toulouse during the month of May in the year 1219, to avenge the death of Count Simon de Montfort; and I shall see to it that the Pope proclaims a Crusade and has it preached throughout the whole world to obtain help and assistance." **The Albigensian war takes on another appearance, due to the death of Pope Innocent III, through the change of the Legate, through the passing of Count *Raymond of Toulouse*, through the death of *Raymond, the Count of Foix*, and of *Lady Philippe de Moncade*, the mother of the Count of Foix, and the death of the *Monk Dominic*.**

Count Raymond of Toulouse died of an illness, mourned more than any other man by his subjects. He was Just, kind, brave, and courageous. His Epitaph, consisting of two Gascon <note>Gascon is a dialect of the Occitan language spoken in southwest France.</note> verses, was this:

> *There is no man on earth, however great a Lord he be,*
> *Who could cast me from my land, had the Church not done so.*

**That is:**
There was no man on earth,
Of power or great Lordly worth,
Who could drive me from my land,
Had the Church not lent a hand.

### Chapter Five.

*Amaury de Montfort has surrendered to King Louis VIII the lands obtained from the Albigensians; the siege of Avignon; the King installs a Governor in Languedoc. War is still waged against the Albigensians, Toulouse is besieged; peace talks held with Count Raymond and the people of Toulouse.*

Amaury de Montfort <note>Amaury VI de Montfort (1192–1241), son of the famous crusader Simon de Montfort, who struggled to maintain his father's conquests.</note> did not have the luck or the prosperity of his father in the war against the Albigensians. For he no longer had King Philip Augustus <note>Philip II of France (r. 1180–1223).</note>, who allowed the recruitment of Pilgrims <note>In the context of the Albigensian Crusade, "pilgrims" referred to the crusaders who took up the cross for a limited term of service.</note>, nor did he have Pope Innocent III, who had ordained the same. Furthermore, there was not a city or village in all of France that had not been filled with widows or orphans by the preceding wars against the Albigensians.

In addition to this, the prelates <note>High-ranking clergy such as bishops and abbots.</note> there likewise frequently had to endure great fear during the harsh battles that commonly occurred there. Many Bishops had left behind their mitres or episcopal hats, and some Abbots their croziers or staffs; so much so that people did not speak of the <term>Crusades: military expeditions sanctioned by the Church</term> or the Crusaders as often as before. This resulted in Amaury being unable to enjoy his acquired lands for a long time. This grieved him, and he hurried to

<column-break/>

France and surrendered to Louis the Eighth of that name, King of France, all the rights and justice that belonged to him in these lands, which the Pope and the Councils of Lavaur, Montpellier, and the Lateran <note>referring to the Fourth Council of the Lateran in 1215</note> had given and granted to him. Therefore, in recognition of this, King Louis made him the Constable of France, which took place in the year 1224.

To establish himself in possession of these lands, King Louis came to Languedoc, passing before the gates of Avignon, where he was not permitted to enter because they were excommunicated or banished for holding to the faith of the Albigensians; for this reason, they had also been given over by the Pope to whoever should first obtain or conquer them. At that time, Avignon was not yet the capital of the <term>Comtat Venaissin: a territory in the Provence region that later became a papal enclave</term> as it is now; but it belonged to the King of Naples and Sicily. The King, being enraged by this refusal, besieged the city stubbornly for eight months, at the end of which they surrendered themselves around the feast of Pentecost in the year 1225.

During this siege, nearly all the cities of Languedoc recognized the King of France through the efforts of Master Amelin, the Archbishop of Narbonne. The King appointed Imbert de Beaujeu as Governor in Languedoc and departed again for France; but on the way, being at Montpensier, he died in December of the year 1226.

### The Second Book

The young Raymond, Count of Toulouse <note>Raymond VII (1197–1249), who spent much of his life fighting to regain the lands his father lost during the Albigensian Crusade.</note>, had committed himself by promise to the King that he would seek his absolution from Pope Honorius <note>Pope Honorius III, who succeeded Innocent III and continued the crusade against the Cathars.</note>, and that he would thereafter be restored to the peaceful possession of all his lands. However, as the King had died in the meantime, he saw that the Kingdom of France had then fallen into the hands of King Louis the Ninth <note>Later known as Saint Louis (r. 1226–1270).</note>, who was still a minor, and under the government and leadership of his mother <note>Blanche of Castile, who served as a powerful and effective regent for her son.</note>. He therefore judged—since he now had to deal with a King who was still a child and with a woman—that he could regain by force what he had surrendered by agreement. This caused him to resolve to take up arms, being strengthened and driven to do so by the help of the Albigensians, his subjects, who hoped to bring their side back to its former power and strength while the minority of the King of France lasted. But they were deceived in their plan. For although Louis the Ninth was a minor, he was nevertheless accompanied by the good fortune of having a mother as wise and prudent as any who had ever lived. For King Louis the Eighth had, before his death, appointed her as the guardian of his son and Governess of the Kingdom, having recognized and known her ability and sufficiency for the same.

Furthermore, Imbert de Beaujeu <note>Humbert V de Beaujeu, a French military commander appointed by the Crown to maintain control in the southern territories.</note> maintained his position in Languedoc; for he took up arms and set himself

<column-break/>

against Count Raymond and the Albigensians. The Queen sent troops to him, by which he conquered the Castle of Bonteque near Toulouse, which had greatly harassed Imbert and those who held his side. All the Albigensians who were inside were put to death. A certain Deacon, along with those who would not renounce their faith, were set apart; these, by order of the same Imbert and of Amelin, the Legate of the Pope <note>Amalric (or Amelin), the Papal Legate who coordinated the spiritual and political efforts of the crusade.</note>, and upon the advice of Guyon, the Bishop of Carcassonne, were all burned alive. They suffered death with a wonderful constancy <note>This "constancy" or steadfastness in the face of fire was often noted by chroniclers, though viewed by the Church as a sign of stubborn heresy rather than true martyrdom.</note>, which occurred in the year 1227. And as the persecution became greater, so also did the number of Albigensians multiply. Noticing this, Imbert de Beaujeu went to the Court to demonstrate that without assistance, he could no longer defend and protect the lands and places that had recently been attached to the Crown and Patrimony of France against the Albigensians and Count Raymond. During his absence, Count Raymond captured the Castle of Sarrazin <note>Castelsarrasin, a stronghold northwest of Toulouse.</note>, which was one of the strongest places Imbert held. And being master of the field, he greatly damaged his enemies.

### Of the History of the Albigensians

Where the Archbishop of Bourges, the Archbishop of Auch, and the Archbishop of Bordeaux, each summoned the Crusaders <note>original: "Pelgrims." Participants in the Albigensian Crusade were legally considered pilgrims, earning indulgences for their service.</note> from their respective districts.

Count Raymond then withdrew into Toulouse, where he was immediately blockaded, and the entire countryside was laid waste until the harvest. Having been driven to the utmost extremity, the Abbot of Grandselve <note>The Cistercian Abbey of Grandselve was one of the wealthiest and most influential in the region of Toulouse.</note>, named Elie Garin, came on behalf of Amelin <note>Cardinal Romano Bonaventura, the Papal Legate (1225–1229), who coordinated the final stages of the crusade.</note>, the Papal Legate, to offer peace to Count Raymond and the inhabitants of Toulouse. Nevertheless, the farsighted clearly noticed that as soon as Count Raymond was snatched and taken from them, he would be used as a tool to persecute them and restore the Inquisition <note>The Medieval Inquisition was formally established in the wake of this conflict to root out the Cathar "heresy" in the Languedoc.</note>; the fires would be lit once more, and they would all miserably perish and be ruined in both body and soul. But the reasoning of such men was outvoted by the untimely cries of the starving common folk, who could not perceive their misfortune until they were already entangled and the noose with which they were to be strangled was around their necks. Furthermore, within Toulouse itself, there was no lack of people who also made Count Raymond afraid, saying that he was no longer dealing with an Amaury de Montfort <note>Son of Simon de Montfort; Amaury was less successful than his father and eventually ceded his claims to the French King.</note>, but with the King of France himself, who was

In the meantime, a ceasefire <note>original: "stil-stant van Wapenen"</note> was granted and conceded to the people of Toulouse. Count Raymond then appeared on the appointed day and at the place, where likewise the Abbot of Grandselve appeared. After many arguments held between them concerning the peace, the Abbot convinced him that he would obtain far more advantage by being in France than in that place. He argued that because the matter concerned the King, the Queen Mother—as guardian and Governess—would have to be present, and that one would achieve more there in a few days than by remaining in the south, where much going and coming would be required that might be lengthy and fruitless. The Abbot pledged himself and his word that, if the Count went there, he would receive nothing but good satisfaction. Being then overcome by such promises, he consented and promised to go to France, wherever it should please the Queen Mother to appear. ## The Second Book

The young Raymond, Count of Toulouse, had bound himself by promise to the King to receive his absolution from Pope Honorius <note>Pope Honorius III (reigned 1216–1227) was a staunch supporter of the crusade against the Cathars.</note>, and that he would thereafter be restored to the peaceful possession of all his lands. But the King having died in the meantime, he saw that the Kingdom of France had then fallen into the hands of King Louis the Ninth, who was still a minor and under the regency and guidance of his mother <note>Blanche of Castile, who served as regent during the minority of her son, Saint Louis.</note>. He therefore considered—since he now had to deal with a King who was still a child and with a woman—that he might regain by force what he had yielded by agreement. This led him to resolve to take up arms, being strengthened and urged to do so by the help of the Albigensians, his subjects, who hoped to restore their side to its former strength and power while the minority of the King of France lasted; but they were deceived in their plan. For although Louis the Ninth was a minor, he was nevertheless accompanied by the good fortune of having a mother as wise and prudent as any who had ever lived. King Louis VIII had therefore, before his death, appointed her as the guardian of his son and Governess of the Kingdom, having recognized and known her ability and sufficiency for the task.

Furthermore, Humbert de Beaujeu <note>Humbert V de Beaujeu was the Constable of France and a key military leader in the Languedoc during this period.</note> maintained his position in Languedoc; for he took up arms and set himself against Count Raymond and the Albigensians. The Queen sent him troops, with which he conquered the Castle of Bonteque <note>Possibly Labécède-Lauragais, which fell in 1227.</note>, situated near Toulouse, which greatly harassed Humbert and those who held his side. All the Albigensians who were inside were put to death. And a certain Deacon, along with those who would not renounce their faith, were set apart; these, by order of the same Humbert and of Amelin, the Legate of the Pope, and following the advice of Guy, the Bishop of Carcassonne, were all burned alive together, suffering death with a marvelous constancy. This occurred in the year 1227. And as the persecution became greater, so also did the number of Albigensians multiply. Noticing this, Humbert de Beaujeu traveled to the Court to demonstrate that without support, he could no longer defend and protect the lands and places that had recently been attached to the Crown and Patrimony of France against the Albigensians and Count Raymond. During his absence, Count Raymond took Castle Sarrazin <note>Castelsarrasin, a strategic stronghold northwest of Toulouse.</note>, which was one of the strongest places held by Humbert. And being master of the field, he caused great damage to his enemies.

But Humbert returned from France in the springtime or early summer of the year 1228, being accompanied by a great army of Crusaders <note>original: "Pelgrims." Participants in the crusade were legally termed "pilgrims" to qualify for spiritual indulgences.</note>, among whom also

### Of the History of the Albigensians

## The Second Book

The young Raymond, Count of Toulouse, had bound himself by promise to the King, that he would go to receive his absolution from Pope Honorius, and that the King would thereafter restore him to the peaceful possession of all his lands. But as the King had died in the meantime, he saw that the Kingdom of France had then fallen into the hands of King Louis the Ninth, who was still a minor and under the government and management of his Mother <note>Blanche of Castile (1188–1252), who served as regent and was renowned for her political skill and firm rule during her son's youth.</note>. He therefore considered—since he now had to deal with a King who was still a child and with a woman—that he might recover by force what he had surrendered by agreement. This caused him to resolve to take up arms, being strengthened and urged to do so by the help of the <term>Albigensians</term> <note>A dualist Christian sect in Southern France, also known as Cathars, who were the targets of this Crusade.</note>, his subjects, who hoped to restore their side to its former power and strength while the minority of the King of France lasted; but they were deceived in their plan. For although Louis the Ninth was a minor, he was nevertheless accompanied by the good fortune of having a mother as wise and prudent as any who had ever lived. King Louis the Eighth had therefore, before his death, appointed her as guardian of his son and Governess of the Kingdom, having found and recognized her capability and sufficiency for the task.

Furthermore, Imbert de Beauieu <note>Humbert de Beaujeu, the Constable of France and lieutenant for the King in Languedoc.</note> maintained his position in Languedoc; for he took up arms and set himself against Count Raymond and the Albigensians. The Queen sent him troops, by which he captured the Castle Bonteque <note>Likely the Castle of Bécède, located near Toulouse.</note>, which had greatly harassed Imbert and those on his side. All the Albigensians who were inside were put to death: and a certain Deacon, with those who would not renounce their faith, were set apart; these, by order of the same Imbert and of Amelin, the Pope's Legate, and upon the advice of Guyon, the Bishop of Carcassonne, were all burned alive, suffering death with a wonderful constancy <note>Original: *volstandicheyt*, meaning steadfastness or unwavering commitment to their faith even in the face of death.</note>, which occurred in the year 1227. And as the persecution grew greater, so also did the number of Albigensians multiply. Perceiving this, Imbert de Beauieu traveled to the Court to demonstrate that without assistance, he could no longer defend and protect the lands and places that had recently been attached to the Crown and Patrimony of France against the Albigensians and Count Raymond. During his absence, Count Raymond took the Castle Sarrazin <note>Castelsarrasin</note>, which was one of the strongest places held by Imbert. And being master of the field, he greatly damaged his enemies.

But Imbert returned from France in the springtime or early summer of the year 1228, accompanied by a large army of Pilgrims <note>In this context, "pilgrims" refers to the Crusaders who took up the cross to fight against heresy, often for a period of forty days.</note>, among whom

# of the History of the Albigensians.

...themselves come to refuse, they shall then be punished as Heretics. And if it is found that they, having taken this oath, have harbored any Heretic, been well-disposed toward them, or given them counsel, they shall be punished with the same penalty ordained by the Council <note>original: *Concilium*</note>.

Likewise, we will and ordain (he says) that if it be found that anyone, being dead, has died a heretic, and if the same be legally proven before the Bishop: then all of his goods shall be confiscated, and furthermore, the houses which they inhabited since the conclusion of the Peace of Paris, or which they shall inhabit from now on, shall be entirely razed to the ground.

That was what they made **Count Raymond** sign and ordain. And at that same time, from then on, they began to destroy and tear them away piece by piece—those whom they could not move or shake even once while they remained united and bound together.

Moreover, to give the Inquisition even greater authority and power, they gathered a Council in Toulouse in the year 1229, in which the Archbishops of Narbonne, Bordeaux, and Auch, and many Bishops and Prelates allowed themselves to be bound. And among other articles concluded there, the following sufficiently proves by what spirit these prelates were driven.

<column-break/>

<margin>The 7th article of the Council of Toulouse.</margin>
We forbid (they say) the laity from reading the books of the Old and New Testaments, only granting and allowing them, for the sake of their devotion, the psalter or some Breviary or book of hours for worship, or the Hours of the Blessed Virgin Mary, if they perhaps desire to have them. Explicitly forbidding them from having those same books translated into the common tongue <note>The "common tongue" refers to the vernacular languages spoken by the people, such as Occitan or French, as opposed to the Latin used by the Church. This was a pivotal moment in restricting direct access to scripture.</note>.

**Pope Gregory the Ninth** also made certain ordinances against the Albigensians at that same time. Specifically, wishing to stop and shut the mouths of the Albigensian pastors—who did not cease to cry out against human institutions <note>The Albigensians often argued that many Church rituals and hierarchies were "human inventions" rather than divine commands.</note>—he ordained: that preaching should be forbidden and unlawful for any and every layperson, of whatever quality or state they might be.

**King Louis the Ninth** likewise issued his placards <note>Official public proclamations or decrees.</note>, which were identical in content to those of Count Raymond. **Emperor Frederick** did the same, whose [edicts] we do not produce here, so as not to be tedious or troublesome to the reader: since they all have one and the same origin in content. Thus, he who has seen one of them has seen them all: for they—specifically the Popes—did nothing else but [compel] Kings, Princes, Emperors, and powers...

## The Second Book

...mighty Lords, to sign what they deemed appropriate, in order to persecute all those who resisted the commands of the Pope. These individuals would not have dared to refuse to sign such things, for fear that the same measures would have been used against them in a different manner.

Once the agreement between the Pope and **Count Raymond** was made and finalized, he was forced to remain in prison until the sums of money mentioned therein were paid in full. Meanwhile, Lord **Peter de Colmieu**, the Legate’s Lieutenant, hurried to **Toulouse** to restore the city to the King’s obedience. He had the city’s walls destroyed and the towers cast down, so that they would no longer have any means to rebel against the King. He also took with him to the Queen Mother, **Jeanne**, the only daughter of **Count Raymond**, who was then only nine years old, so that she might be raised by her until she reached marriageable age <term>marriageable age; original: *honbaer*, meaning of an age fit for marriage</term>, and then be married to **Alphonse**, the brother of King **Louis**. The removal of this young princess greatly distressed all the subjects of **Count Raymond**, clearly foreseeing that such a change of lordship would also cause a change and disturbance of their general peace, as indeed happened.

There still remained the **Counts of Foix** and **Cominges**, along with the **Prince of Béarn**, who were yet to be conquered or drawn in by cunning. The Legate **Colmieu** considered that **Count Raymond** was suited to attempt this final means; he therefore commanded him to admonish the **Count of Foix** through his writing, that he should follow his example, or otherwise resolve to perish miserably. He then wrote to him in a friendly manner <note>original: *vrientelijc*; the catchword "vrient-" at the bottom of the previous page anticipates this word</note> that the friendship and unity which had at all times existed between their Houses obligated him to be concerned for his well-being as much as his own. # of the History of the Albigensians.

...offering friendship, which was namely this: that if he submitted himself to the aforementioned submission and obedience of the Pope and the Church of Rome, he would then and for all time to come release and exempt him from the homage or recognition of vassalage <term>vassalage; the feudal obligation of a subordinate to a lord</term> that he had historically shown him on account of the County of Foix. He likewise prayed him that he would promote the same advantage for the benefit of the Count of Comminges and the Prince of Béarn.

To this the Count of Foix replied that he could not abandon either his side or his faith, especially at such a time when it might give the impression that it happened more out of fear than out of reason. And that much depended on achieving a fruitful change, such as was expected of him: that truth had conquered and drawn him, not the allurements of promises, nor the force of arms. He would therefore await the arrival of a world of Pilgrims <note>In the context of the Albigensian Crusade, "pilgrims" (*pelgrims*) was the common term for the crusading soldiers who took a religious vow to fight.</note> with which he was threatened, and he hoped that God would make the justice of his cause known and make them regret the arrogance of their promise.

Count Raymond was not satisfied with this answer, and much less so the Legate, who devised another means to involve him. Namely this: there were certain of his subjects living within his lands and around the aforementioned County; these men, being terrified by the apprehension or imagination of their ruin, humbly begged him that he might have compassion for himself and his poor subjects, who would undoubtedly be oppressed by this final violence. ...powerful Lords, caused to be signed whatever they deemed appropriate to persecute all those who resisted the commands of the Pope. These individuals would not have dared to refuse signing such documents, for fear that the same measures would have been used against them in another way.

The peace with Count Raymond now being made and finalized, he was required to remain in prison until the sums of money mentioned therein were paid in full. Meanwhile, Lord Peter of Colmieu, the Legate’s Lieutenant, traveled to Toulouse to restore the city to the King's obedience; he ordered the city walls to be destroyed and the towers to be cast down, so that they would no longer have the means to rebel against the King. He also took with him to the Queen Mother <note>Blanche of Castile, who acted as regent for her son, Louis IX.</note>, Joan, the only daughter of Count Raymond, she being only nine years old, so that she might be raised alongside her until she reached marriageable age, at which point she would be married to Alphonse, the brother of King Louis. The removal of this young princess greatly distressed all the subjects of Count Raymond, as they foresaw that such a change in rule would also cause a change and disruption to their general peace, as indeed came to pass.

### The Ninth Chapter.
### The last war led by Trencavel, the Bastard of the Count of Béziers: the progress of the same: the last Crusade against the Albigensians; negotiations between the Legate Amelin and the same Trencavel: End of the war.

The English Historian Matthew Paris <note>Matthew Paris (c. 1200–1259) was a Benedictine monk and chronicler known for his *Chronica Majora*, though he often reported exaggerated figures for distant battles.</note> has written that in the year 1234, arms were taken up again against the Albigensians, and that a great army of Pilgrims <term>Pilgrims: in this context, the term refers to Crusaders who took a vow to fight for the Church</term> came against them, so that they supposedly lost over a hundred thousand people at once, along with all their Bishops who were present in this battle, without a single one remaining or escaping. But he must be poorly informed in this regard. For the Historian of Languedoc, who described the events occurring at this time, makes no mention of this at all; and yet one must believe that he would not have forgotten such an outstanding victory over the Albigensians, whom he hated unto death. It is true that during the time that the Counts of Toulouse, Foix, Comminges, and the Prince of Béarn held their side and were named as their leaders, Trencavel—the bastard son of the Count of Béziers—showed himself as nothing more than a private soldier

<column-break/>

and even one of little standing. But when the Albigensians were abandoned by all support, there were some who stirred up this soldier, telling him that if he would remember the injustice done to his Father—whom they had unrighteously stripped of his lands, treacherously imprisoned, and finally brought to his end by poison—then they would help and assist him. He then took to the field, saying that he wished to avenge his Father’s death and reconquer with the sword all that had been snatched from him through injustice. He was assisted and helped by a number of brave and valiant captains, namely Lord Olivier de Termes <note>original: "Fumees"; likely a transcription error for de Termes, a famous knight of the era</note>, Bernard-Hugon de Serrelongue, Bernard de Villeneuve, and Jordan de Saissac <note>original: "Satiat"</note>, all of whom were impressive and spirited captains who also had great multitudes of people in their service who were devoted and loyal to them. These had already taken the Castles of Montréal, Saissac, Montolieu, Limoux, and others, before the enemy had well noticed his intention or come to be on his guard against it.

Pierre Amiel <note>original: "Melin"</note>, Legate of the Pope and Bishop of Toulouse, being greatly terrified because he saw the side of the Albigensians growing and increasing again, took recourse to the ordinary means of the Pope and his followers and servants; namely, by causing the Pardons and Indulgences <term>Indulgences: grants by the Church claimed to reduce the temporal punishment for sins, often used to recruit soldiers for Crusades</term> for sins to be preached in all haste for all those who would join the Crusade or Cross-bearing

### The tenth Chapter.
#### Many Monks, Inquisitors, or Heresy-masters, and Officers of the Inquisition killed: the reason why: Pope Innocent the Fourth treats the **Count Raymond** unworthily: the **Count Raymond** goes to Rome, and why: He travels to Rhodes, but he dies in Milan.

IN the year 1243, **Count Raymond**, having paid all his fines and having returned to his subjects, some of his countrymen complained bitterly about the unfair procedures and unjust actions of the **Monks**, the **Inquisitors**; specifically that they, without any distinction, bound all sorts of people together and placed them on the same level, tormenting them either as heretics, or as those who were favorable to them, or those connected by blood or other kinship. They were not content with directing their procedures against those who made open confession of the faith of the **Albigensians**, so that under the cloak of the **Office of the Inquisition**, they were committing an exceedingly great robbery and perversion of justice. This report and complaint against the **Inquisitors** or **Heresy-masters** was made to the **Count Raymond** in the presence of five **Inquisitors** and four **Officers of the Inquisition**, namely **Guillaume Arnoldi**, monk and Inquisitor, and two other **Jacobin Monks** <note>Jacobin Monks: Members of the Dominican Order, so named because their first house in Paris was in the Rue St. Jacques.</note>. Therefore, Amelius <note>original: "Amelin." Likely referring to Amelius of Lautrec, the Bishop of Albi and a papal legate.</note> finally realizing that one could not overcome such a man—who, even when he seemed to be safely and firmly shut in, would nevertheless find himself several days' journey outside that place, strengthening himself anew—pleaded with the Count of Foix that he would, through friendly means, bring him back to obedience and service, and enter into negotiations with him for that purpose. This man [the Count of Foix] employed himself in this matter and advanced it, such that he [the subject of the negotiation] promised him to no longer carry arms against the aforementioned Legate, nor against the Roman Church. That was the last resistance and violence that we find to have been carried out by the Albigensians, as well as the last Crusade of Pilgrims that was mounted against them. Afterward, the persecutions were resumed only by the <term>Inquisitor Monks</term><note>Primarily members of the Dominican Order, whom the author later refers to as Jacobins.</note>. Who caused the fires to blaze again much more than before. And this poor people, being so unarmed, was caught one by one; it was impossible for them to survive. And even if they occasionally struck out at the Inquisitors or <term>Heresy-masters</term><note>A literal translation of the Dutch "Kettermeesters," referring to the inquisitorial judges.</note>, laying hands on them, this did not happen except out of necessity and from a feeling of intolerable and extreme violence, of which we have a notable example in the following chapter.

### Chapter Ten.
#### Many Inquisitor Monks or Heresy-masters, and Officers of the Inquisition killed: the cause thereof: Pope Innocent IV treats Count Raymond unworthily: Count Raymond goes to Rome, and why: He travels to Rhodes, but dies in Milan.

In the year 1243. Count Raymond <note>Raymond VII, the last sovereign Count of Toulouse.</note>, having paid all his fines and having returned to his subjects, certain of his countrymen complained greatly about the unfair procedures and unjust dealings of the Inquisitor Monks; namely, that without any distinction, binding all sorts of people together and placing them on the same level, they tormented them either as heretics, or as those who were favorable [to heresy], or as those connected by blood or other kinship. They were not contenting themselves with directing their proceedings against those who were making public confession of the Albigensian faith. In such a way that, under the cloak of the Office of the Inquisition, they were committing an exceedingly great robbery and perversion of justice. # The Second Book

<meta>catchword: To</meta>

Count Raymond of Toulouse: the persecution was continued against the Albigensians until the Gospel was received in France, and then most of these places where the Albigensians had previously lived immediately accepted the <term>Reformation</term><note>The 16th-century religious movement that led to the establishment of Protestant churches. The author suggests a direct lineage between medieval dissenters and later Protestants.</note>.

The change brought by the Lord also changed the condition of the Albigensians. For when Count Raymond had died, Alphonse—the brother of King <term>St. Louis</term><note>King Louis IX of France, who reigned from 1226 to 1270.</note>—took possession of all the lands, goods, and income of the said Count. Consequently, the great hatred and ill-will that the Popes and their clergy bore toward the House of the Count of Toulouse also ceased. And as for the places that, according to the treaty, were to be placed in the hands of the <term>Legate</term><note>A personal representative of the Pope.</note>, it was no longer necessary to insist further on those terms, since this Alphonse—not being under suspicion by the Pope or the Church—peacefully possessed that which belonged to him.

And just as one hand washes the other, so too was Alphonse—having conquered and obtained the goods of Count Raymond through the war the Church had waged against the Count—obliged to promote the honor of the Pope within his lands. To this end, he redoubled the efforts of the <term>Inquisition</term><note>A judicial system established by the Catholic Church to find and suppress heresy.</note>, as the monk <term>Rainerius</term><note>original: "Rainerius." Referring to Rainerio Sacconi (c. 1200–1262), a former Cathar who became a Dominican friar and a prominent inquisitor.</note> (who was himself an Inquisitor in the year 1250) testifies. He left behind a written record of all the forms and methods of procedure, from which we have taken everything written regarding this in the second book of the *History of the Waldensians*.

->**To the honor of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, Creator of all things visible and invisible, and to the honor of the Glorious Mother of God, who has brought to naught and destroyed all Heresies.**<-

We, Guillaume de Gourdon, Captain, <term>Seneschal</term><note>A high-ranking administrative official and judge acting as the King's representative in a province.</note>, or chief judge and governor of Carcassonne and Beziers. Make known to every person: that we, desiring on behalf of our most excellent Lord Philip, by God’s grace the most illustrious King of France, in the region near the Castle of Lombes in the Diocese of Albi, called Realmont, to promote the exaltation of the Catholic Faith and the uprooting of wicked <term>Heresies</term><note>Beliefs or doctrines that contradicted the official teachings of the Catholic Church, specifically referring here to the Albigensian or Cathar movement.</note>, as well as the benefit of our Lord the King and his subjects: and so that also all dens and hiding places of those who believe and are favorable to heretics might be entirely cast out from among these people on behalf of our Lord the King; and principally concerning the innumerable multitude of the children of heretics and fugitives: seeing that the perversity of heretics is so damnable that they must not only be punished in their own persons, but also in their descendants. We have ordained and do ordain measures, that the children of heretics who, of their own will and movement, do not return to the purity of the Catholic faith and the unity of the Church, forsaking their errors, shall in no way be admitted into the city of Realmont to any honor, or public office, or administrative service. Which likewise, in all places and in all things, must be fully observed and maintained regarding the children of those who have fled because of heresies, and who before their death did not convert again of their own will and goodwill. Furthermore, that those who believe, harbor, or are favorable to heretics (after they have been revealed and declared as such by the Church) shall be sent out from the City of Realmont and eternally banished, all their goods forfeited and confiscated, and their children completely excluded from all honors, public dignities, or high offices; unless someone among them should reveal such heretics and allow himself to be used in the service of the <term>Inquisition</term><note>The judicial system and office established by the Church to find, try, and sentence those suspected of heresy.</note> in seeking them out.

# The Second Book

That is the last piece that we have obtained as proof of the persecution against the **Albigensians**<note>A name given to the Cathar religious movement in Southern France, named after the city of Albi.</note>. Although it is certain that they were continually persecuted by the **Inquisition**, their enemies could nevertheless not prevent them from remaining hidden, like glowing embers and sparks under the ashes. They wished and longed to be able to see that over which their descendants have since rejoiced—namely, the freedom to call upon God in purity and freedom of mind, without being forced to adhere to any superstition or idolatry. By teaching their little children in secret in their religion in this manner, the fruit of their holy devotion was finally plucked when it pleased the Lord that the clarity of his **Gospel** should shine and light in the midst of the darkness of the **Antichrist**<note>In the context of this 17th-century text, "Antichrist" is a polemical term used by Protestant authors to refer to the Papacy or the Roman Catholic Church.</note>. For at that time, many were found from those same places who had previously confessed that they accepted the faith of the Albigensians, and who embraced the Evangelical teaching with great desire and longing. This was especially true of the city of **Realmont**, located in **Albigeois**, where the aforementioned lightning bolt <note>The "lightning bolt" refers to the harsh decree of Guillaume de Gourdon mentioned on the previous page.</note> had been shot forth. For notwithstanding the long intervening time in which they were not visibly seen, nevertheless the eternal God did not fail to carry out his work. He showed thereby that he knows well how to keep and preserve his faithful in the midst of the Babylonian confusions, just like diamonds in a dung-heap, or a grain of wheat in the straw and chaff,

<column-break/>

and like gold in the heat of the fire. And even if it were the case that the instruction had not passed from father to child until the time of the **Reformation**, it remains a matter of wonder to note the goodness of God. Many of the inhabitants of these places, upon which the first dew of his grace had descended, have likewise in this latter time been abundantly enriched through his heavenly blessings. This must serve them as a good track and a spur to cause them doubly to love the truth which has been graciously revealed to them, and to bring forth fruit worthy of the same. Just as this should also produce an extreme sorrow and repentance in the places that have cursed, denied, and rejected the same: for God has given them over to a depraved mind and left them in the darkness they loved. He thus punishes the contempt for his word through the denial of it, letting those go down and perish in error who preferred it over the truth.

->of the History, of the Albigensians.<-
n ij

They held the same faith as those who elsewhere were called the **Waldensians**<note>A medieval religious movement, similar to the Albigensians, founded by Peter Waldo; both groups were precursors to the Protestant Reformation.</note>; for their enemies declared and testified to this, and persecuted them as Waldensians. Most of the torments inflicted upon them came from the Popes, whose corruptions they denounced and whose abuses they exposed and brought to light. They defended the **Gospel** in its purity against the Pope and the **Roman Church**, refusing to adhere to the idolatries then in vogue, and above all, the **Mass** and the fabrication of **Transubstantiation**<note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist are substantially changed into the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> or "essential change." They cursed and shook the power and dominion of the Popes, considering it all an abuse, deception, and tyranny. They argued this power did not resemble the humility that is becoming of true Pastors and teachers, nor did it agree with the teaching and the calling of the **Apostles**; rather, it was nothing but sheer excess and pomp, fitting and worthy only of those who love the world and perish along with it. Because of this boldness, by which they rebuked those who believed that they alone—and no one else—had the right to rebuke, they were burdened with slanders. They were denounced as headstrong and wanton people, godless and worldly laymen who had forced themselves into the office of teaching, whereas it was only their place to learn from others in silence and be instructed. And since the Popes had not been able to

<column-break/>

silence them through the commands they had issued, nor had they been able to overcome them or convict them of error through the Word of God, they had them persecuted by **Monks** and **heresy-masters**<note>Original: *kettermeesters*. These were the Inquisitors, specialized officials tasked with identifying and punishing deviation from Catholic doctrine.</note>. These men handed over everyone they could catch from among these people to the secular Judge. But as this process was much too slow to reduce their numbers and see an end to them quickly, the Popes brought forth the sword against them, arming their Cardinals and Governors. They enticed and drew the Kings and Princes of the earth into these bloody wars, offering Heaven as a reward or wage to all those who would take up arms against them for their extermination and wage war for a period of forty days<note>The "forty days" refers to the traditional term of service for a crusader to earn a plenary indulgence, or full remission of sins.</note>. Consequently, many great lords became curious and desired to learn the cause of this irreconcilable enmity between the Pope and his subjects. Understanding that passion and bitterness drove the authorities so far because they were offended by the truth, these lords took up and defended the cause themselves. They saw that the Albigensians' position rested on this logic: that if they were overcome and convicted by the Word of God, they would then give the glory to God. This protection also greatly angered the Popes, who therefore turned their wrath against such Princes and great lords, banning and oppressing these protectors, even to the complete extermination of their houses. That was the origin of the wars.

**D.** Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?
**A.** I believe in him, for the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and he is one person of the Trinity; and according to his Divinity, he is equal to the Father and the Son.
**D.** You believe that God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are three persons. Do you then have three Gods?
**A.** No, I do not have three Gods.
**D.** Nevertheless, you have named three.
**A.** That is by reason of the distinction of the Persons, but not by reason of the essence of the Divinity. For although there are three persons, there is nonetheless only one essence. <note>The text here navigates the complex theology of the Trinity, emphasizing that while the Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct in personhood, they share a single divine "substance" or nature.</note>

**D.** In what manner do you worship and serve God, in whom you believe?
**A.** I worship him through the worship of outward and inward <term>Latria</term>, which is Divine honor. <note>Latria is a theological term referring to the highest form of worship, which is reserved for God alone, as opposed to "dulia," which is the veneration given to saints.</note> Outwardly through the bowing of my knees, through the lifting up of my hands, through prostration, through songs of praise and spiritual songs, through Fasting, and through invocation. But inwardly, I worship through a holy affection and through a will that is ready to do whatever pleases Him; and I serve him through faith, through hope, and through love in his commandments.

**Q.** Whereby must you recognize the church of Christ?
**A.** By the orderliness and fitness of the ministers / and by the people who become partakers of the truth through the ministry.

**Q.** Whereby do you now know the false ministers?
**A.** By their fruits / by their blindness / by their evil works / by their perverse teaching / and by the improper administration of the Sacraments.

**A.** When they, not knowing the truth / which is necessarily required for salvation / maintain human institutions / as commandments.

**D.** By what means is the people recognized who are not in truth in the Church?

**R.** By public sins and by erroneous Faith. For such are to be fled from, so that defilement from them does not occur <note>original: "sozura de lo meseimes"; refers to the spiritual "filth" or "uncleanness" contracted by associating with a corrupt institution</note>.

**D.** Why must you communicate with the holy Church?

**R.** I must communicate with the Church by reason of Substance <note>original: "Substantia"; in this context, it refers to the essential spiritual union of believers</note> through Faith, through Hope, through Charity, and by the observance of the commandments, and by final perseverance in good.

**D.** How many are the ministerial things? <note>These are the outward tools or "means of grace" used by the church ministry.</note>

**R.** Two: the word and the Sacraments.

**D.** How many are the Sacraments?

**R.** Two, that is to say, Baptism and the Eucharist.

**D.** What thing is the third virtue necessary to salvation?

**R.** Hope.

**D.** What thing is Hope?

**R.** It is a certain expectation of grace, and of the glory to come.

**D.** Through what is grace hoped for?

**R.** Through the Mediator Jesus Christ, of whom Saint John says in chapter 1: Grace was made through Jesus Christ. And again: We have seen the glory of him, full of grace and truth, and we all have received from his fullness.

**D.** What thing is that grace?

**D.** Whereby is the people known that in truth is not in the Church?

**A.** Through open sins and through erroneous faith. For one must avoid such people, so that one is not defiled thereby.

**A.** I must have fellowship with the Church in view of its essence <note>Dutch: "wesen"; the essential nature or being of the true spiritual church</note>, through Faith, hope, and through love, and through the keeping of the commandments, and finally persevering in the good.

**A.** Through the Mediator Jesus Christ, of whom St. John says in John 1: Grace is through Jesus Christ. Also, John 1: We have seen his glory, full of grace and truth. And from his fullness we have all received.

### Of the History of the Albigensians.
->Offer-<-

...offerings, through pilgrimages, through invocations, etc., they trust they will acquire grace, which no one is to give except God alone in Christ. And so, laboring in vain, they lose their money and their life—and certainly not only the present life, but the one to come; for which reason it is said, "the hope of the wicked shall perish." <note>original: "l'Esperança de li felon perire"</note>

**D.** And what do you say of the blessed Virgin Mary? For she is full of grace, as the angel testifies: "I greet you, full of grace." <note>original: "plena de gratia"</note>

**R.** The blessed virgin was and is full of grace as pertains to her own need, but not as pertains to communicating it to others. For her son alone is full of grace in terms of participation <note>The text suggests that Christ alone is the source from which others "participate" in or receive grace.</note>, as is said of himself: "and we all have received grace for grace from his fullness." <note>original: "gratia per gratia de la pleneta de luy"</note>

**D.** Do you not believe in the communion of the Saints?

**R.** I believe that there are two things in which the faithful communicate. Some are substantial, some are ministerial. <term>Substantial: relating to the direct spiritual essence of salvation; Ministerial: relating to the outward service and rituals of the church.</term> They communicate in the substantial things through the Holy Spirit in God through the merit of Jesus Christ. But they communicate in the ministerial or ecclesiastical things through the ministries duly performed, such as they are through words, through the Sacraments, through prayers. I believe in both of these communions of the Saints. The first is only in God, and in Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit by the Spirit.

<column-break/>

...through invocation, etc., they trust to obtain grace, which no one can give but God alone in Christ. And so they labor in vain and waste or squander both their money and their life—and truly not only the present life, but the coming one; wherefore it is said that "the hope of the fools shall be lost."

**D.** And what say you of the blessed Virgin Mary? For she is full of grace, as the Angel testifies: "I greet you, full of grace."

**A.** The blessed Virgin has been and is full of grace in herself. But not to share it with others. For her son alone is full of grace, to distribute from it, just as it is said of him in John 1 <note>The source text cites "Ia. 1.", referring to John 1:16.</note>: "we have all received from his fullness, grace for grace."

**D.** You do not believe in the communion of the saints?

**A.** I believe that there are two kinds of things in which the believers have communion. The one is substantial, the other belongs to the ministry. They have communion in the substantial through the Spirit in God, through the merit of Jesus Christ. But in the things that are ecclesiastical or belong to the ministry, they have communion through the lawful exercise of the ministry, namely through the word, through the Sacraments, and through prayer. I believe in both the one and the other of these two kinds of the Communion of the Saints.

# A Declaration which the Waldensians and Albigensians have published concerning the Ten Commandments of the Law of God, which is extracted from a book of theirs titled: *The Book of Virtues*.

The first commandment of the law of God is this. You shall have no strange God before me. Exodus 20, etc. <note>original: "Le Premier Commandament de la ley de Dio es aquest. Non aures Dio strang devant mi Exod. 20. &c." This is written in the original Occitan language used by the Waldensians.</note>

### Explanation of the First Commandment.
->You shall have no other gods before my face.<-

All those who love the creature more than the Creator do not keep this commandment. That which everyone honors and serves more than God, that is their God or in the place of God. And therefore St. Chrysostom says on Matthew: that same evil of which man is a slave, or that which he serves, is in the place of God to him <note>Saint John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was an influential early Church Father; the Waldensians frequently cited such authorities to support their claims of returning to early Christian purity.</note>. If someone now says: "I cannot know when I love God more or less, or the thing that God forbids me to love." That which a person loves least, in case of necessity, is that which he most willingly loses; and that which he loves most is that which he most prefers to preserve and protect. In the same way as a merchant does when in danger of drowning; when he fears death, at which time he gladly throws out his merchandise to save his life, he shows that he loves his life more than his merchandise. In the same way, consider for yourself whether in any circumstance you would rather lose temporal <note>Temporal things refer to worldly, material possessions that exist only within time, as opposed to eternal spiritual matters.</note> things or suffer some damage

<column-break/>

received and suffered in the soul / namely in your money / in your house / or in your cattle / in your wife and children / yes, even in your own body / rather than that you would want to commit any sin / by which you would lose God! If so! then you love God more than all the aforementioned things. But on the contrary, if you would rather sin than lose such temporal things / then you worship and serve such things, truly much more than God / and have become an idolater <note>An "idolatry servant" or idolater, meaning someone who prioritizes worldly things over the divine.</note>. Which the Lord confirms in the Gospel <note>original: "Euangelio"</note>, saying in Luke 14: *If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and also his own life, he cannot be my disciple.* All those who act against this commandment, etc.

### Explanation of the Second Commandment.
->You shall not make for yourself any image, nor any likeness, etc.<-

# A Declaration/ which the Waldensians and Albigensians/ have published regarding the Ten Commandments of God’s Law, which is drawn from a Book of theirs titled:
->The Book of Virtues.<-

The first Commandment of the law of God is this. You shall have no strange God before me. Exodus 20. &c. <note>original: "Le Premier Commandament de la ley de Dio es aquest. Non aures Dio strang devant mi" — this is written in Occitan, the Romance language used by the Waldensians in the Alpine regions.</note>

### Explanation of the First Commandment.
->You shall have no other Gods before my face.<-

All those/ who love the Creature more than the Creator/ do not keep this commandment. That which each person honors and serves more than God/ that is his God, or stands in the place of God. And therefore St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching; the text refers to his commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew.</note> says regarding Matthew, that the very evil to which a man is a slave, or which he serves, is to him in the place of God. Now if anyone says: I cannot know when I love God more or less/ than that/ which God forbids us to love. That which a person loves least/ in a case of necessity/ is that/ which he most willingly loses; and that which he loves most is that/ which he most desires to preserve and protect. In the same way as a merchant does/ being in danger of drowning; when he fears death/ at which time he gladly casts out his merchandise/ to save his life/ so he demonstrates/ that he holds his life dearer/ than his merchandise. In this same way, consider within yourself/ whether in any occurrence you would rather lose temporal things/ or suffer and receive some damage

<column-break/>

to the soul/ namely in your money/ in your house/ or in your cattle/ in your wife and children/ yes even in your own body/ rather than that you would want to commit any sin/ through which you would lose God! If yes! then you love God more/ than all the aforementioned things. But on the contrary, if you would rather sin/ than lose such temporal things/ then you worship and serve such things/ truly far more than God/ and you have become an idolater <note>The term "afgoden dienaer" literally translates to "servant of false gods."</note>. Which the Lord confirms in the Gospel/ saying. Luke 14.

You shall not make any graven or carved image/ whether it be of stone/ wood or of any other matter/ that one can carve or hew into any likeness/ nor also of paintings or in any other manner that it might be. Nor of what is above in heaven/ as are/ the angels/ the sun/ the moon/ and the stars. Nor of what/ is here below on the earth: as are men and other creatures/ just as the Egyptians did <note>The text refers to the ancient Egyptian practice of zoomorphism, where gods were depicted with animal heads.</note>. Nor of what is in the waters: Just as are the fish/ for the Philistines served Dagon <note>Dagon was a major Northwest Semitic deity, often represented by the Philistines as having the body of a fish with a human head and hands.</note>, which was an idol/ that had a head resembling a fish. Nor of what is under the earth: as are the devils, like those of Acheron <note>In Greek mythology, Acheron is one of the rivers of the underworld; here, the author associates it with the dwelling of demons.</note>, who worshipped Beelzebub. You shall not worship them. Showing them outward reverence/ and you shall also not serve them/ with inward reverence. Thus God clearly forbids making any graven image of any thing/ in order to serve it or worship it. And therefore it is a wonder/ that there are still some/ who make likenesses or images/ and that they through their ignorance and against the command of God show their images honor and service/ which belong to God alone.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But there are/ those who say/ that the images are the books of the laity <note><term>laity</term>: Common people who are not members of the clergy. The phrase "images are the books of the illiterate" was a common medieval justification for religious art.</note>/ who not being able to read in books/ can read on the walls.

<margin>Answer</margin>
To whom one may say and answer/ that which the Lord says to his disciples. Matthew 5. You are the salt of the earth. For the life and the conduct or walk of the Pastors, must be, the books of the flocks. Even if one grants/ that the images are books/ then they would still be false and poorly written. For if the laity must take an example of the lives of the saints from these images and likenesses/ so it is certain that the same will be impossible for them. For the virgin (Mary) was an example of humility, of poverty, of purity, and yet they clothe the images of her/ more with garments of pride than of modesty. And thus the laity do not read in their clothes/ humility/ but pride and greed: If they conform themselves to these corrupt and poorly written books. For because the Priests <note>original: "Papen" — a derogatory term for Catholic clergy used by Reformers.</note> and the people of the present time/ are greedy/ proud and excessive/ therefore they have the images painted after their own likenesses. And therefore it is that David says: You think foolishly, that I am like you.

<column-break/>

<margin>Another Objection.</margin>
But there are others who say. We worship the visible images in honor of the invisible God.

<margin>Answer 6.</margin>
Which is false. For if we in truth wish to honor the image of God, by doing good to men/ so shall we honor and serve the image of God/ for the image of God is in every man: but the likeness of God, is not in everyone, but only there/ where the thoughts are pure/ and the soul is kind. But if we truly wish to serve God/ so we must give place to the truth/ that is/ so must we do good to men/ who are created after the image of God. We show God honor/ when we give food to the hungry/ and give drink to those who are thirsty/ and clothe those who are naked. Which being the case/ what

Honor is shown to God, while serving him in wood and stone, when one worships idle, soulless images, as if some divinity dwelt within them, while in the meantime one despises the human being, who is the true image of God. St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) was an important Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching; his name means "golden-mouthed."</note> says in his commentary on Matthew: the blood of God is not painted upon gold, but it is depicted in man. The Emperor's coin is gold: but God's coin is man. Therefore, since it was commanded to the Jews in the Old Law to break all images and likenesses, and that they should listen to no one but God alone, just as it is written in the first book of Kings <note>In the Dutch and many older Bibles, the books of Samuel are called the First and Second Books of Kings.</note>: Samuel spoke to the whole house of Israel: If you return to the Lord with all your hearts, then put away from you the foreign gods, and direct your hearts to the Lord, and serve him alone, so shall he deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines; how much less may we then, who are Christians, stand staring at such signs and images, which the Jews do not do: but we must much more lift up our minds to Christ, who sits at the right hand of God.

<margin>1 Sam. 7:3</margin>

### Explanation of the Third Commandment.

->You shall not misuse the name of the Lord your God, etc.<-

In this Commandment all false swearing of oaths is forbidden, for the confirmation of untruth; also vain swearing, and swearing out of habit: just as it is written, Leviticus 19, etc. The man who often swears shall be filled with wickedness, and the punishment shall not depart from his house. Through the swearing of an oath, one confesses that God knows the truth, and the oath serves to confirm a doubtful matter: for the swearing of an oath is an act of religious service. And therefore those who swear by the elements commit wickedness. And that is the reason why Christ forbids swearing by any thing, to wit, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other thing: but wants our word to be, Yea Yea, Nay Nay, saying that everything that is more than this is of evil. And St. James says in James 5:12: Above all things, brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other thing, so that you do not fall into any condemnation.

<column-break/>

### Explanation of the Fourth Commandment.

->Remember the Sabbath day, etc.<-

Those who wish to celebrate and keep the Sabbath of the Christians, that is, to hallow the Sunday, must observe four things. The first is, to leave off or abstain from all earthly and worldly things. The second is not to sin. The third is not to be idle, so far as good works are concerned. The fourth is to do such works as are profitable to the soul. Of the first it is spoken: Six days shall you labor and do all your work: but the seventh day is the Sabbath or rest day of the Lord your God; then shall you do no work. And in Exodus it is said:

# The First Book of the Third Part

"Keep my Sabbath, for it is holy. He who defiles it shall die the death." And in the Book of Numbers it is written that when one of the children of Israel had found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath, he was brought before Moses. <note>This refers to the episode in Numbers 15:32–36 where a man is executed for gathering sticks on the Sabbath, illustrating the strictness of the Mosaic Law.</note> Moses, looking upon him and not knowing what he should do, heard the Lord speak: "This man shall die the death; the whole multitude shall stone him with stones, and he shall die." They then brought him out of the camp and stoned him, and he died. God willed that the Sabbath should be observed with such great reverence that even the children of Israel did not dare to gather the Manna at that time, even though it was given from Heaven. <note>Manna was the miraculous food provided by God to the Israelites in the desert. On the day before the Sabbath, they were commanded to gather a double portion so they would not have to work on the holy day (Exodus 16).</note>

The second point is: That we must guard ourselves from sins, as is said in Exodus: "Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day," that is, that you observe or celebrate it, diligently guarding yourself from sinning. And therefore St. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), an influential Christian theologian. He argues here that physical labor is less sinful than moral corruption on a holy day.</note> says: that it would be better to farm the land, or to labor and dig on Sunday, than to get oneself drunk or commit any other sins. For sin is a work of slavery, in which one serves the Devil. Likewise, he says that it is better to labor with profit than to wander in idleness; for Sunday was not instituted so that man should abstain from good earthly works and give himself over to sinning, but so that he should give himself over to spiritual works, which are better than earthly ones,

<column-break/>

and that he should then improve himself from the sins he committed throughout the whole week. For idleness teaches much evil. Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), a Stoic philosopher. The Waldensians, like many medieval and Renaissance groups, frequently cited classical philosophers alongside scripture.</note> says that idleness is the burial of a living man.

The fourth point is: To do that which is useful to the soul. Such as thinking upon God, worshiping him with devotion, diligently listening to his commandments and holy teachings. To thank God for all his benefits, to instruct the ignorant, to rebuke the erring, and to avoid all sins for oneself, so that the saying of the Prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Turn away from doing evil, and learn to do well." <note>Isaiah 1:16–17.</note> For rest is not good when it is not accompanied by good works.

Therefore, one must fulfill what is commanded in this commandment because of the honor one owes to Father and Mother; for through them we receive excellent gifts, namely: our being, our upbringing, and our instruction, which we could never

Therefore, first honor your Father who created you, and then your father who begot you, and your mother who carried you in her body and gave birth to you, so that you may live long upon the earth, and that by persevering in good, you may pass from this world into the eternal inheritance.

### Explanation of the Seventh Commandment.

->Thou shalt not commit adultery.<-

Which commandment forbids all unlawful lust, etc. <note>original Occitan: "Loqual Commandament deffend tota non licita cubititia etc." This is the Waldensian dialect of Occitan, the language of the original medieval tracts being translated here into Dutch.</note>
