And [in] 1 Corinthians 5:11: If there is anyone among you who is called a brother and is a fornicator, or a covetous man, etc., with such a one you shall not even eat. Yet one commits fornication and adultery physically, just as there is also a spiritual fornication—namely, when a person separates himself from God.

### Explanation of the Ninth Commandment.

> Thou shalt not bear false witness.

*In this Commandment, not only is the lie forbidden, but every offense.* <note>original Occitan: "En aquest Commandement non es solament deffendu la messogna, ma tota offensa." The author includes the original Waldensian dialect before the Dutch translation.</note>

In this commandment, lying is not only forbidden, but also every kind of damage that can be done to one's neighbor through words or false deeds. For all those who love lies are the Children of the Devil, just as are all those who rob a neighbor’s honor through lying speech, and those who give false testimony for the sake of evil. Through false testimony—as St. Augustine says—three are harmed. First, God, whose presence is despised. Secondly, the judge, who is deceived by the one who lies. And thirdly, the innocent person is harmed, who is oppressed by the false testimony.

In this commandment, it is not only forbidden to lie, but also every kind of harm that can be done to one's neighbor through words or false deeds. For all who love lies are the children of the Devil, as are all those who rob their neighbor's honor through lying talk and who give false witness for the sake of the wicked. Through false witness, as St. Augustine says, three are harmed. First, God, whose presence is despised. Second, the judge, who is deceived by the one who lies. And third, the innocent person is harmed, who is oppressed by the false testimony.

**The First Book of the Third Part**

Slanderers and reputation-thieves <note>original: "faem-roovers," literally "robbers of fame." This refers to those who destroy another's good name.</note> sin against this commandment. The slanderer is compared to an open grave, as David says: *Their throat is an open grave.* <note>original: "Henne kele is een open graf." Reference to Psalm 5:9.</note> There is no grave that is so stinking before God as the mouth of a slanderer. And this is the same thing that St. Ambrose was moved to say: that a thief is more tolerable than a slanderer. For the thief only robs or steals physical goods, but the slanderer robs one of their good name. The slanderer is worthy of being hated by both God and men. The wound of the tongue crushes the bones.

### Explanation of the Tenth Commandment.

->You shall not covet.<-

*In this Commandment, the coveting of all goods is forbidden, etc.* <note>original: "En acquest Commandement es d'effendua la Cubititia de tui li bien etc." This is written in the original Occitan/Waldensian dialect.</note>

In this Commandment is forbidden all kinds of desiring of any of the neighbor's goods, namely: of the housewife, manservant, maidservant, land, vineyards, houses, etc. And the lust of the eyes and of the flesh is also forbidden. The lust of the flesh is like flowing water: but the lust of the eyes is like the earth, because of earthly affections. And just as natural slime and mud arise from earth and water, so likewise from covetousness arises that spiritual filthiness of the soul, which makes man hateful before God. After this follows the pride of life, which blows through the innermost part of the soul like a strong storm wind, by which the soul is turned to ashes; and by that same wind, it is taken away and scattered like the dust of the earth.

<column-break/>

### Conclusion of the Explanation of the Commandments.

*These are the ten Commandments of the law, etc.* <note>original: "Aquesti son li dies Commandament de la ley &c." This is the conclusion of the section in the Waldensian dialect.</note>

These are now the Ten Commandments of the Law. Of which the first [table] ordains what belongs to God, and the others what concerns the neighbor. And whoever wishes to be saved must keep these Commandments. Many excellent blessings are promised to those who shall keep these commandments, and for those who shall transgress the same, many heavy and terrible curses are prepared.

<margin>Deuteronomy 28.</margin>
If it be that we truly confess our sins, then we acknowledge that we are far from God. For salvation is far from sinners, and the knowledge of sin leads to repentance; for no one repents who does not know himself. The first grace toward salvation is the knowledge of sin. And therefore, acknowledging our sins, we approach with confidence to the throne of God's grace and confess our sins before him. For he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all wickedness, and to lead us to the life of grace. Amen.

### The fifth Chapter.

## The explanation which the Waldensians and Albigensians have given concerning the Lord’s Prayer.

St. Augustine, having been requested by a fine spiritual daughter that he would teach her how to pray, wrote and said: That there must not be a multitude of words in prayer, and yet you do not pray any less if you persevere in such an intention. It is praying much when the prayer is fiery. <note>The term "fiery" (vyerigh) here refers to prayer that is passionate, earnest, and filled with spiritual zeal rather than just length.</note> And therefore, speaking much is nothing else than presenting one's necessities with excessive words. To pray much is the same thing for which we pray, requesting it with long-sustained devotion and a heartfelt inclination, which is achieved better through the shedding of tears than through words. Because God, who beholds the most hidden parts of our hearts, is moved more by a sigh, by groaning, and by tears poured out from the heart, than by a thousand words. But many today are like the Heathens, whom Christ did not want his disciples to resemble—namely, those who think and

<column-break/>

believe that they shall be heard much sooner if they use many words in their prayers. Because of this, it happens that they lose much time under the cloak of prayer. Job says, and furthermore experience proves, that man in this life never remains in one state, but that he is now better disposed toward one matter, and immediately again better disposed and more fit to perform another. And therefore there is no one who can keep his spirit bound to prayer for a whole day and night, unless God helps him through a special grace. If a man does not think with his heart on what he says, then he wastes his time, because he prays in vain, and his soul is weary and reluctant. And therefore God has also established for his servants other virtuous, spiritual, and physical exercises in which man must exercise himself daily. At one time in one, and at another time in the other, either for themselves or for their neighbor, having their heart toward God according to all their power...

->Your Kingdom come.<-

Here you must know that God the Father has two Kingdoms: one of Glory and eternal life, the other of virtue and the Christian life. And these two kingdoms are joined together, so that between these two there is no other midpoint except death. But according to the order of Divine justice, the kingdom of virtue precedes the kingdom of honor <note>The author uses "honor" (eerlickheyt) here as a synonym for the state of being in Glory.</note>. Therefore, those who live in the Kingdom of virtue—through which we must pass if we wish to go to the Kingdom of Glory or honor—the same shall undoubtedly also reign in the Kingdom of honor, and no one shall attain the dominion through any other means. And for this reason, Christ said to his Disciples: *Seek first the Kingdom of God and his righteousness*, that is, the kingdom of virtue, such as Faith, hope, and love, and the other virtues of Righteousness. But as you are not capable of this of yourself without heavenly grace, so pray and desire, saying: *O our Father, who art in Heaven. Thy kingdom come* in us; which is namely the love of virtues and the hatred of the world.

No one should think that it is difficult or annoying to forgive a neighbor’s misdeeds. For even if as many misdeeds as have been committed against all the people in the world were committed against one single man, they would still, when placed in a balance scale all together, not weigh as heavily as the smallest misdeed or sin committed against God. But the **Pride** of Man prevents one from thinking rightly on this and noticing such things. And therefore, do not fail to forgive your neighbor, so that you may also receive forgiveness from God. Christians shall fulfill this when they forgive lovingly, praying to God that he will not repay according to the greatness of the misdeeds of their debtors—or those who have wronged them—but that he may grant them grace so that they may acknowledge their sins and show repentance for them, so that they are not damned. Regarding injuries and evil as nothing other than a dream and a fantasy, <note>The author encourages the reader to view worldly insults as fleeting and unreal compared to spiritual matters.</note> such that they do not intend to repay them according to their worth, nor do they seek to avenge them, but show them every service, interacting with those who had angered them as before—yes, even with greater friendliness—and in such a way as if they were their brothers. And therefore, for those who, through a proud spirit, in no way [forgive] their debtor...

For there is a saying of God’s **Holy Scripture** which is true: *that a judgment without mercy shall happen to him, who shall have shown no mercy.* <note>James 2:13. The author emphasizes that human forgiveness is a prerequisite for divine mercy.</note> Such a mind and inclination as you bear toward your debtor, such has God also toward you, and you should hope for no other.

*Lead us not into temptation.* <note>original Occitan: "Non nos amenar en tentation &c." The author uses the vernacular dialect of the Waldensian people for the prayer itself.</note>

**Lead us not into temptation.**

No one should pray to God that He should never let him be tempted. For the Apostle **St. Paul** says that no one shall be crowned who has not fought lawfully and faithfully against the world, the flesh, and the devil. And **St. James** says that he is blessed who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, then he shall receive the crown of life. Yet no one can resist the power of the devil without God’s grace. We must then humbly and devotedly pray constantly to the Heavenly Father that He does not let us fall into temptation or testing, or succumb in the struggle, but that He gives us the strength to overcome while fighting, and that through His grace we may be preserved and obtain the crown which He has prepared to give us. One must not believe that He would sooner or more willingly hear the devil than the Christian believer. For as the Apostle **St. Paul** says: *God is faithful, who will not let you be tempted beyond your ability.*

<column-break/>

*But deliver us from evil.* <note>original Occitan: "Mas desliora no del mal &c."</note>

**But deliver us from evil.**

That is, deliver us from our own evil will of sin, and from the temporal and eternal punishments of the devil. So that we may remain free from his invisible and countless snares and deceptions.

**Amen.** This last word signifies a fervent desire of the one who prays, so that what he prays for might be given to him. And this word **Amen** is worth as much as if one said: *Let it be so or happen,* and this same little word may be placed at the end of all kinds of prayers.

---

->The Last Chapter.<-

### Of the Sacraments / What the Waldensians and Albigensians believed and taught concerning them.
#### Just as the same has been drawn from their own books.
#### *A Sacrament according to the saying of St. Augustine &c.* <note>original Occitan: "Sacrament second lo dire de Sanct Augustin &c."</note>

A **Sacrament**, according to the saying of **St. Augustine** in the book **The City of God**, is an invisible grace, set before the eyes or shown through a visible thing. Or a **Sacrament** is a sign <note>The definition provided here is a classic medieval theological distinction: the *signum visibile* (visible sign) of an *invisibilis gratia* (invisible grace).</note>

### of the History of the Waldensians and Albigensians.
<margin>r-ij</margin>
<meta>catchword: gen-</meta>

of a holy matter. <note>original: "vã eene heylige sake"</note> **There is a great distinction between the bare Sacrament and the cause of the Sacrament; indeed, as great as there is between the sign and the signified thing itself.** For the cause of a Sacrament is the Divine grace and the merit of the crucified **Jesus Christ**, who is the restoration of those who had fallen. This cause of the Sacrament resides powerfully and essentially in God—by virtue of His authority and institution—and meritoriously in **Jesus Christ**. For through His bitter suffering and the shedding of His blood, He obtained grace and righteousness for the Believers. **But the reality of the Sacrament resides in the soul of the believer through participation or fellowship, just as St. Paul says: We have become partakers of Christ.** <note>Hebrews 3:14</note> Namely, through the word of the Gospel, by means of the preaching or revelation thereof, and through the Sacraments in a sacramental manner. For the Lord Jesus instituted and gave the Sacraments as outward aids, so that the ministers might edify the people through instruction in the faith, adapting and accommodating themselves to human dullness and weakness, and instructing or teaching through the word of the Gospel.

There are two <term>Sacraments</term> <note>The Waldensians, like later Protestants, rejected the seven sacraments of the Roman Church, recognizing only these two as biblically mandated.</note>. One of which is of Water, the other of Nourishment, that is, of Bread and Wine.

The first is called **Baptism**, that is in our language, the washing away by Water, whether from a river or spring water. And this must be administered in the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,

<column-break/>

so that first, through the grace of God the Father—looking upon His Son—and through the fellowship of **Jesus Christ**, who has redeemed us, and through the renewal of the **Holy Spirit**, who impresses living faith upon our hearts; the sins of those who are baptized might be forgiven, and they might be accepted into grace. And through perseverance in the same, they might be saved in **Jesus Christ**.

The baptism with which we are baptized is the very same with which Christ Himself willed to be baptized, just as He also willed to be circumcised to fulfill or complete all righteousness; and it is the same baptism with which He willed His Apostles likewise to baptize.

The things that are unnecessary in the administration of Baptism are <term>Exorcism</term> <note>The ritual of driving out demons from the infant before baptism.</note> or adjurations, the breathings, and the signs of the cross on the child’s chest and forehead; the salt that is placed in the child’s mouth; the spittle which is smeared on the child’s ears and nose; the anointing with oil on the chest; the <term>chrism-cloth</term> <note>original: "huyfken of capken," a small white cap or veil placed on the head after baptism.</note> or cap, and the smearing of the **Chrism** <note>Consecrated oil used in Roman Catholic and Orthodox rituals.</note> on the top of the head; and all other such things consecrated by the **Bishop**, as well as sticking a wax candle in the child’s hand, clothing it with a small white garment, the hallowing or conjuring of the Water, the triple immersion of the child, and the questions asked of the **Godparents**. <note>original: "Peeters voorders"</note> All these things are not necessary for the administration of Baptism, nor do they belong to the essence of baptism, nor are they required for Baptism. From all these things, many have taken far more occasion for error than for godliness.

Namely, we must purely confess: that the bread which **Christ** took in his hand at his last supper, which he blessed, broke, and gave to his **Disciples** to eat—and by the receiving of which, through the service of faithful **Pastors**, he left the memory of his suffering—is, in its nature and essence, true bread. ### Concerning the Holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Just as baptism, which is received visibly, is like an enrollment on the register of Christian believers—containing within itself a protestation and a promise to follow Jesus Christ, to uphold his holy ordinances, and to live according to his Holy Gospel—so too is the Holy Supper, the holy receiving of our Lord, the breaking of the bread, and the thanksgiving. It is likewise a visible fellowship made with the members of Jesus Christ: for those who break and eat one bread are also one body, and members of one another. They are grafted and planted in Him, in whose service they promise with high protestation to persevere until the end, without separating themselves from the Evangelical faith or from the union they have all promised to God through Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as all the members are nourished with one and the same food, and just as all believers receive one and the same Spiritual Bread from the Holy Word of life—the Gospel of salvation—so they likewise live by one spirit and by one faith.

This Sacrament of the fellowship of the body and blood of Christ is called in Greek *Eucharistia* <note>original: "Eucharistia", meaning "thanksgiving"</note>, of which Matthew testifies that Jesus, taking the bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: "Take and eat, this is my body." And Saint Luke says: "This is my body which is given for you, do this in remembrance of me; this is my blood of the new and eternal covenant, which shall be shed for many for the forgiveness of sins."

Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. Regarding which Sacrament, we must hold and believe the following, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture. We must namely confess purely: that the bread which Christ took in his hand at his supper, which he blessed, broke, and gave to his disciples to eat—and through the receipt of which, by the service of faithful pastors, he left a memorial <note>original: "ghedachtenisse"</note> of his suffering—is, in its nature and essence, true bread. And that by the pronoun **"this,"** this sacramental proposition is indicated: **"This is my body."** These words are not to be understood identically <note>original: "Identice"</note>, by numerical identity <note>original: "de numerica Identitate," a technical term in logic and theology meaning that two things are exactly the same substance</note>, as if it were said "this my body, is my body." Rather, it is to be understood sacramentally—that is, according to the way and manner common to the Sacraments: both effectively and truly, yet not according to physical measure and size. This same Body of Christ, being seated at the right hand of his Father in Heaven, must also be beheld there by all believers through the understanding, lifting the spirit upwards; and the same must likewise be eaten through a firm faith. All of this must also be understood in the same way regarding the drinking cup.

Saint Augustine says that the eating and drinking of this Sacrament

<column-break/>

must be understood spiritually, for Christ says: "The words that I speak to you are spirit and life." And Saint Jerome says: "the flesh of Christ is understood in two ways: either spiritually, of which Christ says: 'My flesh is food indeed and my blood is drink indeed'; or it is understood as that flesh which was crucified and buried." Regarding spiritual eating, Christ says: "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him." Thus, there are two ways of eating: one happens in a sacramental manner, in which way both the good and the evil eat; the other happens spiritually, and in this way, only the good eat. And therefore Augustine says: "What is that? To eat Christ? This is not only receiving his body in the Sacrament, for many eat unworthily, who do not desire to remain in him, nor wish to have him remaining with them; but he eats spiritually who perseveres in the truth of Christ." And therefore, regarding the eating of the sacramental bread: that is to eat the body of Christ in a figure <note>original: "in figure," meaning figuratively or as a representation</note>. Just as Jesus Christ says: "As often as you shall do this, do it in remembrance of me." For if this eating did not happen through a figure, then Christ would have bound himself perpetually to such an act as he did then. Yet it is also necessary that spiritual eating happens continually: as Saint Augustine

In the keeping of this Sacrament, prayer is useful and beneficial, as is also the preaching of Holy Scripture in the common tongue <note>The Waldensians were famous for insisting that the Bible and services be in the language of the people rather than Latin</note>, which is suitable for edification, and that according to the requirement of the Gospel law, so that peace and love might increase and grow among the people. ->The Seventh Chapter.<-

### About Marriage: what the Waldensians and Albigensians taught regarding it in a certain book of theirs called the *Spiritual Almanac*.

Marriage is holy, and was instituted by God in the beginning of the world. And therefore it is an honorable thing when it is maintained as it should be, and in all purity; and when the man, who is the head of the woman, loves her, protects her, and provides for her honorable upkeep, keeping and proving his loyalty and faith; and when the woman, who was made as a helper to the man, is subject to her husband, obedient to him in all good things, honors him just as God commands her, taking care of her household, guarding herself not only from doing evil, but also from all appearance of evil: keeping and proving loyalty and faith to him, both persevering together according to the teaching of God in what is good, laboring to live honorably and doing no one wrong, teaching and instructing the little children whom God gives them in the fear and teaching of our Lord, and to live as God has commanded.

<column-break/>

Prayer and fasting are useful and beneficial when one intends to enter the state of marriage, along with the demonstrations, instructions, and warnings concerning the same. But the **laying on of hands**, and the **binding together of hands with the Popish stole** <note>original: "Paepsche Stoolle." The stole is a narrow strip of fabric worn by priests; the Waldensians rejected its use in the marriage ceremony as a human invention</note>, and other things which are commonly maintained in the same through human ordinance, beyond the express command of Scripture, do not belong to the essence of marriage, nor are they required as being necessary for it.

Regarding the unlawful or **forbidden degrees** <note>referring to 'prohibited degrees of kinship,' which are rules determining how closely related two people can be and still legally marry</note> and other things that must be observed and maintained in marriage, these shall be spoken of in the treatise on **Discipline** or **Church Order**.

The one who carries the word of God our Lord must be diligent to attract everyone and bring them to the Lord, applying all possible industry and labor toward that end, presenting himself as a good example of a godly life and sound teaching before the people. It is not enough that he teaches in the assembly; but furthermore, he must also teach from house to house and in all places, just as Christ and his Apostles did, comforting the oppressed and especially those who are sick. He must exhort them regarding the goodness and mercy of God, pointing out that from Him—who is the fountain and origin of all good—nothing but good can come. He must show that the same one who is almighty is also our merciful Father, much more concerned and caring for us than any father or mother has ever cared for their little children. He himself testifies that:

*even if it were possible that a mother should forget her child, or the nurse the child she suckled and carried in her womb, yet our Father shall not forget us.* He does everything for our benefit and sends us everything for our best; if it were more advantageous for us that things went differently than they do now, he would surely grant it and let it happen so. Therefore, we must submit our souls to his guidance and firmly believe that he loves us, and that because he loves us, he chastises us. Consequently, we must not be distracted by the pains or the poverty that we suffer at present, nor think that God hates or rejects us. Instead, we should consider ourselves to be all the more in his grace, looking not at those who flourish in this world and find their comforts within it, but much more at Jesus, the most beloved and well-favored of the Father, above any other. # Concerning the third part of the History of the Waldensians and Albigensians.
### Containing the Discipline or Order under which they lived.

->The First Chapter.<-

### On Discipline | On the Discipline or Christian Order.

<note>In the original text, the left column is written in the Occitan (Waldensian) dialect and the right column is in 17th-century Dutch. Both have been translated here into English.</note>

DISCIPLINE contains within itself all moral doctrine, according to the teaching of Christ and the Apostles, showing in what manner each person, living according to their calling, may walk worthily in present righteousness.

And of this Discipline, the Holy Scriptures recount abundant teachings; not only in what way each person must live for themselves, in whatever state, rank, and condition they may be, but also what the unity, the unanimity, and the bond of love should be in the community of the Faithful. And regarding this, if anyone wishes to know, let them read the Apostle in the Epistles, and there they will find laid out abundantly and specifically in what manner each person was intended to preserve themselves in unity, and to walk worthily so that they might not be a scandal or an occasion for the ruin of their neighbor, by evil word or evil deed; and in what

<column-break/>

THE Discipline or Order <term>Discipline (Dutch: Tucht)</term> <note>The Dutch word 'Tucht' refers to communal discipline and the moral regulation of a church body, a central concept in Reformed and Waldensian tradition.</note> encompasses all moral or ethical instruction, or all the teachings of conduct, following the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles—demonstrating how everyone, in their calling through faith, must live and walk worthily in present righteousness.

The Holy Scripture recounts many lessons concerning this Discipline, and shows not only how each individual in particular must live, of whatever status, office, and age they may be: but also what unity, harmony, and bond of love is required in the community of the Believers. If anyone desires to have knowledge of these things, they may read what the Apostle says of them in his epistles, and they will find at length and in particular, in what manner each is bound to keep themselves within the bounds of unity, and so to walk that they are no offense, and no cause of the de- <note>original catchword: "t'ber-", likely for "t'bederf" meaning ruin or destruction, matching the Occitan "ruina" in the left column.</note>

## Concerning the Pastors or Teachers.

All those who shall be accepted as teachers among us, while they are still among their own people, ask our elders that they would be willing to receive them into the Ministry <note>Original Dutch: "Dienst," meaning service or office.</note>, and that it might please them to pray to God that they may become worthy of such a great office: which request they make in order to show their humility.

We then give them their lessons, and have them learn by heart <note>Original Dutch: "van buyten leeren." The Waldensians were famous for their ability to recite entire books of the Bible from memory, a necessity in an era when Bibles were often confiscated.</note> all the chapters of St. Matthew and of St. John, and all the Epistles which are called Canonical, as well as a good portion of the writings of Solomon, of David, and the Prophets.

<column-break/>

## Of the Pastors.

All those who are to be received as Pastors among us, when they are still with their people, they pray, if it pleases our people, that they receive them into the ministry, and that it would please them to pray to God that they be made worthy of so great an office: but the aforesaid petitioners do not do the aforesaid things for any other purpose, except to demonstrate humility.

We teach them lessons and make them learn by heart all the chapters of St. Matthew, and of St. John, and all the Epistles which are called Canonical: a good part of Solomon, of David, and of the Prophets.

The second <note>The junior or more recently ordained minister.</note> must not do anything without the permission of the one placed before him: and similarly, those placed before must not do anything without the permission of their companions, so that all things among us may be done in good order.

## Of the Pastors or Teachers.

All those who shall be accepted as teachers among us, while they are still among their own people, request of ours that they might be received into the Ministry, and that it would please them to pray to God that they might become worthy of such a great office: which request they make in order to demonstrate their humility.

We then give them their lessons, and make them learn by heart all the chapters of St. Matthew and St. John, and all the Epistles which are called the Canonical Epistles, along with a good portion of the writings of Solomon, of David, and the Prophets.

<column-break/>

...in what way [one] is understood not only to flee evil, but also the occasion of evil and the appearance of evil: and if anyone has erred, in what way they are reformed, so they can be amended.

By many such universal teachings, by which the domestic people of the Faith <note>Occitan: *poble domesti de la Fe*, referring to those within the church community.</note> should be taught, so that they behave worthily in the house of the Lord, and do not make of the temple of the Lord a den of thieves <note>Occitan: *balma de lairos*, a cave or den of robbers.</note>, through evil and perverse conversation, and through the toleration of evil.

## The Second Book of the Third Part

...they who are not faithful / or do not believe / are punished and separated / whether it be for their evil life / or for their erroneous faith / or for the lack of their love / or because they have too little hope / or because some of these aforementioned sins / are found together in someone. That it is indeed necessary / to put such a rebuke into practice / and to exercise it / the Lord Jesus teaches, saying: *If your brother sins, go and rebuke him between you and him alone, if he hears you, then you have won your brother.* ***Matthew 18 verse 15.*** The Apostle confirms the same / saying to the ***Galatians 6:1***: *If a man is fallen into any transgression, you who are spiritual, instruct him with the spirit of Gentleness.* <note>The Dutch term "sachtmoedicheyt" implies a mild, humble, and patient disposition when correcting others.</note>

But if they will not accept all the rebukes in love / then the Lord teaches / what the spiritual leaders <note>The leaders mentioned here are the "Barbes" or pastors who oversaw the moral life of the community.</note> must then do further: saying: *and if he does not hear you, then take one or two more with you, so that every word may stand in the mouth of one or two witnesses.*

And the Lord understands that this must be done / when the sin is known to only a few people alone. But he takes it much differently / when the sin is public / and recognized as sin by everyone. In such a case the rebuke must also happen publicly. The Apostle indicates this, saying: ***1 Timothy 5:20.*** *Those who sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the others also may have fear.*

<column-break/>

...be punished, and separated, either for the evil life, or the evil doctrine, whether it be against the Faith, or whether it be against charity, or whether it be against Hope, or in every manner of evil together. And that this ought to be done in correction, the Lord Jesus taught: <note>original Latin/Occitan: *Si lo teo fraire peccare...*</note> *If your brother should sin, go you and correct him between you and him himself alone: if he hears, you have gained your brother. Matthew 18:15.* This same thing the Apostle confirms, saying to the Galatians: *If a man be first caught in any forfeit, or sin, you who are spiritual, teach him in this manner in a spirit of gentleness.* <note>original: *soivefsa* — a Waldensian term for sweetness or mildness of character.</note>

But as all do not charitably receive correction, the Lord teaches what thing the spiritual rulers <term>regidors spirituals (spiritual leaders or guides)</term> ought to do, saying: *If he does not hear you, join with you one or two, that every word stands in the mouth of two and of three witnesses.*

And the Lord understands this here where the fault would not be known to many. But much more is it otherwise where someone sins manifestly <note>Manifestly here means "openly" or "obviously."</note>, and it is manifest to all as sin. Over such, manifest correction must be made. The Apostle shows this, saying: *Reprove those sinning before all that the others may have fear.*

->The Seventh Chapter.<-

### On Marriage.

Marriage must be contracted according to the degrees that are permitted by God and not according to those which God has forbidden: but one must not have a burdened conscience regarding those prohibitions of the Pope <note>The Waldenses rejected the complex Roman Catholic "prohibited degrees" of kinship, which often required expensive papal dispensations (payments) to bypass.</note>, despite the fact that no money was given to him to obtain his dispensation. For that which God has not forbidden may well take place without the Pope's permission.

The bond of Marriage may not be entered into or sealed without the permission and consent of the parents on both sides; for the children belong to the fathers and mothers.

<column-break/>

### Of Marriage.

Marriage must be performed according to the degrees which God has permitted, not according to the degrees which He has forbidden: but there must be no hesitation of conscience regarding those of the Pope, even if nothing of gold or silver has been given to him to have a dispensation. For what God has not forbidden can be done without him.

The marital bond of holy Marriage must not be made without the consent of the parents, from both parties: for the children belong to the father and the mother.

---

->The Eighth Chapter.<-

### Against the excess that is committed in the Taverns.

The Tavern <term>Herberghe</term> <note>While "Herberghe" usually means an inn, in this context it specifically refers to a drinking-house or tavern.</note> or the drinking-house is a fountain of sin and a school of the Devil, in which he performs his miracles, just as it suits him. God usually shows His powers in the Church and does His miracles there, namely to enlighten the blind, to make the lame walk, to make the mute speak, to make the deaf hear—

### Of the Tavern.

The Tavern is a fountain of sin and the Devil's school; there he performs his miracles just as they belong to him. In the holy Church, God is accustomed to show His virtues, or His miracles: to enlighten the blind, to make the lame walk, to make the mute speak, to make the deaf hear: but the Devil does in the Tavern the total contrary. For when the glutton <note>The text likely continues on the next page to describe how the drunkard/glutton loses their senses, inverting God's healing miracles.</note>

### The Second Book of the Third Part

...made, where their Godparents declared on their behalf that they renounced the devil and all his pomp. Now, the dance is the pomp and finery of Satan; and whoever comes to the dance enters into the devil's finery and his mass. For the woman who sings during the dance is like a prioress or choir leader of the devil, and those who sing in response are like her clerics or choir-members; and those who watch this spectacle are like the parishioners; and the voices, flutes, or instruments in the dance are like the church bells; and the flutists or musicians are the devil's ministers. For just as when the pigs are scattered and lost, the pig-herder makes a piglet <note>original: "baudien"; likely referring to a specific distress call or a young pig used to draw the herd together.</note> squeal to entice the others to gather together, and they all run together at the sound of that squealing—so the devil also acts in the Dance. He makes a woman sing or play the flute so that all his pigs—that is, the male and female dancers—might gather together.

Furthermore, in the dance, one breaks and transgresses the ten commandments of God, namely the first: *You shall have no other gods before me.*

1. In the dance, one serves the person whom one seeks to please; and therefore St. Jerome <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his asceticism and translation of the Bible into Latin.</note> says that each person's God is that which they serve and love above all else.

2. One likewise sins in the dance against the second commandment, seeing as one makes an idol of that which one loves most.

3. Against the third: *You shall not use the name of the Lord your God in vain.* For in the dance, one serves the vanity of sin.

4. Against the fourth: For through the dance, the Sabbath <note>original: "Sondach"; Sunday.</note> is desecrated and defiled.

<column-break/>

...his pomp and his mass. For the woman who sings at the dance is the Prioress of the Devil, and those who respond are the Clerks, and those who watch are the parishioners; the sounds and the pipes are the bells, and the minstrels <note>original: "joglar"; musicians or performers.</note> who play are the Ministers of the Devil. For just as when the pigs are scattered, the shepherd makes one of them squeal so that the others hear and gather together, so the Devil makes a woman sing so that all his pigs—that is, the dancers—might gather.

Likewise, at the dance, the ten Commandments of the law of God are transgressed. Against the first: *You shall have no God but me.*

1. At the dance, one worships the person whom one strives to serve; of which Saint Jerome says that the God of each one is that which he worships and loves above all things.

2. Against the second Commandment one sins at the dance when one makes an idol of what each one loves.

3. Against the third: *You shall not take the name of your Lord God in vain.* <note>original Latin/Occitan: "Non recebris lo nom del teo Seignor Dio en Van."</note> At the dance one serves the vanity of the flesh.

4. Against the fourth: By the dance, the Lord’s Day <note>original: "Dia mengea"; literally "Sunday" or "the Day of the Lord."</note> is defiled by dancing.

### The First Book, of the third part, etc.

...steps or paces as he makes in the Dance, he also approaches Hell by just as many leaps. They sin through their adornment or jewelry in five ways. First, by making themselves proud. Second, when they ensnare the hearts of those who behold them. Third, when they make others who do not have such jewelry blush with shame, causing and inciting them to desire the same. Fourth, when they cause women to become difficult and burdensome to their husbands, desiring such jewelry likewise. Fifth, because they cause women who cannot obtain it from their husbands to seek to acquire it through other evil and sinful means.

They sin singing and playing on instruments: For singing breaks the hearts, making them as if drunk with fleeting joy, meanwhile forgetting God, and presenting nothing but lies and foolishness in their songs. And all the stirrings and movements that happen in the dance give testimony of the evil one.

And one must also know that the Dance is a procession of the Devil, and that he who goes into the Dance goes into the procession of the devil; the devil is the leader, the middle-dancer, and the follower in the dances. # of the History of the Waldensians and Albigensians.

### The Tenth Chapter.

->In what manner the people ought to conduct themselves toward those who are on the outside.<-

1. **D**o not love the world.

2. Flee evil company.

3. If it is possible, have peace with all.

4. Do not contend in judgment <note>This refers to avoiding legal disputes or secular lawsuits.</note>.

5. Do not avenge oneself.

6. Love your enemies.

7. Be willing to endure labors, calumnies, threats, reproaches, shames, injuries, and all types of torments for the sake of the truth.

8. Possess your souls in patience.

9. Do not be yoked together with the unfaithful.

10. Do not communicate with evil works, and especially not with those that savor of Idolatry <term>Idolatria: the worship of idols or participation in Roman Catholic rituals perceived by the Waldensians as superstitious</term>, and the services relating to it, and likewise of other such things.

---

->Furthermore, in what manner the faithful ought to rule their bodies.<-

1. **D**o not serve the mortal desires of the flesh.

2. Guard your members so that they do not become weapons of iniquity.

<column-break/>

->How one shall interact with those who are on the outside.<-

1. **O**ne shall not love the world.

2. One shall shun evil company.

3. With all men—so far as it is possible—one shall keep the peace.

4. One shall not contend before the court.

5. One shall not avenge oneself.

6. One shall love one's enemies.

7. One shall gladly endure labor, slanders, threats, rejections, shame, wrongs, and all manner of torments for the sake of the truth.

8. One shall possess one's soul with patience.

9. One shall not pull a yoke with the unbelieving.

10. One shall have no fellowship with evil works, and especially not with those that taste of Idolatry <term>Afgoderije: idolatry or false worship</term> and all services that tend toward it; and one shall judge other similar matters in the same way.

---

->Moreover, how the Faithful <term>Gheloovighen: the "believers" or members of the Waldensian church</term> must govern their own bodies, or rule themselves.<-

1. **T**hey shall not serve the deadly lusts of the flesh.

2. They shall guard their limbs, so that they do not become weapons of wickedness.

# The Third Book,
# Of the third part of the History of the Waldensians and Albigensians.

### Containing the answer or refutation of many doctrines of the Roman Church.

<margin>
*As smoke goes before the fire, battle before victory, so the temptation of the Antichrist goes before glory.* <note>original: "Enaima lo Fum va devant lo fuoc: la batailla devant la victoria: enaimi la tentation de l'Antechrist devant la gloria." Just as smoke precedes the fire, and battle precedes the victory: so also the temptation of the Antichrist precedes Glory or Splendor.

->The First Chapter.<-
### A treatise of the Waldensians and Albigensians, written against the Antichrist.

<note>Two large decorative woodcut initials 'A' and 'D' featuring floral and architectural motifs.</note>

The Antichrist is a falsehood leading to eternal damnation, covered with an appearance of truth and the righteousness of Christ and his bride <note>The "bride" refers to the Church.</note>: opposing the very way of truth, of righteousness, of faith, of hope, of charity, and the moral life, as well as the ministerial truth of the Church administered by false apostles, and defended stubbornly by both one arm and the other <note>The "two arms" typically refer to the "two swords" of medieval theory: the spiritual power of the Church and the secular power of the State.</note>. Or, it is a hidden deception concerning the truth of salvation in substantial and ministerial matters; or it is a fraudulent opposition to Christ and his bride, and to every faithful member. And thus it is not any one specific person ordained...

<column-break/>

<margin>
This treatise on the Antichrist is found in a certain manuscript <note>Dutch: *geschreven boec*</note> in which many sermons of the Barbes <note><term>Barbes</term>: The Waldensian pastors, from the dialect word for "uncles," a title of respect.</note> are also found, dated the Year 1120. It therefore appears to have been written before the time of Waldo <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140–1205) is often considered the founder of the movement, but Waldensian tradition often claims an older lineage.</note>, around the time of Pierre <note>Likely Pierre de Bruys, an early 12th-century reformer.</note>.
</margin>

The Antichrist is the deceit leading to eternal damnation, clothed with a semblance of truth, and of the righteousness of Christ and his bride: fighting and contrary to this same way of truth, of righteousness, of faith, of hope, and of love; as well as against the moral life, and the truth and purity of the service of the church, which Antichrist is promoted by false apostles, and protected by both the one and the other arm. Or otherwise: The Antichrist is a deceit through which the truth of salvation is hidden and obscured by physical things and outward ministrations.

Or otherwise: The Antichrist is a deceptive opposition against Christ, his Bride <note>A common metaphor for the Church.</note>, and every individual faithful member. The gathering of such people is called the Antichrist, or Babylon, or the fourth Beast <note>A reference to the visions in the Book of Daniel.</note>, or the Harlot, or the man of sin, and the Son of perdition.

# Of the History of the Waldensians and Albigensians.

...secular, through riches, honors of dignity, through delicacies and through the delight of the world, and opposes [Christ] through these ways.

Therefore it is manifest to everyone that in no way can the Antichrist be complete nor come except when all these aforementioned things are joined together to make a perfect **Hypocrite** <note>In this context, hypocrisy refers to the outward appearance of holiness used to mask inward corruption.</note> and falsehood; that is, when the wise of the world, the religious orders, **Pharisees**, ministers, Doctors, the secular power, and the people of the world were joined together. Then they created the **man of sin** <note>original: "l'home de pecca"; a reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:3, identifying the Antichrist with the corruption of the church.</note> and complete error. For in the time of the Apostles, although the Antichrist was already conceived, yet being an infant, he lacked the necessary internal and external limbs.

Therefore he was known and destroyed and excommunicated more easily, as he was made like a rustic and coarse mute; for he lacked rational, excusatory, definitive, and sententious wisdom. And because he lacked the false ministers who lack truth, and lacked human statutes, he lacked the outward religious orders. Therefore he had come into error and sin, but did not have that with which he could cover the filth or shame of errors or sin; as he lacked riches and endowments, he could not maintain any minister for himself, nor could he multiply, preserve, or defend their...

<column-break/>

...of the world / through false religion / through feigned goodness / through spiritual power / and temporal tyranny / through riches / honor and dignities / through pleasures and delights of this world.

### The Third Book, of the Third Part

**Answer: These are the following.**

The first is that he perverts the true service of God—which belongs to God alone—and transfers and attributes it to his own works and to the poor rational or irrational, sentient or non-sentient creature. To the rational, such as to men, deceased saints <note>original: "Sancten of Sanctinnen." The Dutch text specifies both male and female saints.</note>, and to images, dead bodies, or relics. His works are his sacraments, but especially the sacrament of the Eucharist—that is, of thanksgiving or of the Lord’s Supper—which he worships as God and as Jesus Christ; he serves the consecrated or hallowed things and forbids worshiping God alone.

The second work of the Antichrist is that he takes away and robs the merits of Jesus Christ, along with all the sufficiency of grace, righteousness, rebirth, forgiveness of sins, sanctification, confirmation <note>original: "vormsel oft vroomsel." A rite intended to strengthen the believer's relationship with God.</note>, and spiritual nourishment: and attributes these to his own authority or power, to certain forms or ways of speaking and words, to his own works, and to the saints and their intercession, and to the giver of things: and by separating and turning the people away from Christ, he leads them to the aforementioned things, so that they should not seek those things in Christ, nor through Christ: but only in the works of their hands, and not through living faith in God, nor in Jesus Christ, nor in the Holy Spirit, but in the will and the works of the Antichrist, just as he preaches that the whole of salvation consists in his own works.

# The Third Book, of the third part

...unity is neither governed nor protected by the Holy Spirit, but by worldly power, and he joins spiritual matters to his aid.

The eighth work of the Antichrist <note>In Waldensian theology, the "Antichrist" was seen as the entire corrupt institutional system of the medieval Church rather than a single individual.</note> is that he persecutes and hunts the members [of Christ], seizes them, and puts them to death.

And these things are among the principal of his works which he commits against the truth, all of which could not well be counted nor properly described; yet for the present, it is enough to have pointed them out in general. Now follow those things through which he covers this, his malice and cunning.

First and foremost, this occurs through the outward confession of Faith. Of which the Apostle <note>The "Apostle" usually refers to St. Paul in this context.</note> speaks: *For they confess that which they have known of God, but they deny that same thing through their works.* <note>original: "Want sy belyden tgene dat sy van Gode bekent hebben, maer dat selve verloochené sy door de wercken." This is a paraphrase of Titus 1:16.</note>

Secondly, he covers his injustice and malice by the length of time, and because he is maintained by some wise and ingenious Monks, by some virgins, women, widows, and honorable persons. And moreover, he is further strengthened and maintained by the innumerable multitude of people, of whom it is spoken in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>: *and power was given to him over every tribe, tongue, and nation, and all who dwell on the earth shall worship him.* <note>Refers to Revelation 13:7-8.</note>

Thirdly, he covers his injustice through the spiritual power of the Apostles, against which the Apostle says: *We can do nothing against the truth, and no power is given to us for destruction.* <note>Refers to 2 Corinthians 13:8.</note>

<column-break/>

...[not] united by the Holy Spirit, but by secular power, and joins spiritual things to it as an aid.

The eighth work of the Antichrist is, that he singles out, and persecutes, and accuses, robs, and puts to death the members of Christ. These things are nearly the most principal of his works, which he does against the truth, which can in no way all be numbered or written. But let it suffice at present to have spoken of these as being most general, through which things this iniquity is covered.

Firstly and mostly through the outward confession of faith. Of which the Apostle says: *for they confess to have known God in words, but they deny Him by deed.*

Secondly, through the length of time, and through the maintenance of the wise, of the Religious <term>Religious: In this historical context, "Religious" (Latin: *religiosi*) specifically refers to members of monastic orders, such as monks or friars.</term>, of the virgins (male and female), of the widows and of the honorable, etc. And the numberless people, of whom it is said in the Apocalypse: *And power was given to him over every tribe, and tongue, and nation, and all those who inhabit the earth worshipped him.*

Thirdly, by the spiritual authority of the Apostles, against which he says: *We can do nothing against the truth, and power is not given for destruction.*

<column-break/>

Fourthly, through many miracles / performed by this or that person / of which the Apostle says: *Whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in all power and signs and wonders of lies, and in all deception of unrighteousness.*

Fifthly, through outward pseudo-holiness / through prayers / through fasts / vigils and alms / against which the Apostle says: *having a form, gesture, or appearance of godliness, but they have denied the power thereof.*

Seventhly, through the administration of the Sacraments / through which they vomit up the bulk of their errors.

Eighthly, through rebukes and Sermons against gross misdeeds / for what they say, they do not do.

Ninthly, through an apparently virtuous life / of some who live with hypocrisy / and others who live with sincerity. For God’s elect / who desire and do good / are held within Babel / and they are like the gold with which the Antichrist covers and clothes his vanity / not allowing them to serve God alone / nor to place their hope on Christ alone / nor that they should devote themselves to the true Divine service / or grant it their support.

All these things / with many others besides / are like a cloak <note>original: "deckmantel" — literally a "cover-mantle," meaning a pretext or a facade used to hide the truth.</note>

### The Third Book, of the Third Part

...brotherhood and unity out of free will, with a sincere intention and firm resolve to desire to please the Lord uprightly and purely, and to be saved; and we transport ourselves through the Lord’s help to or upon the Christian truth and His knowledge and science <note>In this 17th-century context, "science" refers to systematic knowledge or spiritual understanding.</note>, notwithstanding that the same be very humble and small. Therefore we have undertaken to point out what the causes of our separation are, as well as what our brotherhood and gathering <note>original: "vergaderinghe"</note> are: so that, in case it pleases the Lord to share the knowledge of this truth with others, those who shall have received this alongside us may love Him with us. And if by chance they are not sufficiently enlightened, they may be helped through this aid and service, and being sprinkled or made new by the Lord, they may obtain growth. And if to anyone more abundantly and higher is given, from such a person we wish to be instructed with humility, to be able to learn better, and to receive report of our misunderstanding or error. The things then that follow hereafter are the causes of our separation.

Let it be known then to everyone in general and in particular, that the cause of our separation is thus, namely for the essential truth of faith, and the inward knowledge of the only true God, and the unity of the Divine essence, in three persons or substances <note>original: "self-standigheden," a Dutch theological term for "subsistences" or "hypostases" within the Trinity.</note>, which knowledge is neither by flesh nor by blood...

Therefore we ordain to note what the things of our separation are, and also of our congregation, so that if the Lord has given to others to have this same truth: they may carry the love for it together with us. And if by chance they are not well enlightened, they may receive help through this ministry, the Lord watering <note>original: "arrofant," a metaphor for divine grace nourishing the soul like water on a plant.</note> them. And if it is given more to anyone, and more highly; then we desire to be taught more humbly, and to know better from him, and to be corrected in our defects. Therefore these things that follow are the cause of our separation.

Let it be manifest to all and to each that the cause of our separation is this, both for the essential truth of faith, and the ministerial truth; the Essential truth of the faith is the interior knowledge of one true God, and unity of Essence in three persons, which neither flesh nor blood gives. ...the love of Him above all things, the sanctification and the honoring of Him above all things and above all names: living hope through Christ in God; the inner regeneration and renewal through Faith, through Hope, and through Charity; the merit of Jesus Christ with all sufficiency of grace and righteousness; the participation or the communion of all the elect; the remission of sins; holy conversation, and the faithful fulfillment of all the Commandments in the faith of Christ; the true Penance <note>original: "Penitentia," referring here to heartfelt repentance rather than the Roman Catholic sacrament of penance.</note>, and final perseverance, and eternal life. The ministerial truths are these: The external gathering of the Ministers, with the subject people, in place and in time, in the truth, through the ministerial things, in the truth touched upon above, leading, establishing, and preserving through faithful and nourishing company; the good Ministers by their faith and life, being in custom and obedience, and wakefully performing the practice and usage of the Lord over the flocks. <note>original: "grecs," a dialect variant of the Latin "grex" for flock.</note>

The things which the Ministers are understood to serve to the people are these: The Evangelical word, and the word of reconciliation, or the law of grace in the sense or intention of Christ. For they must notify the Evangelical word: the Sacrament added—

<column-break/>

—to give: likewise for the divine service <note>original: "Godsdienst"</note> which is owed to the one God, and the love for God above all things: for the sanctification and the honor of God above all things, and above all names: for the living hope in God through Christ: for the rebirth and the inward renewal through faith, through hope, and love: for the merit of Jesus Christ, accompanied by the sufficiency of grace and righteousness: For the sharing or fellowship <note>original: "ghemeyn-schap," referring to the "communion of saints."</note> with all the elect: For the forgiveness of sins: for the holy walk, and the faithful fulfillment of all the commandments, through faith in Christ: for true repentance: for perseverance unto the end, and for eternal life. The truths then that concern the ministry are these: The external gatherings and meetings of the servants, with the submissive people, in suitable places, at the proper time, and in truth, through the ministry in the aforementioned truth. The same servants, thus leading the church, confirming or strengthening, and converting through their faithful and constant company and interaction, serving to strengthen faith and the piety of life, conducting themselves according to good customs and dutiful obedience, and bravely applying themselves to the practice of godliness, maintaining and carrying out such works as Christ Himself practiced over His flocks.

->Of the Invocation of the Saints.<-

NOW it is to be said of the invocation of the Saints, which the Masters with their followers preach and promote with great public diligence as an article of Faith, saying that the Saints existing in the celestial homeland are to be prayed to by us living in that manner which the Priests and other common people are accustomed to use by their instruction, enjoining upon themselves and other things for the aid of invocation. By which invocation, authorization, and magnification, the people are seen to feel this carnally and foolishly: believing that just as it happens before an earthly King when he is angry, others who are not so angry intercede for someone, mitigating his anger before him—

### The Third Book, of the third part

[They] do not share their anger; [they] pray for others, and sweeten <note>original: "versoeten"; meaning to soften or appease</note> their anger: [teaching] that it also happens exactly like that before God / namely / that the saints sweeten the wrath of God against the sinner.

But one must not believe such things / for if that were so and were to happen / then there would be no conformity or equality / between the will of the Saints / and the will of God : For it would thus appear / that the Saints / against those with whom God is angry / would likewise not be angry.

Secondly / through this glorification and invocation of the Saints / the People fall into Idolatry / trusting themselves more in the Saints / than in God / and serving them with much greater affection than God himself. Which they show by their actions / through the excessive and costly decorations of the Altars / through the loud ringing and sounding of bells / through the multitude of Church lights / and through other honors. Through which things the simple folk allow themselves / to believe / that the Saints are much more Merciful / than God himself / as they deliver [people] from damnation / through their prayers which they make to God / those / whom God had already damned. Furthermore / to maintain such matters / the simple folk <note>original: "slecht volcxken"; literally 'humble little people', a common term for the uneducated laity</note> are taught / that the Saints desire / that one presents offerings to them / and that they take pleasure when one praises them / and that they primarily pray for those who offer them Incense / and other Hymns and show honor / all which things one must carefully avoid / and have an abomination of.

<column-break/>

[They] themselves, and even so the people estimate it to be done before God, that the Saints, by praying for the sinner, mitigate His <note>original: "lei"; referring to God</note> anger.

And this is seen to be not worthy of belief, as it would not be seen to be true conformity of the will of the Saints with the will of God: for against that person with whom God is indignant, it would not be seen that they themselves were also angry.

Secondly, through this magnification and invocation of the Saints, the people fall into idolatry, trusting themselves more to some of the Saints than to God, and serving them more affectionately than God alone. And they demonstrate this through deeds, both by the most precious decoration of altars, and by more resounding sounds [of bells], and multiplications of candles, and by other solemnities. By which things it appears to the simple that they themselves are more merciful than God, and that those whom He Himself would have condemned, they themselves deliver still from damnation through prayers. For which reason, beyond this, the simple learn that the Saints desire gifts, offerings, and specific praises, and that they intercede more greatly for those who give them incense, offerings, and other praises and honors, which things are to be entirely avoided and abominated with great diligence.

<meta>This page continues the theological argument against the Roman Catholic practice of the invocation of saints. While the previous page critiqued the popular belief that saints "appease" God’s wrath, this page provides the positive Waldensian definition of prayer (invocation) as something directed to God alone through the sole mediation of Jesus Christ.</meta>

# of the History of the Waldensians and Albigensians-

Now we are to speak of this invocation of the Saints, and to make known our intention regarding it. First and before all things, we set forth what the name of that invocation is. To invoke is itself the desire of the whole mind and the whole soul, sent by voice in prayer to God alone.

Secondly, we maintain that the man Christ is the mediator <note>original: "megécier"; a middleman or intermediary</note> between God and men, and the Advocate before the Father, and the payer for our sins. Appropriating [this] to God for himself, ever living to pray for us. No one comes to the Father except through him. And "whatever you ask the Father in my name, I will do it." Who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach. And he is the Advocate before the Father, and the forgiver of our sins. Therefore, he presents himself in some manner to us before we move. He stands at the door and knocks, and knocks so that it might be opened to him; who, wishing to close the way of all idolatry <note>original: "idolatria"</note> existing in heaven at the right hand of the Father, wants all the faithful to have him in mind and to attend to him alone: as the care of the faithful must be toward Christ by thought and by affection, and by resemblance in understanding that which is above. Just as it is said: "If you are then raised with Christ, seek those things which are above, in which place Christ is, seated at the right hand of God." He is the door through which, if anyone enters, he shall be saved. No one comes to the Father except through me.

<column-break/>

Regarding this Invocation / we have therefore now to speak / and to make known / what we hold concerning the Invocation of the Saints. And first we shall say beforehand / what Invocation is. ### Of the Chrism, or Confirmation.

Now we must speak of the Chrism, which at present is called the Sacrament of Confirmation, lacking foundation in Scripture in this: that it must first be consecrated by the Bishop, and made of olive oil and balsam, applied to the baptized person on the forehead in the figure of the cross with this form of words: *I sign you with the sign of the cross, and confirm you with the sign of salvation: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit* <note>original Latin: "Signo te segno tu del seng de la croz, & confermo tu per ség de salu: In nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti."</note>; which is done with the laying on of hands, and the binding of a white garment <note>original: "vestiment blanc," a cloth traditionally tied around the head of the confirmed person to protect the holy oil.</note> on the head: which they now call the Sacrament of Confirmation, but it is not seen to be ordained by Christ, nor by his Apostles. For Christ, the example for the whole Church, was not confirmed in such a manner in his person, nor did he require Chrism in this way for his Baptism, but only water. Therefore such a Sacrament is not seen to be of—

<column-break/>

—sacraments properly to minister, the ordination is named <note>This continues the sentence from page 194: "the power given to man by God to... properly minister the sacraments is called the ordination."</note>. But we do not have in the Scripture that which serves as proof (namely of the Roman church) of such ordinations: but only the custom of the church. And the certification letters, the anointing of the hands, the gift of the belt, and of the vials <note>original: "Ampullen."</note>, and the other things which one commonly maintains therein outside of the express Scripture, these do not belong to the essence of the same, nor are they necessary for the Ordinations.

### Of the Chrism or the Confirmation.

We must now speak of the Chrism, which is currently called a Sacrament, which nevertheless has no foundation in the Scripture; and namely in this, that it must first be consecrated by a Bishop, and be made of olive oil and balsam, and thereafter smeared on the forehead of a baptized person with a sign of the cross and these words: *I sign you with the sign of the cross, and I confirm you with the Chrism of salvation: in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit* <note>original Latin: "Signo te signo crucis, & confirmo te Chrismate salutis: in nomme Patris & fily & spiritus sancti."</note>. That is: I sign you with the sign of the cross, and form or strengthen <note>original: "vorme of verstercke." The Dutch term for Confirmation is 'Vormsel', meaning 'shaping' or 'forming'.</note> you with the Chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: which the Bishop ministers with the laying on of hands, and binds a white cloth around the head. And that is what they then call the Sacrament of Confirmation, which one does not find to have been instituted by Christ or his Apostles. For Christ, who is the pattern <note>original: "patrōō."</note> and example—

# The Third Book, of the third part. 196

an image of the whole Church is / who
was not formed in His own person
<note>The text argues that because Christ himself was not "confirmed" with chrism, the ritual lacks divine necessity.</note> : nor did He command
that such Chrism / should be used
in His baptism : but only pure water.

In which one commits blasphemy against God / and which was introduced through the instigation and movement of the devil / so that
the people would be thereby deceived and robbed or drawn away from the faith of the church / and to make them believe the more in the Bishops’ solemnity and necessities.

### Of Extreme Unction.
<note>Also known as "the last anointing" or Last Rites.</note>

The seventh Sacrament of the Roman church / is the last Anointing of the Sick / which they labor to prove / through the saying of St. James. It is not found that this was instituted by Christ / nor by His Apostles. For if it were the case / that this Anointing were a Sacrament / as they wish to make us believe / neither Christ nor His Apostles / would have remained silent regarding the presentation of the execution and the use of the same. Being mindful of this / we must not be so bold as to hold / or confess as an article of faith / that this Sacrament was instituted by Christ or by His Apostles.

### Of Fasting.

Now follows Fasting / which is of two kinds / namely Spiritual or Physical. The Spiritual is / abstaining from sin: the Physical is abstaining from eating. But the Christian person has the freedom / to be able to eat at all times / just as they may fast on all days / provided that the fasting is not done superstitiously or out of malice and superstition / as

<column-break/>

necessity of salvation, in which God is blasphemed, and it is a means through Diabolic movement, so that the people may be mocked in the Faith of the Church, and be more inclined toward the falsehood or necessity of the Bishops.

### Of Extreme Unction.

The seventh Sacrament of the Roman Church is the extreme Unction of the infirm, which by force they attempt to found upon the word of Saint James the Apostle. It is not seen to be ordained by Christ nor by His Apostles. For if this corporal Unction were a Sacrament, in the way that it is feigned, Christ or the Apostles would not remain silent regarding the proper manifestation of its execution. Thinking well on these things, one ought not to dare, hold, nor confess as an article of Faith, that this Sacrament was ordained by Christ and by the Apostles.

### Of Fasting:

NOW follows Fasting, which is double, that is spiritual and corporal. The spiritual is to abstain from sin, the corporal is to abstain from eating. But there is liberty to the Christian to eat in all times, as all days are fit for the act of fasting, not observing it superstitiously as if by the virtue of continence.

# Of the History of the Waldensians and Albigenses. 197

Note that there are some Fasts <note>original: "Deiunis"</note> which are not to be kept, nor to be praised by the faithful, but are rather to be excommunicated and shunned. Such are the Fasts of the Scribes and Pharisees, and those ordained by the Antichrist <note>In Waldensian and Albigensian polemics, the "Antichrist" was frequently identified with the institutional Roman Church and the Papacy.</note> savoring of idolatry. The Fasts of the heretics and superstitious, which are observed by charmers, sorcerers, and necromancers; and the Fasts directed toward created things rather than the Creator, which are not founded in the Law of God. Also, those Fasts disordered in specific ways, particularly with rare, more precious, and delicate items; such as sea-creatures, figs, raisins, grapes, and almonds, of which the poor are deprived while the rich are gorged <note>original: "engorzela"</note>. Thus, alms are stolen from the poor; if the children of God fasted in simpler and more common ways, they could more easily and readily provide for their own families and other poor people. For one should not fast from any physical thing as if it were inherently evil or unclean. For all things are pure to the pure, and nothing is to be refused that is received with thanksgiving: for it is sanctified by the word of God and by prayer. All such decreed Fasts are excommunicated and not encouraged among the faithful. For these things, one should not be reproached or blamed.

-> LOVE BE TO GOD. <-

<column-break/>

...a virtue of abstinence be maintained.
And mark well, that there is some Fasting that one may not maintain, nor also praise among the believers, but which must be avoided as an abomination. Just as there is the fasting of the Scribes and Pharisees, and of those who are appointed by the Antichrist, as savoring of idolatry. Likewise the Fasting of heretics and the superstitious, which is maintained by conjurers, sorcerers, and practitioners of the black arts <note>original: "swarte constenaers"</note>: together with the Fasting that is dedicated to the creature and not to the Creator, which is not founded in the Law of God. Furthermore, disordered Fasting, which is kept with the rarest, most expensive, and most delicious foods, such as sea-fish, figs, raisins, almonds, etc. These are foods that the poor people must do without, and which the rich vomit from over-fullness <note>The Dutch "uptspouwen" implies the rich eat so much "fasting food" that they become physically ill from gluttony.</note>: whereby alms are withheld from the poor, who—if the rich fasted by eating the most common and inexpensive foods instead of others—could more easily be provided for, along with their households and other poor. Since then Fasting does not consist in the abstaining from any physical food as if it were unclean. (For to the pure all things are pure, and there is nothing to be rejected of all that is enjoyed with thanksgiving: For the food is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.) Therefore all such instituted Fasts are cursed and rejected by the believers; by these things, one ought not to be contaminated or to sin.

-> God be praised. <-

### My Lords,

<margin>Song of Solomon 6:8 <note>Original: Cantic. 6. 8.</note></margin>
<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'G' contains a swan nestled among swirling leafy vines and floral scrolls.</note>
Just as there is but one God and Lord, so there is but one faith and one church. "My dove, my perfect one, is unique; she is the favorite of her mother," says the Bridegroom in the Song of Solomon. Her beginning was in Paradise; her progress continued through Abel, Seth, and all the Patriarchs and Prophets—yes, in all true believers until the time of Christ—from whom the Church of the New Testament took her beginning and was continued in all those who, like good sheep, hear and obey the voice of their Shepherd.

How wondrously the Wondrous One <note>A reference to God as the "Wonderful Counselor" from Isaiah 9:6.</note>, who is wise in counsel and mighty in deed, leads and preserves these fine Saints is a matter more for wonder than for human understanding. That which seems intended to cause their downfall becomes their rise: when they are pruned, they become more fruitful; when they are mowed down, they are simultaneously sown; when they are burned, their scattered ashes give birth to Christians in other places once again. Their blood fertilizes the spiritual field of the church. The sparks from the faggots <note>Bundles of wood used for fuel in executions by fire.</note> create a new blaze and fire, to kindle which Christ came into the world.

This is evident, among other things, from the history of the Waldensians and Albigensians <note>Two significant medieval groups who were labeled as heretics by the Catholic Church for their dissenting views and faced severe persecution.</note>, who, despite the horrible persecutions incited against them since the year 1160 until the present day, still have their seed and have not been able to be completely rooted out.

The history of the faith and the persecutions they endured for it, even unto the shedding of blood, is one of the most notable points in ecclesiastical history. It clearly shows that before the time of Luther, God had His church not only in Asia and Africa but also in various parts of Europe—even in those places that stood under the authority of the Roman Pope. And that the church, being like a burning bush, and like the three
