# PREFACE.

[Christian] youths in the fire, as in Daniel 3, and like Daniel in the middle of the lions' den, Daniel 6, who were nevertheless preserved and in no way consumed.

But just as this history is useful and wondrous, so the devil has greatly sought to obscure it and to diminish the luster of the Waldensian Churches—even to wipe away the memory of these things. Yet behold in this work God’s wondrous providence. Just as the Jews have been the librarians and book-keepers for the Christians <note>The author refers to the theological idea that Jewish preservation of the Old Testament benefited Christianity; he compares this to how Catholic records unintentionally preserved the history of those they persecuted.</note>, so have the Papist scribes <note>original: "Paepſe Scribenten"; a contemporary Protestant term for Roman Catholic writers.</note> been the historians of the *Waldensians*. Thus, from their histories and the books they wrote against the "heretics" <note>original: "Ketters"</note>, the history of the *Waldensians* and *Albigensians* can be "fished out" when those accounts are compared against one another.

But how much effort this work involves, and how great the expenses required to collect all these books, to read them, to make extracts from them, and then to balance those things against one another—no one knows better than he who has put his hands to this work. As for me, I have always racked my brain over this history of the *Waldensians*, sparing neither expense nor effort to bring it to light in due time. However, in view of my other occupations (of which I need not say much to your Excellencies, as they are well known to each and all of you), I have not been able to make enough progress according to my own desire and the longing of many others. Nevertheless, several years ago, I brought to light two pieces on this matter in the Latin language; but what was handled in those two pieces only concerned the matter of the faith of the descendants of the Waldensians in Bohemia <note>Referring to the "Bohemian Brethren," a proto-Protestant group the author links to the Waldensian tradition.</note>. To have a complete history, one must above all speak of Waldo’s <note>Peter Waldo, the 12th-century merchant from Lyon credited with starting the Waldensian movement.</note> teaching and faith, and the spreading of the same into various kingdoms and lands, as well as the persecutions inflicted upon them up to these times; therefore, I promised then to do so hereafter.

I have also partially fulfilled my promise through another person: for when the author of the great Dutch *Martyr’s Book* <note>Likely the "Martelaers-boeck" by Haemstede, a famous collection of stories of those persecuted for their faith.</note>, my very dear friend, reached the history of the *Waldensians* and *Albigensians*, I served him with advice, books, papers, records <note>original: "Munimenten"</note>, and extracts as much as I could or might, just as he has acknowledged the same both orally and in writing. On this occasion, various matters concerning several centuries were also brought to light in our language, which had never been known before.

Thereafter, this history by *Perrin* <note>Jean Paul Perrin, a French Huguenot historian whose work is being introduced here.</note> came to light, composed throughout from the Waldensians’ own papers and the legal proceedings <note>original: "Procedueren"</note> held against them by their adversaries, which were recently found in France to the great fortune of our church. When I read them, I thanked God with hot tears that it had pleased His Supreme Majesty to bring these things so clearly to light. To that end, I have also written letters to Geneva to let *Perrin* be thanked for his labor, and prayed for that which he still has in greater measure serving this cause, such as...

# PREFACE.

To bring the books of the *Waldensians*, their sermons, and their polemical writings to light. And so that this treasure, which is contained in the book by *Perrin* <note>Jean Paul Perrin, a French Reformed minister and historian of the Waldensians.</note>, might be shared with our Dutch people, I requested one of our visitors of the sick <term>Sieckebe-soecker: a lay office in the early Dutch Reformed Church responsible for the spiritual care and comfort of the ill and dying</term>, namely *D. I. M. V.*, who understands the French language, to be willing to translate this book. This he took in hand for the glory of God, notwithstanding his demanding service, and through the Lord’s blessing, he has completed it. This being done, I reviewed and collated his translation against the original, and for a broader knowledge of these matters, I added this appendix, even though my service in this city was becoming increasingly difficult. I have done three things therein. First, I point out that the *Waldensians* were not the first to bring such doctrine to light, but that there were several others before them, from the times of the Apostles until their own emergence, who held the same views.

Secondly, as many different opinions exist among scholars of both sides regarding the various bynames <note>Alibienses, Leonists, etc.</note> of the *Waldensians*, I have brought many things to light here from my promised *Onomatologia* <note>A Greek-derived term for a study or treatise on names.</note> or Name-Book of the *Waldensians*, which were previously in darkness, by which the history of the *Waldensians* can be greatly illuminated.

Thirdly, I have confirmed from various Papist scribes <note>Protestant term for Roman Catholic writers.</note> what is said of the faith of the *Waldensians* in this treatise by *Perrin*, so that no one might doubt the truth of his narrative.

I also wished, herewith, to offer this labor of mine to your Excellencies, not only because the book to which this is an appendix is dedicated to your Excellencies, but also to declare my affection for your Excellencies, as well as to be grateful for various favors shown to me and my family. I also hope by my example to stir others, who have received greater talents from the Lord and have more time, to willingly apply and spend their time on the illumination of Church history.

I wish from my whole heart that this book be diligently read and considered by all Reformed Dutchmen, to which I also hereby exhort each and every one, not doubting that they will later thank me for this good advice.

In conclusion, I pray God to increasingly bless your highly honorable and praiseworthy government and your persons, to the honor of His name and the temporal and eternal welfare of these pious citizens.

In Dordrecht, July 12, Anno 1624, on which day in the year of Christ 455 the city of Rome was taken by *Gaiseric* <note>original: "Genfericho"; the Vandal king who sacked Rome in 455 AD.</note>, and the tyrant *Maximus* was thrown into the Tiber, in the 77th year of his tyrannical reign <note>Lydius likely includes this historical note as a symbolic parallel to the fall of perceived religious tyranny.</note>.

-> Your Excellencies’ humble servant, <-
-> *Balthasar Lydius.* <-

But just as this History is useful and wonderful, so has the devil greatly sought to obscure it, and to diminish the luster of the Waldensian Churches, indeed to take away the memories of these things. Yet see in this work God's wonderful providence. Just as the Jews have been the Librarians and Book-keepers for the Christians <note>Lydius refers to the historical idea that Jewish preservation of the Old Testament benefited the Christian church.</note>, so have the Papist scribes <note>A polemical term used by reformers to refer to Roman Catholic writers and chroniclers.</note> been the Historians of the Waldensians, so that from their History and Books written against the "Heretics," when these are compared against each other, the History of the Waldensians and Albigensians can be weighed.

For my part, I have always racked my brain over this History of the Waldensians, sparing no cost nor effort to bring it to light at a favorable time; but in view of my occupations (of which I need not speak much to your High Mightinesses, as they are well enough known to each and every one of you), I have not been able to advance enough in this according to my own, and many others', longing and desire. # Eusebius in the Ecclesiastical History, Book 3, Chapter 32.
->relates these following words from Hegesippus.<-

The church remained until this time (namely, from the reigns of Nero and Domitian) a pure and uncorrupted virgin, because those who wished to falsify the doctrine hid themselves in darkness. # The Friar Minor <term>A member of the Franciscan Order (Ordo Fratrum Minorum), known for their vow of poverty.</term> Petrus Merssaeus in his History of the Bishops, page 437.

In the year 1216, through the envy of Satan, the heresy of the Albigensians <note>A medieval dualist sect in Southern France that the Catholic Church sought to suppress during the Albigensian Crusade.</note> began to grow and sprout so powerfully around Toulouse that all the grain of the faith of that nation seemed to be changed into a weed of error. Regarding the point of the Justification <term>The theological doctrine concerning how a person is made righteous before God; a central dispute during the Reformation.</term> of man, it has fared as it does with the lands situated under the pole, where the darknesses follow one another in such a way that as soon as the sun has set, it immediately rises again. For no sooner had the darkness obscured the eye of Religion on this point than the light of truth immediately broke through again. <meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, shifting from the specific history of the Waldensians to a broader claim: that the Reformed faith aligns with the early Church of the first 600 years, whereas the Roman Catholic Church drifted into error, culminating in the year 666.</meta>

This History of the Waldensians and Albigensians proves this clearly from the Year of Christ 1160 until these present times; but so that we may give the Papists full measure <note>The author uses a measuring metaphor, suggesting they will provide more evidence than is strictly necessary to settle the argument.</note>, we shall prove that from the times of the Apostles until the times of the Waldensians (which Reinerius, being a Papist writing against the Waldensians, admits), similar teaching to that of the Waldensians—and our own today—has always had its defenders.

To prove this briefly, we say that regarding the first 600 years, those of the Papacy can give no luster <note>original: "luyster," meaning authority or prestigious backing.</note> to their teachings (in those points where they differ from us) from any authentic writers. This has been proven in many notable points by John Jewel <note>original: "Johanne Ivello," John Jewel (1522–1571), the Bishop of Salisbury, whose *Apology of the Church of England* was a foundational defense of the Reformation.</note>, Bishop of Salisbury in England, in a very large and concise treatise, to which the Papists have not yet provided a relevant answer. Thomas Stapleton <note>A prominent English Catholic controversialist who fled to the Continent during the reign of Elizabeth I.</note> and others of the Papacy, knowing that the times of the Apostles and the first centuries after the Apostles are not in their favor, insist strongly that we should point out writers who lived within the last thousand years who were conformed to our teaching. Why do they not wish to hear of the first hundred or 200 years? Answer: Those do not serve them; therefore, they leave them aside.

We gladly acknowledge that even

<column-break/>

<margin>f 2 Thessalonians 2:7.</margin>
<margin>g Hegesippus in Eusebius’s *Church History*, book 3, chapter 32, and Nicephorus Callistus, book 3, chapter 16, and book 4, chapter 1.</margin>
<margin>h Revelation 13:18. How the Roman church is to be judged until the year 666.</margin>
<margin>i Daneau, *On the Antichrist*, chapter 20; 2 Thessalonians 2:4.</margin>
during the lives of the Apostles, f the mystery of iniquity <note>original: "verborghentheyt der ongherechticheyt," a reference to the secret growth of the Antichrist's power mentioned in 2 Thessalonians.</note> was already at work. And just as g various Church historians (whom our opponents claim as their own) testify: That the Church, regarding every point of doctrine, remained a virgin only under the Apostles. Nevertheless, we consider the public Church of these first centuries to be the Church of Christ. For the number of the beast is h six hundred and sixty-six. That is, from the time of Christ’s suffering, or from when John wrote the Revelation, until the time of the Emperor Constantine Pogonatus <note>original: "Constantini Pogonati," referring to Constantine IV (reigned 668–685). must lean, and consider that we are thereby made justified before the throne of God, and held as holy and righteous; and is it through such a righteousness that suits the children of God and satisfies the eyes of God—either the righteousness and love that is within us, or much more the righteousness of Christ, bestowed and reckoned to us?

I am entirely of the opinion that it is said in a Christian and godly manner that we must lean—lean, I say, as if upon a firm and immovable ground—upon the bestowed righteousness of Christ, and not upon the holiness and grace that is within us. For our righteousness is only just begun and is imperfect, which cannot protect us, so that in view of it we sin daily and must therefore pray: "forgive us our debts." But the righteousness of Christ is a true and perfect righteousness, which fully pleases God, in which there is nothing that displeases God, but everything that pleases Him to the highest degree. Therefore we must lean **ALONE** on this righteousness of Christ as being certain and firm, and believe that through it we are justified before God. This is the precious treasure of the Christians, which when someone has found it, he sells all that he has so that he

<column-break/>

might buy it. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Hidden Treasure in Matthew 13:44.</note> This is the precious Pearl, which he who has found it leaves all things to have <margin>c Philippians 3:8, 9.</margin> it. The Apostle Paul says: that he has considered all things to be loss, and considered them dung <note>original: "dreek"; a strong term for refuse or excrement, following Paul’s language in the Greek *skybala*.</note>, so that he might win Christ and be found in him, not having his own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ—namely, the righteousness which is from God in faith. But to those who lean on their own holiness, it is said in the Revelation <margin>d Apocalypse 3:16.</margin>: because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I shall spit you out of my mouth, for you say "I am rich and have no need." <margin>e Apocalypse 2:17.</margin> **Also**, I shall give you a white pebble <note>original: "keurſteen"; referring to the white stone given to the victor in Revelation 2:17, signifying acquittal or a special invitation.</note>, and on the pebble a new name written, which no one knows except he who receives it. This name is the name of Christ, and no one knows it except he who has it. From this it arises that the Saints (as experience teaches us) the more they increase in holiness, the less they please themselves, and the more they understand that they have need of Christ and His righteousness bestowed upon them; and, abandoning themselves, they lean alone on Christ.

You will (he says) object this to me, <margin>f Psalm 18:21, 22, 23.</margin> that David says: "reward me Lord according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands before his eyes, for I keep the ways [of the Lord]."

David sang the 18th Psalm, as the Title indicates, when he had conquered his enemies, among whom the principal ones

<column-break/>

were Saul and Absalom. Toward these men David was always friendly; he never attempted or plotted anything against them. <meta>This page continues the argument that the opposition to religious images (iconoclasm) was not a new invention of the 16th-century Reformers, but had deep roots in the early medieval French and Greek churches, often in direct opposition to the Papacy.</meta>

...but that the French Churches acted stubbornly <note>original: "de beeste gespeelt hebben" - literally "played the beast," meaning they were unruly or defiant towards Papal authority</note>, and until that time, they could not be brought to a different opinion by the Roman Pope.

<margin>m In the year 787, no. 57.</margin>
In another $^m$ place, Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) was a powerful Cardinal and historian who wrote the *Annales Ecclesiastici* to defend Catholicism.</note> says that the opinion of some Frenchmen regarding images sprang from the school of Serenus, Bishop of Marseille, the first iconoclast <note>A person who destroys religious images or opposes their veneration.</note> in France. For this, he was rebuked by Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (the Great), who famously argued that images were the "books of the illiterate."</note>. Afterward, those Frenchmen, in the Council of Frankfurt, gave their writings—in which they sharply criticized the Second Council of Nicaea—into the hands of Charlemagne <note>Carolo Magno; King of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor.</note>. From these, he composed his book against images and sent it to Pope Hadrian.

It should be noted here that the Reformed are wrongly accused of being the first iconoclasts, since previously in Greece and in France, at various times, very substantial and earnest resolutions were made by the Empire and in the Councils against the veneration and service of images. These were collected in chronological order by Melchior Goldast <note>A Swiss jurist and historian (1578–1635).</note> in his excellent book titled *Imperial Decrees on the Cult of Images* <note>original: "Imperialia Decreta de cultu imaginum"</note>. It is a great impudence that Sixtus Senensis <note>A converted Jew and Dominican scholar (1520–1569) who wrote the *Bibliotheca Sancta*.</note>, in the preface of his *Library*, dares to write that the book against images, bearing the name of Emperor Charlemagne, was actually written by Carlstadt <note>Andreas Karlstadt (1486–1541), a contemporary of Luther who was known for his radical opposition to images.</note>.

In the preface to that book, he admits that the style of the work itself reveals it was made in the time of Charlemagne. Furthermore, it is found in Rome in the Pope's Library, written in Lombardic script <note>A medieval style of handwriting used in Italy before the Carolingian script became standard.</note>, as Steuchus Eugubinus, the Librarian in Rome, admits in his treatise on the *Donation of Constantine*.

<meta>This page continues the argument against the antiquity of Roman Catholic doctrines, specifically focusing on how Indulgences were dependent on the later development of the concept of Purgatory, and contrasting Roman practices with those of the Greek and Abyssinian churches.</meta>

**Indulgences.** <term>Indulgences</term><note>In Catholic theology, an indulgence is a way to reduce the amount of punishment one has to undergo for sins; the author argues they are useless without the concept of Purgatory.</note> If you take away **Purgatory**, for what purpose would **Indulgences** be useful? For if there is no Purgatory, we shall have no need for Indulgences. Considering this, then, that Purgatory was unknown for a long time, and that it gradually became known—partly through revelations and partly through scripture—so shall we be able to understand Indulgences. Since Purgatory became known so late and was only then accepted by the universal church, who can wonder that Indulgences had no use in the beginning of the church?

Indulgences began when people had started to be fearful of Purgatory for some time. Thus far <term>Rossensis</term>. <note>Original: "Rossenfis." This refers to John Fisher (1469–1535), the Bishop of Rochester (Latin: Roffensis), who wrote on the origins of these doctrines.</note>

<margin>On the sacrifice of the Mass. Chytraeus in his *Oration on the State of the Church*, page 18. <note>David Chytraeus (1530–1600) was a prominent German Lutheran theologian.</note></margin>
The **Greek church** knows of no offering of the body and blood of Christ in the **Lord’s Supper**, much less of the application of the sacrifice of the **mass** for the living and the dead.

<margin>Private Masses.</margin>
**Private mass** is also unknown to them: for they hold the Lord’s Supper with the communion of the entire congregation.

<margin>On the Host.</margin>
They know nothing of any **Hosts**, through which the disappearance of the substance of the bread <note>This refers to the doctrine of Transubstantiation, where the bread is believed to literally become the body of Christ.</note> is forced upon people; but use common bread in their Lord’s Supper.

<margin>On the tonsure.</margin>
They know of no **tonsures** <note>The practice of shaving the top of the head as a clerical symbol.</note> or the shaving of beards, out of fear that the blood of Christ might happen to hang therein. <note>This refers to the Greek Orthodox practice of priests wearing long beards; the author suggests they avoid the Roman practice of shaving because they fear desecrating the wine (the Blood) if it were to spill during communion.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Marriage of Priests.</margin>
Nor do they forbid their **Priests** the state of marriage. In short, they are much purer than the Roman church.

Regarding the doctrine of **Free Will** and **Justification**, which is of the highest importance, I know well that they commonly speak and preach about it using the very words of **Chrysostom**, <note>Saint John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> and also use inappropriate ways of speaking in that matter; but against that I say again, that the same Chrysostom softens these absurd ways of speaking in other places of his many writings, indeed, he sufficiently recants them. Therefore, following the nature of Christian love, I wish to hope for them—as well as for many under the **Papacy**—that they feel better than they speak. Indeed, the hearts of many listeners are purer than the tongues of the Teachers, and especially that through the fire of trial, at their end, the chaff in these people is consumed, and that they are saved through this means, though as if through fire.

**Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> noted this well: That the gates of hell have not overwhelmed those who have not turned away from Him who says, "I am the door." From this it appears (he says) that the Church does not consist of people in respect of their ecclesiastical or worldly power or dignity: for many Princes and Popes have been found to have deviated from the true faith. Therefore, the Church consists of persons in whom the true knowledge is, and the confession of faith and the truth.

If the Papists observed this well, they would not [condemn] the churches that have departed from them, such as the churches in Africa under **Prester John** <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king said to rule over a nation in the East or Africa, often associated with Ethiopia in the late Middle Ages.</note>, the Greeks, the Waldensians, and the Albigensians.

It uses the testimony of Catholic scholars and popes to defend the legitimacy of the Waldensians and other dissenting groups.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the naming and historical reputation of the Waldenses, specifically addressing and debunking the false charges of witchcraft and clarifying the origin of the term "Leonists."</meta>

The opponents said that they held fellowship with unclean spirits. Under this pretext, many pious people were suppressed, but finally the Council of Paris, investigating the matter, found that these were slanders, and released the unhappy prisoners and accused persons, and condemned the accusers and the unjust judges. One still finds that same Decree <note>original: "Arrest"</note> taken on May 20, Anno 1491.

<margin>n Page 54 of the Gretser edition.</margin>
The Waldenses are sufficiently excused in this matter by their opponent Reinerius <note>Reinerius Saccho was a 13th-century Inquisitor and former Cathar whose writings are a primary source for medieval heresy, despite his bias.</note>, when he says in n, "that they led a pious life," which he would not have written about them if they had practiced witchcraft.

<margin>On the name Leonists.</margin>
From the city of Lyon, where Valdo lived, the Waldenses were called Leonists, as much by <margin>o Rein. page 54.</margin> o Reinerius, as in many Constitutions of Frederick II <note>Frederick II (1194–1250) was the Holy Roman Emperor who issued several harsh edicts against heretics.</note> issued against them. <margin>p In the *Authenticae* regarding statutes and customs against the liberty of the Church. Book 1. Letter of Peter de Vinea, chapter 27.</margin> p It is known to the learned that the city of Lyon is called *Leon* in old books. Claude de Rubis, who wrote a large book about this city (Book 1, chapter 30, page 113), says that just as the Piceni are so named from *Pico*—that is, a woodpecker—which they bore [on their standards], so too Lyon got its name from a lion, called *Leo* in Latin, which a colony that settled near that city bore on its banner.

<column-break/>

<margin>q History, Book 6.</margin>
The learned q Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617) was a famous French historian and statesman.</note> is misled by others when he thinks that because of the Greek Emperor Constantine's son, Leo the Fourth—who opposed the use of images in the churches—the Waldenses, holding the same view, were therefore called Leonists.

The observation of the Jesuit Gretser <note>Jacob Gretser (1562–1625) was a German Jesuit scholar and polemicist.</note> is good when he says that although "Leonists" and "Waldenses" are named distinctly in the Constitution of Frederick II, it does not follow from this that different opinions of men are signified thereby; rather, these two names are joined together only for the sake of clarity, just as if one said "Huguenots and Gueux," <note>The "Gueux" (Beggars) were the confederated nobles who resisted Spanish rule in the Netherlands, often associated with the Protestant Huguenots.</note> even though they are both of one opinion.

<margin>The name or the Poor of Lyon.</margin>
Regarding the name *Pauperum de Lugduno* <note>Latin: "The Poor of Lyon."</note>, that is, The Poor of Lyon, it is quite necessary that it be explained; for through a misunderstanding of this name, an obscurity has crept into the history of the Waldenses and their faith.

The Popish <note>The author uses the term "Paepsche" (Popish), a common 17th-century Protestant designation for Roman Catholic historians.</note> historian Conrad of Lichtenau, Abbot of Ursberg, says that in the year 1212, he saw in Rome some from the number of those who were called the "Poor of Lyon," with their Master named—if he remembered it correctly—Bernard, desiring that their sect be confirmed and privileged by the Apostolic See <note>The "Apostolic See" refers to the office and authority of the Pope in Rome.</note>. Likewise, that while wearing hoods as the livery <note>Livery: a distinctive uniform or clothing worn by a specific group or religious order.</note> of a religion or order, they nevertheless shaved their hair like other laymen, without tonsures <note>A tonsure is the practice of shaving the top of the head, which was the standard mark of a Roman Catholic cleric or monk.</note>. This is clearly evident from the *Expurgatory Index* <note>original: "indice expurgatorio," a list of books banned or required to be edited by the Catholic Church</note>, made by certain book censors or "book-correctors" under the **Duke of Alba** <note>Fernando Álvarez de Toledo (1507–1582), the Spanish governor of the Netherlands known for his harsh suppression of religious and political rebellion.</note>, who were appointed for that purpose. **Plantin** <note>Christophe Plantin (c. 1520–1589), an influential Renaissance printer based in Antwerp.</note> printed this in the **year 1571**, but since it was hardly available anymore, it has been reprinted by our people in various places and paper formats, because it shows how, by order of the **Council of Trent**, all good books were corrupted and mutilated. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Arnold of Brescia's radical teachings against the temporal power of the Church. The previous page established Arnold as a companion to Peter Abelard and an ascetic critic of the Papacy. This page provides a poetic summary of his platform and discusses the historical judgment of his execution in 1155.</meta>

<note>The following is a translation of a Latin poem summarizing Arnold’s reforms:
It was right that monks should follow their rule, and that to no one should the fiscal rights of the Pontiffs belong, nor to any the honor of popular care, but that the holy laws of the Abbots should be yielded. All things should be subject to earthly princes, and should only be committed to and ruled by secular men; while to the clergy only the first-fruits, and what the devotion of the people offers, and the tithes for the chaste needs of the body should be granted—not for luxury or the pleasures of the flesh. Granting neither soft foods, nor the splendor of dress, nor illicit jests, nor the lewd joys of the clergy, he utterly condemned the pride of the Pontiffs, the loose morals of the Abbots, and the proud monks. *And indeed, he advised many true things (had not our times rejected faithful warnings), though they were mixed with falsehoods.*
original: "Iure sequi monachos, nulli fiscalia jura..."</note>

**That is, he, Arnold of Brescia, deceived the simple through his eloquence. He was a bitter enemy of the clergy and the monkhood; he attacked the Pope and taught that the clergy possessed temporal goods unjustly. He held that the spirituality stood under the authority of the Princes. That spiritual goods were not given to be swallowed up or wasted in wantonness and excess in clothing. That he rebuked the pride of the Pope and the Abbots**

<column-break/>

**and their way of life, and said many things according to the truth; but those corrupt times could not endure such bold rebukes.**

Gerhohus of Reichersberg <note>Gerhohus (1093–1169) was a Bavarian provost and influential theologian who, while a reformer, often tried to find a middle ground between the Church and its critics.</note> (as the Jesuit Gretser <note>Jacob Gretser (1561–1625), a prominent counter-reformation scholar.</note> acknowledges in the previously cited place) wishes that Arnold of Brescia had not been put to death for his points of doctrine, but rather held in perpetual imprisonment or sent into exile, or at least killed in such a way that the Roman Court and Church could not be accused of having stained themselves with bloody judgments. For (he says) their wish to excuse themselves by saying that it happened without their consent, by the hand of the chief Governor of the city, and that he escaped from their prison, cannot help them. Sagarelli of Parma, Fratricelli, Beghards, Beguines: but considering the matter more closely, I remain by my former opinion. For it is the manner of the Papists <note>A term historically used by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics, often highlighting their allegiance to the Pope.</note> even today, that they blame and attribute to the Reformation all sects that have arisen after it—such as the Schwenckfeldians <note>Followers of Caspar Schwenckfeld, a 16th-century Protestant reformer who emphasized the inner spirit.</note>, Anabaptists, and those of the Family of Love <note>original: "huys der liefde" — a mystical religious group founded by Hendrik Niclaes in the 16th century.</note>—and call such people Lutherans, even though they differ entirely from them. Thus, it has no conformity with the same.

However, although they were not Waldensians, I shall state here in their defense that this sect in general was not guilty of such impurities as are attributed to them by the Papist historians. This appears from the Constitution of Pope Clement V in the Council of Vienne: for in the 3rd chapter of that Constitution, it is said of these Beghards and Beguines that they taught that to kiss a woman, unless nature pulls one toward it, is a sin, but that sleeping together through natural lust is no sin. The Papists relate this very hatefully, as if they had permitted all sleeping together and impurity, whereas they seem to have taught nothing else—

<column-break/>

—than that the married state is an undefiled bed, and that outside the married state, all things, even the smallest, which can provoke a person to impurity, ought to be avoided.

Since Gabriel Prateolus <note>Gabriel Du Préau (1511–1588), a French writer who cataloged various heresies.</note>, treating of the Fratricelli, says that one Hermannus from Italy was the author of the heresy of the Fratricelli, the history of this Hermannus of Ferrara should be related here at length, whom Abraham Bzovius <note>A Polish Dominican church historian (1567–1637) who continued the *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note> calls Hermannus Pungilupus <note>original: "Hermnanū Pungilupum" — Armanno Pungilupo (d. 1269), a popular holy man who was posthumously declared a Cathar heretic.</note>. <margin>Annals, Year 1301, num. 1</margin> This man, having been buried as a holy man, was dug up after twenty years and burned to ashes, and that by order of Pope Boniface VIII. But time does not permit this; I will add this: that the Fratricelli and their followers did not overthrow the foundations of the Papacy as the Waldensians did, although they set themselves against Boniface and his successors as those who were not lawfully elected.

...word, but a High German word *Kaetzer*, in which the letter T is changed into a Z, as also happens in other words, as appears from the following examples: *Catus* <note>Latin for cat</note>, *Katz* <note>German for cat</note>; *Platea* <note>Latin for a wide street or courtyard</note>, *Platz* <note>German for place or square</note>. These Waldensians were called by the Germans *Kathar* or *Kazar*; in Latin, they fashioned the name *Cathari* from this. From this word sprang again the word **Gazari**, the C being changed into a G, for these two letters are frequently swapped for one another. The Italians say *Gaspar* instead of *Caspar*, and *Gato* for *Catus*, and *Gatter* <note>German for a gate or lattice</note> for *Clathri* <note>Latin for bars or a trellis</note>.

Serarius writes in the cited passage: that *Kaetseren* signifies to divide or to tear, and that therefore those who cause divisions and schisms in the church are called *Kaetzer*, or as we Netherlanders say, **ketters**.

In these regions of Germany (says Gretser), this definition of the word *Kaetzer* is unknown, although we High Germans use *Kaetzeren* to mean tor-

menting and plaguing. For example:

### Oh, Shameless Lie.

1. **Mani** <note>original: "Manes"; the 3rd-century founder of Manichaeism, a religion depicting a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> was a Persian, and lived about the year 247 after Christ’s suffering, in the time of the Emperor Aurelian and the Roman Bishop Felix—or, as Augustine writes in Book 13 of *Against Faustus*, Chapter 4, under the Emperor Probus. There was never a Mani in Italy. **Francisco Peña** <note>A Spanish canonist and investigator for the Inquisition.</note>, wishing to polish this lie of **Eymeric** <note>Nicolau Aymerich, a 14th-century Inquisitor General of Aragon known for his harshness.</note>, first admits that Eymeric erred in this account, and that in the time of Pope Innocent III, in the year 1200, there were no Manichaeans in Italy, but shortly thereafter. Wishing to help Eymeric out of the mire, he invents this lie: that Eymeric called the author of some wandering spirits in Italy by the ancient name of Mani. He acts then like the story told of an accomplished liar, who, when his master boasted that he had hit a stag with one shot through its right ear and left hoof, said it was true—but that precisely at that moment, the stag was scratching its right ear with its left hoof. However, he added: "Master, lie no more like that, or I shall not know how to help you." Peña has been more cautious and did not want to brand Eymeric so, but all sensible people can see that he wanted to dress up Eymeric’s lie with a

<column-break/>

far-fetched and trumped-up fiction, in order to smear the "new Manichaeans" whom the Papists have invented with the heresies of the ancient Manichaeans.

->That he wants to avail himself of<-
the testimonies of **Guido the Carmelite**, **Bernardo Corio**, and **Reinerius** cannot help him; for those writers do not say that there was a Mani in Italy. Furthermore, Guido and Reinerius wrote not only against the Waldensians but against all sorts of wandering spirits. Guido does not say a single word about the Waldensians being Manichaeans, but recounts other opinions of the Manichaeans that have no resemblance to the teachings of the Waldensians.

->Reinerius deals with the<-
**Cathars** <note>A dualist medieval religious sect; the name was often used as a catch-all slur for heretics.</note>, and speaks of the **Albanenses**, who were not Albigenses, but came from the valleys near Bergamo named Albe de Sensa or Senzano, as the Jesuit **Gretser** has well noted in his annotations on Reinerius.

->As for what is recounted by the<-
**Papist Scribes** regarding the "new Manichaeans," it is a completely confused tale which we would refute more extensively if time allowed; but we believe that what we have recounted will serve well enough as a warning to the sensible reader.

insultingly called Manichaeans, held other points of doctrine.

Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini (1405–1464), a renowned humanist scholar who was later elected Pope Pius II.</note>, who, having become Pope, was named **Pius II**, writes in his *History of Bohemia*, Chapter 35: That **Hus** <note>Jan Hus (c. 1369–1415), the Czech reformer whose followers, the Hussites, were often linked by historians to the Waldensians.</note> and his followers, having cause to speak ill of some negligent Priests who were full of flaws, began to bark against all Priests; and departing from the Roman Church, they embraced the godless Sect of the Waldensians, and taught these following points of doctrine:

<margin>Of the Pope.</margin>
1. That the Roman Pope is not above other teachers, but is only their equal.

<margin>Priests.</margin>
2. That there is no distinction between Priests, but that they should only be held in higher regard in respect to the holiness of their lives.

<margin>Purgatory.</margin>
3. That souls, upon departing from the Body, are immediately either eternally damned or eternally blessed.

<margin>Praying for the dead.</margin>
4. That there is no Purgatory. <note>A central tenet of the Waldensians was the rejection of the medieval concept of an intermediate state where souls are purified before entering heaven.</note>
5. That it is not necessary—indeed, it is useless—to pray for the dead;

<column-break/>

and that this praying for the dead has sprung from the greed of the Priests.

<margin>Images.</margin>
6. That one ought to remove the images of God and the Saints.

<margin>Holy water.</margin>
7. That the consecration of water and Palm branches is a mockery.

<margin>Mendicant orders.</margin>
8. That the Devil invented the **mendicant orders** <note>Religious orders such as the Franciscans or Dominicans who took vows of poverty and lived by begging.</note>.

<margin>Wealth of the priests.</margin>
9. That Priests ought to be poor and should content themselves with only alms.

<margin>Doing no evil.</margin>
10. That no outstanding sin should be permitted in order to avoid a greater evil.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
11. That **Confirmation** <note>original: "Vormsel."</note> and the anointing of the dying are not Sacraments.

<margin>Auricular confession.</margin>
12. That **auricular confession** <note>The practice of confessing sins privately to a priest.</note> is a trifle, because one must confess their sins to God alone.

<margin>Water baptism.</margin>
13. That baptism should be administered with Water alone, and not with the mixing of any other things, such as Oil, etc.

<margin>Consecration of churches.</margin>
14. That the consecration of churchyards is useless and was invented for financial gain; and that it matters not in what earth dead bodies are buried.

<margin>Founding of cloisters.</margin>
15. That the entire world is a Temple of God; and that those who found churches, monasteries, and houses of prayer restrict the Majesty of God, as if God showed His goodness more closely or dearly within them.

Lij <meta>16. That</meta>

**Reinerius**, who wrote against the Waldensians, gives them this testimony (as the Jesuits acknowledge in their own printed works): "Among all the Sects that have been, or still are, none is more harmful to the Church than the Sect of the **Leonists** (for so he calls the Waldensians), and this for three reasons." <note>Reinerius Sachoni was a former member of the sect who became a Dominican inquisitor. First, because it is the very oldest; for some say that it has lasted from the times of **Sylvester** <note>Pope Sylvester I (reigned 314–335 AD). The Waldensians traditionally claimed the Church became corrupted when Sylvester accepted the "Donation of Constantine."</note>, while others say it has existed since the times of the Apostles.

Second, because it is more widespread than other Sects:

<column-break/>

for there is no land where this Sect is not found.

Third, because while all other Sects, through their horrible blasphemies against God, cause a loathing in those who hear them, this one, on the contrary, has a great appearance of godliness. They have this appearance of godliness because they live righteously before men, believe all things concerning God correctly, and hold sound views on all twelve Articles of the Faith <note>Referring to the Apostles' Creed</note>; they only blaspheme the Roman Church and the clergy, in which the laity all too readily place their faith.

1. Blasphemies against the Roman Church and her institutions.

<margin>Concerning the Roman Church regarding its teaching and life.</margin>

Also, that all human rules of orders, persons, and Pharisaic institutions are [invalid].

This is how the writings of the Church Fathers are treated nowadays. <note>The author is accusing Catholic printers of deleting the phrase "that they may be what they were" to remove Ambrose's support for the idea that the bread remains bread.</note>

Also, they reject the kissing of the Easter board and the altars.
<margin>Auricular confession</margin>
Regarding Confession, they say that even a common man has the power to absolve, and that through the laying on of hands they can forgive sins and grant the Holy Spirit.
Note: that they reject the power which Confessors <note>Priests acting as confessors in the sacrament of Penance.</note> attribute to themselves to forgive sins, and they only lay on hands as a sign of the forgiveness of sins, which God grants to those who have true repentance for their sins; and through prayer they seek to obtain the Holy Spirit for the people, and not through the laying on of hands as an effective cause.

Regarding Marriage, they say that those who come together without hope of having children sin gravely.
So sensitive were the consciences of many Christians immediately after the time of Christ, as appears from several of their *Apologies* against the Heathen: we acknowledge that there are also other ends of marriage, and among those, not the least is to avoid fornication and burning [lust], for it is better to marry than to burn. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:9, "it is better to marry than to burn with passion."</note>

<margin>Prayer in a foreign tongue</margin>
<margin>God's word is sufficient</margin>

<margin>Latin language in the service</margin>
The text of the New Testament, and a large part of the Old Testament, they know by heart in their mother tongue.
<margin>They are firm in the text</margin>

The Decrees and Decretals <note>The body of papal laws and letters that make up Canon Law.</note>, as well as human interpretations of Scripture, they reject, and they hold to the Text alone.

They reject all excommunications.

excommunications (meaning the Papal lightning-bolts) and do not care for Absolution <note>The formal release from guilt or punishment for sin pronounced by a priest.</note>. They also refuse Indulgences and pardons, and laugh at dispensations.

Concerning the third part, regarding the customs of the church, they hold these errors:

<margin>Customs of the church</margin>
All customs approved by the church of which they do not read in the Gospel, they despise, such as Candlemas, Palm Sunday, and the adoration of the cross; they say that one ought not to establish many Feast days, because one day is like another; 

<margin>Feast days</margin>
therefore they work secretly on feast days.

<margin>Fasting</margin>
They do not observe any fasts of the church. They use for this the words of *Isaiah 58*: *Is that the fast that I have chosen?*

<margin>Consecrations</margin>
All church consecrations <note>The OCR reads "Wipinghen," a likely transcription error for "Wijinghen," meaning hallowings or blessings.</note>, blessings of candles, of meat, of palm branches, oil, beer, of the lamb made of white wax <note>The *Agnus Dei*, a wax disc stamped with the figure of a lamb and blessed by the Pope.</note>, of clothes, salt, water, or of certain persons, they despise; as they also do the churches with stone walls (understand this as when the buildings themselves are thought to be holy); they call these a "stone house" and say that God does not dwell in Temples made with hands, and that the prayers offered there have no more power than those offered in a room, because it says in *Matthew 6*: *When you pray, go into your room,* etc.

<summary>This page details the Waldensian rejection of Catholic "human institutions," including the veneration of saints, church traditions, and the physical holiness of church buildings. They argue that the Bible alone is sufficient for salvation and mock the allegorical interpretations used by the Roman clergy.</summary>
<keywords>Waldensians, anti-Catholic polemic, cult of saints, iconoclasm, Matthew 15, Isaiah 58, church consecrations, religious feast days, Pharisees</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Waldensian beliefs and their rejection of Roman Catholic liturgical practices. The previous page discussed their disdain for church traditions, allegorical interpretations, and the cult of saints; this page focuses on church ornamentation, the use of Latin, and the rejection of Purgatory.</meta>

<margin>Popish Trumpery.</margin>
They say that the decorations of the Church are unseemly, and that it would be better to clothe the poor than to decorate the walls. They also say it is poorly done to lay cloths upon the Altars and let them rot upon a stone, and that Christ gave neither Capes nor Chasubles <note>A sleeveless outer vestment worn by a priest when celebrating Mass.</note> to his Disciples.

<margin>Chalice.</margin>
In place of a Chalice, they use a common beaker. Note that for this reason the Waldensians are called Piccards: for the High German word *Becher* <note>original: "Becher", meaning cup or beaker.</note> was translated by the Papists as *Picarium* <note>original: "Picarium", a Latinized form of beaker.</note>, just as Reinerius does here. Reinerius, Page 59, Ingolstadt edition.

<margin>Wax lights.</margin>
Regarding the candles and lights, they say that Christ is the true light, and that he has no need of light, and that it is only useful so that one does not strike their foot or stumble.

<margin>Incense.</margin>
They reject the use of incense.

They value Holy Water as little as common water.

<margin>Images.</margin>
Images and paintings they regard as instruments of Idolatry.

<margin>Popish singing.</margin>
They mock the chants of the Church and say that the power is not in the melody, but in the words.

<margin>Processions.</margin>
All processions on Feast days and at burials they reject.

They say that the songs used day and night in the Roman Church

<column-break/>

were instituted by Pope Gregory and did not exist before his time.

<margin>Masses in one day.</margin>
They also despise the practice of performing many different Masses in a single day.

<margin>Pilgrimage.</margin>
They despise pilgrimages to the Holy Sepulcher <note>The tomb of Christ in Jerusalem.</note> and to the graves of any other Saints; likewise the ceremonies used at burials. <margin>Churchyards.</margin> They would also rather be buried in a field than in a churchyard, if they did not fear the church authorities.

<margin>Funeral rites.</margin>
They also say that Masses for the souls, funeral rites, anniversaries, etc., do not benefit the souls of the deceased.

All these errors arise because they deny Purgatory <note>The intermediate state where souls are purified before entering Heaven.</note>, saying there are only two ways: one for the elect, leading to Heaven; the other for the damned, leading to Hell. They cite that where the tree falls, there it lies. *Ecclesiastes 11*. <margin>Purgatory.</margin> And that if a person is good, he has no need of intercession <note>Prayers said on behalf of another.</note>; if he has been evil, then no intercession can help him. <margin>Praying for the dead.</margin>

They believe that all sin is by its nature mortal <note>A "mortal sin" in Catholic theology is a grave sin that leads to damnation; the Waldensians argued against the distinction between "mortal" and "venial" (lesser) sins.</note>. <margin>All sin is mortal.</margin>

They believe that one "Our Father" <note>The Lord's Prayer.</note> has more power than the ringing of ten bells and all the masses. <margin>Ringing of bells.</margin>

Guido the Carmelite, a Bishop in the Roman Church, in his *Summary Against Heretics* <note>original: "summa contra haereticos"</note>, speaking of the Waldensians, acknowledges that they believe these things.

<meta>This page continues the list of accusations and beliefs attributed to the Waldensians, contrasting their rejection of Roman Catholic ecclesiastical authority with their adherence to foundational Christian creeds.</meta>

<margin>The Pope.</margin> 1. That they do not stand under the Roman Pope, nor under the Prelates <note>High-ranking clergy members such as bishops or abbots.</note>, and that they are not bound to obey them, nor to renounce and abjure their faith upon their command.

<margin>Decrees.</margin> 2. That the Canons, Constitutions, and Decrees of the Popes are of no value and do not bind them.

<margin>Absolution.</margin> 3. That the authority to absolve someone of sin comes from no one but God, and that therefore one layman can proclaim the forgiveness of sins to another.

<margin>Indulgences.</margin> 4. That the Indulgences and Pardons <note>Documents or acts sold or granted by the Church to reduce punishment for sins.</note> proclaimed on behalf of the Pope and other prelates are powerless.

<margin>All Christians are priests.</margin> 5. That even if someone is not ordained, they may distribute the Holy Supper, and that all laypeople are also Priests.

<margin>Communicating frequently.</margin> 6. That one ought not to partake of the Holy Supper only once a year, but many times, for the strengthening of one's faith and the forgiveness of sins.

<margin>Purgatory.</margin> 7. That they deny Purgatory <note>original: "Vaghevier", the place of purification for souls before entering heaven.</note> and say that Alms, Prayers, masses, and similar services do not benefit the dead.

<margin>Roman Church.</margin> 8. That they abhor the entire state of the Roman Church in its members, calling it the "house of lies."

<margin>Church ministry.</margin> 9. That there are only three degrees of ministry in the church, namely Deacons, 

<column-break/>

Elders, and Teachers <note>original: "Leeraren", referring to pastors or ministers.</note>, and that the calling of the same does not depend on the Roman Church.

<margin>Miracles.</margin> 10. That in the Roman Church, no true miracles occur.

<margin>Praying to the dead.</margin> 11. That the Saints in heaven do not hear our Prayers and do not pray for us.

<margin>Saints' Feast Days.</margin> 12. That one ought not to celebrate the Feast Days of the Saints; therefore, they also work with their hands on such days.

<margin>Hail Mary.</margin> 13. That they despise the Angelic Salutation, or the *Ave Maria* <note>original: "Ave maria", the prayer to the Virgin Mary based on the greeting of the angel Gabriel.</note>.

<margin>Fasting.</margin> 14. That during Lent, and on Fast days instituted in honor of the Saints, it is permitted to eat meat, since Christ did not forbid such a thing.

<margin>Absolution.</margin> 15. That the priests have no power to absolve people from their sins.

By these points, Guido <note>Guido de Brès (1522–1567), a prominent Protestant reformer in the Low Countries.</note> attaches a remarkable lie, saying that they reject all 12 Articles of the faith <note>The 12 Articles refers to the Apostles' Creed, the foundational statement of Christian belief.</note>, which contradicts the confession of Reinerius <note>Reinerius Saccho, a 13th-century inquisitor and former member of a "heretical" group who wrote extensively on their actual beliefs.</note> mentioned above, who himself lived for a long time among those called **Cathars** <note>original: "Catharos", a medieval dualist sect often conflated with Waldensians by the Church.</note>, and roundly confessed that they accept all 12 Articles of the faith, and only set themselves against the doctrines of the Roman Church. Which of these two is more to be believed is easily gathered from all the books written against the Waldensians, among which no one but this man [Guido] accuses them of this...

accuses them of this grave error. As more books of the Waldensians and their Barbs <note>original: "Barben", a term for Waldensian pastors, derived from the word for "uncles."</note> or Teachers come to light—as is to be hoped—this lie shall vanish more and more, like smoke.

Nicholas Eymeric, in the second part of his *Directory of Inquisitors* <note>original: "Diretorio inquisitorum", a manual for inquisitors written in the 14th century to help identify and prosecute heretics.</note>, printed in Rome with the permission of the Pope, in Question 14, section: states that these are the heresies of the Waldensians:

<margin>Pope’s power rejected.</margin>
1. That they do not consider themselves subjects of the Roman Pope, and that they are being unjustly persecuted by him.

2. That they do not stand under the Pope’s Ban <note>An official exclusion from the church; excommunication.</note>, and are not bound to obey him when he commands them to renounce their beliefs.

<margin>Decrees.</margin>
3. That the Decretals <note>original: "Decretale", papal decrees that form part of canon law.</note> of the church regarding Fasting and Feast days must not be obeyed.

<margin>Indulgences.</margin>
4. That the Indulgences of the Roman See are of no value.

<margin>Transubstantiation.</margin>
5. That Bread and Wine do not change into the true Body and Blood of Christ <note>This refers to the rejection of Transubstantiation, the belief that the substance of the bread and wine literally becomes Christ's flesh and blood.</note>.

<margin>All Christians are priests.</margin>
6. That every one of their members is a priest.

<margin>Purgatory.</margin>
7. That souls go immediately either to Heaven or to Hell, and that there is no Purgatory <note>original: "Vaghevier", a middle state of purification after death.</note>.

<margin>Praying for the dead.</margin>
8. That Alms and prayers for the dead do not benefit them.

<margin>Invocation.</margin>
9. That the Saints who are in

<column-break/>

Heaven do not hear our prayers, nor do they pray for us, and therefore one must not invoke them, nor hold Feast days in their honor; and that the miracles told about them are merely trifles <note>original: "speulkens", meaning little plays or fictional stories.</note>.
<margin>Saints.</margin>
<margin>Feast days.</margin>
<margin>Miracles.</margin>

<margin>The 12 articles of faith are not a prayer.</margin>
10. That one should not recite or read the Twelve Articles of the Faith <note>The Apostles' Creed.</note> as a prayer, and that such a practice was established by the Roman church.

Note: From this was spun the slander of Guido <note>Likely referring to the inquisitor Bernard Gui or the polemicist Guido de Brès.</note> that they supposedly rejected the Twelve Articles of faith; whereas these are actually two different things: things that must be believed, and things that should not be muttered as a prayer.

<margin>Mary.</margin>
11. That one must not recite the *Ave Maria* <note>The "Hail Mary" prayer.</note>, nor any other prayers except the prayer that Christ taught us <note>The Lord's Prayer (Our Father).</note>.

This last point should not be believed so crudely, as they use other prayers themselves, and only require that all prayers must be regulated according to the pattern of the Our Father, as the author of the preceding book has indicated and proven.

<margin>Wealth of the Clergy.</margin>
12. <meta>This page continues the list of accusations against the Waldensians from the previous page, concluding the section on inquisitorial charges before moving to a defense of the group against contemporary historians.</meta>

...that they must not be believed, nor obeyed.

I shall conclude this chapter with the words of Alfonso de Castro <note>Alfonso de Castro (1495–1558) was a Spanish Franciscan theologian and jurist, famous for his works against heresies.</note> in book 6 of *Concerning Heresies*, in the chapter on Exorcism.

> The Waldensians seem to have been born for the sole purpose of overturning the highest authorities in the Church, if it were possible; for there is no custom used by the Church which they do not strive with all their effort to overthrow.

> They were then true opponents of the Roman Church, and not of the Christian Religion.

These matters regarding the faith of the Waldensians needed to be recounted more extensively, because the slanders or calumnies of the papist historians, and the articles they falsely attributed to them, have led astray a very learned man. In a history and chronology published in the Dutch language—containing many excellent rarities which no one but he, or someone like him, could bring to light—this man was moved to accuse Waldo of heresy. For when he speaks of the *Fratricelli de opinione* <note>original: "Fratricellos de opinione," a group of dissident Franciscans who emerged in the 13th century; the author here clarifies they were distinct from the Waldensians.</note> (who were nonetheless not Waldensians), he says: Some hold it to be **ONE** people with the "Poor Men of Lyons" or Waldensians, originating from an eminent citizen of Lyons in France named Peter Waldo, around the year 1160, **WHOSE**

<column-break/>

**HERESIES ARE WELL ENOUGH KNOWN** and unnecessary to recount here.

Afterward, speaking of Dulcino <note>Fra Dolcino (c. 1250–1307) was the leader of the Dulcinian movement, which the Catholic Church condemned as heretical.</note>, he says: > I believe it is also wished by some that the entire sect had remained in the shadows, **AS WELL AS THE TEACHING OF THE VAUDOIS AND THEIR FOLLOWERS. CERTAINLY, IT WOULD HAVE BEEN GOOD, AND THUS I WOULD NOT FEEL LOATHING AT THE MERE MEMORY OF ALL THESE HERETICS.**

We hope that from now on the contrary shall be evident to the reader, and that he shall not consider the Waldensians to be heretics, nor wish that their teaching and following had remained in the shadows. Rather, on the contrary, we hope he might thank God for their teaching and faith, and wish that their affairs might come to light more and more clearly. Finally, let him set against the judgment of this misled author the judgment of the highly learned and no less godly Paul Merula <note>Paulus Merula (1558–1607) was a prominent Dutch scholar and historian at the University of Leiden.</note> in his *Treasury of Time* <note>original: "Tijtthresoor," referring to Merula's *Tydt-thresol*, a major historical work.</note> page 762, who defends the Waldensians against all accusers.

Regarding the history of their persecutions, as well as those of the Albigensians in various regions, the reader has the extensive account in the preceding book; yet in such a way that an even greater book...

<meta>This page concludes Balthasar Lydius's treatise on the Waldensians. It transitions from a Dutch-language defense of the historical legitimacy of their doctrine to a Latin-language petition and rhetorical challenge directed at his opponents, specifically the Jesuits, before concluding the work.</meta>

...as the preceding, about this matter could be written and published by me, gathered from the histories of various chroniclers of the times. But for this time, this treatise shall suffice. If the papists <note>original: *papiste*, a contemporary term used by Protestants to refer to members of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, through any contradiction or refutation of this history or our appendices, should require further diligence from us, and the Lord grants us life and time, we will not fail to expand upon the honor and teaching of the Waldensians more broadly in another treatise. Praying in the mean-

<column-break/>

time to the Lord that this writing may serve many, to clearly understand that for many centuries before the latest Reformation <note>The author refers to the Protestant Reformation of the 16th century as the "latest Reformation," viewing the Waldensians as a "pre-reformation" movement.</note> of the church, the doctrine of the Papacy has been contested, and ours—both in private and through the public church—has been maintained through the books of the prophets and Apostles; and therefore it is no new doctrine, but the very oldest, founded on the true cornerstone Jesus Christ, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be praise and honor for eternity. Amen.

### *By Balthasar Lydius*

### A just petition on behalf of the Waldensians to any reader of this book and its Appendix.

**S**ee these things of ours, you Jesuits <note>original: *Iesuitæ*</note>, and do not envy them. And all you who, with the Jesuits, go far from Jesus <note>The author uses a Latin pun here: *Iesu-itis* (Jesuits) and *Iesu itis* (you go from Jesus).</note>. We desire a disciple of truth; you are a trap <note>original: *decipulum*, a snare or trap; another Latin wordplay on *discipulum* (disciple).</note>. What are your insults against us but your own vices? Truth is pressed down by them, but not crushed; for truth grows stronger when under pressure. 

If Jesus be ours, let the pig <note>original: *sus*; likely a derogatory reference to opponents of the faith</note> grunt at us, but never let him be his own. You who are the plague of the world, eat yourselves up; remain as bran. Here is fine flour <note>original: *simila*, the finest quality of wheat flour, used here as a metaphor for pure doctrine.</note>, but yours is altogether different. We are no cymbal to your ears, for whom the Creed <note>original: *Symbolum*, referring to the Apostles' Creed or the fundamental confession of faith.</note> is filth.

<column-break/>

But you pious ones, lend us your ears, as we entrust our reputation to YOU. Discern and distinguish, proscribe the prescription, put on and bring in new minds; but measuring all things justly, with a fearless brow, 
->pronounce against the<-
->guilty, and the<-
->innocent,<-
->release.<-

<insert>
1 volume. XXXII, 152; VIII, 200; VIII, 96 pages, printed in two columns in <term>Gothic type<note>Also known as Blackletter, this was a traditional typeface used for Dutch religious and scholarly texts during the 17th century.</note></term>. Negligibly browned with marginal water stains, otherwise a very well-preserved copy in <term>quarto<note>A book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice, creating four leaves or eight pages; typically a sturdy, medium-sized volume.</note></term>. <note>Price listed as 1800 guilders.</note>
</insert>

J.P. PERRIN is considered, along with <term>Leger<note>Jean Léger (1615–1670) was a Waldensian pastor and historian whose works, like Perrin’s, were vital in documenting the history of his people during times of persecution.</note></term>, as the preeminent historian of the <term>Albigensians<note>Also called Cathars; a medieval Christian group in Southern France whose beliefs were deemed heretical by the Catholic Church, leading to the Albigensian Crusade.</note></term> and <term>Waldensians<note>A movement founded by Peter Waldo in the 12th century that practiced apostolic poverty and translated the Bible into the common tongue.</note></term>. This very rare work is particularly sought after because it contains fragments from ancient Waldensian treatises, thereby providing a wonderful depiction of the nature and meaning of the <note>original: "ware kercke Christi"</note> "true church of Christ." See further, among others, the *Bibliotheca Esoterica* and Caillet, Volume III, pages 263-264 <note>These are standard bibliographic reference works for rare and esoteric books.</note>.
